AI.method: The authors conducted a rapid review to identify existing guidelines for evaluating and using GenAI/LLMs in SLRs. They then combined thought experiments, relevant guidance from the literature, and their own SLR and tool-evaluation experience to develop a set of process recommendations.
AI.result: The paper identifies key problems researchers face when evaluating GenAI for SLRs, explains process issues for planning, conducting, and reporting both GenAI-assisted SLRs and GenAI tool evaluations, and synthesizes these into the GUEST (GenAI Use and Evaluation in SLR Tasks) recommendations.
AI.conclusion: GenAI is not yet capable of unsupervised systematic studies and requires human oversight. However, it offers cost-effective assistance for repetitive tasks and additional validation for complex tasks. The GUEST recommendations aim to help researchers conduct trustworthy GenAI-assisted SLRs and rigorous independent evaluations.

title: Stop Writing for Me: Generative Refusal in AI Tools for Thought
comment: Workshop on Tools for Thought at CHI 2026
summary: In creative domains where the labor of articulation is central to the craft, how should we design Tools for Thought that enhance rather than bypass human cognition? Current GenAI paradigms often prioritize "cognitive offloading"-writing on behalf of users-risking the erosion of the constructive thought process essential to artistic training. In this position paper, we explore AI as a Maieutic Partner through "Generative Refusal"-strategically withholding text generation to demand user articulation. We discuss Actor's Note, a journaling tool that generates context-aware questions instead of draft text. Our field study suggests that this constraint significantly reduced cognitive burden while fostering a residual effect of internalized questioning habits. We use these findings to discuss broader design implications for protecting human cognition against the tendency of generative efficiency.

AI.tldr: This position paper proposes "Generative Refusal" — AI tools that strategically withhold text generation and instead ask context-aware questions — as a design paradigm to enhance rather than bypass human cognition in creative domains. A field study using Actor's Note, a journaling tool embodying this approach, showed reduced cognitive burden and fostered internalized questioning habits.
AI.motivation: The authors are concerned that current GenAI tools prioritize cognitive offloading by writing on behalf of users, which risks eroding the constructive thought processes essential to artistic training and creative articulation. The core problem is designing Tools for Thought that amplify rather than replace human cognition in domains where the labor of articulation is central to craft.
AI.method: The paper adopts a position paper format, articulating the concept of AI as a "Maieutic Partner" via "Generative Refusal" — strategically withholding text generation to demand user articulation. This is instantiated in Actor's Note, a journaling tool that generates context-aware questions instead of draft text. A field study was conducted to evaluate the tool's effects on cognitive burden and questioning habits.
AI.result: The field study suggests that the Generative Refusal constraint significantly reduced cognitive burden while producing a residual effect: users internalized the questioning habits promoted by the tool, continuing reflective practices beyond direct interaction.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that deliberately constrained AI — refusing to generate content and instead prompting user reflection — offers a viable design direction for protecting and cultivating human cognition against the tendency of generative efficiency to short-circuit creative thinking.

title: Behavior-Driven Explainability
summary: As system complexity has vastly increased, it has become significantly more challenging for a single person or a team to fully understand all aspects of an entire system. Particularly, this holds when considering all the different stages of a system's development life cycle, such as, e.g., design or maintenance. But especially for safety-critical systems it is essential that the final design can be trusted. Because of this, explainability is becoming an important requirement for modern systems. In this paper, we aim to achieve this goal by utilizing Behavior-Driven Development (BDD), where the expected system behavior is given in the form of structured scenarios. These scenarios give a sequence of actions for each functionality, and by this can be directly translated into explanations. We introduce this method of deriving explanations based on the specification as Behavior-Driven Explainability (BDX). While applicable at any development stage or abstraction level, a case study for the explanation of exceptions in a RISC-V processor shows the support this concept adds during system design.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Behavior-Driven Explainability (BDX), a method that derives system explanations directly from Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) specifications. BDX uses structured scenarios to generate explanations for system behavior, demonstrated through a case study on exception handling in a RISC-V processor design.
AI.motivation: Increasing system complexity makes it difficult for individuals or teams to fully understand all aspects of a system across its development lifecycle. For safety-critical systems, trust in the final design is essential, making explainability a critical requirement. Current approaches lack a systematic way to generate explanations from behavioral specifications.
AI.method: The authors propose Behavior-Driven Explainability (BDX), which leverages Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) specifications—structured scenarios describing expected system behavior as sequences of actions per functionality. These scenarios are directly translatable into explanations. The method is applicable at any development stage or abstraction level.
AI.result: A case study applying BDX to explain exceptions in a RISC-V processor demonstrates the practical support this concept provides during system design, validating its utility in real hardware development contexts.
AI.conclusion: BDX offers a systematic approach to achieving explainability in complex systems by reusing BDD specifications as a source of explanations, thereby enhancing design trustworthiness without requiring separate explainability infrastructure.

title: CHaystack: Benchmarking Chinese Document Retrieval and VQA
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has made substantial progress in extending the memory of large language models (LLMs), and recent advances have further pushed RAG from pure text settings toward multimodal scenarios. In the document understanding domain, document visual question answering (DocumentVQA) has evolved from question answering over a single document to retrieval-and-generation pipelines over large-scale document collections. However, a benchmark specifically designed for Chinese large-scale document retrieval and question answering is still lacking. To bridge this gap, we introduce CHaystack, a new Chinese DocumentVQA benchmark that covers four document categories, namely academic papers, advertisements, web pages, and real-world photographed documents, enabling a more comprehensive evaluation of DocumentVQA systems. In addition, we present CDocRAG, a Chinese DocumentVQA system that uses a VLM-based relevance filter to verify retrieved document images before answer generation. We evaluate representative open-source embedding and generation models on CHaystack. The results reveal a clear contrast in category-wise strengths: Qwen-family models perform best on text-rich documents such as webpages and papers, whereas other models only achieve competitive results on visually rich categories such as advertisements and degrade sharply on text-dense documents. For retrieval, Qwen3-VL reaches 71.91 Recall@1 while the best non-Qwen model achieves only 14.40. These results indicate that the core challenge of CHaystack lies in Chinese textual encoding, and that Chinese large-scale DocumentVQA still leaves substantial room for improvement. Our code and dateset is available at https://github.com/hanxi19/CHaystack.

AI.tldr: CHaystack is a new Chinese DocumentVQA benchmark spanning four document categories (academic papers, advertisements, web pages, photographed documents), accompanied by CDocRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation system with a VLM-based relevance filter. Evaluation reveals Qwen-family models dominate on text-rich documents, while non-Qwen models struggle, highlighting that Chinese textual encoding remains a core challenge for large-scale DocumentVQA.
AI.motivation: Existing DocumentVQA benchmarks lack a dedicated Chinese-language setting for large-scale document retrieval and question answering. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing a comprehensive evaluation benchmark that tests both retrieval and generation capabilities across diverse Chinese document types.
AI.method: The authors construct CHaystack, a benchmark with four document categories: academic papers, advertisements, web pages, and real-world photographed documents. They also propose CDocRAG, a Chinese DocumentVQA system that employs a VLM-based relevance filter to verify retrieved document images before answer generation. Representative open-source embedding and generation models are evaluated on this benchmark.
AI.result: Qwen-family models achieve the best performance on text-rich documents (webpages, papers), with Qwen3-VL reaching 71.91 Recall@1 for retrieval, while the best non-Qwen model reaches only 14.40. Other models perform competitively only on visually rich categories (advertisements) but degrade sharply on text-dense documents.
AI.conclusion: The core challenge in Chinese large-scale DocumentVQA is Chinese textual encoding. There remains substantial room for improvement in this domain, as current non-Qwen models significantly underperform on text-dense Chinese documents.

title: Kernel Forge: An Agent Harness for LLM-based Generation and Optimization of CUDA Kernels
summary: Machine learning models are increasingly embedded in everyday software, and most of their runtime is spent in a small set of compute kernels such as matrix multiplication, convolution, and normalization. Optimizing these kernels is one of the most direct ways to reduce latency and cost, but it has traditionally required expert engineers to hand-write low-level GPU code. Agentic systems built on large language models (LLMs) can now generate and optimize kernels with far less human effort, yet existing tools are largely evaluated on randomly generated tensors and isolated kernels, emit standalone CUDA code that developers must manually reintegrate, mostly target only LLM PyTorch models, and offer limited support for inspecting and debugging results. We present Kernel Forge, an open-source, end-to-end agentic harness that accepts any unmodified PyTorch model in place. Kernel Forge supports vision, diffusion, and LLM workloads, uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to explore multiple optimization paths rather than a single linear refinement chain, and ships with a graphical user interface for monitoring progress, inspecting candidate kernels, and debugging failures. We evaluate Kernel Forge on four PyTorch models spanning vision, diffusion, and LLM workloads on an NVIDIA DGX Spark with GB10 GPU. With only 50 optimization iterations per kernel, it optimizes 14 kernels to outperform PyTorch eager mode, reaching $1.52\times$ on adaptive\_avgpool2d in ResNet-50, $1.70\times$ on group\_norm in Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium, $2.83\times$ on softmax in Gemma 4 E2B, and $1.54\times$ on softmax in Qwen 3.5 35B-A3B.

AI.tldr: Kernel Forge is an open-source agentic system that uses LLMs with Monte Carlo Tree Search to automatically optimize compute kernels across vision, diffusion, and LLM PyTorch models, achieving up to 2.83× speedup over eager mode with only 50 iterations per kernel.
AI.motivation: Optimizing compute kernels (matrix multiplication, convolution, normalization) is critical for reducing latency and cost in ML models, but traditionally requires expert hand-written GPU code. While LLM-based tools now automate kernel generation, existing solutions are limited: they evaluate on random tensors, emit standalone CUDA code requiring manual reintegration, target only LLM models, and lack debugging support. A holistic, end-to-end system that works on unmodified models across diverse workloads is needed.
AI.method: Kernel Forge is an end-to-end agentic harness that accepts any unmodified PyTorch model. Key design elements include: (1) support for vision, diffusion, and LLM workloads; (2) Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to explore multiple optimization paths instead of a single linear refinement chain; (3) a graphical user interface for progress monitoring, candidate inspection, and failure debugging. The system is evaluated on an NVIDIA DGX Spark with GB10 GPU, running 50 optimization iterations per kernel across 14 kernels from four models.
AI.result: Across four PyTorch models evaluated on NVIDIA DGX Spark with GB10 GPU, Kernel Forge achieved speedups over eager mode: 1.52× on adaptive_avgpool2d in ResNet-50, 1.70× on group_norm in Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium, 2.83× on softmax in Gemma 4 E2B, and 1.54× on softmax in Qwen 3.5 35B-A3B. All 14 kernels were optimized to outperform PyTorch eager mode within 50 iterations each.
AI.conclusion: Kernel Forge demonstrates that an MCTS-guided, LLM-powered agentic system can effectively optimize compute kernels across diverse model architectures end-to-end, eliminating the need for manual CUDA expertise, standalone code reintegration, and workload-specific tooling.

title: Evaluating Communicative Belief Updates in Large Language Models via Implicature Recognition and Cancellation
summary: Human language is driven by unspoken beliefs and belief updates, making these critical to model for successful communication between large language models (LLMs) and their users. In this paper, we evaluate the ability of LLMs to recognize unspoken beliefs made through implicatures and to understand their updates through implicature cancellation: the pragmatic phenomenon whereby an utterance's implied meaning is weakened or negated. We create the first expert-annotated implicature cancellation dataset, [DatasetName], crowdsourced for human judgements of implicatures and their corresponding cancellations. We find that LLM belief update understanding lags behind that of humans, especially in more naturally-occurring scenarios. Additional control experiments suggest that successes in LLM belief updates may stem in part from a reliance on prior beliefs, and that failures in belief updates may depend on their type and on their form. Overall, our study suggests that current LLMs have not yet reached human-level understanding of unspoken beliefs and belief updates. Code and data are available at https://github.com/cesare-spinoso/ImplicatureX.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the first expert-annotated implicature cancellation dataset (ImplicatureX) to evaluate LLMs' ability to recognize unspoken beliefs conveyed through implicatures and understand their cancellation. Results show LLMs lag behind humans, especially in naturalistic scenarios, with successes partially attributable to reliance on prior beliefs rather than genuine pragmatic reasoning.
AI.motivation: Human communication relies heavily on unspoken beliefs and belief updates conveyed through pragmatic phenomena like implicatures and their cancellation. For LLMs to communicate successfully with users, they must model these implicit belief dynamics. However, no prior work has systematically evaluated whether LLMs can understand implicature cancellation — where an utterance's implied meaning is subsequently weakened or negated.
AI.method: The authors create ImplicatureX, the first expert-annotated dataset crowdsourced for human judgments on implicatures and their cancellations. They evaluate multiple LLMs on this dataset to assess belief update understanding. Additional control experiments are conducted to probe whether model performance stems from genuine pragmatic reasoning or reliance on prior beliefs, and to examine how failure patterns vary by cancellation type and form.
AI.result: LLMs consistently underperform humans in understanding implicature cancellation, with the gap widening in more naturally-occurring (ecologically valid) scenarios. Control experiments reveal that successful belief updates may be partly driven by models defaulting to prior beliefs rather than true pragmatic comprehension. Failures are systematically related to both the type and linguistic form of the cancellation.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs have not yet achieved human-level understanding of unspoken beliefs and belief updates. The work highlights a significant limitation in LLMs' pragmatic competence and motivates further research into modeling implicit belief dynamics for more natural human-AI communication.

title: ARCHER: Agentic Rule and Compliance Harness for Executable Regulations
summary: Verifying building compliance requires validating thousands of rules against large Building Information Modeling (BIM) designs, which is laborious, capital-intensive, and unscalable. Existing Automated Compliance Checkers (ACCs) are often difficult to generalize across different scenarios, as they are typically developed for highly specific rule sets and use cases. In addition, many ACCs are proprietary, meaning the underlying verification code is not released to end users, so users cannot verify whether their regulatory intent can be accurately captured. We introduce ARCHER (Agentic Rule and Compliance Harness for Executable Regulations), a test-driven, deterministically orchestrated multi-agent program-synthesis harness that generates auditable verification code from regulatory Codes of Practice, enabling transparent, adaptable, and scalable compliance checking. To characterize what makes agentic synthesis work, we evaluate a taxonomy of six harnesses of increasing agentic sophistication across four backbone models, spanning realistic data-governance tiers (from frontier third-party APIs to a fully on-premise open-weights model) on a novel dataset derived from real-world compliance scenarios. ARCHER's deterministic multi-agent orchestration achieves the highest accuracy for every backbone, improving mean union accuracy by 82% over a naive single-pass prompting baseline. Our cost-accuracy analysis further shows that using the ARCHER harness, a self-hosted open-weights model can reach 97.8% of frontier-API accuracy at a quarter of the cost, making data-sovereign compliance checking practical.

AI.tldr: ARCHER is a test-driven, multi-agent system that generates auditable verification code from regulatory codes of practice for automated building compliance checking. It achieves 82% improvement over naive prompting and enables cost-effective, data-sovereign compliance using self-hosted open-weights models at 97.8% of frontier-API accuracy for one-quarter the cost.
AI.motivation: Manual building compliance verification against BIM designs is labor-intensive and unscalable. Existing Automated Compliance Checkers (ACCs) suffer from two key limitations: (1) they are rule-specific and hard to generalize across scenarios, and (2) many are proprietary, preventing users from verifying whether regulatory intent is accurately captured. There is a need for transparent, adaptable, and scalable compliance checking with auditable code generation.
AI.method: The authors introduce ARCHER, a test-driven, deterministically orchestrated multi-agent program-synthesis harness. They evaluate a taxonomy of six harnesses with increasing agentic sophistication across four backbone models (ranging from frontier third-party APIs to fully on-premise open-weights models). The evaluation uses a novel dataset derived from real-world compliance scenarios and includes a cost-accuracy analysis across data-governance tiers.
AI.result: ARCHER's deterministic multi-agent orchestration achieves the highest accuracy for every backbone model tested, improving mean union accuracy by 82% over a naive single-pass prompting baseline. The cost-accuracy analysis demonstrates that a self-hosted open-weights model with ARCHER reaches 97.8% of frontier-API accuracy at 25% of the cost.
AI.conclusion: ARCHER demonstrates that test-driven, deterministically orchestrated multi-agent synthesis is an effective approach for generating transparent, auditable compliance checking code. The framework makes data-sovereign compliance checking practical by enabling open-weights models to approach frontier-model performance at significantly lower cost.

title: Trusting-Trust Attack against an Entire Linux Distribution through Binary Manipulation
summary: Ken Thompson's trusting-trust attack, in which a compromised compiler backdoors the programs it builds and reproduces the backdoor in subsequent rebuilds of itself, is widely regarded as a threat specific to compilers. We show that it is not. We construct a complete trusting-trust attack around GNU strip, an ordinary build utility that neither inspects nor generates source code, using only manipulations of finished ELF files. In the bootstrap of the NixOS Linux distribution, a single tampered strip in the binary seed implants a payload that propagates from one generation of strip to the next and survives into the final standard environment after the seed leaves the dependency closure. On a real nixpkgs revision, the attack builds a complete graphical installer without failures and backdoors almost every one of its binaries, enabling arbitrary malicious behavior of the subverted packages.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that the trusting-trust attack is not unique to compilers by constructing a complete attack using GNU strip, a binary utility that manipulates ELF files, to propagate a backdoor through the NixOS bootstrap chain and into the final system images.
AI.motivation: To challenge the prevailing assumption that trusting-trust attacks are compiler-specific threats, thereby broadening the security community's understanding of bootstrap chain vulnerabilities to include ordinary binary utilities.
AI.method: The authors construct an end-to-end trusting-trust attack centered on GNU strip (an ELF binary manipulation tool). A single tampered strip binary in the NixOS binary seed implants a payload that self-propagates: when the compromised strip processes the next-generation strip binary, it reinjects the backdoor. This propagation survives the entire bootstrap process, persisting even after the original seed leaves the dependency closure. The attack was validated against a real nixpkgs revision, producing a full graphical installer with nearly all binaries backdoored.
AI.result: The attack successfully produced a complete, bootable NixOS graphical installer from a real nixpkgs revision without build failures. Almost every binary in the resulting system was backdoored, demonstrating arbitrary malicious capability across the subverted packages.
AI.conclusion: Trusting-trust is a general property of the bootstrap problem, not a compiler-specific phenomenon. Any utility capable of self-referential processing within a bootstrap chain—even one that merely manipulates binary structures—can serve as an attack vector, implying that defenses must extend beyond compiler verification to the entire binary seed and build toolchain.

title: Authoring Agent Skills: A Software-Engineering Approach
summary: Agent Skills are an emerging way to extend large language model agents with reusable procedural knowledge that the agent loads on demand. Anthropic introduced Agent Skills and published the format as an open specification supported across several agent tools. This note argues that a skill is a software artefact and that its construction should follow software-engineering principles, with qualifications: single responsibility, separation of interface from implementation, low coupling, and economy in a shared token budget, together with behavioural evaluation in place of deterministic testing. Using Claude Code as the reference implementation, it describes how a skill is structured, how its contents are loaded in stages, and how to write the description on which selection depends. It places skills against the other mechanisms a developer can use to shape agent behaviour, like project memory files, slash commands, subagents, external tool connections, and hooks, and gives a rule for choosing between them based on who decides that a mechanism runs and what guarantee it provides. It then sets out an evaluation-driven authoring process, a set of patterns and faults commonly encountered in authoring, and the trust question raised by using skills from third parties. We illustrate the comparison drawn in UML class style, the loading model, the anatomy of a skill, the relative position of each mechanism, and the points at which skills and hooks act during a session.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that Agent Skills should be treated as software artefacts built with software-engineering principles. It analyzes the structure, loading model, and authoring patterns of skills using Claude Code as reference, situates skills among other agent-shaping mechanisms, and proposes an evaluation-driven development process while addressing trust concerns with third-party skills.
AI.motivation: With the emergence of Agent Skills as a mechanism for extending LLM agents with reusable procedural knowledge, there is a need for principled guidance on how to design, structure, and evaluate skills properly. The paper addresses the lack of software-engineering rigor in skill construction and the need to understand how skills relate to other agent-behavior mechanisms.
AI.method: The paper takes an analytical and prescriptive approach: (1) it defines software-engineering qualifications adapted for skills (single responsibility, interface-implementation separation, low coupling, token budget economy, behavioral evaluation); (2) it uses Claude Code as a reference implementation to detail skill structure, staged loading, and selection descriptions; (3) it taxonomizes other agent-shaping mechanisms (project memory files, slash commands, subagents, external tools, hooks) using a decision rule based on who decides execution and what guarantee is provided; (4) it proposes an evaluation-driven authoring process and catalogs common patterns and faults; (5) it uses UML-style diagrams to illustrate the comparative architecture.
AI.result: Key results include: a structured anatomy of a skill, a staged loading model, a comparative taxonomy of agent-shaping mechanisms with a decision rule (who decides × what guarantee), a catalog of authoring patterns and common faults, and identification of the third-party trust problem. The paper provides diagrammatic illustrations in UML class style covering the comparison, loading model, skill anatomy, mechanism positioning, and skill/hook action points during a session.
AI.conclusion: Skills are properly understood as software artefacts demanding engineering discipline. Their construction should follow adapted principles — single responsibility, interface-implementation separation, low coupling, token economy, and behavioral evaluation. Developers should choose among skills and other mechanisms based on the decision-maker and guarantee provided. An evaluation-driven, pattern-aware authoring process mitigates common faults, while third-party skill use raises unresolved trust questions.

title: Development and applications of Generative AI in architectural design studios
summary: Recent advancements in deep generative models, with their capacity to yield outputs that are both visually appealing and semantically coherent, have served to further intricate the nexus between Artificial Intelligence (AI) and creativity. This integration of these models into creative disciplines, most notably within the domain of design, has been rapidly escalating. Nevertheless, a prevailing gap remains in our understanding of the impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) on design creativity. To address this gap, a longitudinal study was initiated, encompassing the development of a user-friendly GenAI interface. This interface was designed to facilitate the integration of GenAI models into design education, following a cyclical process of experimentation and refinement. The study involved the utilization of GenAI models in design studios, the collection of feedback, the development and evaluation of the GAI-A platform, and subsequent implementation in design education. The findings of the study provide a discussion based on the views and observations of students on the extent to which they use GenAI models, their perspectives and expectations of these models, and the extent to which this process improves their creativity in the context of the final product.

AI.tldr: A longitudinal study developed and deployed a GenAI interface (GAI-A platform) in design education to investigate how generative AI models influence student creativity, gathering feedback through iterative design studio experimentation.
AI.motivation: Despite rapid adoption of generative AI in creative design disciplines, there remains a significant gap in understanding how GenAI actually impacts design creativity. The authors seek to empirically investigate this relationship.
AI.method: A longitudinal study involving: (1) development of a user-friendly GenAI interface, (2) iterative cycles of experimentation and refinement, (3) deployment of GenAI models in design studios, (4) collection of student feedback, (5) development and evaluation of the GAI-A platform, and (6) implementation in design education settings.
AI.result: Findings discuss students' usage patterns of GenAI models, their perspectives and expectations regarding these tools, and the extent to which GenAI integration improved creativity in their final design products.
AI.conclusion: The study contributes empirical insights into the GenAI–design creativity nexus through a structured educational intervention, though specific conclusive claims are not detailed in the abstract.

title: Eliminating Propagation Delay: Attention-Based Spatial-Temporal Fusion Graph Convolution Network for Traffic Flow Prediction
summary: Predicting traffic flow is crucial to optimizing transportation systems and improving urban mobility. Many graph convolution-based models have been proposed to extract spatial-temporal features and predict traffic flow. However, most focus on spatial-temporal and semantic correlation in topological relationships. There are two primary problems to address. Firstly, the convolutional structure in the model focuses on utilizing static spatial dependencies and spatial-temporal relationships in topological structures, while neglecting the different information propagation delays between adjacent nodes in the convolution. Secondly, these methods often stack a large number of complex structures, resulting in a substantial increase in computational time during the model training phase, thereby disregarding the model's requirements for timeliness. In this paper, we propose a novel network called the Attention-Based Spatial-Temporal Fusion Graph Convolution Network (A-STFGCN). We design a spatial-temporal fusion block to extract the spatial-temporal feature correlations with propagation delay errors removed and to capture both long-term and short-term temporal characteristics of the data within a multi-head self-attention mechanism based on a mask matrix. Extensive experiments on five real-world datasets demonstrate that our method achieves the best overall performance while having good computation and data utilization efficiency compared with the eight baseline methods.

AI.tldr: A-STFGCN proposes an attention-based spatial-temporal fusion graph convolution network that addresses propagation delay errors between adjacent nodes and model complexity issues, achieving state-of-the-art traffic flow prediction with high computational efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing graph convolution-based traffic flow prediction models suffer from two key limitations: (1) they neglect varying information propagation delays between adjacent nodes during convolution, relying only on static spatial dependencies; (2) they stack numerous complex structures, causing excessive training time and poor timeliness.
AI.method: The authors propose A-STFGCN, which introduces a spatial-temporal fusion block to extract spatial-temporal feature correlations while removing propagation delay errors. This block also captures long-term and short-term temporal characteristics using a multi-head self-attention mechanism with a mask matrix.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on five real-world datasets show that A-STFGCN achieves the best overall performance compared to eight baseline methods, while maintaining strong computational and data utilization efficiency.
AI.conclusion: A-STFGCN effectively balances predictive accuracy and computational efficiency by addressing propagation delay errors and avoiding excessive structural complexity, making it a practical solution for real-world traffic flow prediction tasks.

title: The Effect of Text Chunk Size on Retrieval-Augmented Generation Performance
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems have emerged as a powerful process for allowing large language models (LLMs) to retrieve relevant information to use as source material during text generation. A critical yet under-explored component of these systems is the granularity at which source documents are segmented into retrievable chunks. The size of these chunks has the potential to significantly influence generation quality, contextual correctness, retrieval precision, and computational efficiency. Despite its importance, chunk size is often selected without proper evaluation of its impact on generation quality. Smaller chunks, such as individual sentences, may allow for precise retrieval by narrowing the focus of each chunk. However, they contain less information, which may limit the model's ability to generate coherent responses. Larger chunks, such as entire chapters, contain lots of broad information that may improve correctness, but also introduce additional noise and increase computational cost. Because larger chunks contain more information, the number of chunks returned to the model must also be considered. This paper evaluates how chunk size, along with the number of retrieved segments, influences generation quality and retrieval effectiveness. By comparing these configurations, this study seeks to better understand how document segmentation affects the performance and efficiency of Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems. segmentation affects the performance and efficiency of Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how document chunk size and the number of retrieved chunks impact the generation quality, retrieval precision, and computational efficiency of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, addressing an under-explored but critical design decision.
AI.motivation: Chunk size in RAG systems is a critical yet under-explored hyperparameter. It is often selected arbitrarily without rigorous evaluation of its impact on generation quality, contextual correctness, retrieval precision, and computational cost. The trade-offs between small chunks (high precision, low context) and large chunks (rich context, more noise) warrant systematic study.
AI.method: The paper conducts a comparative evaluation exploring how varying chunk sizes (from individual sentences to entire chapters) and the number of retrieved segments jointly influence generation quality and retrieval effectiveness in RAG systems.
AI.result: The abstract does not specify quantitative results; the study aims to provide a better understanding of how document segmentation affects RAG system performance and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The abstract presents the research agenda and motivation but does not state definitive conclusions. The work seeks to inform better chunking strategies for RAG systems.

title: CaRE Compute-aware Remasking Evaluation Protocol for Masked Diffusion Language Models
summary: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) are advancing rapidly, yet the evaluation standards needed to reliably interpret their progress have not kept pace. Despite MDLMs becoming competitive with autoregressive language models, seven recent remasking papers evaluate under incompatible settings, varying nominal step counts, metrics, and sampling temperatures without jointly controlling these factors, rendering their strategy rankings largely incomparable and leaving open whether reported gains reflect algorithmic improvements or evaluation artifacts. We present CaRE, a compute-aware evaluation framework that audits MDLM remasking strategies by standardizing actual number of function evaluations (NFE), enforcing multi-metric reporting, and explicitly controlling stochasticity. Applied to 7 remasking strategies across LLaDA-8B-Base and Dream-7B-Base at 4 stochasticity levels and 3 step budgets on OpenWebText and LM1B, CaRE reveals that: (i) temperature explains the majority of MAUVE variance, (ii) compute-matched comparisons reverse several published strategy rankings, and (iii) informed remasking and stochastic unmasking are in tension, with high-entropy remasking reducing MAUVE by 0.296 at 256 steps at unmask_temp=0.25 (p=0.020). A CaRE leaderboard covering 12 open-weight MDLMs (150M to 8B parameters) shows that this interaction direction holds across architectures and scales. These findings demonstrate that current MDLM evaluations can systematically conflate algorithmic improvements with hidden choices of compute and stochasticity. We release the evaluation protocol, implementation, and leaderboard to ensure future remasking claims are reproducible and comparable.

AI.tldr: CaRE is a compute-aware framework that standardizes MDLM evaluation by controlling NFE, temperature, and metrics, revealing that reported remasking strategy gains are often artifacts of evaluation inconsistency rather than algorithmic superiority.
AI.motivation: Recent MDLM remasking papers use incompatible evaluation settings (varying step counts, metrics, sampling temperatures) without joint control, making strategy rankings incomparable and obscuring whether improvements are genuine or evaluation artifacts.
AI.method: CaRE standardizes actual NFE, enforces multi-metric reporting, and explicitly controls stochasticity. Applied to 7 remasking strategies on LLaDA-8B-Base and Dream-7B-Base across 4 stochasticity levels and 3 step budgets (OpenWebText, LM1B), plus a leaderboard of 12 open-weight MDLMs (150M–8B).
AI.result: (i) Temperature explains most MAUVE variance; (ii) compute-matched comparisons reverse several published rankings; (iii) high-entropy remasking reduces MAUVE by 0.296 at 256 steps (unmask_temp=0.25, p=0.020), revealing tension between informed remasking and stochastic unmasking, a pattern consistent across architectures and scales.
AI.conclusion: MDLM evaluations systematically conflate algorithmic improvements with hidden compute and stochasticity choices. CaRE provides a standardized protocol, implementation, and leaderboard to ensure future claims are reproducible and comparable.

title: Deep Label-Wise Attentive Temporal Convolutional Networks Improve Medical Coding
comment: Work carried out in 2019; posted as a record of the work. Baselines and state of the art reflect the 2019 literature
summary: Medical coding is the task of assigning a set of diagnosis and procedure codes for a hospitalization using recorded notes. It requires aggregating information from different parts of the text and focus to different sections for each individual code, making it a very difficult problem even for professional human coders. We model the task as a multi-label text classification problem. To overcome the mentioned difficulties, we propose a deep neural model consisting of a multi-layer temporal convolution network (TCN) followed by label-wise attention. While multi-layer TCN helps extract a global document representation with the ability to learn relations over very long sequences, label-specific attention mechanism allows the model to focus on different aspects of the same document for each individual label. Our method achieves significantly better F-1 scores (9% increase) compared to the previous state-of-the-art model, with a remarkable increase in recall score (28% increase), which we believe is the more important metric for a clinical decision support setting.

AI.tldr: Proposes a deep model combining multi-layer Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN) with label-wise attention for medical coding, achieving 9% F1 improvement and 28% recall increase over prior state-of-the-art.
AI.motivation: Medical coding requires aggregating information across different text sections and focusing on different parts for each code, making it extremely challenging even for expert human coders. Prior models struggled with long-range dependencies and lacked code-specific focus mechanisms.
AI.method: A multi-layer Temporal Convolution Network (TCN) extracts global document representations capable of modeling long-sequence relations, followed by a label-wise attention mechanism that enables the model to attend to distinct, relevant sections of the clinical note for each individual diagnosis/procedure code. The task is framed as multi-label text classification.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves a 9% increase in F1 scores and a remarkable 28% increase in recall compared to the previous state-of-the-art model.
AI.conclusion: The combination of TCN for long-range dependency modeling and label-specific attention for targeted information extraction yields substantial performance gains. The dramatic recall improvement is particularly valuable for clinical decision support, where missing relevant codes is more costly than over-coding.

title: CHILL-Harness: Counterfactual Harness Learning for Efficient Reasoning in Long-Horizon Agents
summary: Agent harnesses have become the operational infrastructure of modern large language model agents, coordinating context, tools, verification, and execution control to translate latent model capability into reliable long-horizon behavior. However, reliable long-horizon behavior requires harness control to adapt to task demands, execution environments, and evolving execution states, whereas current harnesses predominantly rely on hand-crafted or globally fixed policies; this mismatch manifests as unnecessary computational overhead and, in adverse cases, reduced task success. To address this limitation, we formulate the task of enabling adaptive orchestration in harness systems as a causal learning problem and propose Counterfactual Harness Intervention Learning for Long-Horizon Agents (CHILL-Harness). CHILL-Harness intervenes at the orchestration layer to enable advantage-guided workflow adaptation, thereby improving reasoning and execution efficiency while preserving task performance. Specifically, we develop causal intervention effect learning as the effect-estimation component of CHILL-Harness to estimate intervention-relative workflow advantage from confidence-weighted execution evidence and identify advantageous workflow adaptations. We further introduce advantage-realizing causal orchestration as its realization component to adaptively allocate counterfactual reasoning and realize only workflow adjustments supported by sufficient expected advantage. Finally, we incorporate a success-preserving objective and advantage-margin authorization constraints into CHILL-Harness to promote reliable adaptation. Extensive experiments on heterogeneous long-horizon tasks spanning information seeking, software engineering, and terminal interaction show that CHILL-Harness consistently preserves or improves task success while substantially reducing token consumption and execution time.

AI.tldr: CHILL-Harness formulates adaptive orchestration in LLM agent harnesses as a causal learning problem, using counterfactual intervention effect estimation and advantage-guided workflow adaptation to improve reasoning efficiency while preserving task success across long-horizon tasks.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agent harnesses rely on hand-crafted or globally fixed orchestration policies that cannot adapt to task demands, execution environments, or evolving states. This mismatch causes unnecessary computational overhead and reduced task success, motivating the need for adaptive orchestration.
AI.method: CHILL-Harness consists of two core components: (1) causal intervention effect learning, which estimates intervention-relative workflow advantage from confidence-weighted execution evidence to identify beneficial adaptations; (2) advantage-realizing causal orchestration, which adaptively allocates counterfactual reasoning and only applies adjustments with sufficient expected advantage. A success-preserving objective and advantage-margin authorization constraints promote reliable adaptation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on long-horizon tasks spanning information seeking, software engineering, and terminal interaction demonstrate that CHILL-Harness consistently preserves or improves task success while substantially reducing token consumption and execution time.
AI.conclusion: CHILL-Harness effectively bridges the gap between static harness policies and dynamic execution demands through causal intervention learning, enabling reliable, efficient adaptive orchestration for long-horizon LLM agents.

title: Early Detection of Distributed Backdoors in Multi-Agent LLM Systems: A Characterization Study
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems can be attacked by a payload that no single agent ever holds in full: a poisoned tool hides encrypted fragments in its observations, spreads them across several agents, and an external step reassembles and executes them after the run. Per-step safety checks that judge each action in isolation may fail to recognize the complete distributed payload. We investigate how early such an attack can be detected while the run is still unfolding, and how robustly it can be caught once its most obvious cues are stripped away. We build a working instance on a hierarchical multi-agent system, run it under benign and attacked conditions across five language models and two task domains, and record when each fragment is injected and when the payload is assembled and executed. Detection is a race against assembly. Before the first fragment is injected, attacked and benign runs are indistinguishable; once injection begins, a prefix detector flags $99.3\%$ of successful attacks with a median of five steps remaining and a $10.3\%$ safe-run false-positive rate. Because assembly occurs only after the run, these alarms arrive in time to abort nearly every successful attack. We then measure how much of that warning rests on removable surface cues of the attack rather than on its distributed structure. Generic zero-shot and behavior-trained detectors provide almost no warning at all; the detectors that do work lean in part on removable surface cues, chiefly the ciphertext's length and entropy, and once the entropy cue is removed from the payload and the length features from the detector, detection arrives later and transfers poorly across domains, though a fine-tuned model recovers some of the loss.

AI.tldr: Multi-agent LLM systems are vulnerable to distributed payload attacks where encrypted malicious fragments are spread across agents and assembled post-run, evading per-step safety checks. The study measures detection timing: a prefix detector catches 99.3% of attacks with ~5 steps remaining but relies partly on surface cues (ciphertext length/entropy). When these cues are removed, detection degrades significantly, though fine-tuning partially recovers performance.
AI.motivation: Current per-step safety mechanisms in multi-agent LLM systems examine each action in isolation, making them blind to distributed attacks where no single agent ever holds the complete malicious payload. The authors aim to understand (1) how early such distributed attacks can be detected during an unfolding run, and (2) how much of that detection capability depends on superficial cues versus the actual distributed structure of the attack.
AI.method: The authors built a hierarchical multi-agent system capable of executing distributed payload attacks: a poisoned tool injects encrypted fragments into observations across multiple agents, and an external step reassembles and executes the payload after the run completes. They tested this under benign and attacked conditions across five language models and two task domains. Detection was framed as a race against assembly, with fragment injection timestamps recorded. They evaluated prefix-based detectors, generic zero-shot detectors, and behavior-trained detectors, then systematically removed surface cues (ciphertext entropy, length features) to isolate structural detection signals. A fine-tuned model was tested for recovery.
AI.result: Before fragment injection, attacked and benign runs are indistinguishable. Once injection begins, a prefix detector flags 99.3% of successful attacks with a median of 5 steps remaining and a 10.3% false-positive rate on safe runs — early enough to abort nearly all successful attacks. However, generic zero-shot and behavior-trained detectors provide almost no warning. The effective detectors rely partially on removable surface cues (ciphertext length and entropy). When entropy is removed from the payload and length features from the detector, detection arrives later and transfers poorly across domains. A fine-tuned model partially recovers the lost detection capability.
AI.conclusion: Distributed payload attacks represent a genuine and stealthy threat to multi-agent LLM systems that per-step safety checks cannot address. While prefix-based detectors can provide early warning, their effectiveness is substantially attributable to surface-level features rather than robust detection of distributed structure. Removing those cues significantly weakens detection and cross-domain transfer, highlighting the need for more structurally-aware detection methods. Fine-tuning offers a partial path to recovery but does not fully close the gap.

title: What Motivates Whom? A Survey of Newcomers to OSS and Experienced OSS Practitioners
summary: Open source software (OSS) development continues to expand, yet software practitioners often struggle to select suitable projects, leading to inefficient onboarding and disengagement. Understanding how contributors select OSS projects is important for supporting contributors onboarding, engagement, and long-term participation within OSS communities. This study investigates contributors' project-selection preferences in OSS projects and examines how these preferences correlate with contributors' motivations and demographic backgrounds. Through an online survey of 208 practitioners, we found that demographic factors, such as age, gender, and the OSS role they held, significantly correlate with their motivations. Additionally, preferences for project characteristics such as project age, development stage, and documentation quality vary based on specific motivations. Importantly, our findings are presented through a comparative lens, analyzing the responses of newcomers to OSS and experienced OSS practitioners separately to uncover their distinct preferences. Lastly, we explore software practitioners' perspectives on how existing recommendation systems could better support project selection and align with their motivations. By disentangling the unique needs of newcomers to OSS and OSS practitioners, our findings provide insights for researchers, OSS project owners, and software practitioners to improve contributor onboarding, engagement, and retention, while also informing future project recommendation systems and improving the OSS ecosystem.

AI.tldr: This study surveys 208 OSS practitioners to examine how contributors' motivations and demographics (age, gender, role) influence their project-selection preferences, revealing distinct patterns between newcomers and experienced contributors, with implications for recommendation systems and onboarding.
AI.motivation: OSS contributors often struggle to select suitable projects, leading to poor onboarding and disengagement. Understanding the factors that drive project selection—and how these differ between newcomers and experienced practitioners—is critical for improving contributor retention and the health of the OSS ecosystem.
AI.method: An online survey of 208 software practitioners was conducted. The study analyzed how demographic factors (age, gender, OSS role) correlate with motivations, and how those motivations in turn correlate with preferences for project characteristics (project age, development stage, documentation quality). Responses from newcomers and experienced OSS practitioners were compared separately.
AI.result: Demographic factors significantly correlate with contributor motivations. Preferences for project age, development stage, and documentation quality vary based on specific motivations. Newcomers and experienced practitioners exhibit distinct project-selection preferences. Practitioners also provided perspectives on how existing recommendation systems could be improved to better align with their motivations.
AI.conclusion: By disentangling the unique needs of newcomers versus experienced OSS practitioners, the findings offer actionable insights for researchers, project owners, and tool builders to improve contributor onboarding, engagement, and retention, and to inform the design of future project recommendation systems.

title: Language as a Material Interface for Creative LLM Interaction
comment: Paper accepted at Creativity and Cognition '26, London 13-16 July 2026
summary: Although directive prompting is the predominant way to interact with Large Language Models (LLMs), many creative practices rely on language that is open-ended, associative, phonaesthetic, symbolic, and that unfolds across multiple temporalities. In this work, we explore how creative practitioners might work with AI systems when language is treated not merely as instruction but as material. We conducted an ecological two-week study with four creative practitioners using a design probe: the Memetic Mixer, a tangible interactive device that constrains interaction with an LLM. Analysis of post-study interviews and device logs identified distinct modes of material language use and temporalities that shaped each participant's engagement with AI and their creative practice. We reflect on these findings and contribute design considerations that support open-ended interaction with AI in creative practice.

AI.tldr: Explores how creative practitioners use language as material (not just instruction) when interacting with LLMs. A two-week study with a tangible device (Memetic Mixer) revealed distinct modes of material language use and temporalities, leading to design considerations for open-ended AI interaction in creative practice.
AI.motivation: Directive prompting dominates LLM interaction, but creative practices often employ open-ended, associative, symbolic, and phonaesthetic language that unfolds over time. The authors seek to understand how creative practitioners engage with AI when language is treated as material rather than simply as instruction.
AI.method: An ecological two-week study with four creative practitioners using a design probe called the Memetic Mixer — a tangible interactive device that deliberately constrains LLM interaction. Data was gathered through post-study interviews and device logs, then analyzed to identify distinct modes of material language use and temporal patterns.
AI.result: The study identified distinct modes of material language use and varying temporalities that shaped how each participant engaged with AI and their creative practice. These patterns revealed how constrained, tangible interaction can foster non-directive, materially-oriented language practices with LLMs.
AI.conclusion: The authors contribute design considerations for supporting open-ended, material-language-based interaction with AI systems in creative contexts, moving beyond the dominant directive prompting paradigm.

title: Mechanisms of Width Scaling in Normalized Residual Networks: The Effective Alignment Dimension
summary: Existing theories of neural-network width characterize asymptotic limits, but provide limited guidance on whether an expansion direction identified from finite training data remains beneficial on unseen data. We study this problem for function-preserving residual expansion and introduce the effective alignment dimension, a measurable quantity describing the signal-noise geometry of activation gradients. By deriving the exact mean and variance of the inner product between independently estimated training and test gradients, we obtain a finite-sample upper bound on misalignment probability. The bound depends only on the effective alignment dimension and an effective sample size, requiring finite second moments and a nonzero population gradient, without covariance spectral assumptions or prescribed width-growth rates. We integrate this certificate into the train-test residual-expansion framework, yielding a high-probability condition for test-risk improvement. Experiments across width-controlled LLaMA-style Transformers, Pythia, and ResNet-20 show that wider models exhibit larger effective alignment dimensions and lower empirical misalignment. Direct residual interventions confirm that the alignment statistic predicts the sign and magnitude of held-out loss changes.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the "effective alignment dimension," a measurable quantity characterizing activation gradient geometry, and derives finite-sample bounds on misalignment probability for residual expansion directions. The bound, requiring only mild moment conditions, is integrated into a train-test residual-expansion framework that certifies test-risk improvement. Experiments on LLaMA-style Transformers, Pythia, and ResNet-20 validate the theory.
AI.motivation: Existing neural-network width theories characterize asymptotic limits but fail to provide guarantees on whether a residual expansion direction estimated from finite training data will remain beneficial on unseen test data. This gap motivates a finite-sample analysis of gradient alignment across train/test splits.
AI.method: The authors define the effective alignment dimension to capture signal-noise geometry of activation gradients. They derive the exact mean and variance of the inner product between independently estimated training and test gradients, yielding a finite-sample upper bound on misalignment probability. This bound depends only on the effective alignment dimension and an effective sample size, requiring only finite second moments and a nonzero population gradient (no covariance spectral assumptions or prescribed width-growth rates). The certificate is integrated into a train-test residual-expansion framework providing high-probability conditions for test-risk improvement.
AI.result: Experiments across width-controlled LLaMA-style Transformers, Pythia, and ResNet-20 demonstrate that wider models exhibit larger effective alignment dimensions and lower empirical misalignment. Direct residual interventions confirm that the alignment statistic predicts both the sign and magnitude of held-out loss changes.
AI.conclusion: The effective alignment dimension provides a practical, theoretically-grounded certificate for guiding residual expansion decisions in finite-sample settings. Wider networks naturally yield better alignment, and the proposed statistic reliably predicts out-of-sample performance improvements from function-preserving expansions.

title: JKO-RAG: Distributional Retrieval as Wasserstein Free-Energy Gradient Flow
summary: RAG pipelines return a \emph{ranked list} of passages. We argue this is a mismatch: the downstream language model conditions on a \emph{set}, and the selection problem is fundamentally geometric. We propose \jko, which frames reranking as minimising a free-energy functional $F(p)=\text{relevance}+\text{entropy}+\text{redundancy}$ under Wasserstein-2 gradient flow via the Jordan--Kinderlehrer--Otto proximal scheme. The ground metric $C_{ij}=(1-\cos\langle z_i,z_j\rangle)^2$ encodes the semantic geometry of the embedding manifold. Our central contribution is a \emph{linear-response theory} explaining \emph{why} the Wasserstein geometry helps: the Wasserstein and KL retrieval maps differ only in their proximal Hessian -- dense and geometry-aware for $W^2$, diagonal and geometry-blind for KL -- and this difference damps the mass transport that query paraphrase induces. The theory yields a falsifiable prediction: the stability advantage is monotonically decreasing in step size $h$. We verify this empirically via free-energy descent, frequency-resolved perturbation response, the predicted $h$-dependence, and a certified-radius analysis. Four extensions are introduced: \textbf{\nmjko} (learned ground metric), \textbf{\bwjko} ($W^2$--KL interpolation), \textbf{\samjko} ($2\times$ speedup), and \textbf{\dualrank} (OT dual potentials as confidence signals). Across five BEIR benchmarks, \jko\ outperforms the cross-encoder on all five; the decisive advantage is robustness -- 22--38\% more stable under paraphrase, $2\times$ fewer leaked distractors.

AI.tldr: The paper reframes RAG passage reranking as a geometric optimization problem over sets, proposing JKO — a Wasserstein gradient flow method minimizing a free-energy functional that balances relevance, entropy, and redundancy. A linear-response theory explains why Wasserstein geometry yields superior robustness to query paraphrasing compared to KL-based methods, with predictions verified empirically. JKO outperforms cross-encoders on five BEIR benchmarks, showing 22–38% greater paraphrase stability.
AI.motivation: RAG pipelines produce a ranked list of passages, but downstream language models condition on a set. This rank/set mismatch, coupled with the inherently geometric nature of passage selection, motivates reframing reranking as a geometric optimization problem rather than a sequential scoring task.
AI.method: The core method, JKO, frames reranking as minimizing a free-energy functional F(p) = relevance + entropy + redundancy under Wasserstein-2 gradient flow via the Jordan–Kinderlehrer–Otto proximal scheme. The ground metric uses cosine-distance-based squared cost C_{ij} = (1 − cos⟨z_i, z_j⟩)². A linear-response theory is developed to explain the advantage, showing that Wasserstein vs. KL retrieval maps differ in their proximal Hessian (dense/geometry-aware vs. diagonal/geometry-blind), damping mass transport from query paraphrasing. Four extensions are proposed: learned ground metric (MetaJKO), W²–KL interpolation (BW-JKO), a 2× speedup variant (SamJKO), and OT dual potentials as confidence signals (DualRank).
AI.result: JKO outperforms the cross-encoder on all five BEIR benchmarks. The key advantage is robustness: 22–38% greater stability under paraphrase and 2× fewer leaked distractors. Empirical verification includes free-energy descent, frequency-resolved perturbation response, monotonic h-dependence of stability advantage, and certified-radius analysis.
AI.conclusion: Wasserstein geometry provides a principled framework for set-based passage reranking in RAG, with its robustness advantage rooted in a geometry-aware proximal Hessian that damps paraphrase-induced mass transport. The linear-response theory yields falsifiable predictions confirmed empirically, establishing JKO as both theoretically grounded and practically superior to existing methods.

title: GrocLM: Grocery Category Recommendation in E-Commerce with Large Language Models
summary: The rapid growth of online grocery shopping requires recommendation systems that capture cyclical purchasing behavior and diverse user intents. Traditional item-level methods face scalability and accuracy challenges, motivating category-level recommendation as a more structured and practical alternative. We present GROCLM, a fine-tuned language model for grocery category recommendation in a real-world production environment. GROCLM employs a two-stage LoRA-based training strategy to encode cyclical purchasing patterns directly into model parameters, enabling more effective utilization of rebuying signals compared to prompt-based conditioning. To ensure valid and controllable outputs, we further introduce a trie-based constrained decoding mechanism over a predefined category space. Experiments on both proprietary production data and a public benchmark demonstrate that GROCLM consistently outperforms strong baselines. In a live production restocking task, GROCLM achieves a 7.5% relative improvement in cart-adds per impression, while maintaining efficient inference by generating all categories jointly. These results highlight the effectiveness and practicality of integrating large language models into structured recommendation systems.

AI.tldr: GROCLM is a fine-tuned LLM for grocery category recommendation that uses LoRA-based training to encode cyclical purchasing patterns and trie-based constrained decoding for valid outputs, achieving a 7.5% relative improvement in cart-adds per impression in production.
AI.motivation: Online grocery recommendation faces scalability and accuracy challenges with traditional item-level methods. Category-level recommendation offers a more structured alternative, but existing approaches struggle to capture cyclical (rebuying) purchasing behavior and diverse user intents effectively.
AI.method: GROCLM employs (1) a two-stage LoRA-based fine-tuning strategy that encodes cyclical purchasing patterns directly into model parameters rather than relying on prompt-based conditioning, and (2) a trie-based constrained decoding mechanism that ensures all generated outputs fall within a predefined, valid category space, enabling joint generation of all categories.
AI.result: On proprietary production data and a public benchmark, GROCLM consistently outperforms strong baselines. In a live production restocking task, it achieves a 7.5% relative improvement in cart-adds per impression while maintaining efficient inference via joint category generation.
AI.conclusion: Integrating large language models into structured recommendation systems via parameter-efficient fine-tuning and constrained decoding is both effective and practical for real-world grocery recommendation, offering significant performance gains without sacrificing inference efficiency.

title: TabRank: Chain-of-Thought Distillation for Table Re-Rankers
summary: The ability to retrieve relevant tables for answering questions is a key task for structured information retrieval. Multi-stage retrieval systems rely heavily on rerankers to refine candidate lists produced by efficient first-stage retrievers. As a result, neural rerankers and LLM-based reranking methods have become increasingly important due to their superior capacity for semantic understanding and reasoning compared to conventional sparse or dense retrieval models. Recently, Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) equipped with explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning have shown strong improvements in ranking quality in unstructured passage retrieval. In this work, we present TabRank, a framework for training reasoning rerankers for Tabular Retrieval. We first present a comprehensive dataset of 6728 reasoning traces for tabular reranking on the Natural Questions Tables dataset. We then explore two variants of training a compact reasoning model on these reasoning traces: explicit CoT distillation and conditioning the student reranker on the teacher's reasoning trace within the prompt. We stress-test TabRank on several out-of-distribution generalization settings on diverse domains and multi-table scenarios. Our approach significantly improves performance across a variety of table retrieval datasets, increasing Acc@10 by 30.5% on HybridQA, 15.2% on SQA, 52.9% on TabFact, and 13.1% on TATQA subsets of the Multi-Table QA Benchmark compared to the base model. Notably, TabRank generalizes effectively to multi-table reasoning. Our code, data and models are available at https://github.com/AdarshSingh7647/TabRanker

AI.tldr: TabRank trains compact reasoning rerankers for table retrieval using distilled chain-of-thought reasoning traces, achieving substantial accuracy gains (up to 52.9% on TabFact) and strong out-of-distribution generalization across diverse table QA datasets.
AI.motivation: Multi-stage retrieval systems for tabular data lack effective neural rerankers that leverage explicit reasoning. While Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) with chain-of-thought reasoning improve passage retrieval, no analogous approach exists for table retrieval. The authors aim to bridge this gap by enabling reasoning-based reranking for structured tabular data.
AI.method: The authors construct a dataset of 6,728 reasoning traces for tabular reranking using the Natural Questions Tables dataset. They then train compact reasoning rerankers via two approaches: (1) explicit CoT distillation, where a student model learns to generate reasoning chains, and (2) conditioning the student reranker on the teacher's reasoning trace provided within the prompt. The resulting TabRank framework is evaluated under out-of-distribution and multi-table settings.
AI.result: TabRank significantly outperforms the base model across multiple table retrieval datasets on the Multi-Table QA Benchmark: Acc@10 improves by 30.5% on HybridQA, 15.2% on SQA, 52.9% on TabFact, and 13.1% on TATQA subsets. TabRank also demonstrates effective generalization to multi-table reasoning scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Distilling reasoning capabilities into compact rerankers via CoT traces is a highly effective strategy for tabular retrieval, yielding robust performance and strong generalization across diverse domains and multi-table settings without requiring large, computationally expensive reasoning models at inference time.

title: Towards a Systems Foundation for Agentic Cloud Management
summary: Agentic cloud management is emerging as a practice to automate laborious operations, minimize toil, and improve responsiveness. Despite the rapid development of autonomous management agents, we argue that the fundamental missing piece is a systems foundation to enable safe, effective operations across agents and between agents and human operators. In this paper, we advocate for the need of such a systems foundation and share our efforts on developing CloudWeaver, an agentic management substrate that works across existing cloud-user interfaces and future agent-native interfaces. Specifically, we discuss how CloudWeaver (1) scopes the context of individual agent sessions with local views of cloud resources and (2) coordinates concurrent management operations on shared cloud resources. CloudWeaver offers strong safety guarantees and attributable feedback in the presence of conflicting intents, while preserving concurrency between independent operations. We validate CloudWeaver using a representative Azure API workload.

AI.tldr: CloudWeaver is a systems substrate that provides safe, concurrent coordination for autonomous cloud management agents, offering scoped resource views and conflict resolution with safety guarantees, validated on Azure APIs.
AI.motivation: Current agentic cloud management lacks a foundational systems layer to safely and effectively coordinate operations across multiple agents and between agents and human operators, risking conflicts and unsafe operations on shared cloud resources.
AI.method: CloudWeaver introduces two key mechanisms: (1) local resource views that scope each agent session's context, and (2) a coordination layer for concurrent management operations on shared resources, providing safety guarantees and attributable feedback when conflicting intents arise while preserving concurrency for independent operations.
AI.result: The system was validated using a representative Azure API workload, demonstrating its ability to handle concurrent agent operations safely.
AI.conclusion: A systems foundation like CloudWeaver is essential for enabling safe, effective autonomous cloud management, bridging existing cloud-user interfaces with future agent-native interfaces.

title: Latent Stability Analysis of Malware Representations Under Feature-Space Perturbations
summary: Static malware detectors are commonly evaluated using clean-sample metrics such as accuracy, F1, ROC AUC, and PR AUC. However, these metrics provide limited insight into how learned malware representations behave when feature vectors are perturbed, how close samples move toward uncertain decision regions, or whether compressed representations preserve security-relevant structure. This paper presents a latent-stability analysis pipeline for malware perturbation assessment in EMBER feature space. The pipeline compares full EMBER features, PCA-based compression, beta/denoising variational autoencoder representations, Mandelbrot-inspired escape-time descriptors, and a PINN-style latent-flow module. We define Latent Escape Divergence (LED) to measure changes in escape-time profiles under perturbation, and use PINNFlow-derived residual, velocity, risk, and gradient-shift metrics to characterize latent movement. Experiments are conducted on EMBER static PE feature vectors using 180,000 training samples, 180,000 test samples, and 240,000 holdout samples. Full EMBER features achieve the strongest clean classification performance with ROC AUC of 0.9962 and F1 of 0.9713, while PCA-64 is the strongest compressed baseline with ROC AUC of 0.9846 and F1 of 0.9347. The proposed VAE+Mandelbrot+PINNFlow representation does not outperform these baselines for clean classification, but it provides additional diagnostic value under controlled feature-space perturbation probes.

AI.tldr: Standard malware detection metrics (accuracy, F1, AUC) fail to reveal how learned representations behave under perturbation. This paper introduces a latent-stability analysis pipeline using VAE, Mandelbrot-inspired escape-time descriptors, and PINN-style latent-flow to assess representation robustness in EMBER feature space, defining a novel Latent Escape Divergence (LED) metric.
AI.motivation: Existing static malware detector evaluation relies on clean-sample metrics (ROC AUC, F1, PR AUC) that do not capture how learned representations respond to perturbations, drift toward decision boundaries, or retain security-relevant structure after compression. A diagnostic framework is needed to probe latent-space stability under adversarial or noisy conditions.
AI.method: The authors construct a latent-stability analysis pipeline operating on EMBER static PE features. It compares: (1) full EMBER features, (2) PCA-based compression, (3) beta/denoising variational autoencoder representations, (4) Mandelbrot-inspired escape-time descriptors, and (5) a PINN-style latent-flow module. They define Latent Escape Divergence (LED) to quantify changes in escape-time profiles under perturbation, and derive PINNFlow-based metrics (residual, velocity, risk, gradient-shift) to characterize latent movement. Experiments use 180K training, 180K test, and 240K holdout samples.
AI.result: Full EMBER features yield the best clean classification: ROC AUC 0.9962, F1 0.9713. PCA-64 is the strongest compressed baseline (ROC AUC 0.9846, F1 0.9347). The VAE+Mandelbrot+PINNFlow representation underperforms on clean classification but provides additional diagnostic value under perturbation probes, revealing latent-space stability characteristics invisible to standard metrics.
AI.conclusion: Clean-sample metrics alone are insufficient for evaluating malware detector robustness. The proposed latent-stability pipeline, while not improving classification accuracy, offers meaningful diagnostic insight into representation stability under perturbation — a critical complement to traditional evaluation in security-sensitive ML applications.

title: Learning from 53.6K Real-World Developer Edits of AI-Generated Code
summary: Imperfections in AI-generated code require that software developers modify the generated code manually, or by re-prompting an AI programming assistant. Manual code edits provide more realistic and granular information on editing behavior than Git commits, which only contain final successful code snippets. Yet, due to a lack of high-quality, realistic code editing data, LLMs are mostly trained on publicly available Git data (e.g., commits). To address this gap, we introduce DECODE (Developer Edits of Code Dataset), a dataset of 53.6K real-world in-IDE code edits of AI-generated code in Python, TypeScript, and JavaScript, sourced from 1K+ developers. First, we demonstrate the utility of DECODE for data analysis, obtaining insights on when, why, and how AI-generated code is edited. We find that most edits occur within the first 15 minutes after accepting an AI completion, resulting in the removal of AI completions in 31% of edit trajectories. Second, we use DECODE to benchmark the ability of LLMs to predict code edits. We find that finetuning on DECODE enables open-source 3B models to perform code edit prediction tasks significantly better than frontier LLMs. We then discuss implications of this work, emphasizing the necessity of developer-centric machine learning approaches for future AI programming assistants.

AI.tldr: DECODE is a dataset of 53.6K real-world in-IDE code edits of AI-generated code (Python, TypeScript, JavaScript) from 1K+ developers. It reveals that edits occur mostly within 15 minutes of AI completion acceptance, with 31% of edit trajectories removing the AI completion entirely. Fine-tuning on DECODE enables 3B models to outperform frontier LLMs on code edit prediction, highlighting the need for developer-centric ML approaches in AI programming assistants.
AI.motivation: Current LLM training relies heavily on Git commit data, which only captures final, successful code snapshots and misses the rich, granular, and realistic editing behavior that occurs during development. There is a lack of high-quality, realistic code editing data that reflects how developers actually interact with and modify AI-generated code in their IDE.
AI.method: The authors construct DECODE, a dataset of 53.6K real-world in-IDE code edits of AI-generated code across Python, TypeScript, and JavaScript, collected from over 1,000 developers. They then (1) conduct empirical data analysis to understand when, why, and how developers edit AI-generated code, and (2) benchmark LLMs on code edit prediction using DECODE, comparing open-source models fine-tuned on DECODE against frontier LLMs.
AI.result: Analysis shows most edits happen within 15 minutes of accepting an AI completion, and 31% of edit trajectories result in complete removal of the AI-generated code. For code edit prediction, fine-tuning on DECODE allows open-source 3B-parameter models to significantly outperform much larger frontier LLMs.
AI.conclusion: DECODE fills a critical gap in training data for code editing models.
