summary: Specula is a push-button agentic system that generates high-quality formal specifications for large, complex system code and uses the specifications for highly effective model checking and bug finding. Specula employs large language model (LLM) based coding agents to autonomously develop TLA+ specifications, including invariants that describe correctness properties of the target system and formal models that describe the system implementation with the right level of abstractions. Specula is fully autonomous and thus eliminates the barrier of applying formal methods to real-world system code (as in traditional human-centric approaches). Meanwhile, Specula addresses limitations of LLM-driven techniques like reward hacking and hallucinations through self-evolving loops that iteratively improve specification quality by enabling the agents to deepen their understanding of system code and its behaviors. We have used Specula to check 48 open-source system projects; Specula found 249 bugs including many deep bugs that are hard to find by existing approaches. Specula has been used by several companies and is maintained at https://github.com/specula-org/Specula.

AI.tldr: Specula is an autonomous, LLM-based agentic system that generates TLA+ formal specifications from system code and uses them for model checking, finding 249 bugs across 48 open-source projects through iterative self-improvement loops.
AI.motivation: Applying formal methods to real-world system code is traditionally human-intensive and thus rarely done. LLM-driven approaches offer automation but suffer from reward hacking and hallucinations. Specula aims to bridge this gap by providing a fully autonomous, push-button system that eliminates the adoption barrier while mitigating LLM limitations through self-evolving refinement loops.
AI.method: An agentic architecture where LLM-based coding agents autonomously produce TLA+ specifications — both invariants (correctness properties) and formal models (implementation abstractions). The system employs self-evolving loops that iteratively deepen the agents' understanding of system code and its runtime behaviors, thereby improving specification quality and counteracting reward hacking and hallucinations.
AI.result: Evaluated on 48 open-source system projects, Specula discovered 249 bugs, including many deep bugs that existing approaches struggle to find. The system has also seen industrial adoption by several companies.
AI.conclusion: Specula demonstrates that autonomous, LLM-driven formal specification generation paired with model checking is practical and effective for large, complex systems, achieving significant bug-finding results while overcoming both the human cost of traditional formal methods and the reliability issues of naive LLM application.

title: From Idea to Classroom in Days: Using "Vibe Coding" to Create a Programming Process Visualizer from IDE Activity Logs
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures. Accepted for presentation at the 2026 IEEE Frontiers in Education Conference (FIE 2026)
summary: This paper reports on the rapid development and classroom deployment of a Thonny log visualizer built using AI-assisted ``vibe coding'' to make students' programming processes easily visible to teachers. We developed a web application that analyzes log files generated by Thonny (an IDE for Python) and produces interpretable views of students' programming processes. Teachers can upload a log, a ZIP archive, or a folder containing logs for a group or the course; the system parses all logs, generates results per student, and provides student-by-student navigation for reviewing cases. Each student's view includes an interactive activity timeline, a compact session summary, a code-size graph, a programming-process replay, and more. These views support teacher decision-making by enabling the identification of learning-support situations and flagging sessions for academic-integrity clarification. The tool was initially evaluated using logs from previous courses; a February 2026 pilot in an introductory programming course with 160 participants provided teachers' feedback and informed iterative usability improvements.

AI.tldr: A Thonny log visualizer was rapidly built via AI-assisted "vibe coding" to help teachers see students' programming processes. It parses Thonny IDE logs and provides per-student interactive views (timeline, session summary, code-size graph, replay), aiding in identifying learning-support needs and academic-integrity issues. Piloted with 160 students, teacher feedback drove iterative improvements.
AI.motivation: Teachers lack visibility into students' actual programming processes when using IDEs in introductory programming courses. Thonny generates detailed logs, but raw log data is cumbersome to interpret. There is a need for a tool that transforms these logs into interpretable, actionable visualizations to support teacher decision-making—both for identifying students needing learning support and for flagging potential academic-integrity concerns.
AI.method: The authors developed a web application using AI-assisted "vibe coding" for rapid prototyping. The system accepts Thonny log files (individual logs, ZIP archives, or folders), parses them, and generates per-student visual analytics: an interactive activity timeline, a compact session summary, a code-size graph, and a programming-process replay. Navigation supports student-by-student review. The tool was initially evaluated on historical course logs, then piloted in February 2026 in an introductory programming course with 160 participants, with teacher feedback collected for iterative usability refinement.
AI.result: The tool successfully produced interpretable visualizations from Thonny logs, enabling teachers to distinguish learning-support situations and flag sessions warranting academic-integrity clarification. The February 2026 pilot with 160 students yielded actionable teacher feedback that informed iterative usability improvements to the application.
AI.conclusion: AI-assisted "vibe coding" proved effective for rapidly developing a functional educational analytics tool. The Thonny log visualizer fills a practical gap by making student programming processes transparent to instructors, supporting both pedagogical intervention and academic-integrity monitoring in introductory programming courses.

title: Multiclass Classification without Labels via Posterior Simplex Geometry
summary: In many classification problems, reliable instance-level labels are unavailable. However, it is often possible to construct weakly enriched unlabeled samples: datasets selected by different cuts, sources, populations, or experimental conditions that change latent class proportions without revealing them. Classification without Labels (CWoLa) shows that, in the binary case ($K=2$), a classifier trained to distinguish two impure mixtures with different class proportions can recover an optimal class discriminator without knowing the mixture proportions. We extend this principle to multiclass learning from several unlabeled mixtures ($K>2$), where the learner observes only mixture identity and neither latent class labels nor class-prior matrices. We prove that, for a multiclass mixture model, the Bayes-optimal mixture classifier $g^\star$ maps data points into a $(K-1)$-simplex embedded in mixture-posterior space. The $K$ vertices of this simplex are induced by the latent classes through the unknown mixing matrix. Leveraging this geometry, we propose prior-free procedures that train a standard classifier to distinguish mixture identities and then extract latent class structure using either post-hoc simplex fitting or a bottleneck architecture. Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Galaxy10 DECaLS show that mixture identity alone can recover latent classes and their fractions in the mixture. By narrowing the gap between weakly supervised and fully supervised performance, we provide a mathematically grounded, scalable tool for multiclass discovery in label-scarce domains.

AI.tldr: This paper extends Classification without Labels (CWoLa) from binary to multiclass settings, showing that a classifier trained to distinguish unlabeled mixtures with unknown class proportions can recover optimal latent class structure through geometric properties of the Bayes-optimal mixture classifier.
AI.motivation: In many real-world classification problems, instance-level labels are unavailable, but datasets can be partitioned into mixtures (cuts, sources, populations) that differ in latent class proportions. Prior CWoLa work handled only binary cases; extending to multiclass (K>2) enables broader applicability for label-scarce discovery.
AI.method: The authors prove that the Bayes-optimal mixture classifier maps data to a (K-1)-simplex in mixture-posterior space, with K vertices induced by latent classes through the unknown mixing matrix. They propose two prior-free procedures: (1) post-hoc simplex fitting on the classifier's posterior outputs, and (2) a bottleneck architecture that directly embeds this geometry into the network. No knowledge of mixture proportions or class priors is required.
AI.result: Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Galaxy10 DECaLS demonstrate that mixture identity alone suffices to recover both latent classes and their mixing fractions. The approach narrows the gap between weakly supervised and fully supervised performance.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a mathematically grounded, scalable tool for multiclass discovery in label-scarce domains by leveraging only mixture-level supervision, with theoretical guarantees rooted in the simplex geometry of the Bayes-optimal mixture classifier.

title: From Naive RAG to Deep Agentic Retrieval: An Evolving Context Engineering Pipeline for Regulatory Compliance
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE the 14th International Conference on Smart Energy Grid Engineering (SEGE 2026)
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is the dominant paradigm for applying large language models (LLMs) to enterprise document corpora, yet naive implementations encounter hard limits as corpus scale and query complexity grow. This paper traces the evolution of a production retrieval pipeline at Ontario Power Generation (OPG) for regulatory compliance and rate case analysis under Ontario Energy Board (OEB) reporting requirements. We examine successive stages: naive RAG, hybrid retrieval with re-ranking, agentic function-calling retrieval, and a deep multi-agent architecture with code-based tool synthesis and explicit planning, and identify the failure modes and tradeoffs that motivated each transition. We formalize the mature architecture as Progressive Evidence Acquisition with Cost-Aware Escalation (PEA-CAE): begin with low-cost, high-precision retrieval and escalate to full-document reads only when the expected evidence gain justifies latency and cost. Our findings show that context engineering is a more tractable and economically viable path than domain-specific fine-tuning for large, evolving regulatory corpora. More broadly, the progression toward deep agentic retrieval mirrors classical information retrieval ideas, introducing adaptive query reformulation, progressive document discovery, and hierarchical subagent summarization as practical system primitives. Operational traces further support the search-based nature of modern retrieval systems, where iterative evidence acquisition and adaptive planning increasingly replace single-pass retrieval as the foundation for enterprise-scale question answering.

AI.tldr: This paper traces the evolution of a production RAG pipeline at Ontario Power Generation across four stages (naive RAG → hybrid with re-ranking → agentic function-calling → deep multi-agent with planning), formalizing the mature system as Progressive Evidence Acquisition with Cost-Aware Escalation (PEA-CAE), which argues that context engineering is more practical than fine-tuning for large regulatory corpora.
AI.motivation: Naive RAG implementations encounter hard limits as enterprise document corpora scale and query complexity increase. The authors aim to identify failure modes at each stage of retrieval pipeline maturity and establish practical design principles for cost-effective, high-accuracy retrieval in regulatory compliance settings, particularly under OEB reporting requirements.
AI.method: The paper presents a case-study analysis of four successive retrieval architectures deployed at OPG: (1) naive RAG, (2) hybrid retrieval (sparse + dense) with re-ranking, (3) agentic function-calling retrieval, and (4) a deep multi-agent architecture incorporating code-based tool synthesis and explicit planning. The mature architecture, PEA-CAE, uses cost-aware escalation — starting with low-cost, high-precision retrieval and escalating to full-document reads only when expected evidence gain justifies the added latency and expense.
AI.result: Context engineering emerges as a more tractable and economically viable approach than domain-specific fine-tuning for large, evolving regulatory corpora. The progression toward deep agentic retrieval mirrors classical IR concepts, with adaptive query reformulation, progressive document discovery, and hierarchical subagent summarization proving effective as practical system primitives. Operational traces confirm the search-based nature of modern retrieval systems, where iterative evidence acquisition and adaptive planning increasingly replace single-pass retrieval.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that enterprise-scale question answering over regulatory corpora benefits most from architectural sophistication in retrieval rather than model customization. The PEA-CAE framework — escalating retrieval cost only when evidence gain justifies it — provides a principled design pattern, and the broader trend toward agentic, search-based retrieval represents a convergence with classical IR principles.

title: ProcAgent: An Agentic Framework for Procedural Task Guidance on Edge with Human-in-the-Loop
summary: Procedural tasks such as furniture assembly and home repair impose substantial cognitive demands because users must interpret instructions, track task progress, reason about spatial state, and recover from errors while performing physical actions. Prior multimodal assistants have shown promise for procedural guidance, but most rely on cloud inference and fixed always-on perception, making them poorly suited to privacy-sensitive, latency-critical domestic settings. We present ProcAgent, a fully on-device, agentic, vision-based procedural assistant for real-time adaptive guidances on a single NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. ProcAgent uses a propose-and-verify architecture that combines low-latency continuous perception, a symbolic task graph, on-demand vision-language verification, and an LLM-based interaction agent. The system continuously proposes user progress, invokes expensive visual reasoning only when ambiguity or likely deviation arises, and supports both reactive question answering and proactive intervention with human-in-the- loop confirmation. We evaluate ProcAgent along four dimensions: perception accuracy, reasoning, task-level performance, and user experience. Despite running entirely on-device, the system maintains responsive interaction, resolving text-only queries in approximately 2 seconds and visually grounded queries in approximately 8 seconds. In a user study with 10 participants completing assembly tasks, ProcAgent receives positive ratings for comprehensibility, actionability, and privacy comfort. These results show that adaptive procedural assistance can be achieved entirely on edge hardware without sacrificing usability.

AI.tldr: ProcAgent is a fully on-device procedural assistant running on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin that uses a propose-and-verify architecture to provide real-time adaptive guidance for tasks like furniture assembly. It combines continuous perception, a symbolic task graph, on-demand vision-language verification, and an LLM agent to balance low latency with occasional deep visual reasoning, achieving responsive interaction (~2s for text, ~8s for visual queries) and positive user ratings.
AI.motivation: Procedural tasks impose high cognitive demands (interpreting instructions, tracking progress, spatial reasoning, error recovery). Existing multimodal assistants rely on cloud inference and always-on perception, which are unsuitable for privacy-sensitive, latency-critical domestic environments. There is a need for an on-device solution that preserves privacy while maintaining usability.
AI.method: ProcAgent employs a propose-and-verify architecture with four components: (1) low-latency continuous perception for real-time user progress tracking, (2) a symbolic task graph for structured task representation, (3) on-demand vision-language verification that invokes expensive visual reasoning only when ambiguity or deviation is detected, and (4) an LLM-based interaction agent supporting both reactive Q&A and proactive intervention with human-in-the-loop confirmation. The entire system runs on a single NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin.
AI.result: The system achieves responsive on-device performance: ~2 seconds for text-only queries and ~8 seconds for visually grounded queries. In a user study with 10 participants performing assembly tasks, ProcAgent received positive ratings for comprehensibility, actionability, and privacy comfort.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive procedural assistance with strong usability can be achieved entirely on edge hardware, eliminating cloud dependency without sacrificing interaction quality or user experience.

title: Interpretable Column Annotation with LLM-Symbolized Decision Process Materialization
summary: Column annotation (CA), including column type annotation (CTA) and column property annotation (CPA), aims to identify the meanings of table columns and the semantic relationships among them. Recent CA methods usually use various neural models to learn column representations and directly map them to label categories, thereby (1) sacrificing model interpretability and adaptivity, and (2) overlooking rich label semantics and ultimately limiting accuracy. To address these limitations, we propose SymCA, an LLM-empowered interpretable CA framework that materializes column annotation as a global-to-local symbolic decision process. SymCA consists of two components: (1) global skeleton induction, which constructs a semantic skeleton over the label space, and (2) local substrate evolution, which evolves predictive substrates within the skeleton. Specifically, to exploit label semantics while preserving an interpretable decision process, the global skeleton induction module leverages LLMs to generate candidate hypernym-inspired tree-structured semantic skeletons and employs a Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR)-based consensus strategy to select a robust skeleton against generation variance. Since different internal nodes require different evidence to distinguish among their child nodes, the local substrate evolution module materializes each internal node as an executable and evolvable predictive substrate. Over multiple evolution rounds, each substrate trains an interpretable random forest classifier with the current operator set, leverages the LLM to propose node-specific operator modifications, and uses an exploration-exploitation strategy to prioritize promising substrates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SymCA is accurate, robust, and interpretable, outperforming the strongest baselines by an average of 6.42% in Micro-F1 and 11.03% in Macro-F1.

AI.tldr: SymCA proposes an LLM-empowered interpretable column annotation framework that transforms the task into a global-to-local symbolic decision process, using tree-structured semantic skeletons and evolvable predictive substrates, achieving significant accuracy gains over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing neural CA methods sacrifice model interpretability and adaptivity while overlooking rich label semantics, which limits accuracy. There is a need for an interpretable framework that fully exploits label semantics in column annotation.
AI.method: SymCA has two components: (1) Global skeleton induction uses LLMs to generate hypernym-inspired tree-structured semantic skeletons over the label space, with MBR-based consensus for robustness. (2) Local substrate evolution materializes each internal node as an evolvable predictive substrate, training interpretable random forest classifiers, using LLMs to propose operator modifications, and applying exploration-exploitation to prioritize promising substrates across multiple evolution rounds.
AI.result: SymCA outperforms the strongest baselines by an average of 6.42% in Micro-F1 and 11.03% in Macro-F1, demonstrating accuracy, robustness, and interpretability.
AI.conclusion: SymCA successfully addresses the limitations of existing neural CA methods by materializing column annotation as an interpretable symbolic decision process, leveraging LLMs for both global structure induction and local classifier evolution, and achieving state-of-the-art performance.

title: How Affect Propagates among LLM Agents: Emergent Emotional Contagion in Crowd Simulation
summary:
This paper studies the behavior of language models in a multi-agent crowd simulation, focusing on how affect propagates among agents that perceive and appraise one another. Each agent perceives its neighbors through visual, auditory, and tactile channels, then appraises these perceptions in light of its prompted personality profile, memory, current affective state, and situational context. Appraisal is carried out by an LLM, which updates the agent's internal affective state and selects its outward expression. The architecture contains no hand-authored mechanism for directly transferring affective state between agents; instead, inter-agent influence arises through the perception-appraisal-expression loop. The agent representation draws on the Big Five personality model and Russell's circumplex model of affect. To limit latency, low-level steering and navigation are handled by a conventional crowd simulator operating independently of the LLM-based cognitive layer.
  We evaluate the architecture across five scenario environments spanning alarming, joyful, and neutral situations in different spatial layouts. The results show that the system produces emotional contagion dynamics with spatial, temporal, and personality-dependent structure in sparse, small crowds. Alarm spreads from seeded agents as a traveling front, the mean alarmed fraction settles at a nonzero plateau, and the distribution of prompted personality profiles determines whether an ambiguous alarm ignites panic and whether a provocation is interpreted as anger or fear. We further evaluate the appraisal step through controlled experiments across prompt variants, sampling temperatures, and four model backends, showing that the dynamics are backend-dependent.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent simulation where LLM-driven agents perceive and appraise neighbors through sensory channels, with affective state propagation emerging purely from perception-appraisal-expression loops—no direct emotion transfer. Emotional contagion dynamics exhibit spatial, temporal, and personality-dependent structure, and are backend-dependent.
AI.motivation: To investigate how affect propagates among language-model-based agents in a crowd simulation without any hand-authored direct emotion transfer mechanism, instead relying on emergent contagion through perception, appraisal, and expression loops shaped by personality profiles.
AI.method: Each agent uses visual, auditory, and tactile channels to perceive neighbors; an LLM appraises these perceptions considering the agent's Big Five personality profile, memory, current affective state (Russell's circumplex model), and situational context; outward expression is selected by the LLM. Low-level steering/navigation is offloaded to a conventional crowd simulator. Evaluated across five scenario environments (alarming, joyful, neutral) with varied spatial layouts. Controlled experiments manipulate prompt variants, sampling temperatures, and four model backends.
AI.result: Emotional contagion emerges with spatial, temporal, and personality-dependent structure. Alarm spreads as a traveling front from seeded agents; mean alarmed fraction plateaus at a nonzero level. Personality profile distributions determine whether ambiguous alarms trigger panic and whether provocations are interpreted as anger or fear. Dynamics vary significantly across model backends.
AI.conclusion: LLM-mediated perception-appraisal-expression loops can produce realistic emotional contagion dynamics in sparse, small crowds, with emergent properties shaped by personality distributions and backend model characteristics, demonstrating that affective propagation need not be explicitly programmed.

title: An Attack on High Rate McEliece Cryptosystems Using Generalized Reed Solomon Codes with Weight $2$ Mask
summary: Due to the insecurity of McEliece cryptosystems instantiated with Generalized Reed-Solomon codes, there have been several proposals of McEliece type systems that replace the permutation matrix by a matrix $M$ with larger row and column weight. In many of them, the secret key is still a GRS code. There have been successful attacks on some of those schemes with row and column weight between $1$ and $1 + R$, where $R$ is the rate of the code. The case of weight two and larger has been left open in these works. Subsequently, several authors proposed schemes with weight exactly two and with even higher weight. We provide distinguishers for the public codes appearing in these cryptosystems in the high rate regime. In addition, we give a framework to turn a good enough distinguisher into a key-recovery attack. In the case where the matrix $M$ has row and column weight $2$, we can successfully attack the scheme in the high rate regime using a cube code distinguisher.

AI.tldr: The paper presents distinguishers and key-recovery attacks against McEliece-type cryptosystems using GRS codes with a matrix M of row/column weight ≥2, focusing on the high-rate regime. A cube code distinguisher successfully breaks the weight-2 case.
AI.motivation: Prior attacks on McEliece variants replacing the permutation matrix with a higher-weight matrix M (while still using GRS secret codes) only succeeded for weight between 1 and 1+R. The security of schemes with weight ≥2 remained open, and several proposals subsequently adopted weight exactly 2 or higher. This paper aims to close that gap.
AI.method: The authors construct distinguishers for the public codes in these cryptosystems operating in the high-rate regime. They then provide a general framework that converts a sufficiently effective distinguisher into a full key-recovery attack. For the specific case where M has row and column weight 2, they deploy a cube code distinguisher to mount a successful attack.
AI.result: Distinguishers are provided for public codes when M has weight ≥2 in the high-rate regime. The weight-2 case is successfully attacked using the cube code distinguisher, yielding a complete key-recovery break.
AI.conclusion: McEliece variants using GRS codes with a matrix M of row/column weight 2 are insecure in the high-rate regime. The framework demonstrates that any sufficiently strong distinguisher can be leveraged for key recovery, undermining the security rationale behind these proposed schemes.

title: CodeNib: A Multi-View Data System for Serving Repository Context to Coding Agents
summary:
Coding agents repeatedly search, navigate, and retain context from evolving repositories, but disconnected indexes, language servers, and task-local histories force repeated discovery and obscure lifecycle costs. CodeNib builds reusable lexical, dense, and structural views per repository commit, maps outputs to repository-relative source ranges, maintains selected views across edits, and serves ranked search, symbol navigation, and bounded context through one runtime.
  Across 100 snapshots, we map quality-cost frontiers across the repository-context lifecycle. When outputs match an independent rebuild, graph and vector updates are $8.7\times$ and $25.4\times$ faster at the median. On the static-navigation subset matching normalized live-server locations (63% of 1,000 requests), the median per-request live/static latency ratio is $4.7\times$. Across five models, selected context policies preserve localization with 50--87% fewer trajectory tokens than paired grep/read. Together, these results support multi-view repository-context serving with explicit, operation-specific validity boundaries.

AI.tldr: CodeNib introduces a multi-view repository context system that maintains reusable lexical, dense, and structural indexes per commit, serving ranked search, symbol navigation, and bounded context through a single runtime. It significantly outperforms disconnected approaches in update speed, navigation latency, and token efficiency for coding agents.
AI.motivation: Coding agents waste effort repeatedly rediscovering repository structure because existing tools rely on disconnected indexes, language servers, and task-local histories. This fragmentation obscures lifecycle costs and forces redundant context reconstruction across evolving codebases.
AI.method: CodeNib builds three reusable views per repository commit: lexical (sparse), dense (embedding-based), and structural (AST/symbol). It maps all outputs to repository-relative source ranges, maintains selected views across edits, and serves ranked search, symbol navigation, and bounded context through a unified runtime. Evaluation spans 100 repository snapshots, measuring update speed, navigation latency, and context policy effectiveness across multiple models.
AI.result: Graph and vector updates are 8.7× and 25.4× faster at the median compared to independent rebuilds. On static-navigation matching live-server locations (63% of 1,000 requests), median live/static latency ratio is 4.7×. Selected context policies preserve localization while using 50–87% fewer trajectory tokens than paired grep/read across five models.
AI.conclusion: Multi-view repository-context serving with explicit, operation-specific validity boundaries is both feasible and efficient, enabling coding agents to reuse context rather than repeatedly rediscovering it across evolving repositories.

title: Verification Without Distrust: Reframing User-Side Oversight as Routine Epistemic Governance in Everyday Human-Chatbot Interaction
summary: Research on human-AI interaction has long framed verification of system outputs as a trust-contingent behavior that better-calibrated trust should reduce. We test this assumption in everyday human-chatbot interaction through a mixed-methods survey of 153 frequent chatbot users. Contrary to the canonical prediction, we find no detectable association between trust and verification, with the result robust across sensitivity analyses. Three further user-side practices - refinement, correction, and approval before automated actions - are widely endorsed and positively associated with satisfaction. The data reveal a substantive distinction between evaluative oversight (trust-decoupled, weakly tied to satisfaction) and interventionist oversight (weakly trust-correlated, strongly tied to satisfaction). A medium-to-large satisfaction-control gap shows that effective task outcomes do not produce a felt sense of agency. Qualitative findings identify instrumental mental models, failure-mode-specific doubt, and demand for epistemic infrastructure. We reframe user-side oversight as routine epistemic governance compatible with trust, and derive four design directions for scaffolded oversight in conversational AI.

AI.tldr: Contrary to canonical HCI assumptions, a survey of 153 frequent chatbot users finds no association between trust and output verification. Users instead engage in refinement, correction, and pre-action approval—practices positively linked to satisfaction. The study reframes user oversight as "routine epistemic governance" compatible with trust, distinguishing evaluative from interventionist oversight and deriving four design implications.
AI.motivation: Prior human-AI interaction research frames verification as a trust-contingent behavior—i.e., better-calibrated trust should reduce the need for verification. The authors challenge this assumption, questioning whether verification in everyday chatbot use is actually trust-driven or something else entirely.
AI.method: Mixed-methods survey of N=153 frequent chatbot users. Quantitative analyses (association tests between trust and verification, sensitivity analyses) combined with qualitative thematic coding of open-ended responses.
AI.result: (1) No detectable association between trust and verification, robust across sensitivity analyses. (2) Three user practices—refinement, correction, and pre-automation approval—are widely endorsed and positively associated with satisfaction. (3) A clear distinction emerges: evaluative oversight (trust-decoupled, weakly satisfaction-tied) vs. interventionist oversight (weakly trust-correlated, strongly satisfaction-tied). (4) A satisfaction-control gap: effective task outcomes do not yield felt agency. (5) Qualitative themes: instrumental mental models, failure-mode-specific doubt, and demand for epistemic infrastructure.
AI.conclusion: User-side oversight should be reframed not as a trust deficit to eliminate but as routine epistemic governance. This implies designing for scaffolded oversight, including epistemic infrastructure that supports refinement, correction, and approval workflows in conversational AI.

title: Stable FP4 Training via Transposition-Invariant Block Quantization
summary: Reducing training precision is a key lever for improving the e ciency of large language model (LLM) training, but pushing beyond FP8 to 4-bit oating point (FP4) remains challenging due to instability during optimization. We identify a fundamental source of this instability in existing microscaling approaches: scale inconsistency induced by tensor transposition. In conventional 1D block quantization, forward and backward passes assign di erent scaling factors to the same values after transposition, leading to biased and unstable gradient updates. To address this issue, we propose a low-precision training framework based on 2D block FP4 quantization, which enforces transposition-invariant scaling and preserves consistency between forward and backward computations. We further combine this with truncation-free scaling and stochastic rounding to control quantization error and maintain unbiased gradients. To handle the sensitivity of attention mechanisms, we adopt MXFP8 quantization for query and key projections, yielding a practical mixed-precision design. We evaluate our method on dense LLMs up to 7B parameters and a 30B Mixture-of-Experts model, trained on up to 100B tokens. Across all settings, our approach achieves stable end-to-end FP4 training and closely matches BF16 performance, with less than 1.3% degradation in perplexity and downstream accuracy. These results demonstrate that enforcing forwardbackward scaling consistency is su cient to enable practical FP4 training at scale, providing a simple and e ective pathway toward more e cient LLM training.

AI.tldr: Identifies scale inconsistency from tensor transposition as the root cause of FP4 training instability in LLMs, and proposes 2D block quantization with transposition-invariant scaling to enable stable 4-bit training that matches BF16 performance within 1.3% degradation.
AI.motivation: Reducing training precision below FP8 (to FP4) promises significant efficiency gains for LLM training, but existing microscaling approaches suffer from optimization instability. The authors diagnose that conventional 1D block quantization causes scale inconsistency when tensors are transposed between forward and backward passes — the same values receive different scaling factors, producing biased gradients that destabilize training.
AI.method: The paper proposes a low-precision training framework built on 2D block FP4 quantization that enforces transposition-invariant scaling, ensuring forward and backward passes apply consistent scaling factors. This is combined with truncation-free scaling and stochastic rounding to control quantization error and preserve unbiased gradients. For attention mechanisms (query/key projections), MXFP8 is used as a mixed-precision fallback due to their higher sensitivity.
AI.result: Evaluated on dense LLMs up to 7B parameters and a 30B Mixture-of-Experts model, trained on up to 100B tokens. The method achieves stable end-to-end FP4 training with less than 1.3% degradation in perplexity and downstream accuracy compared to BF16 baselines across all settings.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing forward-backward scaling consistency via 2D block FP4 quantization is sufficient to enable practical FP4 training at scale, offering a simple and effective path toward more efficient LLM training.

title: AI-Assisted Knowledge Access for Legacy Enterprise Asset Management in Energy Operations: A Practical Retrieval System
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE the 14th International Conference on Smart Energy Grid Engineering (SEGE 2026)
summary: Energy utilities still run engineering work management, engineering procurement, and inventory processes on long-lived enterprise asset management platforms. Replacing these platforms is often cost prohibitive and operationally disruptive, so practical improvement layers are required. This paper presents a retrieval assistant that improves day-to-day knowledge access across three operational modes: vendor documentation question answering, operational data store (ODS) schema question answering, and user interface usage and how-to question answering. The runtime method combines intent understanding, query rewriting, hybrid semantic and vector retrieval, context engineering under token limits, grounded answer generation, and deterministic hyperlink conversion for panel identifiers and cited documentation. The data preparation pipeline emphasizes semantic enrichment as the primary quality lever by adding table and field descriptions, normalizing acronyms across sources, and indexing representative row-level context when useful. A measured pilot shows consistent gains in retrieval quality and user outcomes. Precision at five improved from 0.56 to 0.72, mean reciprocal rank from 0.43 to 0.58, and normalized discounted cumulative gain (nDCG) at five from 0.51 to 0.66. Median task completion time dropped from 14.2 to 8.3 minutes, while usefulness and confidence both increased to 4.0 on a five-point scale. Results are based on a small sample and are reported as pilot findings, but they indicate that intent understanding and semantic enrichment can deliver meaningful operational value in legacy environments while also establishing reusable foundations for future analytics and automation tools.

AI.tldr: A retrieval assistant is proposed to enhance knowledge access on legacy enterprise asset management platforms used by energy utilities, demonstrating significant improvements in retrieval quality and user efficiency through intent understanding and semantic enrichment.
AI.motivation: Energy utilities rely on aging enterprise asset management systems where full replacement is cost-prohibitive and disruptive. A practical, non-invasive improvement layer is needed to enhance day-to-day knowledge access without replacing the underlying platforms.
AI.method: A retrieval assistant with three operational modes: vendor documentation QA, ODS schema QA, and UI how-to QA. The runtime combines intent understanding, query rewriting, hybrid semantic and vector retrieval, context engineering under token limits, grounded answer generation, and deterministic hyperlink conversion. The data preparation pipeline uses semantic enrichment (adding table/field descriptions, acronym normalization, row-level context indexing) as the core quality lever.
AI.result: In a pilot evaluation, Precision@5 rose from 0.56→0.72, MRR from 0.43→0.58, nDCG@5 from 0.51→0.66. Median task completion time dropped from 14.2→8.3 minutes. Usefulness and confidence scores both reached 4.0/5.0. Results are from a small sample and reported as pilot findings.
AI.conclusion: Intent understanding and semantic enrichment deliver meaningful operational value in legacy environments while establishing reusable foundations for future analytics and automation, though results require validation at larger scale.

title: RoCo-ACE: Rollout-Conditioned Online Distillation for Retention-Aware Knowledge Injection
summary: Knowledge injection updates pretrained MLLMs with new factual or domain-specific knowledge, but fitting full authoritative answers can cause drift in non-updated behavior. Online distillation mitigates this drift by training on model-generated rollouts, yet uniform reference-conditioned distillation provides coarse supervision: it can under-emphasize reference-supported rollout tokens and supervise omitted facts only indirectly. We introduce RoCo-ACE, a rollout-conditioned online distillation objective for knowledge injection. RoCo uses same-rollout reference-free/reference-conditioned likelihood contrast to reallocate additional distillation weight to reference-supported rollout tokens, while ACE adds sparse reference-side anchored correction for authoritative anchors omitted from the rollout without full-answer imitation. Across three knowledge-injection settings, six retention benchmarks, multiple baselines, and multiple base models, RoCo-ACE achieves the best injected-knowledge accuracy among compared methods while keeping evaluated retention close to the base model.

AI.tldr: RoCo-ACE introduces a rollout-conditioned online distillation objective for knowledge injection into MLLMs. It combines reference-supported token reweighting (RoCo) with sparse anchored correction for omitted facts (ACE), achieving superior injected-knowledge accuracy while preserving retention across multiple benchmarks and base models.
AI.motivation: Knowledge injection into pretrained MLLMs via full-answer imitation causes behavioral drift. Online distillation with model-generated rollouts mitigates drift, but uniform reference-conditioned distillation is too coarse: it under-emphasizes reference-supported tokens and only indirectly supervises omitted facts. A finer-grained objective is needed to target specific token-level supervision gaps.
AI.method: RoCo-ACE has two components: (1) RoCo (Rollout-Conditioned Contrast) uses same-rollout reference-free versus reference-conditioned likelihood contrast to reallocate higher distillation weight to reference-supported rollout tokens; (2) ACE (Anchored Correction with Entailment) adds sparse, reference-side anchored correction targeting authoritative anchors that are omitted from the rollout, without resorting to full-answer imitation.
AI.result: Across three knowledge-injection settings, six retention benchmarks, multiple baselines, and multiple base models, RoCo-ACE achieves the best injected-knowledge accuracy among all compared methods while maintaining retention performance close to the original base model.
AI.conclusion: RoCo-ACE provides a more precise online distillation signal for knowledge injection by token-level reweighting and sparse correction of omitted facts. It successfully balances the trade-off between injecting new knowledge and preserving existing model behavior.

title: VisualPatchWorld: Code World Models as Latent Structured Representations for Planning
summary: Different research lines use the term world model in different ways, yet they share a common aim: to capture how the world evolves under action in a form that supports perception, simulation, and planning. Two prominent realizations are neural predictors that learn dynamics in continuous vector spaces, and hand-built physics engines that expose explicit state and physical laws. Neural predictors scale from data but leave the form of the dynamics implicit; physics engines are inspectable and editable but difficult to construct at scale. We introduce VisualPatchWorld (VPW), which represents world dynamics as code. VPW first selects a qualitative dynamical form with short active probes, then fits that form's free parameters from recorded state-action traces by minimizing multi-step prediction error. The resulting programs can be rolled forward like a simulator, inspected in source form, and used inside model-predictive control; image-derived scene graphs can supply the live state at replan time. Across comparisons with prior code-based world models, VPW attains 69.0% mean planning success and exceeds the strongest code baseline by 23.5 points. The largest gains arise when choosing the correct qualitative dynamics is essential. Under the same planner, the induced models approach ground-truth engine success on navigation and grasp-rich control; a residual gap remains for contact-rich pushing, and checking a shortlist of promising plans in the engine closes most of that gap. These results establish a practical route toward automatically constructed code world models that are useful for planning. Code is available at https://github.com/HKBU-KnowComp/VisualPatchWorld/.

AI.tldr: VisualPatchWorld (VPW) introduces code-based world models that represent dynamics as executable programs. It probes the environment to select qualitative dynamics, fits parameters from state-action traces, and uses the resulting code for simulation and model-predictive control. VPW achieves 69.0% planning success, outperforming prior code-based world models by 23.5 points.
AI.motivation: Existing world models fall into two camps: neural predictors that learn implicit dynamics from data but lack inspectability, and hand-built physics engines that are explicit and editable but hard to scale. The authors seek a middle ground — automatically constructed, inspectable, code-based world models that support planning while scaling from data.
AI.method: VPW operates in two stages: (1) it uses short active probes to select a qualitative dynamical form (e.g., the correct equation structure), and (2) it fits the free parameters of that form by minimizing multi-step prediction error on recorded state-action traces. The resulting programs are executable simulators that can be rolled forward, inspected as source code, and integrated into model-predictive control with image-derived scene graphs providing live state at replan time.
AI.result: VPW attains 69.0% mean planning success, exceeding the strongest code-based baseline by 23.5 points. Gains are largest when selecting the correct qualitative dynamics is critical. Under the same planner, VPW-induced models approach ground-truth engine success on navigation and grasp-rich control tasks. A residual gap remains for contact-rich pushing, but checking a shortlist of promising plans against a ground-truth engine closes most of that gap.
AI.conclusion: VPW establishes a practical route toward automatically constructed, code-based world models that are useful for planning. The approach combines the scalability of learned models with the inspectability and editability of symbolic physics engines, with the main remaining challenge being contact-rich dynamics.

title: KQFuzz: Knowledge-Guided Fuzzing for Quantum Libraries via Large Language Models
comment: Accepted to the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering. 17 pages, 9 figures. Comments are welcome
summary: As quantum computing continually improves, ensuring the reliability and correctness of quantum libraries has become increasingly critical. To this end, many LLM-based fuzzing approaches towards quantum libraries have been proposed to uncover potential bugs. However, these methods still suffer from limitations such as insufficient flexibility and low efficiency, which hinder the progress of the quantum computing field. To address these challenges, we propose KQFuzz, a novel knowledge-guided fuzzer for quantum libraries. It leverages comprehensive codebase knowledge to ground LLM-based test generation, synergizing this with fitness-guided evaluation and two-level mutations to explore complex execution paths and trigger potential bugs. Firstly, KQFuzz introduces a novel prompting scheme tailored to quantum programs, which strategically incorporates knowledge of the codebase to efficiently generate high-quality quantum seed programs. Moreover, we develop evaluation and mutation strategies to handle the generated seed programs, facilitating efficient fuzzing execution while further enriching the diversity of the resulting test cases. We implement KQFuzz and conduct fuzzing on three popular quantum libraries, including Qiskit, PennyLane, and Cirq. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, with coverage improved by up to 18.44%. During the development of KQFuzz, we discovered 13 bugs, all of which have been confirmed and 12 have already been fixed by the developers.

AI.tldr: KQFuzz is a knowledge-guided fuzzer for quantum libraries that combines LLM-based test generation with codebase knowledge, fitness-guided evaluation, and two-level mutations. It outperforms existing methods with up to 18.44% coverage improvement and found 13 confirmed bugs across Qiskit, PennyLane, and Cirq.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based fuzzing approaches for quantum libraries suffer from insufficient flexibility and low efficiency, limiting progress in ensuring quantum computing reliability. A more effective fuzzing method is needed to uncover bugs in quantum libraries.
AI.method: KQFuzz employs three key components: (1) a novel prompting scheme that incorporates comprehensive codebase knowledge to guide LLM-based generation of high-quality quantum seed programs; (2) fitness-guided evaluation to assess and filter generated test cases; and (3) two-level mutations to explore complex execution paths and enrich test case diversity during fuzzing execution.
AI.result: KQFuzz was evaluated on Qiskit, PennyLane, and Cirq. It achieved up to 18.44% improvement in code coverage over state-of-the-art methods. The approach discovered 13 bugs, all confirmed by developers, with 12 already fixed.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge-guided fuzzing that synergizes LLM-based generation with codebase context, fitness evaluation, and multi-level mutations is highly effective for bug detection in quantum libraries, as demonstrated by significant coverage gains and real-world bug discoveries.

title: MOSAIC-FL, a micro-service based privacy-preserving framework with application to genomics
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Accepted and presented at SECRYPT 2026, 23rd International Conference on Security and Cryptography, Porto, Portugal, 16-18 July 2026. https://secrypt.scitevents.org
summary: Security and privacy are primordial requirements for Federated Learning (FL), especially in fields such as healthcare and genomics where sensitive information has to be analyzed. Our FL framework is designed to address these challenges while proposing a modular, flexible and micro-service architecture. More precisely, it integrates an efficient gRPC communication layer and a Finite State Machine to ensure robust component synchronization and threat detection, while relying on a fault-tolerant secure aggregation protocol using a Threshold variant of the CKKS homomorphic cryptosystem. This allows blind model aggregation by an orchestration server, requiring a minimum of $t$-out-of-$N$ active clients for decryption while minimizing communication overhead thanks to both cryptographic and network protocols. We ensure IND-CPA-D security through noise flooding and mitigate the recent key-recovery attack on synchronized decryptors by renewing the collective key material at every round. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness through diverse use cases, ranging from standard image recognition (EMNIST) to complex genomic classification including breast cancer subtyping on TCGA, evaluating system performance across different threshold values and model scales.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a modular federated learning framework with a micro-service architecture that integrates gRPC communication, a finite state machine for synchronization and threat detection, and a threshold-based CKKS homomorphic encryption scheme for secure, fault-tolerant blind model aggregation requiring t-out-of-N clients for decryption.
AI.motivation: Addressing the critical security and privacy requirements in FL for sensitive domains like healthcare and genomics, where existing approaches lack modularity, fault tolerance, and robust protection against both IND-CPA attacks and recent key-recovery attacks on synchronized decryptors.
AI.method: A modular micro-service FL architecture combining: (1) a gRPC communication layer for efficient networking, (2) a Finite State Machine for component synchronization and threat detection, (3) a fault-tolerant secure aggregation protocol using Threshold CKKS homomorphic encryption enabling blind aggregation with t-out-of-N threshold decryption, (4) noise flooding for IND-CPA-D security, and (5) per-round collective key material renewal to mitigate synchronized decryptor key-recovery attacks.
AI.result: The framework was validated on diverse use cases: standard image recognition (EMNIST) and complex genomic classification including TCGA breast cancer subtyping. System performance was evaluated across varying threshold values and model scales, demonstrating practical effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The proposed FL framework successfully combines modularity, security, and fault tolerance through its micro-service design and threshold CKKS-based aggregation, making it suitable for privacy-sensitive domains while resisting both classical and emerging cryptographic attacks.

title: Repositories, Contributors, and Continuity: An Empirical Study of Foundational Quantum Software
summary: Driven by contributions from academia, industry, and open-source communities, the quantum software ecosystem is rapidly growing. Across this ecosystem, new concepts often emerge through software artefacts accompanying scientific publications as well as through sustained development in larger communities. However, many repositories receive development efforts only over a limited period of time, raising the question whether their concepts persist beyond individual repositories. In this paper, we apply established empirical software engineering techniques to analyse a set of foundational quantum software repositories. We combine cross-repository activity with contributor relationships to study the evolution of communities. Our analysis provides empirical evidence of contributor migration patterns and indications of cross-project knowledge transfer. We observe multiple development paths: projects may evolve into sustained communities, contributors may integrate concepts into established ecosystems, or activity may continue through new and follow-up software artefacts. Our observations provide an initial empirical perspective on how concepts and influence persist across repository boundaries in quantum software ecosystems.

AI.tldr: This paper applies empirical software engineering methods to analyze the evolution of quantum software repositories, examining how concepts, contributor communities, and development activity persist across repository boundaries. It identifies three distinct development paths: sustained community evolution, integration into established ecosystems, and continuation through new follow-up artefacts.
AI.motivation: The quantum software ecosystem is growing rapidly, but many repositories receive development effort only temporarily. The authors are motivated by the question of whether novel concepts introduced through software artefacts persist beyond the lifespan of individual repositories, especially given the fragmented and fast-moving nature of quantum computing research.
AI.method: The authors apply established empirical software engineering techniques, combining cross-repository activity analysis with contributor relationship mapping. They trace contributor migration patterns and examine cross-project knowledge transfer through a selected set of foundational quantum software repositories.
AI.result: The analysis reveals empirical evidence of contributor migration across repositories and indications of cross-project knowledge transfer. Three development paths are observed: (1) projects evolving into sustained communities, (2) contributors integrating concepts into established ecosystems, and (3) activity continuing through new, follow-up software artefacts.
AI.conclusion: Concepts and influence in the quantum software ecosystem persist across repository boundaries through multiple mechanisms. This work provides an initial empirical foundation for understanding how knowledge and community structures evolve in the quantum software domain, despite the transient nature of many individual repositories.

title: Empathy and the Human-Moment Gaps of AI Chatbots: Insights from Empathy Displacement Theory
comment: BRAIN. Broad Research in Artificial Intelligence and Neuroscience, 2025
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly deployed in domains where empathy is essential, including healthcare, education, and customer service. However, their capacity to sustain authentic human moments remains structurally limited. This paper introduces two interlinked conceptual models to explain and address this limitation. First, the Human-Moment Gap Framework (HMGF) identifies three structural empathy deficits in AI-mediated interaction: affective surfaceism (emotional imitation without depth), memory fragmentation (lack of relational continuity), and moral framing mismatch (efficiency prioritised over dignity). Second, the paper develops the Empathy Displacement Theory (EDT), which explains how AI-simulated empathy can progressively substitute, distort, and displace genuine human empathy across individual, relational, and organisational contexts. HMGF serves as the causal foundation of EDT by demonstrating how technical and moral deficiencies in chatbot design may evolve into broader social and institutional consequences. The study is conceptual and exploratory, aiming to develop an integrative theoretical framework rather than provide empirical validation. Together, HMGF and EDT provide a unified framework for understanding AI-mediated empathy, generating testable propositions and implications for the responsible development and governance of empathetic AI systems. The paper concludes that the central challenge of empathetic AI is not whether machines can genuinely care, but how simulated care reshapes human emotional expectations, interpersonal behaviour, and institutional norms.

AI.tldr: This conceptual paper introduces two frameworks — the Human-Moment Gap Framework (HMGF) and Empathy Displacement Theory (EDT) — to explain how AI chatbots structurally fail to sustain authentic empathy and how simulated empathy can progressively displace genuine human empathy across individual, relational, and organizational levels.
AI.motivation: AI chatbots are increasingly deployed in empathy-critical domains (healthcare, education, customer service), yet their capacity for authentic human connection is structurally limited. The paper seeks to provide a theoretical account of these limitations and their broader consequences, moving beyond surface-level critique toward an integrative explanatory framework.
AI.method: This is a conceptual and exploratory study that develops two interlinked theoretical models — HMGF and EDT — through integrative theoretical synthesis. No empirical validation is conducted; the aim is to generate testable propositions and a unified framework for future research.
AI.result: HMGF identifies three structural empathy deficits: affective surfaceism (shallow emotional imitation), memory fragmentation (disrupted relational continuity), and moral framing mismatch (efficiency prioritized over dignity). EDT builds on HMGF to explain how AI-simulated empathy displaces genuine empathy through substitution, distortion, and displacement mechanisms across individual, relational, and organizational contexts.
AI.conclusion: The central challenge of empathetic AI is not whether machines can genuinely care, but how simulated care reshapes human emotional expectations, interpersonal behavior, and institutional norms. The frameworks provide a foundation for responsible development and governance of empathetic AI systems.

title: Generative Distributionally Robust Optimization
summary: Generative models are increasingly adopted in distributionally robust optimization (DRO), but existing approaches trade off model compatibility and adversarial structure: methods that accept arbitrary samplers do not restrict worst-case laws to a generator family, while generator-parameterized adversaries rely on model-specific access such as likelihoods, scores, or training data. We propose Generative Distributionally Robust Optimization (GDRO), a principled framework that accepts any sampleable conditional generator as the nominal model and restricts worst-case laws to a chosen conditional generator family. The key is the sampler-Sinkhorn pairing: samplers represent the conditional laws exactly, while Sinkhorn divergence compares their induced distributions without likelihood access and can be estimated from samples alone. The resulting population problem admits a direct finite-sample approximation and differentiable primal-dual implementation at the active decision context. For Lipschitz losses, the population Sinkhorn radius bounds downstream degradation. Across explicit and implicit generators, our method reduces rare-context inventory regret by 60% and SocialGAN navigation collisions by 50% relative to nominal decisions.

AI.tldr: GDRO introduces a distributionally robust optimization framework that accepts any sampleable conditional generator as the nominal model and restricts worst-case distributions to a generator family, using Sinkhorn divergence as the distributional distance metric to avoid requiring likelihood access.
AI.motivation: Existing DRO methods face a trade-off: sampler-agnostic approaches don't constrain worst-case distributions to a generator family, while generator-parameterized adversaries require model-specific access (likelihoods, scores, training data). A framework is needed that simultaneously supports arbitrary samplers and restricts adversaries to generator families without likelihood access.
AI.method: The proposed GDRO framework pairs samplers (representing conditional laws exactly) with Sinkhorn divergence (comparing induced distributions using only samples, no likelihood needed). This yields a population problem with finite-sample approximation and a differentiable primal-dual implementation at the active decision context. For Lipschitz losses, the population Sinkhorn radius provides downstream degradation bounds.
AI.result: Across experiments with both explicit and implicit generators, GDRO reduces rare-context inventory regret by 60% and cuts SocialGAN navigation collisions by 50% relative to nominal (non-robust) decisions.
AI.conclusion: GDRO successfully bridges the gap between sampler compatibility and adversarial structure in DRO, demonstrating substantial practical improvements in both inventory management and trajectory forecasting tasks.

title: Retrieval, not hallucinations, will be the limiting factor for LLM-based clinical AI tools
summary: Discussions around large language model (LLM) errors in clinical artificial intelligence (AI) generally center around precision errors like hallucinations. This perspective, targeting both clinicians and AI researchers, seeks to shift that discussion to recall errors, particularly in retrieval of patient-level data needed for many clinical AI tools. The perspective outlines types of errors and mitigation strategies, describes research directions in LLMs and retrieval, and provides an overview of retrieval evaluation.

AI.tldr: Shifts the clinical AI discourse from LLM precision errors (hallucinations) to recall errors in patient-level data retrieval, outlining error types, mitigation strategies, research directions, and retrieval evaluation frameworks.
AI.motivation: Current clinical AI discussions overemphasize LLM precision errors (hallucinations) while neglecting recall errors — failures to retrieve relevant patient-level data. Since many clinical AI tools depend on retrieving patient-specific information, inadequate retrieval can undermine clinical decision-making, making recall a critically underexplored problem.
AI.method: This is a perspective/opinion piece rather than an empirical study. The authors conceptually categorize recall error types, propose mitigation strategies, survey research directions at the intersection of LLMs and retrieval, and provide an overview of retrieval evaluation methodologies relevant to clinical AI contexts.
AI.result: The paper delineates recall errors as a distinct and underappreciated class of LLM failure in clinical AI, presents a taxonomy of such errors, and maps out potential mitigation approaches alongside evaluation methods tailored to retrieval performance in healthcare settings.
AI.conclusion: The clinical AI community must broaden its error analysis beyond hallucinations to include recall failures in patient data retrieval, as these pose substantial risks to downstream clinical applications and warrant dedicated research on mitigation and evaluation.

title: RSMeM: Knowledge-Enhanced Memory Evolution for Remote Sensing Agents with Systematic Evaluation
comment: Accepted to ACL 2026 Main. Code: https://github.com/AI9Stars/RSMeM
summary: Geoscience research requires complex analysis and domain expertise, with remote sensing (RS) observations as a key foundation. However, existing RS agents built on general-purpose LLMs remain largely domain-agnostic, resulting in brittle and error-prone workflows. Moreover, these failures are seldom consolidated into a reusable experience for subsequent analyses. To address this issue, we introduce RSMeM, a knowledge-enhanced memory evolution mechanism that bootstraps RS agents with pre-distilled domain knowledge and iteratively integrates online experience for robust multi-step tool execution. RSMeM is composed of two components: (i) Hierarchical Knowledge Grounding, which performs taxonomy-aware retrieval over a hierarchical domain corpus to guide planning and tool selection; and (ii) Failure-Aware Experience Refinement, which distills failure-annotated tool-use traces into reusable constraints for next-round tool execution. By iteratively employing these two processes, RS agents can evolve to absorb task-level domain knowledge and effectively translate it into instance-level execution experience. Extensive experiments on EarthBench demonstrate that RSMeM consistently improves tool-use performance and end-to-end answer across a diverse set of LLM backbones. Notably, RSMeM achieves a 6% accuracy improvement on DeepSeek-V3.2 with less than 1% additional experience tokens, demonstrating the strong knowledge density of our distilled experience. Our code is available at https://github.com/AI9Stars/RSMeM

AI.tldr: RSMeM introduces a knowledge-enhanced memory evolution mechanism for remote sensing (RS) agents that combines hierarchical domain knowledge grounding with failure-aware experience refinement, enabling robust multi-step tool execution and achieving a 6% accuracy gain on DeepSeek-V3.2 with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing RS agents built on general-purpose LLMs are domain-agnostic, leading to brittle, error-prone workflows. Critically, their failures are rarely consolidated into reusable experience for future analyses, limiting continuous improvement.
AI.method: RSMeM consists of two iterative components: (1) Hierarchical Knowledge Grounding — taxonomy-aware retrieval over a hierarchical domain corpus to guide planning and tool selection; (2) Failure-Aware Experience Refinement — distilling failure-annotated tool-use traces into reusable constraints for subsequent tool execution rounds. These processes jointly enable agents to absorb task-level domain knowledge and translate it into instance-level execution experience.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on EarthBench show consistent improvements in both tool-use performance and end-to-end answer accuracy across diverse LLM backbones. RSMeM achieves a 6% accuracy improvement on DeepSeek-V3.2 while using less than 1% additional experience tokens, demonstrating high knowledge density in the distilled experience.
AI.conclusion: RSMeM effectively bootstraps RS agents with pre-distilled domain knowledge and iteratively refines execution through failure-aware experience, providing a compact yet powerful mechanism for robust, evolving remote sensing analysis workflows.

title: Where Steering Signals Come From: Activation Source Selection in Activation Steering
summary: Activation steering controls language models by adding vectors or features to hidden states at inference time, but the upstream source of these steering signals is often treated as a secondary detail. We study this source choice as activation source selection: the combination of source context and activation readout policy used to collect the hidden states from which a steering signal is built. Holding the downstream intervention fixed, we show across three instruction-tuned models and four steering task families that changing only the source activations substantially changes steering success. We further find that effective steering is not explained simply by whether the desired behavior appears in the source text. Instead, strong signals come from execution-boundary states, where the model is about to produce or continue the target behavior. This pre-/post-realization distinction explains why answer-based sources sometimes work: their useful component aligns with execution-boundary directions rather than target appearance alone. Building on this view, we introduce tail subtraction, which removes shared prompt and continuation semantics from boundary states and yields cleaner, more stable steering signals. Overall, our results suggest that steering depends on representations of what the model is about to do, not merely on what has already appeared.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how the choice of source activations (context + readout policy) for building steering vectors significantly impacts steering effectiveness, finding that execution-boundary states—where the model is about to produce target behavior—are most effective, and introduces "tail subtraction" to refine these signals.
AI.motivation: Most activation steering work treats the upstream source of steering signals as an afterthought, focusing instead on the downstream intervention mechanism. The authors argue that source selection is a critical, understudied design choice that can dramatically alter steering outcomes.
AI.method: The authors systematically vary source context and activation readout policies across three instruction-tuned models and four steering task families, holding the downstream intervention method fixed. They analyze which hidden states yield effective steering and introduce "tail subtraction"—removing shared prompt and continuation semantics from boundary states—to produce cleaner steering signals.
AI.result: Source activation choice alone substantially changes steering success. Effective steering is not simply explained by whether desired behavior appears in the source text; instead, execution-boundary states (where the model is about to produce or continue target behavior) provide the strongest signals. Tail subtraction yields cleaner, more stable steering vectors.
AI.conclusion: Steering depends on representations of what the model is about to do—execution-boundary directions—rather than merely on what has already appeared in the text. The pre-/post-realization distinction and tail subtraction offer principled guidance for source selection in activation steering.

title: How to Watermark the RLWE Homomorphic Ciphertexts
summary: In recent years, homomorphic encryption (HE) schemes based on the Ring Learning with Errors (RLWE) problem have rapidly developed and been widely applied to secure computation tasks, including privacy-preserving deep learning inference, privacy-preserving database queries, and related applications. However, most existing HE schemes focus primarily on the feasibility and efficiency of homomorphic computation, often neglecting practical requirements such as copyright protection of ciphertexts, source authentication, and supervision during computation. To address these issues, we propose a watermarking technique for RLWE-based HE ciphertexts. The algebraic structure of RLWE polynomials allows us to embed small noise as watermarking information into the ciphertext polynomials without affecting the plaintext values. However, HE ciphertexts typically undergo multiple homomorphic operations, which can distort or even remove the embedded watermark information. To address this challenge, we propose two practical solutions. The first, ARWMark, is a watermarking scheme based on noise stratification and is robust to homomorphic additive operations. The second scheme, MRWMark, is constructed using the roots of a linear equation and is resilient to both homomorphic additive and multiplicative operations, while supporting zero-bit watermarking. We provide a detailed theoretical analysis, proving that our schemes do not compromise the original security of HE, while ensuring the correctness and robustness of the proposed watermarking techniques. Furthermore, we conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of both watermarking schemes.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes two watermarking schemes (ARWMark and MRWMark) for RLWE-based homomorphic encryption ciphertexts, embedding noise-based watermarks that survive homomorphic operations without compromising security or plaintext correctness.
AI.motivation: Existing RLWE-based HE schemes focus on computation feasibility and efficiency but neglect practical needs like copyright protection, source authentication, and computation supervision. There is a need to embed and preserve watermark information in HE ciphertexts despite the distortions introduced by homomorphic operations.
AI.method: The authors exploit the algebraic structure of RLWE polynomials to embed small noise as watermark information. Two schemes are proposed: ARWMark, which uses noise stratification and is robust to homomorphic additions; and MRWMark, which relies on roots of a linear equation and resists both additive and multiplicative operations while supporting zero-bit watermarking. Theoretical analysis addresses security, correctness, and robustness.
AI.result: Both watermarking schemes preserve the original HE security guarantees, ensure correctness of plaintext values, and demonstrate robustness against homomorphic operations. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of ARWMark and MRWMark.
AI.conclusion: The proposed watermarking techniques successfully address the gap in RLWE-based HE by providing copyright protection, source authentication, and computation supervision without degrading security or correctness, with MRWMark offering broader robustness to both additive and multiplicative homomorphic operations.

title: Input Relation Prompting for Metamorphic Testing on Query-Based Systems
summary: Testing query-based systems (QBSs) presents significant challenges due to the absence of ground truth for validation and the extensive time and effort required for manual testing. This paper addresses these challenges by proposing an approach that assists testers in identifying metamorphic relations (MRs) for metamorphic testing (MT) instead of solely and exhaustively relying on prerequisite domain knowledge. MT is an approach rising in popularity employed to alleviate the oracle problem by applying input transformation rules (MRs) to a program. The proposed approach helps the tester by prompting MRs that describe the relationships between inputs and outputs, enabling fault detection when the expected relationship is not met. Unlike traditional testing approaches, this approach does not rely on pre-defined test cases or concrete ground truth, making it suitable for the testing of real-world QBSs. Furthermore, the proposed approach can be combined with other testing methods such as combinatorial testing and fuzz testing, expanding the possibilities for QBS testing. A conducted case study of a real-world web application demonstrates the applicability and potential of the proposed approach. Overall, this research contributes to advancing the field of metamorphic testing and provides a valuable tool for QBS testers to enhance their testing efficiency.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an approach to assist testers in identifying metamorphic relations (MRs) for metamorphic testing of query-based systems, addressing the oracle problem without requiring ground truth or exhaustive domain knowledge.
AI.motivation: Testing query-based systems is challenging due to the lack of ground truth for validation (the oracle problem) and the high manual effort involved. Traditional approaches depend heavily on prerequisite domain knowledge to define metamorphic relations, which is impractical and inefficient for real-world QBSs.
AI.method: The proposed approach prompts testers with candidate metamorphic relations (MRs) — rules that describe relationships between inputs and outputs — enabling fault detection when expected relationships are violated. It does not rely on pre-defined test cases or concrete ground truth and can be integrated with complementary methods such as combinatorial testing and fuzz testing. A case study on a real-world web application is conducted to evaluate applicability.
AI.result: The case study demonstrates that the proposed approach is applicable and has potential for real-world QBS testing, offering a practical means to identify MRs and detect faults without exhaustive domain expertise.
AI.conclusion: The research advances the field of metamorphic testing by providing a tool that enhances testing efficiency for QBS testers, reducing reliance on domain knowledge and expanding testing possibilities through integration with other techniques.

title: The AI Wave and the Reinvention of Game Discovery: Oversupply, Structural Correction, and Agentic Player-Game Matching
summary:
AI-assisted production has sharply reduced the cost and team size required to ship a video game, producing a supply shock on open marketplaces. Recent estimates put Steam release volume at roughly sixty new titles per day, with median per-title revenue for a large share of releases falling below the platform's own submission fee [1]. This paper asks whether the resulting oversupply constitutes an emerging market crash or a structural correction, and what discovery infrastructure the market will require as a consequence.
