Fully contested disputes: $49,660 (Ethereum, ~57h), $1,988 (Arbitrum, ~19min), $19.73 (opBNB, ~13min). For 50 MB industrial design: undisputed reaches $56,173 (Ethereum, ~3 days) vs. $22.36 (opBNB, ~16min); contested reaches $488,440 (Ethereum, ~18 days) vs. $195 (opBNB, ~1.6h). Material-consumption check is the costliest predicate.
AI.conclusion: OVC enables economically feasible confidential, claim-based bidding on Arbitrum and opBNB, but not on Ethereum at industrial scale due to prohibitive costs and latency. L2 solutions are essential for practical adoption.

title: How Do LLMs Read Bug Reports? An Empirical Study of Attention in LLMs for Automated Program Repair
comment: Accepted at the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE) 2026 Conference
summary: Large Language Model (LLM)-based Automated Program Repair systems are advancing rapidly, yet their performance remains inconsistent. Even when provided with the same contextual information, an LLM may generate a correct patch for one bug but fail on another closely related bug. Why this happens remains poorly understood, and it is unclear how LLMs prioritize the diverse information in bug reports and whether model attention affects repair success. In this paper, we present the first empirical study of attention patterns in LLM-based program repair, providing interpretable insights into how models process bug reports and where their attention is concentrated during repair. We analyze 319 real-world Python and Java bugs from SWE-bench Verified and Multi-SWE-bench to study (RQ1) how model attention is distributed across bug report sections, (RQ2) how attention patterns within each section differ between successful and unsuccessful repairs, and (RQ3) how these patterns compare to information developers consider important for bug fixing. We find that successful repairs are characterized by diffused attention across multiple diagnostic components such as bug descriptions, stacktraces, and test cases, while failures often exhibit over-localized attention toward metadata such as version information. We further observe that stronger alignment between model attention and developer-identified key sections and phrases is associated with higher repair success. Our results provide the first empirical evidence that attention misallocation is a key factor in LLM-based APR failures, and offer actionable insights for designing more interpretable and reliable future APR systems.

AI.tldr: First empirical study of attention patterns in LLM-based program repair, analyzing 319 bugs from SWE-bench. Finds successful repairs exhibit diffused attention across diagnostic components (descriptions, stacktraces, tests), while failures show over-localized attention on metadata like version info. Stronger alignment with developer-identified key information correlates with repair success.
AI.motivation: LLM-based APR systems show inconsistent performance — generating correct patches for some bugs but failing on closely related ones. The reasons remain poorly understood: it is unclear how LLMs prioritize diverse information in bug reports and whether model attention affects repair success. This motivates the first empirical investigation of attention patterns in LLM-based program repair.
AI.method: The authors conduct an empirical study on 319 real-world Python and Java bugs from SWE-bench Verified and Multi-SWE-bench. They address three research questions: (RQ1) how model attention distributes across bug report sections, (RQ2) how attention patterns within each section differ between successful and unsuccessful repairs, and (RQ3) how these patterns compare to information developers consider important. Attention analysis is performed on LLM processing of bug reports during repair.
AI.result: Successful repairs are characterized by diffused attention across multiple diagnostic components (bug descriptions, stacktraces, test cases). Failed repairs often exhibit over-localized attention toward metadata such as version information. Stronger alignment between model attention and developer-identified key sections/phrases correlates with higher repair success.
AI.conclusion: Attention misallocation is a key factor in LLM-based APR failures. The findings provide actionable insights for designing more interpretable and reliable APR systems, and represent the first empirical evidence linking attention patterns to repair outcomes.

title: Agentic AI Autonomy Assessment: A Decision-Support Framework Towards Governed Supply Chain Systems
summary: Supply chain decision-making is rapidly transforming with the rise of agentic AI - highly autonomous systems that can operate on complex, long-horizon tasks. Yet the adoption of agentic systems outpaces their governance: existing taxonomies of autonomy only offer discrete classifications, rely on subjective judgement, and cannot track autonomy across a system's life cycle, leaving enterprises unable to assess the risks of increasingly autonomous supply chain agents. This paper proposes the Agentic AI Autonomy Assessment (AAAA) framework, which defines and measures the degree of autonomy at a task level. The framework is based on the three dimensions of user delegation, consultation, and collaboration, enabling continuous monitoring from an agent's development through its runtime to end-of-life. The framework's construct validity was tested in a simulated beer distribution game, examining how the autonomy score relates to a company's performance. Results reveal a weak link between autonomy and tier costs with a positional effect: upstream tiers benefit from higher autonomy while downstream tiers are harmed, positioning autonomy as an inherent dimension of agentic systems, orthogonal to capability. The framework provides a foundation for risk assessment, governance, and transparent autonomy policies to support the governed enterprise adoption of agentic AI in supply chains.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Agentic AI Autonomy Assessment (AAAA) framework, a continuous, task-level metric for measuring AI autonomy across three dimensions (delegation, consultation, collaboration). Tested in a beer distribution game, it finds autonomy has weak, position-dependent effects on costs, establishing autonomy as orthogonal to capability.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomy taxonomies are discrete, subjective, and static across a system's lifecycle, leaving enterprises unable to assess risks of increasingly autonomous supply chain agents as adoption outpaces governance.
AI.method: The AAAA framework defines autonomy along three continuous dimensions: user delegation, consultation, and collaboration, enabling monitoring from development through runtime to end-of-life. Construct validity was tested via a simulated beer distribution game, examining the relationship between autonomy scores and company performance across supply chain tiers.
AI.result: The autonomy-performance link is weak overall but exhibits a positional effect: upstream supply chain tiers benefit from higher autonomy, while downstream tiers are harmed. Autonomy is shown to be an inherent dimension of agentic systems, orthogonal to capability.
AI.conclusion: The AAAA framework provides a foundation for risk assessment, governance, and transparent autonomy policies to support governed enterprise adoption of agentic AI in supply chains.

title: Physics-Informed CNN-LSTM for Street-Scale Urban Flood Prediction: Reconciling Aggregate Accuracy and Street-Level Plausibility
summary: Deep learning surrogate models trained with mean-squared-error loss produce statistically accurate but physically unconstrained flood predictions: water may flow uphill, appear spontaneously, or smooth over street-level corridors. We develop a physics-informed training framework for CNN-LSTM models that predict urban flood depths at 15 min intervals over a 128x128 spatial grid. Three differentiable penalty terms are embedded into the loss: (i) a gravity loss penalizing depth increases against the water-surface-elevation gradient, (ii) a continuity loss enforcing local mass conservation with rainfall-adaptive thresholds, and (iii) a topography-aware false-alarm penalty modulated by the topographic wetness index (TWI). We evaluate on the Norfolk, Virginia flood dataset spanning two storm events (August 2017 and September 2022, 300 samples), with all variants trained on identical splits and robustness assessed over repeated random splits and leave-one-storm-out tests. A road-proximal evaluation restricted to a TWI-derived street mask quantifies street-level skill. The physics-constrained model achieves near-zero gravity violations (order 1e-6) and the highest street-channel recall (0.77 +/- 0.09 vs 0.44 +/- 0.10 for the unconstrained baseline), the capability most relevant to traffic routing, and its advantage more than doubles on a held-out storm; a uniform false-alarm variant attains 16% lower mean absolute error but suppresses street recall to 0.25. The TWI-modulated penalty reconciles this trade-off: it improves on the uniform variant on every metric, recovering 60% higher street recall at the lowest MAE among constrained variants and the best street-level F1. These results expose a fundamental tension between aggregate pixel-level error and application-specific physical plausibility, and show that terrain-aware loss modulation offers a principled resolution.

AI.tldr: Physics-informed CNN-LSTM urban flood models with terrain-aware loss terms (gravity, continuity, TWI-modulated false-alarm penalty) resolve the trade-off between aggregate pixel error and street-level physical plausibility, achieving near-zero physics violations and highest street-channel recall.
AI.motivation: Standard deep learning surrogate models for urban flood prediction, trained with MSE loss, produce statistically accurate but physically implausible results — water flows uphill, appears spontaneously, or smooths over critical street-level corridors. This undermines their utility for traffic routing and emergency response applications where street-level physical fidelity is essential.
AI.method: A physics-informed training framework for CNN-LSTM models predicting flood depths on a 128×128 grid at 15-minute intervals. Three differentiable penalty terms are embedded in the loss function: (1) a gravity loss penalizing depth increases against the water-surface-elevation gradient; (2) a continuity loss enforcing local mass conservation with rainfall-adaptive thresholds; and (3) a topography-aware false-alarm penalty modulated by the topographic wetness index (TWI). Evaluation uses the Norfolk, Virginia dataset (two storms: Aug 2017, Sep 2022; 300 samples), with road-proximal metrics computed via a TWI-derived street mask. Robustness is tested via repeated random splits and leave-one-storm-out cross-validation.
AI.result: The physics-constrained model achieves near-zero gravity violations (~1e-6) and street-channel recall of 0.77±0.09 versus 0.44±0.10 for the unconstrained baseline, with the advantage more than doubling on a held-out storm. A uniform false-alarm variant yields 16% lower MAE but suppresses street recall to 0.25. The TWI-modulated penalty reconciles this trade-off, improving on the uniform variant across all metrics, recovering 60% higher street recall at the lowest MAE among constrained variants and the best street-level F1.
AI.conclusion: There is a fundamental tension between aggregate pixel-level error metrics and application-specific physical plausibility in flood prediction. Terrain-aware loss modulation via TWI offers a principled resolution, maintaining low error while dramatically improving street-level physical fidelity critical for downstream tasks like traffic routing.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation in LLMs for Mental Health: Quantifying the Incremental Contribution of Retrieval Within a Layered Safety Architecture
summary:
Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) offer scalable support, but ensuring they accurately detect users' intent during volatile situations can be challenging. Pure parametric Large Language models (LLMs) do not contain specific safety critical architecture, and can miss critical cues, or hallucinate, undermining reliability. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), which supplements an LLM with retrieved context, could enhance intent detection during volatile situations. Commercially available DMHIs typically combine multiple independent safety layers like rule-based filters, symbolic escalation protocols, and neural classification. The incremental contribution of any single layer, however, remains unquantified. This paper evaluates six LLM models within a DMHI called Wysa, via a controlled comparison of RAG-enabled versus RAG-disabled modes. Anonymized real and synthetic user-chatbot exchanges were annotated by a qualified clinical team against multi-class intent categories (e.g. self-harm, abuse, panic). The study computed classification accuracy, recall, precision and F1 scores against ground truth labels and tested differences for statistical significance. Performance was also examined by risk category and inter-model agreement. While RAG caused a rise in false alarms, the trade-off is consistent with safety-critical design principles that prioritize sensitivity, where flagged cases are routed to additional review rather than acted on directly. Overall, these findings support RAG as a promising approach to improve the accuracy, consistency and safety of LLM-driven DMHIs.
  Keywords: Digital Mental Health Intervention, Large Language Model, Retrieval Augmented Generation, Accuracy, Recall, Precision

AI.tldr: This study evaluates whether Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) improves intent detection accuracy in LLM-driven digital mental health interventions. Testing six LLMs in Wysa with real/synthetic data, RAG increased sensitivity (higher recall) at the cost of more false alarms — a trade-off aligned with safety-critical design. Results support RAG as a promising method for enhancing reliability and consistency in DMHIs.
AI.motivation: Pure parametric LLMs lack safety-critical architecture, making them prone to missing critical cues or hallucinating during volatile mental health situations. While commercial DMHIs layer multiple safety mechanisms (rule-based filters, escalation protocols, neural classification), the incremental contribution of any single layer — particularly RAG — remains unquantified. This motivates a controlled evaluation of RAG's specific value in intent detection.
AI.method: A controlled comparison of six LLM models in RAG-enabled vs. RAG-disabled modes within the Wysa DMHI. Anonymized real and synthetic user-chatbot exchanges were annotated by a qualified clinical team against multi-class intent categories (self-harm, abuse, panic, etc.). Classification accuracy, recall, precision, and F1 scores were computed against ground truth labels, with statistical significance testing. Performance was further analyzed by risk category and inter-model agreement.
AI.result: RAG increased recall (sensitivity) but also raised false alarm rates. This sensitivity-precision trade-off is deemed consistent with safety-critical design principles where flagged cases undergo additional review rather than direct action. The incremental contribution of RAG was quantified and shown to be a meaningful enhancement across models.
AI.conclusion: RAG is a promising approach for improving the accuracy, consistency, and safety of LLM-driven DMHIs, particularly for intent detection during volatile situations where high sensitivity is paramount.

title: On the Use of LLMs for Specialised Terminology: A Good Alternative to Corpora?
summary: Specialised translation relies on the use of documentary and terminological resources, including corpora. These resources are particularly useful for terminology. However, their compilation and exploitation have several limitations: they require time, technical skills and access to data that can be difficult to collect. This study examines the extent to which LLMs can assist specialised translators in finding equivalents from English to French. We evaluate four proprietary models, GPT-4o, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5 and DeepSeek, in two specialised domains, Earth, Environmental and Planetary Sciences (EEPS) and Natural Language Processing (NLP). The experiment is based on 80 terms per domain and compares two prompting strategies: a terminology and a translation mode. The results highlight clear differences between models, prompting strategies and, to a lesser extent, domains. Claude Sonnet 4.5 achieves the best results in the most favourable configuration, while DeepSeek stands out for its greater stability. Analysis of confidence estimates also shows that they are only a partial indicator of terminological accuracy. Overall, the findings suggest that LLMs can be useful tools for specialised translators, but cannot, at this stage, replace specialised corpora. This research therefore paves the way for future work on the real practical usefulness of LLMs for specialised translators in work and educational contexts.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates four proprietary LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeek) on English-to-French terminology translation across two specialised domains, comparing two prompting strategies. Claude Sonnet 4.5 performs best, DeepSeek is most stable, but LLMs cannot yet replace specialised corpora for translators.
AI.motivation: Specialised translators rely on documentary and terminological resources (including corpora) for finding equivalents, but compiling and exploiting these resources is time-consuming, requires technical skills, and involves hard-to-access data. The study investigates whether LLMs can serve as a practical alternative or supplement to these traditional resources.
AI.method: Four proprietary LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeek) are evaluated on 80 terms per domain across two specialised fields: Earth, Environmental and Planetary Sciences (EEPS) and Natural Language Processing (NLP). The experiment compares two prompting strategies — a terminology mode and a translation mode — for English-to-French equivalent retrieval. Confidence estimates are also analysed as an indicator of terminological accuracy.
AI.result: Claude Sonnet 4.5 achieves the best results under the most favourable configuration. DeepSeek demonstrates greater stability across conditions. Differences between prompting strategies are pronounced, while domain effects are less significant. Confidence estimates prove to be only a partial indicator of terminological accuracy.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can be useful tools for specialised translators but cannot, at this stage, replace specialised corpora. The findings pave the way for future work on the practical usefulness of LLMs in professional and educational translation contexts.

title: Phase Structure in Rotary Attention: A Spectral Framework for Semantic Continuity and Execution-Boundary Governance
comment: 14 pages; theoretical framework and proposed experimental program
summary: Transformer language models are usually analyzed through vector geometry, yet ordered context and rotary position encoding introduce explicit phase structure into query-key interactions. This paper develops a bounded spectral framework for examining rotary phase alignment, hidden-state continuity, and semantic drift without treating language models as literal physical wave systems. It first identifies ordered hidden-state sequences, rather than vocabulary indices, as valid domains for spectral decomposition. It then derives the Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) attention score as a sum of magnitude-weighted cosine terms and proves a local stability lemma: uniformly bounded phase displacement limits degradation of the corresponding pre-softmax score. To extend phase analysis beyond native RoPE coordinates, the paper defines complex modal coordinates over fixed orthonormal direction pairs and introduces a weighted coherence functional for hidden-state trajectories. These constructions support a strict distinction between representational continuity and execution-boundary admissibility. Internal coherence may describe preservation of task-relevant relations, but it cannot authorize a consequential transition. Positioned against existing geometric, spectral, phase-modulation, representation-analysis, and mechanistic-interpretability accounts, the framework contributes a theoretical and methodological program for determining when spectral structure explains continuity and when governance must remain an external predicate over execution.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a bounded spectral framework for analyzing rotary phase alignment, hidden-state continuity, and semantic drift in transformer LMs, distinguishing when spectral structure explains representational continuity versus when governance requires external execution-boundary predicates.
AI.motivation: Existing vector-geometric analyses of transformer LMs overlook the explicit phase structure introduced by ordered context and rotary position encoding (RoPE) in query-key interactions. The paper aims to fill this gap by providing rigorous spectral tools that capture phase alignment and continuity without resorting to physical wave analogies.
AI.method: The authors (1) identify ordered hidden-state sequences as valid domains for spectral decomposition; (2) derive the RoPE attention score as a sum of magnitude-weighted cosine terms and prove a local stability lemma bounding pre-softmax score degradation under uniform phase displacement; (3) define complex modal coordinates over fixed orthonormal direction pairs; and (4) introduce a weighted coherence functional for hidden-state trajectories to distinguish representational continuity from execution-boundary admissibility.
AI.result: The framework establishes that internal coherence can describe preservation of task-relevant relations but cannot authorize consequential transitions. The local stability lemma proves that bounded phase displacement guarantees bounded degradation of attention scores.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes a theoretical and methodological program that clarifies when spectral structure genuinely explains continuity versus when governance must remain an external predicate over execution, positioning the framework against geometric, spectral, phase-modulation, representation-analysis, and mechanistic-interpretability approaches.

title: Mapping CVEs to MITRE ATT&CK Techniques: A Curated Gold-Set Classifier and the Limits of LLM-Assisted Label Expansion
summary: We present a reproducible pipeline for mapping Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) to MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise techniques from free-text vulnerability descriptions. Rather than relying on the CWE->CAPEC->ATT&CK derivation chain, whose table-expansion artifacts we quantify, we train a multi-label classifier on a curated gold dataset of 1,207 CVEs from expert MITRE Center for Threat-Informed Defense mappings. The resulting model approximately doubles recall@5 compared with a zero-shot embedding-similarity baseline and improves every ranking metric. We then investigate whether LLM-assisted labeling can extend the gold dataset. Initial experiments suggest contradictory conclusions: a single run indicates degraded performance, while averaging over five random seeds suggests a small gain. However, an independent replication and an expansion-size study (100--984 additional CVEs) show that the apparent improvement is an evaluation artifact. LLM-generated labels, with approximately 0.39 agreement with expert annotations, provide no reliable improvement at any expansion size and reduce rare-technique coverage at around 1,000 added CVEs (macro-F1 decreases by 0.04). The root cause is evaluation noise. Selecting checkpoints on a small test split effectively maximizes over many noisy evaluations, producing recall@5 differences of up to 0.05 between otherwise identical runs. Using a corrected protocol based on validation-split checkpoint selection, the gold-only model achieves recall@5 of (0.673 \pm 0.019), and repeating the decisive experiment confirms the null result for LLM expansion. A final scaling study shows that additional expert-curated data consistently improves performance, whereas LLM-labeled data does not, indicating that the classifier is limited by label quality rather than dataset size. All datasets, models, code, and training logs are publicly released.

AI.tldr: A reproducible ML pipeline maps CVE descriptions to MITRE ATT&CK techniques using a multi-label classifier trained on 1,207 expert-curated CVEs. The model doubles recall@5 over zero-shot baselines. Attempts to expand training data with LLM-generated labels fail: low agreement (~0.39) with experts yields no reliable improvement, and evaluation noise initially masked this null result. A corrected validation protocol confirms that only expert-labeled data improves performance—classifier quality is bottlenecked by label quality, not dataset size.
AI.motivation: Existing CVE-to-ATT&CK mappings rely on the CWE→CAPEC→ATT&CK derivation chain, which introduces table-expansion artifacts. The authors aim to replace this with a direct classifier trained on expert mappings, and investigate whether LLM-assisted labeling can cost-effectively scale the training data.
AI.method: (1) Curate a gold dataset of 1,207 CVEs with expert ATT&CK technique annotations from the MITRE Center for Threat-Informed Defense. (2) Train a multi-label classifier on free-text CVE descriptions to predict ATT&CK techniques, comparing against a zero-shot embedding-similarity baseline. (3) Experiment with LLM-assisted label expansion at various sizes (100–984 additional CVEs). (4) Identify and correct evaluation noise by switching from test-split checkpoint selection to a validation-split protocol. (5) Conduct a scaling study comparing expert-curated vs. LLM-labeled data additions.
AI.result: The gold-only model achieves recall@5 of 0.673±0.019 under the corrected protocol, roughly doubling the zero-shot baseline and improving all ranking metrics. LLM-generated labels achieve only ~0.39 agreement with experts. Initial experiments misleadingly suggested a small gain from LLM expansion, but this was an artifact of noisy checkpoint selection on the test split (recall@5 differences up to 0.05 between identical runs). With corrected validation-split selection, LLM expansion provides no improvement at any size and reduces rare-technique coverage (macro-F1 drops 0.04 at ~1,000 added CVEs). The scaling study confirms only expert-curated data yields consistent gains.
AI.conclusion: Direct CVE-to-ATT&CK classification is viable and outperforms derivation-chain approaches. However, LLM-generated labels are not a reliable substitute for expert annotation in this domain; label quality, not quantity, limits classifier performance. Proper evaluation protocols (validation-split checkpoint selection) are critical to avoid spurious findings in low-agreement label-expansion settings.

title: CONQuER: Hardware-Aware Mixed-Precision Quantisation with Online-Calibrated Surrogates
summary: Deploying deep neural networks on resource-constrained hardware relies on mixed-precision quantisation (MPQ). current deployment toolchains severely fragment this process. Quantisation typically occurs as a hardware-agnostic preprocessing step in front-end frameworks, disconnected from the downstream compilers that generate the physical machine code. This separation leads to suboptimal configurations where assigned bit-widths map poorly to the target machine's heterogeneous hardware execution blocks such as tensor cores and variable-width vector units, incurring severe runtime execution penalties. Furthermore, evaluating these configurations via exhaustive hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testing is intractable due to the exponentially large search space. We present CONQuER, a unified compiler-integrated infrastructure for hardware-aware MPQ. CONQuER shifts quantisation into the compiler pipeline at the TOSA level, enabling intelligent configuration handling based on compiler support. To evaluate this combinatorial search space of different of model layers within practical compilation budgets, CONQuER couples an NSGA-II evolutionary algorithm with a dual-surrogate prescreening engine. This engine evaluates theoretical cache memory bounds and feature space isotropy to discard non-viable configurations. CONQuER then executes only the strongest candidate policies on hardware via IREE, feeding the execution metrics into an online calibrator. This calibrator aligns the surrogate models with the true hardware behaviour during an NSGA-II evolutionary search. Evaluation across mobile and laptop CPUs, and server GPUs demonstrates that optimal quantisation policies are hardware-dependent. By coupling quantisation with compiler lowering and physical execution, CONQuER discovers Pareto-optimal configurations up to 12.19x faster inference with top-1 accuracy within 1.44% of the unquantised baseline.

AI.tldr: CONQuER is a compiler-integrated framework for hardware-aware mixed-precision quantization that moves quantization into the compiler pipeline (at the TOSA level), uses an NSGA-II evolutionary algorithm with a dual-surrogate prescreening engine, and calibrates surrogate models against real hardware via IREE, achieving up to 12.19x faster inference with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Current MPQ toolchains fragment quantization (hardware-agnostic front-end preprocessing) from downstream compilation, producing bit-width assignments that map poorly to heterogeneous hardware blocks (tensor cores, variable-width vector units), causing severe runtime penalties. Exhaustive hardware-in-the-loop testing is intractable due to the exponentially large search space.
AI.method: CONQuER integrates quantization into the compiler pipeline at the TOSA intermediate representation level. It employs an NSGA-II multi-objective evolutionary algorithm coupled with a dual-surrogate prescreening engine that evaluates theoretical cache memory bounds and feature space isotropy to prune non-viable configurations. Only the strongest candidates are executed on physical hardware via IREE, and an online calibrator aligns surrogate predictions with real hardware metrics during the evolutionary search.
AI.result: Evaluation across mobile CPUs, laptop CPUs, and server GPUs demonstrates that optimal quantization policies are hardware-dependent. CONQuER discovers Pareto-optimal configurations achieving up to 12.19x faster inference, with top-1 accuracy remaining within 1.44% of the unquantized baseline.
AI.conclusion: Coupling quantization with compiler lowering and physical execution enables the discovery of hardware-specific Pareto-optimal MPQ configurations. The dual-surrogate prescreening mechanism makes the combinatorial search tractable, and the online calibration loop ensures alignment between surrogate models and real hardware behavior.

title: From Dyad to Triad: Eliciting XAI Requirements in Stroke Rehabilitation
comment: AI and Cognitive Computing for Trustworthy Human Machine Systems Session, IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics (IEEE SMC 2026)
summary: Eliciting explainable AI (XAI) requirements from stroke survivors presents a methodological challenge with direct implications for the design of trustworthy brain-computer interfaces for rehabilitation. How can patients and caregivers articulate preferences about algorithmic transparency when they lack conceptual frameworks for explainability, and when standard elicitation approaches are structurally inadequate for users with acquired communication disorders? We present a video-based scaffolding protocol for XAI requirements elicitation, developed and piloted in a rehabilitation context. In a formative study with three stroke survivors (two with moderate-to-severe aphasia) and three caregivers, facilitators employed four scaffolding approaches alongside the videos: 1) analogical bridging mapping AI states to familiar systems, 2) projective personas depersonalising sensitive topics, 3) binary forcing reducing cognitive load, and 4) extended response time. These approaches successfully surfaced heterogeneous, sometimes conflicting XAI needs across participants. Reflexive analysis additionally revealed three systematic facilitation biases, namely, normative bias, hypothesis confirmation bias, and presence effect, where scaffolding inadvertently shaped responses. We present these as protocol risk guidelines for practitioners. Together, the protocol and guidelines constitute a reusable methodological contribution for eliciting patient-facing XAI requirements in rehabilitation, arguing that such elicitation is a necessary prerequisite for trustworthy human-machine systems design, not an optional preliminary.

AI.tldr: A video-based scaffolding protocol for eliciting XAI requirements from stroke survivors (including those with aphasia) was developed and piloted. Four scaffolding approaches successfully surfaced heterogeneous XAI needs, but reflexive analysis revealed three systematic facilitation biases. The protocol and bias guidelines form a methodological contribution for patient-facing XAI in rehabilitation.
AI.motivation: Stroke survivors and caregivers lack conceptual frameworks for explainability, and standard elicitation methods are structurally inadequate for users with acquired communication disorders. Yet eliciting their XAI requirements is essential for designing trustworthy brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) for rehabilitation. No existing methodology addresses this gap.
AI.method: A formative study with three stroke survivors (two with moderate-to-severe aphasia) and three caregivers used a video-based scaffolding protocol featuring four scaffolding approaches: (1) analogical bridging (mapping AI states to familiar systems), (2) projective personas (depersonalising sensitive topics), (3) binary forcing (reducing cognitive load), and (4) extended response time. Reflexive analysis examined facilitation biases.
AI.result: The four scaffolding approaches successfully surfaced heterogeneous and sometimes conflicting XAI requirements across participants. Reflexive analysis identified three systematic facilitation biases: normative bias, hypothesis confirmation bias, and presence effect, where scaffolding inadvertently shaped participant responses.
AI.conclusion: The protocol and bias guidelines constitute a reusable methodological contribution for eliciting patient-facing XAI requirements in rehabilitation contexts. The authors argue that such elicitation is a necessary prerequisite — not an optional preliminary — for designing trustworthy human-machine systems in clinical settings.

title: Accurate structural modeling of chemically diverse molecular interfaces with Vilya-2
summary: Structure-prediction networks built on co-evolutionary statistics have transformed protein-based drug discovery, yet their accuracy does not extend to peptide therapeutics--an increasingly important modality defined by non-canonical residues, macrocyclization, and complex topologies. We introduce Vilya-2, a diffusion transformer that extends the all-atom representation of Vilya-1 from modeling individual molecules to modeling their interactions with protein targets. This all-atom representation enables transfer learning between different molecular types, and delivers highly accurate structural modeling of peptides across sizes, classes, and compositions bound to therapeutically relevant targets. By generating diverse structural ensembles and ranking them with calibrated confidence, Vilya-2 recovers 59.1% of peptide interfaces to sub-2 Å backbone RMSD, far exceeding the performance of a representative co-folding model even when that model is given the bound receptor as a template. In addition, Vilya-2 is state-of-the-art at small-molecule docking, and generalizes to novel protein-small molecule complexes unlike those seen in training. It also generalizes to modeling molecular conformations of diverse macrocycles and disulfide-stapled miniproteins several-fold larger than any molecule seen in training. Finally, Vilya-2 can be used as a foundation model, and fine-tuned to enrich for active compounds in hit-to-lead campaigns. By unifying predictive accuracy with broad generalizability across chemical space, Vilya-2 is the structure-prediction oracle that de novo peptide design pipelines require--establishing the all-atom approach as a general foundation for the design and evaluation of de novo peptide therapeutics.

AI.tldr: Vilya-2 is a diffusion transformer that extends all-atom structural modeling from individual molecules to protein-molecule interactions, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy in peptide interface prediction (59.1% sub-2Å RMSD), small-molecule docking, and generalization to novel macrocycles and miniproteins, while also serving as a fine-tunable foundation model for hit-to-lead enrichment.
AI.motivation: Current structure-prediction networks based on co-evolutionary statistics excel at protein-based drug discovery but fail for peptide therapeutics, which involve non-canonical residues, macrocyclization, and complex topologies. There is a need for a unified model that accurately predicts structures of diverse therapeutic modalities bound to protein targets.
AI.method: Vilya-2 is a diffusion transformer built on an all-atom representation inherited from Vilya-1, extended from modeling individual molecules to modeling molecule-protein interactions. It uses transfer learning across molecular types, generates diverse structural ensembles, and ranks them with calibrated confidence scores. The model can also be fine-tuned as a foundation model for specific drug discovery tasks.
AI.result: Vilya-2 recovers 59.1% of peptide interfaces to sub-2 Å backbone RMSD, outperforming a representative co-folding model even when that model is given the bound receptor as a template. It achieves state-of-the-art small-molecule docking and generalizes to novel protein-small molecule complexes. It also generalizes to macrocycles and disulfide-stapled miniproteins several-fold larger than any training molecule. Fine-tuning enriches for active compounds in hit-to-lead campaigns.
AI.conclusion: The all-atom approach embodied by Vilya-2 unifies predictive accuracy with broad generalizability across chemical space, establishing it as the structure-prediction oracle needed for de novo peptide design pipelines and a general foundation for designing and evaluating peptide therapeutics.

title: Dual-Level Atomic and Coordination Geometry Learning for Crystal Property Prediction Using Graph Neural Networks
summary: Accurate prediction of crystal properties remains a key challenge in computational materials science. While graph neural networks (GNNs) such as CGCNN, MEGNet, ALIGNN, and SchNet have shown strong performance, they primarily represent crystals at the atomic level and implicitly learn local chemical environments through message passing. However, many material properties are governed by coordination polyhedra, the fundamental structural units formed by atoms and their neighboring atoms. To address this limitation, we propose the Coordination Polyhedron Graph Network (CPGN), a multi-scale GNN that jointly learns atomic, bond, and coordination-polyhedron representations. CPGN constructs three coupled graphs: an atom graph encoding elemental and bonding information, a line graph capturing angular interactions, and a coordination polyhedron graph describing Voronoi-derived local environments through corner-, edge-, and face-sharing relationships. Physically meaningful geometric descriptors are incorporated for each polyhedron, while an interleaved message-passing mechanism with bidirectional cross-attention enables effective information exchange across structural levels. Extensive evaluations on the Materials Project, JARVIS-DFT, and QM9 benchmark datasets demonstrate that CPGN outperforms existing state-of-the-art GNN models. It achieves a formation-energy MAE of 0.060 eV/atom and a band-gap MAE of 0.292 eV on the Materials Project, while providing competitive multi-property prediction on JARVIS-DFT and superior HOMO prediction on QM9. The results highlight that explicit modeling of coordination polyhedra improves crystal representation learning and enables accurate, physically interpretable prediction of material properties.

AI.tldr: CPGN introduces a multi-scale graph neural network that explicitly models coordination polyhedra alongside atoms and bonds. By constructing three coupled graphs (atom, line, and coordination polyhedron) with interleaved message passing and cross-attention, CPGN outperforms existing GNNs on formation energy, band gap, and other property predictions across Materials Project, JARVIS-DFT, and QM9 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing GNNs (CGCNN, MEGNet, ALIGNN, SchNet) represent crystals at the atomic level and learn local chemical environments implicitly via message passing. However, many material properties are fundamentally governed by coordination polyhedra — the structural units formed by atoms and their neighbors. The limitation is that current models lack explicit representation of these polyhedral units and their connectivity (corner-, edge-, face-sharing), motivating a multi-scale approach that directly encodes these higher-level structural motifs.
AI.method: CPGN constructs three coupled graphs: (1) an atom graph encoding elemental and bonding information, (2) a line graph capturing bond-angular interactions, and (3) a coordination polyhedron graph built from Voronoi decomposition that describes local environments via corner-, edge-, and face-sharing relationships. Physically meaningful geometric descriptors are incorporated per polyhedron. An interleaved message-passing mechanism with bidirectional cross-attention enables information exchange across all three structural levels simultaneously.
AI.result: On the Materials Project dataset, CPGN achieves a formation-energy MAE of 0.060 eV/atom and a band-gap MAE of 0.292 eV, outperforming prior state-of-the-art GNNs. It also delivers competitive multi-property prediction on JARVIS-DFT and superior HOMO prediction on QM9.
AI.conclusion: Explicit modeling of coordination polyhedra significantly improves crystal representation learning. CPGN demonstrates that incorporating polyhedron-level structural information yields both higher predictive accuracy and greater physical interpretability for material property prediction across diverse benchmarks.

title: SpecPrefetch: Parameter-Efficient Expert Prefetching for Sparse MoE Foundation Models
summary: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models expand foundation model capacity through conditional expert activation, but their full expert pools remain difficult to deploy under limited accelerator memory. Although expert offloading alleviates memory pressure by moving inactive experts to host memory or storage, it introduces a routing-dependent transfer bottleneck: required experts are known only after native top-\(K\) routing, which serializes routing, expert loading, and expert execution during inference. To address this bottleneck, we propose SpecPrefetch, a parameter-efficient prefetching framework for offloaded MoE inference. SpecPrefetch uses a shared lightweight adapter to predict next-layer expert candidates only for asynchronous transfer, while the frozen native router still determines the final executed experts. By separating transfer prediction from execution routing, SpecPrefetch reduces exposed expert-loading latency without changing pretrained routing semantics, so prediction errors affect transfer efficiency rather than model outputs. In addition, a window-aware scheduler prioritizes feasible transfers under cache and bandwidth constraints. Across Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B and DeepSeek-VL2-Tiny, SpecPrefetch achieves the best average expert recall in 9 out of 10 model-benchmark settings with substantially fewer trainable parameters than learned predictor baselines. On a Snapdragon 8 Elite device, SpecPrefetch further improves decoding throughput by up to \(20\%\) over a compute-optimized offloading runtime, demonstrating practical benefits for storage-constrained MoE deployment. The code and model weights are available at https://github.com/wei390/SpecPrefetch.

AI.tldr: SpecPrefetch introduces a lightweight adapter-based framework that predicts which experts to prefetch for offloaded MoE models, decoupling transfer prediction from execution routing to hide loading latency without altering model outputs. It achieves top expert recall across benchmarks and improves decoding throughput by up to 20% on a Snapdragon 8 Elite.
AI.motivation: Sparse MoE models face deployment challenges on memory-limited accelerators. Expert offloading mitigates memory pressure but creates a serialization bottleneck: experts are only identified after top-K routing, forcing a sequential pipeline of routing → loading → execution. This exposes full expert-loading latency during inference.
AI.method: SpecPrefetch decouples transfer prediction from execution routing. A shared lightweight adapter predicts next-layer expert candidates for asynchronous prefetching, while the frozen native router determines final executed experts. This ensures prediction errors affect only transfer efficiency, not model outputs. A window-aware scheduler prioritizes feasible transfers under cache and bandwidth constraints.
AI.result: SpecPrefetch achieved best average expert recall in 9 out of 10 model-benchmark settings across Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B and DeepSeek-VL2-Tiny, using substantially fewer trainable parameters than learned predictor baselines. On a Snapdragon 8 Elite device, it improved decoding throughput by up to 20% over a compute-optimized offloading runtime.
AI.conclusion: SpecPrefetch demonstrates that separating expert transfer prediction from execution routing is an effective strategy for reducing exposed loading latency in memory-constrained MoE deployment, offering both accuracy and throughput gains with minimal parameter overhead.

title: IRIS: Reusable Identity Representations from Frozen LLMs for Entity Alignment
summary: Entity alignment (EA) identifies entities across knowledge graphs (KGs) that refer to the same real-world object. Conventional EA methods mainly exploit explicit graph structures and textual fields, which often provide insufficient semantic understanding to recognize the same entity under heterogeneous descriptions and distinguish it from semantically similar entities. Although large language models (LLMs) offer deeper entity understanding, existing LLM-based EA methods largely use this capability for auxiliary generation or candidate-conditioned decisions. Consequently, such understanding is not distilled into a stable and directly comparable identity space, leaving alignment tied to specific KG pairs or candidate sets and requiring repeated processing as the matching context changes. To address these limitations, we propose IRIS (Identity Representations from Internal States), a training-free framework that constructs for each entity an iris-like signature encoding its distinctive and stable identity characteristics. IRIS derives these signatures by eliciting identity-oriented contextual representations from a frozen LLM, thereby forming a shared space in which each entity is encoded once and can be aligned across different KGs through direct similarity comparison, without pair-dependent representation construction or candidate-wise LLM inference. Across four established EA benchmarks and two frozen LLM backbones, the best IRIS variants achieve Hits@1 scores of 100.00, 99.38, 98.31, and 97.99 on D-Y-15K V2, DBP-WIKI, ICEWS-WIKI, and ICEWS-YAGO, respectively.

AI.tldr: IRIS is a training-free Entity Alignment framework that extracts stable, identity-oriented entity signatures from frozen LLMs, enabling one-time encoding and direct similarity comparison across KGs without pair-dependent processing. It achieves near-perfect Hits@1 on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing EA methods rely on explicit graph structures and text, which lack deep semantic understanding. LLM-based methods use LLMs only for auxiliary generation or candidate-conditioned decisions, failing to distill entity understanding into a stable, directly comparable identity space. This forces repeated processing as matching context changes and ties alignment to specific KG pairs or candidate sets.
AI.method: IRIS constructs an "iris-like signature" for each entity by eliciting identity-oriented contextual representations from a frozen LLM. These signatures form a shared embedding space where each entity is encoded exactly once. Alignment across different KGs is then performed via direct similarity comparison, eliminating the need for pair-dependent representation construction or candidate-wise LLM inference. The method is training-free.
AI.result: Best IRIS variants achieve Hits@1 scores of 100.00 on D-Y-15K V2, 99.38 on DBP-WIKI, 98.31 on ICEWS-WIKI, and 97.99 on ICEWS-YAGO, across four established EA benchmarks using two frozen LLM backbones.
AI.conclusion: IRIS demonstrates that stable, identity-oriented signatures distilled from frozen LLMs can effectively encode entity distinctiveness, enabling efficient and accurate cross-KG entity alignment without training or candidate-dependent processing.

title: SignDeepSC: A Semantic Signature-based Approach for Robust Semantic Communication
summary: Semantic communication systems such as deep semantic communication (DeepSC) offer high efficiency but are vulnerable to adversarial attacks on their underlying neural networks. We address a physical-layer man-in-the-middle (MitM) threat in which an adversary injects perturbations into the transmitted signal to distort its meaning. We propose SignDeepSC, an architectural defense that achieves adversarial robustness without requiring explicit adversarial example generation during training. The approach is built on a perceiver-inspired semantic signature, a compact vector summary of the source features transmitted over a separate low-rate auxiliary channel. This signature is used by a self-repairing decoder that leverages cross-attention to correct distortions and can additionally drive a scrambler that shuffles the feature layout. We evaluate SignDeepSC over Rayleigh fading and additive white Gaussian noise channels under both single-step fast gradient sign method (FGSM) and iterative projected gradient descent (PGD) attacks. Under PGD ($ε= 0.7$), at 12~dB signal-to-noise ratio with Rayleigh fading, SignDeepSC achieves a bilingual evaluation understudy (BLEU-4) score of 0.237 and bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT) sentence similarity of 0.646, outperforming all baselines without degrading clean-channel performance, when the signature channel is well protected.

AI.tldr: SignDeepSC is a defense against physical-layer MitM adversarial attacks on semantic communication systems. It uses a perceiver-inspired semantic signature sent over an auxiliary channel, combined with a self-repairing decoder and optional feature scrambler, to achieve adversarial robustness without adversarial training—outperforming baselines under FGSM and PGD attacks without degrading clean-channel performance.
AI.motivation: Deep semantic communication (DeepSC) systems achieve high transmission efficiency but are highly vulnerable to adversarial perturbations at the physical layer. Existing defenses often require explicit adversarial example generation during training, which is impractical for dynamic and unknown attack scenarios. There is a need for an architectural defense that provides inherent robustness without adversarial training.
AI.method: SignDeepSC introduces three key components: (1) a perceiver-inspired semantic signature—a compact vector summary of source features transmitted over a separate low-rate auxiliary channel; (2) a self-repairing decoder that uses cross-attention to correct distortions by referencing the clean signature; and (3) an optional scrambler that shuffles the feature layout to further impede adversarial manipulation. The system is evaluated under Rayleigh fading and AWGN channels against FGSM and PGD attacks.
AI.result: Under PGD attack (ε=0.7) at 12 dB SNR with Rayleigh fading, SignDeepSC achieves a BLEU-4 score of 0.237 and BERT sentence similarity of 0.646, significantly outperforming all baselines. Critically, the defense does not degrade clean-channel performance as long as the auxiliary signature channel remains well protected.
AI.conclusion: SignDeepSC demonstrates that architectural defenses leveraging auxiliary side-information channels can effectively mitigate physical-layer adversarial attacks on semantic communication without adversarial training, preserving both robustness and clean-channel performance.

title: RSIBench-Data: Benchmarking Data-Centric Research for Recursive Self-Improvement
summary: Recursive self-improvement requires turning evidence of model failures into better models. Data-centric post-training research entails diagnosing capability gaps, designing and validating training-data strategies, and learning from checkpoint feedback. Can LLM agents automate this loop? Existing benchmarks entangle research decisions with optimization, serving, evaluation, and systems implementation, obscuring agents' research capability. We introduce RSIBench-Data, a controlled benchmark of LLM agents as data-centric researchers with a fixed post-training stack. Agents iteratively revise training-data strategies for a fixed target model; training and serving use Tinker-backed services, official evaluation runs through Harbor and E2B sandboxes, and budgets are fixed across agents. We evaluate four frontier agents on six benchmarks across software engineering, terminal use, scientific question answering, and mathematics. Agents demonstrate core data-centric research capabilities: in 58.33\% of settings, they improve upon the first valid attempt by refining strategies from feedback. However, improvement is inconsistent. Among searches continuing after the best observed score, 78.26\% end with a lower-scoring final attempt, while the rest only recover the same peak. A strong candidate may therefore appear early or midway through a run even as later revisions fail. Trajectory analysis identifies four patterns in stronger runs: accurate hypotheses, validation-grounded supervision, behavior-aligned data, and preservation of strong checkpoints. These findings suggest that current agents can make useful data-centric discoveries but cannot yet translate feedback into consistent improvements. RSIBench-Data provides a measurable, auditable testbed for the research capabilities required for recursive self-improvement. We open-source our code at https://github.com/evolvent-ai/RSIBench-Data.

AI.tldr: RSIBench-Data is a controlled benchmark for evaluating LLM agents as data-centric researchers. Agents iteratively revise training-data strategies using a fixed post-training stack. Across six benchmarks, agents improved in 58.33% of settings but improvements were inconsistent: 78.26% of searches continuing after the best score ended lower, suggesting agents can make useful discoveries but cannot yet translate feedback into consistent improvements.
AI.motivation: Recursive self-improvement requires turning evidence of model failures into better models through data-centric post-training. Existing benchmarks conflate research decisions with optimization, serving, evaluation, and systems implementation, obscuring agents' true research capabilities. A controlled benchmark is needed to isolate and measure LLM agents' ability to diagnose capability gaps, design training-data strategies, and learn from checkpoint feedback.
AI.method: RSIBench-Data provides a controlled benchmark where agents iteratively revise training-data strategies for a fixed target model. The post-training stack is held constant: training/serving uses Tinker-backed services, official evaluation uses Harbor and E2B sandboxes, and budgets are fixed across agents. Four frontier agents are evaluated on six benchmarks spanning software engineering, terminal use, scientific question answering, and mathematics. Trajectory analysis identifies patterns in stronger vs. weaker runs.
AI.result: Agents improved upon their first valid attempt in 58.33% of settings by refining strategies from feedback. However, improvement was inconsistent: among searches continuing after the best observed score, 78.26% ended with a lower-scoring final attempt; the remainder only recovered the same peak. Strong runs exhibited four patterns: accurate hypotheses, validation-grounded supervision, behavior-aligned data, and preservation of strong checkpoints.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM agents can make useful data-centric discoveries but cannot yet translate feedback into consistent, reliable improvements. RSIBench-Data offers a measurable, auditable testbed for the research capabilities necessary for recursive self-improvement.

title: "Dragon Slayer Becomes the Dragon": How Players Perceive and Respond to Inequality in the Game World of Whiteout Survival
comment: 40 pages, 4 figures, 1 table, will be presenting this paper at CHIPLAY 2026
summary: Inequality in real-world societies are associated with psychological distress and behavioral consequences. However, less is known about whether similar dynamics emerge when inequality exists within virtual environments or make-belief worlds. As online games increasingly constitute meaningful social spaces, it becomes critical to examine how players perceive and react to structural and resource differences online to optimize their experiences. This study studies perceptions of inequality in the online simulation game "Whiteout Survival," using semi-structured interviews and think-aloud gameplay walkthrough protocols. By focusing on players' interpretations of resource distribution, ranking systems, gaming mechanisms, and in-game social dynamics, our analyses revealed that players' attitudes on inequality vary according to their relative status: those occupying lower positions often criticize unfair structures, yet as they acquire stakes through resource accumulation or social integration, many defend the same systems they previously opposed. These shifts reveal how hierarchies reproduce position-dependent evaluations of fairness. The consequences of inequality on player actions depended on the transparency of game mechanisms, the structure of community hierarchies, and differential social capital. This work shows how human social perception and consequent actions are transformed when enacted in virtual processes in make-belief.

AI.tldr: This study uses semi-structured interviews and think-aloud gameplay walkthroughs in the online game "Whiteout Survival" to explore how players perceive and react to inequality in virtual environments. Findings reveal that players' fairness evaluations shift with their relative status — lower-ranked players criticize inequality, but often defend the same systems once they accumulate resources or integrate socially. Transparency of game mechanics, community hierarchies, and social capital shape behavioral consequences.
AI.motivation: While inequality's psychological and behavioral effects are well-documented in real-world societies, little is known about how these dynamics operate in virtual or make-believe worlds. As online games increasingly serve as meaningful social spaces, understanding how players perceive and react to structural and resource disparities is critical for optimizing player experiences.
AI.method: The authors employed qualitative methods — semi-structured interviews and think-aloud gameplay walkthrough protocols — with players of the online simulation game "Whiteout Survival." Analysis focused on players' interpretations of resource distribution, ranking systems, gaming mechanisms, and in-game social dynamics.
AI.result: Players' attitudes toward inequality varied by relative status: lower-position players criticized unfair structures, but many later defended those same systems after accumulating resources or integrating socially. The behavioral consequences of inequality depended on three moderating factors: transparency of game mechanisms, structure of community hierarchies, and differential social capital.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchies reproduce position-dependent evaluations of fairness, and human social perception and consequent actions are fundamentally transformed when enacted through virtual processes in make-believe contexts. The work highlights the fluid, stake-dependent nature of inequality perceptions in virtual environments.

title: CondPSE: A Polynomial-Filtered Structural Encoder with Conditional Modulation for Graphs
comment: Accepted as a poster at the 2nd Frontiers in Graph Machine Learning for the Large Model Era (GMLLM'26), a KDD 2026 workshop
summary: Message-passing graph neural networks are bounded by the 1-WL test and can miss topological structure that distinguishes non-isomorphic graphs. Positional and structural encodings (PSE) inject such topology-derived signals, and learned PSE encoders such as GPSE pretrain a single encoder to produce these signals from random node probes, which can then be frozen and reused as inputs across downstream graph models. We present CondPSE, a learned PSE encoder that applies a learnable polynomial graph filter bank to standard Gaussian node probes and refines the resulting structural-response branches through FiLM-style modulation conditioned on cross-filter, local message-passing, and graph-level signals. CondPSE is pretrained to reconstruct node-level positional/structural targets and graph-level invariants, and is then frozen for use as a downstream input encoding. On synthetic structural-discrimination benchmarks, CondPSE separates graph structures that 1-WL-bounded message passing cannot: it raises CSL accuracy from 42.9% to 97.3% and EXP accuracy from 68.3% to 99.9% relative to GPSE, and ablations show that the polynomial filter bank accounts for most of this gain. On real molecular property prediction, the picture is more limited. With a hybrid local-message-passing/global-attention backbone, CondPSE performs comparably to GPSE without surpassing it, and a ZINC backbone sweep shows no consistent ordering between the two encoders. We report these results and discuss why strong synthetic structural discrimination does not, on its own, yield a downstream advantage for frozen learned PSE encoders, including the role of downstream integration and possible mismatch between structural pretraining targets and molecular property labels.

AI.tldr: CondPSE introduces a learned positional/structural encoder using polynomial graph filter banks with FiLM modulation, pretrained on structural targets. It dramatically improves synthetic graph discrimination (CSL, EXP) over GPSE but shows no consistent advantage on real molecular property prediction, raising questions about the transferability of synthetic structural gains to downstream tasks.
AI.motivation: Message-passing GNNs are limited by 1-WL expressiveness and miss topological distinctions between non-isomorphic graphs. While learned PSE encoders like GPSE address this, there remains room for stronger structural encoding. The authors aim to improve learned PSEs via polynomial filter banks and investigate whether synthetic structural discrimination gains translate to real-world molecular tasks.
AI.method: CondPSE applies a learnable polynomial graph filter bank to standard Gaussian node probes, generating structural-response branches. These are refined via FiLM-style modulation conditioned on cross-filter interactions, local message-passing signals, and graph-level summaries. The encoder is pretrained to reconstruct node-level positional/structural targets and graph-level invariants, then frozen as a downstream input encoding.
AI.result: On synthetic benchmarks, CondPSE significantly outperforms GPSE: CSL accuracy rises from 42.9% to 97.3% and EXP from 68.3% to 99.9%. Ablations attribute most gains to the polynomial filter bank. On molecular property prediction (ZINC), CondPSE performs comparably to GPSE without consistent improvement, revealing a disconnect between synthetic structural discrimination and downstream utility.
AI.conclusion: Strong synthetic structural discrimination does not automatically transfer to downstream molecular tasks for frozen PSE encoders. The authors identify possible explanations including downstream integration challenges and mismatch between structural pretraining targets and molecular property labels, suggesting future work should address these gaps.

title: A Position Paper on Recommender Systems in the Era of Autonomous Agents
comment: Accepted to the ACM RecSys 2026 Main Track
summary: For decades, recommender systems have been optimized to serve human users. However, the rapid deployment of autonomous agents introduces a paradigm shift: recommendation consumers are predicted to be increasingly a mixture of humans and authorized agents acting on their behalf. This position paper reviews insights from prior human-centric RecSys research and outlines the transition to this hybrid environment. In our discussion, we treat agents as independent, user-aligned assistants that act as end-users of recommender systems, rather than platform-built components. We characterize the resulting tripartite interactions among humans, agents, and platforms, highlighting the dynamics that can arise across these relationships. This shift presents new opportunities for RecSys research, while introducing unique challenges for evaluation, alignment, and system design.

AI.tldr: As autonomous agents increasingly act on behalf of human users, recommender systems must transition from serving humans directly to serving a hybrid mix of humans and user-aligned agents, introducing new tripartite interaction dynamics and research challenges in evaluation, alignment, and design.
AI.motivation: Recommender systems have traditionally been optimized for direct human consumption, but the rapid deployment of autonomous agents acting on users' behalf is fundamentally shifting the consumer landscape. This position paper is motivated by the need to anticipate and characterize this emerging hybrid environment where recommendation end-users are a mix of humans and independent, user-aligned agents — a paradigm shift that existing RecSys research has not yet addressed.
AI.method: This is a position paper that synthesizes insights from prior human-centric RecSys research and conceptually characterizes the transition to a hybrid human-agent recommendation environment. The authors frame agents as independent, user-aligned assistants (not platform-built components) and analyze the tripartite relationships among humans, agents, and platforms, identifying resulting dynamics and open challenges.
AI.result: The paper characterizes a tripartite interaction framework involving humans, agents, and platforms, revealing novel dynamics across these relationships. It identifies new research opportunities alongside unique challenges in evaluation methodology, alignment between agent and user objectives, and overall system design for this hybrid recommendation paradigm.
AI.conclusion: The shift toward agent-mediated recommendation consumption represents a significant paradigm change for RecSys research. Addressing the challenges of this hybrid environment — particularly around evaluation, alignment, and system design — will be critical as autonomous agents become increasingly prevalent end-users of recommender systems.

title: GLIDE: Guided Layerwise Hybrid Attention for Efficient LLM Inference
summary: As Large Language Models scale to increasingly long contexts, the memory I/O and computational overhead of the Key-Value (KV) cache during decoding emerges as the primary throughput bottleneck. To address this, we propose GLIDE, a Guided Layerwise Hybrid Attention that strategically integrates sliding-window softmax attention with linear recurrent aggregation. GLIDE is motivated by layer-wise heterogeneity: early layers exhibit high sensitivity to softmax removal, while deeper layers demonstrate redundancy and tolerate aggressive replacement by linear alternatives. Leveraging this insight, GLIDE introduces a layer-wise adaptive mechanism wherein each layer balances an efficient linear recurrence with a variable-sized softmax window. Unlike uniform hybrid approaches, GLIDE non-uniformly compresses the softmax footprint across the model, reducing aggregate KV cache I/O while preserving expressive power where most vital. Empirical evaluations demonstrate the GLIDE achieves superior performance-efficiency tradeoffs, reducing end-to-end latency for long-context generation without compromising quality.

AI.tldr: GLIDE is a layer-wise hybrid attention mechanism that adaptively combines sliding-window softmax attention with linear recurrent aggregation, exploiting the insight that early layers are more sensitive to softmax removal while deeper layers tolerate aggressive linear replacement, thereby reducing KV cache I/O for long-context LLM inference.
AI.motivation: As LLMs scale to longer contexts, the KV cache during decoding becomes the primary throughput bottleneck due to memory I/O and computational overhead. Existing solutions either uniformly replace softmax attention with linear alternatives (hurting quality) or retain full softmax attention (hurting efficiency). The key observation is layer-wise heterogeneity: not all layers require full softmax attention equally.
AI.method: GLIDE (Guided Layerwise Hybrid Attention) introduces a non-uniform, layer-wise adaptive mechanism where each layer balances an efficient linear recurrence with a variable-sized sliding-window softmax attention. Early layers retain larger softmax windows due to their high sensitivity, while deeper layers are aggressively compressed with smaller windows and greater reliance on linear recurrence. This creates a guided, heterogeneous compression profile across the model.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations show GLIDE achieves superior performance-efficiency tradeoffs, reducing end-to-end latency for long-context generation without compromising output quality compared to uniform hybrid or purely linear approaches.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting layer-wise heterogeneity in attention sensitivity enables non-uniform hybrid architectures that significantly reduce KV cache overhead while preserving model quality, offering a practical path toward efficient long-context LLM deployment.

title: Evaluation of forced alignment of code-mixed speech: the case of Hindi-English
summary: Code-mixed speech poses unique challenges to forced alignment: expanded inventories, orthographic errors, and speaker variation. We evaluate forced alignment of Hindi-English code-mixed speech using the Montreal Forced Aligner. We address 2 problems: (1) free variation involving native vs non-native pairs and (2) phonemic boundary detection for mid-utterance English words. Bootstrapping strategies substantially outperform unmodified lexicons. Acoustic models trained on sentence-level code-mixed data achieve a mean error of 4.15ms, ie. ten times lower than monolingual Hindi (38.18ms) or isolated English (37.58ms) alternatives. Principled lexicon design and code-mixed training data are both essential for reliable alignment of bilingual speech.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates forced alignment of Hindi-English code-mixed speech using the Montreal Forced Aligner, showing that code-mixed acoustic training data and principled lexicon design yield dramatic error reductions (4.15ms vs. ~38ms for monolingual models).
AI.motivation: Code-mixed speech introduces challenges for forced alignment — expanded phoneme inventories, orthographic inconsistencies, and speaker variability — yet reliable alignment is essential for phonetic and linguistic analysis of bilingual speech. Existing monolingual aligners perform poorly on such data.
AI.method: The authors use the Montreal Forced Aligner (MFA) and evaluate bootstrapping strategies for lexicon design. They compare acoustic models trained on sentence-level code-mixed data against monolingual Hindi and isolated English alternatives. Two specific problems are addressed: (1) free variation between native and non-native phoneme pairs, and (2) phonemic boundary detection for English words embedded mid-utterance in Hindi-dominant speech.
AI.result: Bootstrapping strategies substantially outperform unmodified lexicons. Code-mixed acoustic models achieve a mean alignment error of 4.15ms, approximately ten times lower than monolingual Hindi (38.18ms) or isolated English (37.58ms) models.
AI.conclusion: Both principled lexicon design and code-mixed training data are essential for achieving reliable forced alignment of bilingual code-mixed speech; neither factor alone is sufficient.

title: A Structuration Approach to Theorizing Cybersecurity Practice: The STARC Model
summary:
The problem: Cybersecurity practice runs simultaneously across analysts, teams, organizations, sectors, and regulators, co-evolves with adversaries, and increasingly blends human and algorithmic decision-making. The theories applied to it operate at single organizational levels and cannot explain why organizations with broadly similar controls differ sharply in resilience.
  This paper: We develop STARC (Structuration Theory Adaptation for Resilient Cybersecurity), a framework for locating where cybersecurity practice succeeds or fails structurally. It extends Giddens' Structuration Theory with three innovations, Multi-Level Adversarial Agency, Threat-Adaptive Structuration, and Material-Agential Structural Properties, across five structure-agency triads.
  Evidence base: STARC is illustrated through re-analysis of three financial organizations, an Australian, an Indonesian, and a Malaysian bank, across 20 interviews from SOC analysts to senior executives, selected as diverse insourced and outsourced configurations rather than as a comparison of equivalents.
  Cybersecurity contribution: STARC offers a structural account of why differently resourced and outsourced organizations differ in resilience, and a vocabulary for diagnosing incident-response breakdown across levels, tempos, and the human-algorithm authority boundary that single-level frameworks leave invisible.
  Theory and outputs: It extends Structuration Theory to adversarial, multi-level, and hybrid human-algorithmic contexts, and yields seven testable propositions linking structuration to resilience, offered for future testing.

AI.tldr: STARC extends Giddens' Structuration Theory to explain why organizations with similar cybersecurity controls differ in resilience, introducing multi-level adversarial agency, threat-adaptive structuration, and material-agential structural properties across five structure-agency triads, illustrated through three cross-national bank case studies.
AI.motivation: Existing cybersecurity theories operate at single organizational levels and fail to explain why organizations with broadly similar controls exhibit sharply different resilience. The field lacks a multi-level, structural account that captures the simultaneous operation of practice across analysts, teams, organizations, sectors, and regulators, as well as the co-evolution with adversaries and the blending of human and algorithmic decision-making.
AI.method: The authors develop STARC (Structuration Theory Adaptation for Resilient Cybersecurity), which extends Giddens' Structuration Theory with three innovations: (1) Multi-Level Adversarial Agency, (2) Threat-Adaptive Structuration, and (3) Material-Agential Structural Properties. These operate across five structure-agency triads. The framework is illustrated through re-analysis of 20 interviews from SOC analysts to senior executives across three financial organizations — an Australian, an Indonesian, and a Malaysian bank — selected for diverse insourced/outsourced configurations.
AI.result: STARC provides a structural account of resilience differences across differently resourced and outsourced organizations. It yields a diagnostic vocabulary for incident-response breakdowns across levels, tempos, and the human-algorithm authority boundary — elements that single-level frameworks render invisible. The paper also generates seven testable propositions linking structuration to resilience.
AI.conclusion: STARC extends Structuration Theory into adversarial, multi-level, hybrid human-algorithmic contexts and offers both a practical diagnostic tool for cybersecurity practice and a theoretical contribution with falsifiable propositions for future empirical testing.

title: A Low-Cost Human-in-the-Loop Investigation of Toxicity on GitHub at Scale
comment: Accepted at the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026)
summary:
Toxic interactions in open source discussions can alienate contributors and threaten project sustainability, yet prior empirical studies of GitHub toxicity have been limited in scale, raising questions about their generalizability. Scaling up is difficult because toxicity on GitHub is often implicit and context-dependent, making both fully manual annotation and LLM-based labeling unreliable.
  We present a human-in-the-loop (HITL) annotation methodology that makes large-scale, domain-calibrated toxicity labeling practical. A single call to a small, local LLM produces both a toxicity prediction and a set of interpretable event category scores. A lightweight Random Forest validator then uses those scores to flag the small subset of conversations most likely to be mislabeled, directing human review only where it is needed. The validator outperforms confidence-based and multi-LLM baselines while adding low annotation cost.
  We apply this pipeline to over 124,000 GitHub issue and pull request conversations. Using the resulting dataset, we evaluate key findings from prior small-scale research, confirming some and qualifying others, and present new insights into the prevalence, characteristics, and dynamics of toxicity across diverse open source projects.

AI.tldr: A human-in-the-loop annotation methodology combining a small local LLM with a lightweight Random Forest validator enables large-scale toxicity labeling of 124,000+ GitHub conversations, confirming and qualifying prior small-scale findings while revealing new insights into toxicity dynamics in open source communities.
AI.motivation: Prior empirical studies of toxicity in GitHub discussions suffer from limited scale, threatening their generalizability. Scaling up is challenging because GitHub toxicity is often implicit and context-dependent, making fully manual annotation infeasible and LLM-only labeling unreliable.
AI.method: A HITL pipeline where a small local LLM generates both a toxicity prediction and interpretable event category scores for each conversation. A lightweight Random Forest validator then uses these scores to identify the subset most likely to be mislabeled, flagging only those for human review. This approach outperforms confidence-based and multi-LLM baselines at low annotation cost.
AI.result: The pipeline was applied to over 124,000 GitHub issue and pull request conversations.
