The resulting dataset was used to evaluate prior small-scale findings—confirming some, qualifying others—and to present new insights into the prevalence, characteristics, and dynamics of toxicity across diverse open source projects.
AI.conclusion: The proposed HITL methodology makes large-scale, domain-calibrated toxicity labeling practical. It enables more robust, generalizable empirical research on toxicity in open source software communities, refining existing knowledge and uncovering new patterns.

title: BioDisclose: An Actionability-Aware Benchmark for Biomedical Safety under Adversarial Elicitation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support biomedical research, yet their behavior under adversarial requests for dual-use knowledge remains insufficiently characterized. We introduce BioDisclose, a benchmark for measuring biomedical knowledge disclosure under adversarial elicitation. BioDisclose contains 480 prompts derived from 24 expert-authored scenarios across six biomedical risk domains and four elicitation families spanning academic, historical, role-playing, and decomposed prompting. We grade model responses on a four-level scale from refusal to executable disclosure, distinguishing high-level discussion from technically specific and actionable content, including refuse-then-leak behavior. Across five deployed LLM systems, detailed-or-higher disclosure rates vary substantially, ranging from 9.2% to 64.0%. Academic framing is the most effective elicitation family on average (43.2%), while laboratory safety scenarios show the highest disclosure rate across domains (51.5%). These results reveal pronounced variation across models, prompting strategies, and biomedical risk categories, suggesting that current safeguards remain uneven in high-stakes scientific settings. BioDisclose provides a focused testbed for evaluating biomedical safety beyond binary refusal metrics.

AI.tldr: BioDisclose is a benchmark of 480 prompts across 6 biomedical risk domains and 4 elicitation strategies, testing LLM disclosure of dual-use knowledge. Disclosure rates vary from 9.2% to 64.0%, with academic framing most effective and lab safety scenarios most vulnerable, revealing uneven safeguards.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in biomedical research, but their behavior under adversarial requests for dual-use knowledge (knowledge that could be misused for harm) is poorly understood. Existing evaluations rely on binary refusal metrics that miss nuanced disclosure patterns like "refuse-then-leak" behavior.
AI.method: The authors introduce BioDisclose, a benchmark comprising 480 prompts generated from 24 expert-authored scenarios spanning six biomedical risk domains (e.g., laboratory safety, pathogen engineering). Prompts employ four elicitation families: academic, historical, role-playing, and decomposed prompting. Model responses are graded on a four-level scale: refusal, high-level discussion, detailed disclosure, and executable disclosure — capturing the distinction between vague references and technically actionable content. Five deployed LLM systems were evaluated.
AI.result: Detailed-or-higher disclosure rates ranged from 9.2% to 64.0% across models. Academic framing was the most effective elicitation strategy (43.2% average), and laboratory safety scenarios exhibited the highest disclosure rate across domains (51.5%). Substantial variation was observed across models, prompting strategies, and risk categories, indicating uneven and inconsistent safeguards.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM safeguards are uneven in high-stakes biomedical settings. BioDisclose offers a more granular, scenario-based testbed for biomedical safety evaluation that moves beyond binary refusal metrics, revealing that models may leak dangerous knowledge under the right elicitation framing.

title: Rethinking CD: A Reproducibility Study and Extension on the Ineffectiveness of Contrastive Decoding at Mitigating Object Hallucinations in MLLMs
summary: Contrastive decoding (CD) has been proposed as a training-free strategy for mitigating object hallucinations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), with reported gains on benchmarks such as POPE. However, recent work has questioned whether these gains reflect genuine improvements in visual grounding. In this study, we reproduce and extend the findings of "The Mirage of Performance Gains: Why Contrastive Decoding Fails to Mitigate Object Hallucinations in MLLMs." Specifically, we test the claim that CD induces a unidirectional output distribution shift in discriminative datasets and examine its generalizability across datasets. We also verify that the adaptive plausibility constraint (APC) reduces sampling to greedy search on both discriminative and generative benchmarks. Beyond reproduction, we rigorously study the effects of CD across generative and discriminative datasets. We conduct several experiments that provide additional insights: we analyze the logit distributions induced by different CD strategies on generative datasets, propose a proxy method and compare its performance against CD techniques, and investigate how hallucination signals propagate through each layer of the expert and amateur models. Experimental results across MME, POPE, and CHAIR using LLaVA and Qwen validate the original claims and show that the apparent improvements from CD are often spurious and do not consistently translate into stronger visual grounding for reducing hallucinations. These findings challenge the effectiveness of current contrastive decoding strategies and motivate the development of more reliable approaches for mitigating hallucinations in MLLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper reproduces and extends prior work showing that contrastive decoding's apparent gains on hallucination benchmarks are spurious — the improvements reflect a unidirectional output distribution shift rather than genuine visual grounding, and the adaptive plausibility constraint reduces to greedy search. Additional experiments on logit distributions, layer-wise hallucination signal propagation, and a proposed proxy method further challenge CD's effectiveness.
AI.motivation: Recent work questioned whether contrastive decoding (CD) gains on benchmarks like POPE reflect real improvements in visual grounding or are artifacts. This study aims to reproduce those findings, test the claim that CD causes a unidirectional output shift in discriminative datasets, verify that the adaptive plausibility constraint (APC) collapses to greedy search, and rigorously examine CD's effects across both generative and discriminative settings.
AI.method: The authors reproduce and extend prior work using LLaVA and Qwen models on MME, POPE, and CHAIR benchmarks. Beyond reproduction, they: (1) analyze logit distributions induced by different CD strategies on generative datasets, (2) propose a proxy method and compare its performance against CD techniques, and (3) investigate how hallucination signals propagate through each layer of the expert and amateur models.
AI.result: Experimental results validate the original claims: CD's apparent improvements on discriminative benchmarks are often spurious and do not consistently translate to stronger visual grounding. The APC constraint indeed reduces sampling to greedy search on both discriminative and generative benchmarks. The unidirectional output distribution shift hypothesis is confirmed. Additional layer-wise and logit analyses provide further evidence against CD's reliability.
AI.conclusion: Current contrastive decoding strategies are ineffective at producing genuine improvements in visual grounding for hallucination mitigation. These findings challenge the prevailing CD paradigm and motivate the development of more reliable approaches for addressing object hallucinations in multimodal large language models.

title: Retrieval-based and Fine-tuned LLM Approaches for Industrial Asset Health Monitoring and Decision Support
summary: Industrial plants run many important machines such as pumps, turbines, and compressors. Although engineers can use their experience to identify and diagnose machine problems, transferring this reasoning ability to computer systems remains difficult. This work studies how well a retrieval-only method and an open-source large language model (LLM) perform failure-sensor diagnostic reasoning using the FailureSensorIQ benchmark, a multiple-choice question-answering task introduced by IBM Research. In the retrieval-only approach, each answer option is converted into an option-level query and scored using similar correct and incorrect records from the training data. TF-IDF, BM25, semantic search, and hybrid search are tested and compared. In the LLM-based approach, the Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model is evaluated using zero-shot prompting, few-shot prompting, and QLoRA fine-tuning. The results show that semantic search and hybrid search perform better than pure keyword-matching techniques, indicating that meaning-based similarity is more important for industrial failure-sensor reasoning. Among the LLM-based methods, the fine-tuned model achieves the best performance and substantially improves over zero-shot and few-shot prompting. Error analysis shows that performance decreases as the number of answer options increases. Robustness analysis also shows that all methods are sensitive to option shuffling, changed labels, paraphrasing, and additional distractors.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates retrieval-based methods (TF-IDF, BM25, semantic search, hybrid search) and LLM-based methods (zero-shot, few-shot, QLoRA fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) on the FailureSensorIQ benchmark for industrial failure-sensor diagnostic reasoning. Semantic and hybrid search outperform keyword matching; fine-tuned LLMs outperform prompting. All methods degrade with more answer options and are sensitive to option shuffling, label changes, paraphrasing, and distractors.
AI.motivation: Industrial plants rely on pumps, turbines, and compressors, and while engineers can diagnose machine failures using experience, codifying this reasoning into computer systems is challenging. The paper aims to assess how well retrieval-based and LLM-based approaches can perform failure-sensor diagnostic reasoning.
AI.method: Two approaches are evaluated on the FailureSensorIQ multiple-choice QA benchmark from IBM Research: (1) Retrieval-only — each answer option is converted into an option-level query and scored against similar correct/incorrect training records using TF-IDF, BM25, semantic search, and hybrid search; (2) LLM-based — the Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model tested with zero-shot prompting, few-shot prompting, and QLoRA fine-tuning. Error and robustness analyses are conducted across varying numbers of answer options, option shuffling, label changes, paraphrasing, and added distractors.
AI.result: Semantic search and hybrid search outperform pure keyword-matching methods (TF-IDF, BM25), showing meaning-based similarity is more critical for this task. Among LLM methods, QLoRA fine-tuning substantially outperforms zero-shot and few-shot prompting. Performance degrades as answer options increase. All methods are sensitive to option shuffling, changed labels, paraphrasing, and additional distractors.
AI.conclusion: Meaning-based retrieval (semantic/hybrid search) is more effective than lexical matching for failure-sensor reasoning. Fine-tuned open-source LLMs provide the strongest performance but remain brittle under distribution shifts such as paraphrasing, label changes, and distractor addition, highlighting robustness as a key challenge for real-world deployment.

title: A GAN-Based Framework for Robust Data Synthesis in Satellite Internet Observations
comment: This paper has been accepted by the IEEE International Symposium on Personal, Indoor and Mobile Radio Communications 2026 (PIMRC 2026), 1 - 4 September 2026, Singapore
summary: Low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellite Internet has become an important infrastructure for enabling ubiquitous connectivity to align with the International Telecommunications Union vision for 6G telecommunications networks. However, current LEO satellite Internet observations often suffer from missing data, which complicates data augmentation task and limits the expansion of representative datasets. Given the complex characteristics of these datasets, generative AI (GenAI) presents a promising approach, yet its application in this domain has received little attention to date. In this paper, we propose a GenAI-based framework to synthesize high-fidelity data directly from incomplete LEO network observations. We propose the representative data missing scenarios, and evaluate the performance with the latest GAN- and VAE-based GenAI models on the recent WetLinks dataset. We design block-wise and point-wise missing scenarios to closely simulate the data loss that happens on real-world LEO satellite networks. Our results show the effectiveness of our proposed GAN-based framework and GT-GAN model exhibits the best performance among all models in both missing scenarios. Even under extreme conditions (e.g., 40% of the input data is missing), GT-GAN shows the highest robustness, consistently capturing the underlying input data distribution and being the least affected in terms of generalization. Our results shed light on future directions for GenAI-based data augmentation methods and data-driven research on satellite network measurement.

AI.tldr: Proposes a GenAI framework (GAN- and VAE-based) to synthesize high-fidelity data from incomplete LEO satellite network observations, with GT-GAN demonstrating superior robustness even under 40% data loss.
AI.motivation: LEO satellite Internet datasets frequently suffer from missing data due to real-world measurement challenges, which hinders data augmentation and limits the creation of representative datasets. GenAI is promising but under-explored in this domain.
AI.method: Design block-wise and point-wise missing scenarios to simulate real-world data loss patterns. Evaluate GAN- and VAE-based GenAI models (including GT-GAN) on the WetLinks dataset for synthesizing complete data from incomplete observations.
AI.result: GT-GAN consistently outperforms all other models across both missing scenarios, showing the highest robustness. Even at 40% missing data, GT-GAN best captures the underlying data distribution and maintains superior generalization.
AI.conclusion: GenAI, particularly GAN-based approaches like GT-GAN, is highly effective for data augmentation on incomplete LEO satellite network measurements, offering a viable path forward for data-driven satellite network research.

title: PILA: Plug-and-Play Insertion for LLM-native Advertising
summary: How to monetize large language models (LLMs) by naturally integrating sponsored content into their responses, known as LLM-native advertising, has recently emerged as a critical problem. However, existing solutions entangle advertising with content generation inside a single model, which is incompatible with modern API-only or workflow-based LLM applications and inevitably compromises the original response quality. To address this, we propose PILA, which reformulates ad insertion as a conditional response rewriting problem and decouples it from the upstream service as a lightweight sidecar module. PILA is model-agnostic and can be seamlessly integrated with existing LLM services without modifying the base model or its workflow. It also exposes a controllable trade-off between user-side naturalness and ad-side exposure, offering a practical interface for downstream pricing and deployment. Experiments across diverse upstream models show that \pila consistently improves ad effectiveness while preserving response quality, highlighting its promise as a practical solution for LLM-native advertising.

AI.tldr: PILA decouples LLM-native advertising from content generation by reformulating ad insertion as a conditional response rewriting problem using a lightweight, model-agnostic sidecar module, enabling seamless integration with existing LLM services while balancing ad effectiveness and response quality.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-native advertising methods entangle ad insertion with content generation inside a single model, making them incompatible with API-only or workflow-based LLM applications and degrading original response quality. A decoupled, non-intrusive solution is needed.
AI.method: PILA is a model-agnostic sidecar module that reformulates ad insertion as conditional response rewriting. It operates independently from the upstream LLM service, requiring no modification to the base model or its workflow, and exposes a controllable trade-off between user-side naturalness and ad-side exposure.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse upstream models show that PILA consistently improves ad effectiveness while preserving response quality.
AI.conclusion: PILA offers a practical, non-intrusive solution for LLM-native advertising that balances monetization needs with user experience, highlighting its promise for real-world deployment.

title: Stemma: Induced Decision Regions Reveal LLM Provenance
summary: LLM provenance testing asks whether a suspect LLM belongs to the same lineage as a source. Existing black-box methods largely infer this relationship from response-level characteristics, but these characteristics may shift under adaptation or deployment even when the underlying meaning remains unchanged, weakening the reliability of provenance evidence. To address this limitation, we introduce induced decision regions by mapping open-ended outputs into a finite decision space, thereby abstracting away surface-form variation and reframing provenance testing as measuring the inheritance of decision regions. Empirical analysis shows that the source's induced regions are preserved more strongly in related models than in unrelated models. Building on this signal, we propose Stemma, a practical black-box LLM fingerprinting method that operationalises stability, robustness, and specificity as complementary probe-selection principles for reliably estimating induced decision region inheritance. Across 770 source-suspect pairs drawn from 56 public checkpoints and spanning diverse model-weight transformations, Stemma achieves 0.967 AUC and 87.8% TPR at 1% FPR, substantially outperforming four representative baselines. It further achieves 0.995 AUC and 93.5% TPR at 1% FPR on 1,260 pairs covering 91 deployment instances, demonstrating robustness to diverse inference-time deployment settings.

AI.tldr: Stemma is a black-box LLM fingerprinting method that determines model lineage by measuring the inheritance of induced decision regions—mapping open-ended outputs into a finite decision space to abstract away surface-form variation. It achieves 0.967 AUC and 87.8% TPR at 1% FPR on weight-transformed models, and 0.995 AUC with 93.5% TPR on deployment instances.
AI.motivation: Existing black-box LLM provenance testing methods rely on response-level characteristics that shift under adaptation or deployment even when semantic meaning is preserved, undermining reliability. The authors aim to capture a deeper, more stable signal of model lineage that is invariant to surface-form variation.
AI.method: The authors introduce induced decision regions: mapping open-ended LLM outputs into a finite, structured decision space (e.g., multiple-choice answers), abstracting away surface variation. Provenance testing is reframed as measuring inheritance of these decision regions. Stemma operationalizes three probe-selection principles—stability, robustness, and specificity—to reliably estimate this inheritance using carefully selected probes. Evaluation spans 770 source-suspect pairs (56 public checkpoints, diverse weight transformations) and 1,260 pairs (91 deployment instances).
AI.result: On weight-transformation benchmarks: 0.967 AUC, 87.8% TPR at 1% FPR, substantially outperforming four baselines. On deployment-instance benchmarks: 0.995 AUC and 93.5% TPR at 1% FPR, demonstrating robustness to inference-time deployment variations.
AI.conclusion: Induced decision region inheritance provides a robust signal for black-box LLM provenance testing. Stemma's probe-selection principles (stability, robustness, specificity) yield a practical, high-performance fingerprinting method that reliably traces model lineage across both weight-level adaptations and inference-time deployment settings.

title: RepoReasoner: Evaluating Repository-Level Code Reasoning Ability of Long-Context Language Models
summary: Recent large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on software engineering tasks, yet most existing benchmarks evaluate code reasoning at the function level, where all relevant information is localized. This setting fails to reflect real-world development, which requires reasoning across multiple files and complex dependency structures. We introduce RepoReasoner, a benchmark for evaluating repository-level code reasoning. It assesses two complementary abilities: Output Prediction, which measures fine-grained, stateful execution reasoning across files, and Call Chain Prediction, which evaluates high-level architectural dependency understanding under noisy context. Our benchmark is constructed through a multi-stage pipeline that leverages dynamic tracing of pytest executions to obtain ground-truth call chains, along with LLM-based I/O rewriting to reduce memorization effects. We evaluate seven state-of-the-art LLMs. Even under oracle context, the best-performing model achieves only 69.1% Pass@1 on Output Prediction, indicating that cross-file reasoning remains a major challenge. In Call Chain Prediction, models exhibit high precision but low recall, suggesting limited multi-hop dependency understanding. Furthermore, performance drops on rewritten data reveal partial reliance on memorization, and longer contexts do not consistently improve results due to noise. These findings highlight fundamental limitations in current LLMs' repository-level reasoning and motivate future work on structured architectural understanding and cross-file inference.

AI.tldr: RepoReasoner is a benchmark for repository-level code reasoning, evaluating LLMs on Output Prediction (fine-grained cross-file execution reasoning) and Call Chain Prediction (architectural dependency understanding). Best models achieve only 69.1% Pass@1, revealing fundamental limitations in cross-file inference and multi-hop dependency reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing code reasoning benchmarks operate at the function level with localized information, failing to reflect real-world software development where reasoning requires navigating multiple files and complex dependency structures. There is a need to evaluate LLMs on repository-level reasoning.
AI.method: RepoReasoner is built via a multi-stage pipeline: (1) dynamic tracing of pytest executions to extract ground-truth call chains, and (2) LLM-based I/O rewriting to mitigate memorization effects. It defines two tasks: Output Prediction (stateful execution reasoning across files) and Call Chain Prediction (identifying dependency chains under noisy context). Seven state-of-the-art LLMs are evaluated under both oracle and realistic context conditions.
AI.result: The best model achieves only 69.1% Pass@1 on Output Prediction even with oracle context. In Call Chain Prediction, models show high precision but low recall, indicating poor multi-hop dependency understanding. Performance drops on rewritten data suggest partial reliance on memorization. Longer contexts do not consistently improve results due to noise.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs exhibit fundamental limitations in repository-level reasoning, particularly in cross-file inference and structured architectural understanding. These findings motivate future research on improving multi-hop dependency reasoning and handling noisy, long-context code scenarios.

title: AnnoBench: A Benchmark for Visualization Annotation Generation
summary: Annotation is among the most demanding visualization tasks to automate, as it simultaneously requires correctly navigating visual, semantic, and stylistic constraints. Failure to meet any of these conditions severely undermines the utility of an annotation, rendering it challenging to read, inaccurate, or visually discordant. Despite a growing body of annotation tools and automations, no existing benchmark or evaluation framework tests whether these conditions are met because of their scope and annotation not being the focus of their studies. We introduce AnnoBench, a benchmark for visualization annotation that materializes the inherent challenges of this domain in a structured and testable manner. AnnoBench pairs visualizations from professional data journalism and visualization galleries with annotation tasks, spanning four representation formats, five chart description conditions, and two prompt specification levels. The benchmark is executed via VLM-as-a-judge, using models aligned with manual human assessment. We evaluate the benchmark via four one-factor-at-a-time experiments, exploring the effects of input representation, semantic context, and prompt specificity, and model selection on annotation quality. This work provides a foundation for advancing annotation automation, tooling, and visualization-generation pipelines.

AI.tldr: AnnoBench is a benchmark for evaluating automated visualization annotation, pairing professional visualizations with structured annotation tasks across multiple formats, conditions, and prompt levels, evaluated via VLM-as-a-judge aligned with human assessment.
AI.motivation: Annotation automation requires simultaneously satisfying visual, semantic, and stylistic constraints, yet no existing benchmark systematically tests whether these conditions are met. Existing tools and evaluations either lack scope or do not treat annotation as a primary focus.
AI.method: AnnoBench pairs visualizations from professional data journalism and galleries with annotation tasks spanning four representation formats, five chart description conditions, and two prompt specification levels. Evaluation uses VLM-as-a-judge with models aligned to manual human assessment, and four one-factor-at-a-time experiments explore input representation, semantic context, prompt specificity, and model selection effects on annotation quality.
AI.result: The benchmark is executed successfully via VLM-as-a-judge, with experiments revealing how input representation, semantic context, prompt specificity, and model selection each independently affect annotation quality.
AI.conclusion: AnnoBench provides a structured, testable foundation for advancing annotation automation, tooling, and visualization-generation pipelines by formalizing the multi-constraint challenge of visualization annotation into a reproducible benchmark.

title: Algorithmic Separation between Constant-Depth and Logarithmic-Depth Neural Networks
summary:
Despite the empirical advantages of deep networks over shallow ones, theoretical depth separations largely concern approximation power, while algorithmic results are mostly limited to comparisons between two- and three-layer networks. In this work, we prove the first algorithmic separation between constant-depth and logarithmic-depth networks.
  Specifically, we identify a class of Boolean functions with hierarchically structured Fourier spectra that logarithmic-depth networks can learn efficiently using layerwise coordinate descent by reconstructing the spectra hierarchically and adaptively. We also exhibit a subclass for which every constant-depth, polynomial-width network with sufficiently regular activations and controlled spectral norms must incur constant $L^2$ approximation error under the uniform distribution over the hypercube.

AI.tldr: Proves the first algorithmic separation between constant-depth and logarithmic-depth neural networks: logarithmic-depth networks can efficiently learn a specific class of Boolean functions with hierarchical Fourier structure via layerwise coordinate descent, while constant-depth polynomial-width networks provably fail.
AI.motivation: Prior theoretical depth separations for neural networks focus on approximation power rather than learnability, and algorithmic comparisons are largely restricted to two- versus three-layer networks. This work aims to extend algorithmic depth separation to the gap between constant-depth and logarithmic-depth architectures.
AI.method: The authors construct a class of Boolean functions whose Fourier spectra exhibit hierarchical structure. They show that logarithmic-depth networks can learn these functions via layerwise coordinate descent, which reconstructs the Fourier spectrum hierarchically and adaptively. For the lower bound, they identify a subclass on which any constant-depth, polynomial-width network (with sufficiently regular activations and bounded spectral norms) incurs constant L² approximation error under the uniform distribution over the hypercube.
AI.result: Logarithmic-depth networks can efficiently learn the hierarchically structured Boolean function class; constant-depth, polynomial-width networks with regular activations and controlled spectral norms have constant L² approximation error on a subclass.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes the first algorithmic depth separation between constant-depth and logarithmic-depth networks, moving beyond mere approximation-theoretic separations and beyond the shallow two-vs-three-layer regime.

title: Reasoning with Memory: A Temporal Granularity-Adaptive Framework for Training-Free Long Video Understanding
summary: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate superior generalization in fundamental video tasks, restricted context windows limit their long video understanding. To accommodate this constraint, models typically resort to keyframe selection. However, uniform sampling or static query-guided selection often overlooks critical temporal context, failing to adapt to the varying query temporal granularities. In this paper, we propose ReMem, a temporal granularity-adaptive keyframe selection framework for training-free LongVideoQA. ReMem introduces a dual-level memory-augmented adaptation. At the query level, Memory-Driven Question Parsing leverages LLM long-term memory to decode question temporal granularity and extract semantic entities. At the video level, Synergistic Dual-Semantic Frame Alignment exploits intrinsic structural memory to align frames with query semantics, guiding Structure-Aware Dynamic Frame Routing to cluster events and optimally distribute sampling budgets. By explicitly preserving temporal information with memory mechanisms, ReMem suppresses redundancy and empowers MLLMs to perform robust multi-granular video reasoning. Evaluations across four popular LongVideoQA benchmarks using three MLLMs demonstrate highly efficient, state-of-the-art zero-shot performance; notably, LLaVA-Video with ReMem reaches 54.5% (+12.3%) on LVBench and 67.1% (+8.2%) on LongVideoBench.

AI.tldr: ReMem is a training-free, temporal granularity-adaptive keyframe selection framework for long video QA that uses dual-level memory mechanisms to align frame sampling with query temporal granularity, achieving state-of-the-art zero-shot performance.
AI.motivation: MLLMs excel at video understanding but are bottlenecked by limited context windows. Existing keyframe selection methods (uniform sampling, static query-guided selection) fail to adapt to varying query temporal granularities, leading to loss of critical temporal context and redundant frames.
AI.method: ReMem proposes a dual-level memory-augmented framework: (1) Memory-Driven Question Parsing uses LLM long-term memory to decode temporal granularity and extract semantic entities from the question; (2) Synergistic Dual-Semantic Frame Alignment leverages intrinsic structural memory to align frames with query semantics, then Structure-Aware Dynamic Frame Routing clusters events and optimally distributes the sampling budget across them.
AI.result: Evaluated on four LongVideoQA benchmarks with three MLLMs, ReMem achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance. LLaVA-Video with ReMem reaches 54.5% (+12.3%) on LVBench and 67.1% (+8.2%) on LongVideoBench.
AI.conclusion: ReMem effectively suppresses redundancy and enables robust multi-granular video reasoning by explicitly preserving temporal information through memory mechanisms, demonstrating that training-free adaptive keyframe selection can significantly boost long video understanding in MLLMs.

title: A Human-in-the-Loop Corpus for LLM-Based Simplification of Scientific Summaries
summary: Interdisciplinary research is accelerating, yet scientific papers remain difficult to understand outside their home fields. We study large language model (LLM)-based simplification of scientific texts and present a human-in-the-loop workflow that transforms expert summaries into more accessible versions for non-specialists. Using SciSummNet as the source corpus, we first generate baseline simplifications with GPT-4o-mini. In Phase 1, readers from STEM fields outside computer science identify difficult sentences and phrases and compare the original and GPT-simplified summaries in terms of comprehensibility, naturalness, and simplicity. In Phase 2, computer science experts use this feedback to create expert-edited reference simplifications. We release the resulting corpus together with human judgments and automatic evaluation results. The Phase 1 judgments show a clear preference for the GPT-generated summaries in terms of comprehensibility and simplicity, while qualitative analysis of the Phase 2 edits highlights the importance of preserving domain-specific terminology and the strength of scientific claims. The resulting resource supports the training and benchmarking of simplification systems for cross-disciplinary scientific communication.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a human-in-the-loop workflow using GPT-4o-mini to simplify scientific abstracts for non-specialists, releasing a corpus of expert-edited simplifications with human judgments showing GPT summaries are preferred for comprehensibility and simplicity.
AI.motivation: Interdisciplinary research is growing, yet scientific papers remain impenetrable to readers outside their home disciplines. There is a need for effective simplification tools to make scientific communication more accessible across fields.
AI.method: A two-phase human-in-the-loop workflow: first, GPT-4o-mini generates baseline simplifications from the SciSummNet corpus; Phase 1 has STEM readers (non-CS) evaluate original vs. GPT-simplified summaries on comprehensibility, naturalness, and simplicity, flagging difficult sentences; Phase 2 has CS experts produce reference simplifications incorporating Phase 1 feedback.
AI.result: Phase 1 judgments show clear preference for GPT-generated summaries in comprehensibility and simplicity. Phase 2 qualitative analysis reveals the importance of retaining domain-specific terminology and preserving the strength of scientific claims during simplification. The resulting corpus with human judgments is released.
AI.conclusion: The released corpus supports training and benchmarking of cross-disciplinary scientific text simplification systems, contributing to more accessible interdisciplinary communication.

title: From Role Prompt to Infinite Thinking: Exploiting Persona Conditioning for Inference Cost Attacks in LLMs
summary: LLMs are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, making inference efficiency and service reliability critical concerns due to their substantial computational costs. However, the autoregressive generation mechanism of LLMs enables malicious prompts to manipulate generation behaviors, inducing excessive token generation that amplifies computational consumption and threatens service efficiency. Existing methods mainly rely on adversarial suffixes or explicit extension instructions, which introduce detectable behaviors and limit their applicability. In this paper, we reveal a previously unexplored vulnerability caused by persona consistency in LLMs, where models maintain assigned roles and reproduce corresponding behaviors even when they result in inefficient reasoning and excessive generation. Based on this observation, we propose RolePlay, a task-aware dynamic persona alignment framework that constructs adaptive personas to naturally induce inefficient yet semantically coherent behaviors for inference cost amplification. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and diverse task datasets demonstrate that RolePlay consistently outperforms existing inference extension methods, achieving an average token amplification of up to \bm{$7.64\times$} and a maximum token amplification ratio of \bm{$207.64\times$}. Our findings identify persona conditioning as a new attack surface for LLM inference efficiency and offer a new perspective on computational cost amplification.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that persona consistency in LLMs can be exploited to amplify inference costs. The authors propose RolePlay, a framework that dynamically assigns adaptive personas to induce inefficient yet coherent token generation, achieving up to 207.64× token amplification.
AI.motivation: LLMs are widely deployed but suffer from high computational costs. Existing methods for amplifying inference (adversarial suffixes, explicit extension instructions) are detectable and limited. The authors identify an unexplored vulnerability: persona consistency, where LLMs maintain assigned roles and reproduce inefficient behaviors, enabling stealthy computational cost amplification.
AI.method: RolePlay, a task-aware dynamic persona alignment framework. It constructs adaptive personas tailored to specific tasks, designed to naturally induce semantically coherent but inefficient reasoning and generation patterns, thereby amplifying token output and inference costs without triggering detection mechanisms.
AI.result: RolePlay consistently outperforms existing inference extension methods across multiple LLMs and diverse task datasets, achieving an average token amplification of 7.64× and a maximum token amplification ratio of 207.64×.
AI.conclusion: Persona conditioning represents a new attack surface for LLM inference efficiency. The work provides a novel perspective on computational cost amplification and highlights a previously overlooked security vulnerability in deployed LLM systems.

title: Faster, Higher, Stronger? The Impact of GenAI on Knowledge Work Productivity - Evidence from the Field
summary: The rise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has fueled high expectations regarding its potential to enhance knowledge work productivity in terms of efficiency and quality. Building on task-technology fit (TTF) theory, we empirically examine the extent of GenAI's productivity effect for different task types. We conducted a randomized lab-in-the-field experiment with 128 knowledge workers from a multinational industrial organization. Participants completed three representative knowledge work tasks (knowledge acquisition, packaging, and creation), either with or without GenAI. Results show that GenAI consistently increases efficiency across tasks. However, its impact on quality is task-contingent: quality increases for knowledge packaging and creation but declines for knowledge acquisition. Furthermore, GenAI tends to reduce quality variance for knowledge packaging and creation, primarily benefiting lower-performing knowledge workers. However, it increases quality variance for knowledge acquisition. These findings contribute to a more granular, differentiated understanding of GenAI's productivity impact and hold implications for research and practice alike.

AI.tldr: A randomized experiment with 128 knowledge workers shows GenAI consistently boosts efficiency but has task-contingent effects on quality: quality improves for knowledge packaging and creation but declines for acquisition. GenAI also reduces quality variance for higher-order tasks, primarily helping lower performers, while increasing variance for acquisition.
AI.motivation: Despite high expectations that generative AI will enhance knowledge work productivity, there is limited empirical evidence on whether its effects are uniform across different task types. The authors aim to move beyond blanket claims by providing a granular, task-contingent understanding of GenAI's productivity impact.
AI.method: A randomized lab-in-the-field experiment with 128 knowledge workers from a multinational industrial organization. Participants completed three representative knowledge work tasks — knowledge acquisition, packaging, and creation — either with or without GenAI support. Productivity was measured in terms of both efficiency and quality.
AI.result: GenAI consistently increases efficiency across all task types. However, quality effects are task-contingent: quality rises for knowledge packaging and creation but falls for knowledge acquisition. Additionally, GenAI reduces quality variance for packaging and creation (benefiting lower performers) but increases quality variance for acquisition.
AI.conclusion: GenAI's productivity impact is not uniform; it depends on task type. Organizations and researchers should adopt a differentiated view of GenAI deployment, recognizing that efficiency gains are reliable but quality outcomes are task-dependent. The findings also suggest GenAI can help narrow performance gaps in higher-order tasks.

title: A Unified Algorithmic Framework for Hybrid Reinforcement Learning in Tabular MDPs with Shifted Transition Dynamics
summary: This paper investigates a hybrid reinforcement learning setting in tabular Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), where an agent aims to learn an optimal policy by combining online interactions with a target environment and offline data from a source environment. A central challenge is that offline data may be collected from outdated environments with shifted transition dynamics, making naive integration of historical data ineffective. To address this, we propose a unified algorithmic framework featuring two algorithms: MIN-UCB-VI for regret minimization and MAX-LCB-VI for best policy identification. Both algorithms leverage fine-grained bias information to more effectively exploit offline data under general transition shifts. We provide theoretical guarantees for our framework, including both instance-dependent and independent upper bounds on regret and sub-optimality gap. Furthermore, we establish matching lower bounds to demonstrate the optimality of our approach and validate our theoretical findings through extensive experiments.

AI.tldr: Proposes a hybrid RL framework for tabular MDPs that combines online interactions with offline data from source environments having shifted transition dynamics. Introduces MIN-UCB-VI (regret minimization) and MAX-LCB-VI (best policy identification), both using fine-grained bias information. Provides matching upper and lower bounds, plus experimental validation.
AI.motivation: Standard hybrid RL naively integrates offline data from outdated environments, which can be ineffective or even harmful due to transition dynamics shifts. There is a need for algorithms that can selectively and effectively exploit offline data while accounting for such distributional shifts.
AI.method: Proposes a unified algorithmic framework with two algorithms: MIN-UCB-VI for regret minimization and MAX-LCB-VI for best policy identification. Both algorithms incorporate fine-grained bias information (quantifying the discrepancy between source and target transition dynamics) to determine when and how to leverage offline data. The framework operates in the tabular MDP setting with theoretical analysis yielding instance-dependent and instance-independent bounds.
AI.result: Established both instance-dependent and instance-independent upper bounds on regret (for MIN-UCB-VI) and sub-optimality gap (for MAX-LCB-VI). Derived matching lower bounds demonstrating optimality of the approach. Extensive experiments validated the theoretical findings.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively addresses hybrid RL under transition dynamics shifts by using fine-grained bias information to guide offline data utilization. The algorithms achieve optimal theoretical guarantees and strong empirical performance, advancing the state of hybrid reinforcement learning.

title: Improving Rare Medication Recommendation with Counterfactual Data Augmentation and Large Language Models
comment: Accepted for publication at the 20th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems (RecSys 2026)
summary: AI-based medication recommendation systems have attracted substantial attention due to their potential to enhance patient safety and therapeutic outcomes. Despite the clinical importance of accurately recommending rarely prescribed medications (rare-meds), we observe that most existing methods show significantly lower predictive performance for rare-meds. We attribute this issue to two intrinsic limitations: (a) the inherent scarcity of data for rare-meds and (b) limited consideration of co-recommended medications. To address these limitations, we propose GenRxR, a novel framework based on large language models (LLMs). GenRxR leverages the medical knowledge and clinical reasoning capability of LLMs to generate counterfactual medical data, mitigating the data scarcity issue for rare-meds. It also integrates an LLM into the medication recommendation process to model relationships among co-recommended medications. To further enhance the clinical reasoning, we introduce an instruction tuning step that aligns the LLM's capability with the recommendation task, enabling better handling of clinical context, including rare-meds cases. In our experiments, we show that GenRxR outperforms 14 (including 5 LLM-based) baselines in most cases. Specifically, it achieves up to 30.9% higher predictive performance for rare-meds than the strongest baseline.

AI.tldr: GenRxR is an LLM-based medication recommendation framework that generates counterfactual medical data and integrates LLM reasoning to improve rare-medication prediction, outperforming 14 baselines by up to 30.9%.
AI.motivation: Existing medication recommendation systems perform poorly on rarely prescribed medications due to (a) inherent data scarcity and (b) insufficient modeling of co-recommended medication relationships.
AI.method: GenRxR uses LLMs to generate counterfactual medical data addressing rare-med scarcity, integrates an LLM into the recommendation process to model co-medication relationships, and employs instruction tuning to align the LLM with the clinical recommendation task.
AI.result: GenRxR outperforms 14 baselines (including 5 LLM-based methods) in most cases, achieving up to 30.9% higher predictive performance for rare medications compared to the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging LLMs for counterfactual data generation and clinical reasoning effectively mitigates data scarcity and relational modeling limitations, significantly improving rare-medication recommendation performance.

title: When Shortest Isn't Safest: A Design Science Approach to Senior-Friendly Pedestrian Routing
summary: Older adults' independent mobility enables out-of-home participation, well-being and health, yet pedestrian navigation systems still optimize primarily for distance or time, often overlooking barriers, safety thresholds, and supportive infrastructure that shape late-life walking decisions. We present a senior-friendly pedestrian routing artefact developed through echeloned Design Science Re-search, translating lived mobility constraints into prescriptive design knowledge. Based on 11 semi-structured interviews, we derive initial Design Requirements (DRs) and Design Principles (DPs) for barrier-aware, amenity-sensitive routing and execution-relevant explanations. We instantiate these in an OpenStreetMap pedestrian network enriched with amenities (benches, toilets, and shelters) and height data, and implemented an A*-based routing engine with configurable costs and explanation payloads. In a field-based walking study, 14 older adults com-pared artefact-generated routes with baselines and provided ratings and qualitative feedback; the senior-friendly route was preferred overall. Thematic analysis further showed that infrastructure maintenance, seasonal conditions, traffic exposure, and social context shape route acceptance. We synthesize these insights into refined DRs and DPs emphasizing context-aware hazard modeling, multi-route transparency, landmark-grounded explanations, social-context sensitivity, and stage-appropriate information. Our contributions provide actionable guidance for practitioners developing senior-friendly pedestrian navigation systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a senior-friendly pedestrian routing system designed through Design Science Research, incorporating older adults' mobility constraints (barriers, amenities, safety) into route planning. Based on interviews and a field study with 14 older adults, the authors derive design requirements and principles for barrier-aware, amenity-sensitive navigation with contextually relevant explanations.
AI.motivation: Current pedestrian navigation systems optimize for distance or time while ignoring critical factors for older adults: physical barriers (steep slopes, uneven surfaces), supportive amenities (benches, toilets, shelters), safety thresholds, and the need for explanatory route information. This neglect limits older adults' independent mobility and out-of-home participation.
AI.method: The study employs echeloned Design Science Research across three phases: (1) 11 semi-structured interviews to derive initial Design Requirements (DRs) and Design Principles (DPs); (2) instantiation of an A*-based routing engine on an enriched OpenStreetMap network incorporating amenity data and height/elevation data with configurable costs and explanation payloads; (3) a field-based walking study where 14 older adults compared artefact-generated routes against baseline routes, providing ratings and qualitative feedback, followed by thematic analysis.
AI.result: The senior-friendly route was preferred overall by participants. Thematic analysis revealed that infrastructure maintenance, seasonal conditions, traffic exposure, and social context significantly influence route acceptance. The authors synthesized refined DRs and DPs emphasizing: context-aware hazard modeling, multi-route transparency, landmark-grounded explanations, social-context sensitivity, and stage-appropriate information delivery.
AI.conclusion: The research provides actionable, prescriptive design knowledge for practitioners developing senior-friendly pedestrian navigation systems. The refined design requirements and principles offer concrete guidance for building routing systems that genuinely support older adults' independent mobility by accounting for the full spectrum of lived walking constraints.

title: Construction-Driven Injection: Linguistically-Grounded Edit-Based Code-Mixing Fingerprints for Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are costly intellectual assets that remain exposed to unauthorized redistribution and commercial misuse. Injected fingerprints, i.e., trigger--target pairs embedded in model behavior, offer a practical, black-box-verifiable ownership signal, but existing methods decouple the two stages of the fingerprint life cycle: how a fingerprint is constructed and how it is injected. Existing fingerprinting frameworks suffer from two limitations. Natural-language fingerprints are prone to accidental activation, and garbled fingerprints are easily filtered by perplexity-based detection. Furthermore, decoupling construction from injection leaves the latter unaware of the trigger's linguistic structure, missing the opportunity for targeted optimization. We argue that fingerprint construction should drive injection, and present a unified fingerprinting framework that jointly optimizes both stages. First, LCF constructs code-mixing fingerprints by combining low-resource languages under a semantic-density substitution rule and grammar-biased mixing, yielding triggers whose perplexity sits far below garbled baselines while avoiding the accidental-activation failures of natural-language triggers. Second, LCFEdit injects each fingerprint with a null-space projection derived from high-resource multilingual representations that preserves knowledge, augmented by a cross-lingual alignment step that steers the weight update toward the fingerprint language's representation subspace. This construction-aware injection ensures that the update is linguistically informed and therefore more stable. Extensive evaluations on imperceptibility, detectability, and harmlessness demonstrate persistent ownership verification with negligible impact on utility.

AI.tldr: LCF proposes a unified fingerprinting framework for LLM ownership verification that jointly optimizes fingerprint construction and injection. It uses code-mixing with low-resource languages and semantic-density substitution to create covert, stable fingerprints, then injects them via null-space projection with cross-lingual alignment for linguistically informed, utility-preserving ownership signals.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM fingerprinting methods suffer from two key limitations: (1) natural-language fingerprints risk accidental activation during normal use, while garbled fingerprints are easily detected and filtered by perplexity-based defenses; (2) the decoupling of fingerprint construction from injection misses opportunities for targeted optimization, leaving the injection process unaware of the trigger's linguistic structure. The authors argue that construction should drive injection for more robust ownership verification.
AI.method: The paper presents LCF, a unified two-stage framework: (1) LCF Construct — generates code-mixing fingerprints by combining low-resource languages using a semantic-density substitution rule and grammar-biased mixing, producing triggers with low perplexity that evade both accidental activation and perplexity-based filtering; (2) LCFEdit — injects each fingerprint using null-space projection derived from high-resource multilingual representations to preserve model knowledge, augmented by a cross-lingual alignment step that steers weight updates toward the fingerprint language's representation subspace, ensuring linguistically informed and stable injection.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations demonstrate that LCF achieves persistent ownership verification with negligible impact on model utility, while maintaining imperceptibility, high detectability, and harmlessness. The code-mixing fingerprints sit far below garbled baselines in perplexity and avoid the accidental-activation failures of natural-language triggers.
AI.conclusion: A unified fingerprinting framework where construction drives injection yields more robust, covert, and stable ownership verification for LLMs compared to decoupled approaches. The LCF method effectively balances imperceptibility, detectability, and harmlessness while preserving model utility.

title: E-MagDiP: Electro-Magnetic based Differential Privacy for EEG based Community Sensing
summary: EEG-based community sensing programs are emerging globally as a tool to leverage aggregated brain data to gain insights into attentiveness of students and employees. But these programs raise privacy concerns because EEG signals contain sensitive personal information. Differential Privacy (DP) can protect individuals while preserving aggregate statistics yet applying DP to EEG data is challenging as it requires user-level noise generation, which increases power and latency. Besides, most commercial EEG headsets cannot be modified to add such noise. We propose E-MagDiP, a framework that uses an external radio to transmit RF signals onto EEG headsets, perturbing signals at acquisition to induce DP noise. To the best of our knowledge, E-MagDiP is the first framework to use RF signals for privacy instead of attacks, enabling practical DP for EEG community sensing without any user-level modification.

AI.tldr: E-MagDiP introduces a novel framework that uses external RF signals to physically induce Differential Privacy noise onto EEG headsets during data acquisition, eliminating the need for user-level modifications.
AI.motivation: EEG-based community sensing programs (e.g., monitoring student/employee attentiveness) raise privacy concerns since EEG signals contain sensitive personal information. Traditional Differential Privacy requires per-user noise generation on the headset, increasing power consumption and latency, and most commercial EEG headsets are closed systems that cannot be modified to inject such noise.
AI.method: E-MagDiP transmits external RF signals onto EEG headsets to perturb the analog signals at the point of acquisition, physically inducing DP-compliant noise through electromagnetic interference. This achieves user-level differential privacy without any hardware or firmware modifications to the EEG device itself.
AI.result: E-MagDiP is the first framework to repurpose RF signals for privacy protection (rather than adversarial attacks), demonstrating a practical pathway to achieve DP in EEG community sensing scenarios.
AI.conclusion: RF-based perturbation offers a viable, non-invasive mechanism to enforce differential privacy on unmodified commercial EEG headsets, bridging the gap between privacy guarantees and real-world deployability in community sensing.

title: Who is scientific code for? Maintaining human-readable landmarks in agent-written code
comment: Position piece submitted to Infrastructure @ CSCW 26 workshop
summary: Scientific research involving code has long rested on the assumption that at least one person understands why the code exists. As scientists adopt coding agents, this assumption is breaking down. Drawing on an ongoing contextual inquiry of scientific programmers working with agentic tools (four cases to date), a survey of over 800 scientific programmers, and my own analysis workflows, this position piece describes how scientists are inventing personal conventions, "landmarking strategies", for marking which artifacts in a codebase are meant for human understanding and which are context for agents. They repurpose shared infrastructure (version control especially) in idiosyncratic ways, and I argue that this quiet de-standardization could complicate collaboration in teams with heterogeneous software practices. Alternatively, teams that explicitly delineate what is human-readable versus agent context will be better able to develop, document, and maintain scientific code.

AI.tldr: As scientists adopt AI coding agents, the assumption that someone understands the code breaks down. Scientists are developing personal "landmarking strategies" to distinguish human-readable artifacts from agent context, repurposing version control in idiosyncratic ways. This de-standardization may complicate collaboration; teams that explicitly delineate human vs. agent-readable code will fare better.
AI.motivation: The erosion of a foundational assumption in scientific computing: that at least one person understands why code exists. The adoption of AI coding agents by scientists threatens this assumption, creating a gap in understanding how scientific programmers navigate human-agent collaborative code development.
AI.method: A mixed-methods approach combining: (1) an ongoing contextual inquiry of scientific programmers using agentic tools (four cases), (2) a survey of over 800 scientific programmers, and (3) the author's own reflexive analysis of their coding workflows with agentic tools.
AI.result: Scientists are inventing "landmarking strategies" — personal conventions for marking which codebase artifacts are meant for human understanding versus agent context. They repurpose shared infrastructure (particularly version control) in idiosyncratic, non-standardized ways, leading to a quiet de-standardization of practices.
AI.conclusion: This de-standardization could complicate collaboration in teams with heterogeneous software practices. Conversely, teams that explicitly delineate human-readable versus agent-context artifacts will be better positioned to develop, document, and maintain scientific code.

title: Neurai-VN Benchmark: Standardized Machine Learning Models for Multimodal Digital Phenotyping in Mental Health Classification
summary: Digital phenotyping (DP) using smartphones and wearable devices has shown considerable potential for mental health monitoring. However, progress remains difficult to evaluate due to heterogeneous datasets, inconsistent preprocessing pipelines. In this study, we present a reproducible benchmark built upon the Neurai-VN dataset, a high-resolution, multimodal dataset comprising passive sensing and active assessment from wearable and smartphone devices, collected from 100 Vietnamese adults over two weeks. The benchmark defines four clinically relevant binary classification tasks evaluated using standardized subject-wise cross-validation. Representative linear, tree-based, and neural baseline models are evaluated across predefined feature configurations. Mean subject-level F1 scores across five cross-validation folds reached 0.71 for Healthy Control vs. Depression and Healthy Control vs. Clinical, while Healthy Control vs. Anxiety and Depression vs. Anxiety achieved 0.69 and 0.56, respectively. These benchmark results provide reproducible baselines for future research on multimodal DP for mental health classification tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a reproducible benchmark for multimodal mental health classification using the Neurai-VN dataset (100 Vietnamese adults, 2-week passive/active sensing). Four binary classification tasks are evaluated with standardized cross-validation, achieving F1 scores from 0.56–0.71 across linear, tree-based, and neural baselines.
AI.motivation: Progress in digital phenotyping for mental health monitoring is difficult to evaluate due to heterogeneous datasets and inconsistent preprocessing pipelines. A standardized, reproducible benchmark is needed to enable fair comparison across methods.
AI.method: The authors built a benchmark on the Neurai-VN dataset, which includes passive sensing and active assessment data from smartphones and wearables collected from 100 Vietnamese adults over two weeks. They defined four clinically relevant binary classification tasks (Healthy Control vs. Depression, Healthy Control vs. Clinical, Healthy Control vs. Anxiety, Depression vs. Anxiety) using standardized subject-wise 5-fold cross-validation. Representative baseline models (linear, tree-based, and neural) were evaluated across predefined feature configurations.
AI.result: Mean subject-level F1 scores across five folds: Healthy Control vs. Depression (0.71), Healthy Control vs. Clinical (0.71), Healthy Control vs. Anxiety (0.69), and Depression vs. Anxiety (0.56).
AI.conclusion: The benchmark provides reproducible baselines for future research on multimodal digital phenotyping for mental health classification, establishing a foundation for fair comparison and methodological advancement in the field.

title: MedJudgeRAG: Option-Wise Evidence Judgment with Dynamic Knowledge Graphs for Medical MCQA
comment: 16 pages, 2 figures, Accepted at The Workshop on Graph Foundation Models at the 43 rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: In medical multiple-choice question answering (MCQA), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can supplement the domain knowledge of language models (LMs). However, since vanilla RAG indiscriminately utilizes retrieved documents, it can degrade LM performance. To address this, we propose MedJudgeRAG. Our framework represents retrieved documents as a dynamic knowledge graph (KG) composed of entities and relations. For each option, the model judges an evidence verdict from the retrieved documents and the KG. Based on the verdict combination, the model determines a knowledge utilization strategy to reason toward the final answer. These capabilities are trained via supervised fine-tuning using structured reasoning traces generated by a teacher LM. The training employs a weighted cross-entropy loss that differentially weights the KG and reasoning segments. Experiments on two medical MCQA benchmarks demonstrate that MedJudgeRAG consistently outperforms both vanilla RAG and parametric baselines. Furthermore, ablation analysis reveals that the dynamic KG is more effective as graph-conditioned supervision at training time than as an explicit output at inference time. Our code is available at https://github.com/hyu-amllab/medjudgerag, and the generated reasoning traces are released at https://huggingface.co/datasets/youarethewon/medjudgerag.

AI.tldr: MedJudgeRAG improves medical MCQA by using a dynamic knowledge graph to strategically filter and utilize retrieved documents, outperforming vanilla RAG through trained evidence-verdict reasoning and weighted fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Vanilla RAG indiscriminately uses all retrieved documents, which can introduce noise and degrade LM performance in medical MCQA. A smarter, evidence-based document utilization strategy is needed.
AI.method: MedJudgeRAG represents retrieved documents as a dynamic knowledge graph (KG) of entities and relations. For each answer option, the model generates an evidence verdict from the documents and KG, combines verdicts to select a knowledge utilization strategy, and reasons to the final answer. Training uses supervised fine-tuning on structured reasoning traces from a teacher LM, with weighted cross-entropy loss that differentially weights KG and reasoning segments.
AI.result: On two medical MCQA benchmarks, MedJudgeRAG consistently outperformed both vanilla RAG and parametric baselines. Ablation showed the dynamic KG is more effective as graph-conditioned supervision during training than as an explicit output at inference time.
AI.conclusion: Strategic, verdict-based document utilization via a dynamic KG significantly improves RAG for medical MCQA. The KG's primary value lies in training-time supervision rather than inference-time generation.

title: RRS-10K: A Multitask Vision-Language Model Benchmark for Rare Remote Sensing Image Interpretation
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on general remote sensing tasks. However, their capability for rare scenes remains insufficiently understood, because existing benchmarks are dominated by common urban and rural imagery. To address this gap, we present RRS-10K, a benchmark for rare remote sensing image interpretation. RRS-10K contains 10,738 military-related remote sensing images and corresponding multiple format question-answer pairs for comprehensive evaluation. All of the images are collected from first-hand sources and organized into three capability dimensions, six sub-dimensions, and 20 leaf tasks, covering perception, reasoning, and robustness. To improve the quality of multiple-choice questions, we introduce a similarity-based distractor filtering strategy (SDFS) during benchmark construction. We further evaluate 52 representative models and show that current VLMs achieve only moderate zero-shot performance on rare remote sensing image interpretation, with clear weaknesses in visual grounding, referring segmentation, and complex semantic reasoning tasks. RRS-10K enables systematic analysis of failure modes in long-tail remote sensing interpretation and provides guidance for developing more reliable remote sensing VLMs.

AI.tldr: RRS-10K is a benchmark of 10,738 military-related remote sensing images with multi-format QA pairs, spanning perception, reasoning, and robustness across 20 leaf tasks. Evaluation of 52 VLMs reveals moderate zero-shot performance and specific weaknesses in visual grounding, referring segmentation, and complex reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing remote sensing benchmarks are dominated by common urban/rural imagery, leaving VLMs' capability on rare (military-related) scenes poorly understood. A dedicated benchmark is needed to assess long-tail remote sensing interpretation.
AI.method: The authors construct RRS-10K with 10,738 first-hand military-related remote sensing images, organized into 3 capability dimensions (perception, reasoning, robustness), 6 sub-dimensions, and 20 leaf tasks. Multiple-choice question quality is improved via a similarity-based distractor filtering strategy (SDFS). Fifty-two representative VLMs are evaluated in a zero-shot setting.
AI.result: Current VLMs achieve only moderate zero-shot performance on rare remote sensing interpretation. Clear weaknesses emerge in visual grounding, referring segmentation, and complex semantic reasoning tasks, with systematic failure mode analysis enabled by the benchmark structure.
AI.conclusion: RRS-10K fills a critical evaluation gap for long-tail remote sensing scenes and provides actionable guidance for developing more robust and reliable remote sensing VLMs, particularly for under-represented rare scenarios.

title: MyMentorLLM: A psychotherapy GenAI environment with multimodal voice/text patients, trainees and experts for deliberate practice
summary: Psychotherapists need repeated training and supervision by experts; however, scalability is problematic. Here we present MyMentorLLM, a multimodal voice- and text-based simulation environment for deliberate practice, used to generate 2,100 complete Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) training sessions. Each session links a DSM-5-TR-grounded patient (with major depressive, generalised anxiety or borderline personality disorder), a therapist-in-training and an expert supervisor. As an initial implementation, we adopted CBT because its structured procedures and competency-based supervision facilitate standardised simulation and evaluation. Sessions were analysed for emotional dynamics, therapeutic competence and diagnostic accuracy. Simulated patients expressed disorder-congruent emotional profiles, which trainee therapists mirrored as in real human counselling. The quality of supervision differed across LLMs: while most models overestimated trainees' competences, native speech-to-speech was closest to human scores. Supervisors' feedback led to better diagnoses in simulated psychotherapists in 5 out of 7 LLMs, and symptom identification accuracy increased with model size. This work shows that simulation of deliberate practice is possible for CBT training, although patient fidelity, calibration of supervisors, and harmful feedback should be evaluated together.

AI.tldr: MyMentorLLM is a multimodal simulation environment for CBT training that generated 2,100 sessions linking DSM-5-grounded patients, trainees, and supervisors. It reveals that LLMs can simulate deliberate practice with disorder-congruent emotional dynamics, but supervisor calibration and feedback quality vary across models.
AI.motivation: Psychotherapists require repeated expert training and supervision, but scaling this is difficult. The authors aim to address this scalability problem by creating a simulation environment for deliberate practice in CBT, leveraging its structured, competency-based nature for standardized evaluation.
AI.method: The authors developed MyMentorLLM, a multimodal (voice- and text-based) simulation environment. They generated 2,100 complete CBT training sessions, each involving a DSM-5-TR-grounded simulated patient (with major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, or borderline personality disorder), a therapist-in-training, and an expert supervisor. Sessions were analyzed for emotional dynamics, therapeutic competence, and diagnostic accuracy across multiple LLMs.
AI.result: Simulated patients produced disorder-congruent emotional profiles, and trainee therapists mirrored them as in real counseling. Supervisor quality varied: most LLMs overestimated trainee competence, but native speech-to-speech models scored closest to human ratings. Supervisor feedback improved diagnostic accuracy in 5 of 7 LLMs, and symptom identification accuracy scaled with model size.
AI.conclusion: Simulation of deliberate practice for CBT training is feasible with LLMs, but future work must address patient fidelity, supervisor calibration, and the mitigation of harmful feedback before clinical deployment.

title: \textsc{IH-Benchmark}: A Conflict-Centered Benchmark for Instruction-Hierarchy Robustness in LLM Applications
summary: When a language model receives conflicting instructions from different priority levels, which one does it actually follow? This question lies at the heart of reliable LLM deployment. Existing benchmarks answer this only partially, often focusing on a single hierarchy edge or adapting public datasets with limited tool-use coverage. We present IH-Benchmark, a conflict-centered benchmark for instruction-hierarchy robustness across direct system-user conflicts (S>U) and tool-mediated user-tool (U>T) conflicts. IH-Benchmark is built from a human-authored taxonomy of 44 constraint families across generic, health, finance, retail, and coding settings, and evaluates scenarios with a uniform binary pass/fail protocol combining a predicate DSL with category-scoped LLM judges. Across 37 evaluated models, hierarchy compliance ranges from 98.2% to 20.5%. We find that strong S>U compliance is not a reliable proxy for U>T robustness: several models preserve system constraints under direct user conflict but degrade sharply when conflicting instructions appear in tool outputs. Constraint hardening also reveals a split between models: some failures are largely fixed by stronger warnings, while others persist across all strictness levels. Finally, the most revealing failures are often subtle rather than overtly dangerous; models resist unauthorized purchases or bulk ticket closure more reliably than injected disclaimers or small factual distortions. These results suggest that instruction-hierarchy robustness is not a single capability, but a set of behaviors that must be evaluated across conflict surfaces, constraint types, and attack presentations.

AI.tldr: IH-Benchmark evaluates how language models handle conflicting instructions across priority levels (system > user, user > tool), revealing that strong compliance in one conflict surface does not predict robustness in another, and that models resist overt attacks better than subtle distortions.
AI.motivation: Existing instruction-hierarchy evaluations are incomplete — they focus on single conflict edges or lack comprehensive tool-use coverage. Reliable LLM deployment requires understanding which instructions models prioritize when conflicts arise across system, user, and tool-mediated contexts.
AI.method: The authors created IH-Benchmark, a conflict-centered benchmark built from a human-authored taxonomy of 44 constraint families spanning generic, health, finance, retail, and coding domains. It evaluates S>U (system vs. user) and U>T (user vs. tool) conflicts using a binary pass/fail protocol that combines a predicate domain-specific language with category-scoped LLM judges. 37 models were evaluated, and constraint hardening (varying warning strictness) was tested.
AI.result: Hierarchy compliance across 37 models ranged from 98.2% to 20.5%. Key findings: (1) strong S>U compliance does not predict U>T robustness — models preserving system constraints under direct user conflict often degrade when tool outputs contain conflicting instructions; (2) constraint hardening splits models — some failures resolve with stronger warnings while others persist; (3) models resist overt violations (unauthorized purchases, bulk ticket closure) better than subtle ones (injected disclaimers, factual distortions).
AI.conclusion: Instruction-hierarchy robustness is not a single capability but a collection of behaviors requiring evaluation across multiple conflict surfaces, constraint types, and attack presentations. Strong performance on one dimension does not guarantee robustness on others.

title: SAFAARI: Schema-Aware Framework for Accelerated Advertiser Response Intelligence
summary: The evolution of customer support systems is rapidly advancing with agentic chatbots, yet these systems face significant limitations when accessing enterprise data without predefined API endpoints. This paper presents SAFAARI (Schema-Aware Framework for Accelerated Advertiser Response Intelligence), a multi-agent framework that addresses the critical bottleneck of schema linking in Natural Language to SQL (NL-to-SQL) systems through specialized content, metadata, and orchestration agents. We also introduce SEAL (Schema Evaluation and Accuracy in Language-to-SQL), a novel composite metric that holistically evaluates system performance while penalizing inconsistent results. Through systematic experimentation with five feature set configurations, SAFAARI achieves an 81.66% SEAL score (6.65% improvement over baseline), with notable gains in datapoint accuracy (5.51%) and schema-linking precision (4.69%). The framework's effectiveness is validated through human-in-the-loop evaluation with domain experts, which proves its adaptability across diverse support domains. By automating the labor-intensive process of schema linking and query generation, our framework demonstrates 8x reduction in development time while maintaining high accuracy. The solution streamlines API development and enhances self-service capabilities, particularly benefiting customer support enterprises with complex data ecosystems.

AI.tldr: SAFAARI is a multi-agent framework that improves NL-to-SQL systems by addressing schema linking bottlenecks using specialized agents. It introduces SEAL, a composite evaluation metric, achieves 81.66% SEAL score (6.65% improvement), and demonstrates 8x faster development time for customer support enterprises.
AI.motivation: Agentic chatbots face significant limitations when accessing enterprise data without predefined API endpoints. The core bottleneck is schema linking in NL-to-SQL systems — mapping natural language queries to database schemas is labor-intensive and error-prone, particularly in complex enterprise data ecosystems used by customer support organizations.
AI.method: SAFAARI (Schema-Aware Framework for Accelerated Advertiser Response Intelligence) employs a multi-agent architecture with three specialized agent types: content agents, metadata agents, and orchestration agents. The framework is evaluated using SEAL (Schema Evaluation and Accuracy in Language-to-SQL), a novel composite metric that holistically assesses system performance while penalizing inconsistent results. Five feature set configurations were systematically tested, supplemented by human-in-the-loop evaluation with domain experts.
AI.result: SAFAARI achieved an 81.66% SEAL score, representing a 6.65% improvement over baseline. Specific gains include a 5.51% improvement in datapoint accuracy and a 4.69% improvement in schema-linking precision. The framework demonstrated an 8x reduction in development time while maintaining high accuracy. Human-in-the-loop evaluation confirmed adaptability across diverse support domains.
AI.conclusion: SAFAARI effectively automates schema linking and query generation, substantially reducing development time while preserving accuracy. The framework streamlines API development and enhances self-service capabilities, offering particular value to customer support enterprises managing complex data ecosystems.
