title: LLM4OSC: Profile-Bound Natural Language Control with Deterministic Validation for Open Sound Control
summary: Open Sound Control (OSC) is the dominant wire protocol for real-time parametric control in professional audio, live performance, and virtual production. Large language models can emit plausible OSC, but they hallucinate addresses, mishandle type tags, and fail under paraphrase- unacceptable in show-critical contexts. We present LLM4OSC, a local-first architecture in which models propose structured intent JSON over a human-reviewed device profile, and deterministic code validates, clamps, and encodes before any UDP send. We introduce a frozen evaluation harness with CI gates on wrong-send rate: mismatches that would still pass validation and transmit. On a Max/MSP hero profile (12 patterns; 8 literal + 8 paraphrase + 4 refusal cases), after profile tag enrichment, symbolic slot fill, NL refine, and a retrieval confidence gate, backends B0--B3 all pass frozen gates (100% semantic accuracy, 0% wrong-send). B0 (rules) remains the production default at ~0.05ms; LLM backends remain ~3-4s. Historical few-shot B2 accuracy of 62.5% rises to 100% on this suite only after symbolic post-processing- not because the 0.5B model alone becomes show-safe. We argue for propose-validate-send and wrong-send rate as first-class metrics for language-to-control systems.

AI.tldr: LLM4OSC is a local-first architecture that uses LLMs to propose structured intent JSON validated against a device profile, then deterministically encodes valid OSC messages. The system introduces wrong-send rate as a metric and achieves 100% semantic accuracy with 0% wrong-send on a Max/MSP test suite, with symbolic post-processing being essential for correctness.
AI.motivation: LLMs can generate plausible OSC messages but hallucinate addresses, mishandle type tags, and fail under paraphrase — unacceptable in show-critical live performance contexts. Existing approaches lack safety guarantees and formal evaluation metrics for language-to-control systems.
AI.method: LLM4OSC employs a propose-validate-send architecture: (1) models emit structured intent JSON constrained by a human-reviewed device profile, (2) deterministic code validates, clamps, and encodes OSC messages before any UDP transmission. A frozen evaluation harness measures wrong-send rate (mismatches that would pass validation and transmit). The pipeline includes profile tag enrichment, symbolic slot fill, NL refinement, and a retrieval confidence gate. Four backends (B0 rules-based, B1–B3 LLM-based) were tested on a Max/MSP hero profile with 12 patterns (8 literal, 8 paraphrase, 4 refusal cases).
AI.result: All backends (B0–B3) achieve 100% semantic accuracy and 0% wrong-send rate on the frozen test suite. B0 (rules-based) operates at ~0.05ms, while LLM backends require ~3–4s. Historical few-shot B2 accuracy of 62.5% rises to 100% only after symbolic post-processing — the 0.5B model alone is not show-safe. The retrieval confidence gate and symbolic slot fill are critical components enabling safe transmission.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that propose-validate-send architectures and wrong-send rate should become first-class design patterns and metrics for language-to-control systems, particularly in safety-critical, show-critical domains like live performance and virtual production.

title: Beyond Single-Episode Optimization: Sliding-Window Aware Generative Auto-Bidding for Long-Term Advertising Effectiveness
summary: Auto-bidding systems optimize bids to maximize value under efficiency constraints such as Cost-Per-Action (CPA). Existing methods treat each day as an independent episode. However, many advertisers produce value so sparsely that per-day efficiency ratios become statistically unreliable, undermining advertiser retention. Platforms therefore evaluate window-level efficiency over sliding windows of $W{=}7$ days, ensuring fair evaluation and long-term advertising effectiveness. This creates cross-episode coupling: each day's bidding decisions affect up to $W$ overlapping windows, so setting daily targets requires anticipating future market conditions. We propose SWAG-Bid (Sliding-Window Aware Generative Auto-Bidding), a hierarchical framework decomposing this challenge into episode-level planning and step-level execution. The planner uses a Masked Trajectory Model to forecast markets and generate candidate plans, scored across all overlapping windows by Multi-Window Model Predictive Control Sampling (MWMS) with exponential confidence decay. The controller adjusts reliance on this guidance through a state-adaptive gate, Per-Step Gated Adaptive Layer Normalization (PSG-AdaLN), complemented by Return-to-Go and Cost-to-Go channels carrying budget and constraint information. Experiments on AuctionNet-Sparse and online A/B tests on AliExpress show that SWAG-Bid achieves competitive constraint satisfaction and value acquisition under sliding-window evaluation.

AI.tldr: SWAG-Bid is a hierarchical auto-bidding framework that optimizes bids under sliding-window (7-day) efficiency constraints, using a masked trajectory planner with multi-window model predictive control and an adaptive controller to handle cross-episode coupling in sparse-conversion advertising.
AI.motivation: Existing auto-bidding methods treat each day independently, but many advertisers have sparse conversions, making daily CPA statistically unreliable. Platforms evaluate bidder performance over sliding windows (e.g., 7 days), which introduces cross-episode coupling: each day's bids affect multiple overlapping windows. This demands anticipatory planning across episodes.
AI.method: SWAG-Bid uses a hierarchical design: (1) an episode-level planner employing a Masked Trajectory Model to forecast markets and generate candidate plans, scored by Multi-Window Model Predictive Control Sampling (MWMS) with exponential confidence decay across all overlapping windows; (2) a step-level controller with a state-adaptive gate (PSG-AdaLN) that modulates reliance on planner guidance, plus Return-to-Go and Cost-to-Go channels that convey budget and constraint information.
AI.result: Experiments on AuctionNet-Sparse and online A/B tests on AliExpress demonstrate that SWAG-Bid achieves competitive constraint satisfaction and value acquisition under sliding-window evaluation.
AI.conclusion: SWAG-Bid effectively addresses the sliding-window evaluation paradigm in sparse-conversion scenarios, offering a principled approach to cross-episode coupling that ensures both advertiser retention and long-term advertising effectiveness.

title: REPREC: Representation Driven Parameter-Efficient Recommendation System
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have been applied to sequential recommendation by formulating it as a natural language task. Previous work has improved personalization by incorporating collaborative and sequential signals through input conditioning or LLM fine-tuning. However, existing approaches often rely on one or more of the following: LLM fine-tuning, additional architectural modules, representation distillation, or item-level conditioning over long interaction histories, increasing training complexity and deployment cost. We propose REPREC, a lightweight framework that reformulates LLM-based sequential recommendation through lightweight user representation alignment. REPREC maps a fixed-size user embedding from a frozen sequential encoder into a small set of learned soft tokens through a lightweight MLP injector that conditions a frozen LLM, leaving both pretrained backbones unchanged while training only the injector. We conducted exhaustive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets and demonstrate that REPREC consistently outperforms LoRA while remaining compatible with different pretrained sequential encoders and LLM backbones, enabling a modular and production-friendly recommendation pipeline without modifying either pretrained component. The gains are particularly pronounced for casual and core users across all datasets, highlighting REPREC's effectiveness in low-data regimes. Finally, when trained on short prompt histories and evaluated with longer contexts, REPREC maintains 85-100% of LoRA's performance while reducing per-epoch training time by an average of 1.51X, demonstrating an effective balance between recommendation quality and computational efficiency for production deployment. The code is available at https://github.com/phdbotcode/REPREC

AI.tldr: REPREC is a lightweight framework for LLM-based sequential recommendation that aligns frozen user embeddings with a frozen LLM via a trainable MLP injector using soft tokens, outperforming LoRA while reducing training cost.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based sequential recommendation methods rely on LLM fine-tuning, extra architectural modules, representation distillation, or item-level conditioning over long histories, all of which increase training complexity and deployment cost. There is a need for a lightweight, modular approach that preserves pretrained backbones.
AI.method: REPREC uses a frozen sequential encoder to produce a fixed-size user embedding, which is then mapped by a lightweight MLP injector into a small set of learned soft tokens. These soft tokens condition a frozen LLM. Only the injector is trained; both the sequential encoder and LLM remain unchanged.
AI.result: REPREC consistently outperforms LoRA across multiple benchmark datasets, is compatible with different pretrained sequential encoders and LLM backbones, shows pronounced gains for casual/core users in low-data regimes, and maintains 85–100% of LoRA's performance with 1.51× faster per-epoch training when evaluated with longer contexts.
AI.conclusion: REPREC offers a modular, production-friendly recommendation pipeline that balances recommendation quality and computational efficiency without modifying pretrained components, making it suitable for real-world deployment.

title: Aletheia: An Offline-First Clinical Decision Support System for Differential Diagnosis in Low-Resource Healthcare Settings
summary: Access to specialist clinical expertise remains severely limited across sub-Saharan Africa, where physician-to-patient ratios can fall below 1:25,000 in rural settings. Existing AI-assisted diagnostic tools predominantly require reliable internet connectivity and high-specification hardware, rendering them impractical for frontline healthcare workers in district hospitals and health centres. This paper presents Aletheia, an offline-first clinical decision support system designed for low-resource healthcare contexts across sub-Saharan Africa. Aletheia is built upon Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, fine-tuned using Quantised Low- Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) on a curated dataset of 27,000 clinical reasoning samples spanning 50 disease conditions with elevated prevalence in East Africa. Evaluation demonstrates a Top-1 diagnostic accuracy of 80.0%, Top-3 accuracy of 100.0%, BERTScore-F1 of 0.909, and METEOR of 0.467 across ten representative clinical case categories. The system achieves an Expected Calibration Error (ECE) of 0.275 and passes the Africa Deep Tech Challenge 2026 (ADTC 2026) memory budget constraint of 7 168 MB, achieving a peak inference RAM of approximately 3 630 MB on the standardised benchmark laptop. These results demonstrate the feasibility of deploying large language model-based clinical reasoning at the primary care level in resource-constrained settings without cloud infrastructure.

AI.tldr: Aletheia is an offline-first clinical decision support system built on a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct model using QLoRA on 27,000 clinical cases across 50 East African diseases. It achieves 80% Top-1 and 100% Top-3 diagnostic accuracy with ~3.6 GB peak RAM, demonstrating feasibility of LLM-based clinical reasoning at primary care level without internet.
AI.motivation: Access to specialist clinical expertise is critically limited in sub-Saharan Africa (physician-to-patient ratios below 1:25,000 in rural areas). Existing AI diagnostic tools require reliable internet and high-spec hardware, making them impractical for frontline healthcare workers in district hospitals and health centres.
AI.method: The authors developed Aletheia using Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct as the base model, fine-tuned with Quantised Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) on a curated dataset of 27,000 clinical reasoning samples covering 50 disease conditions prevalent in East Africa. The system is designed to operate offline on standard benchmark hardware.
AI.result: Top-1 diagnostic accuracy: 80.0%; Top-3 accuracy: 100.0%; BERTScore-F1: 0.909; METEOR: 0.467; Expected Calibration Error (ECE): 0.275. Peak inference RAM of ~3,630 MB, well within the ADTC 2026 memory budget of 7,168 MB.
AI.conclusion: Deploying LLM-based clinical reasoning at the primary care level in resource-constrained, offline settings is feasible. Aletheia demonstrates that a compact, fine-tuned language model can deliver clinically meaningful diagnostic support without cloud infrastructure, directly addressing the access gap in sub-Saharan Africa.

title: SpeechLLM Meets Federated Learning for End-to-End ASR: English and Italian Case Studies
comment: Accepted at the 2nd International Conference on Federated Learning and Intelligent Computing Systems (FLICS2026)
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving training of automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems across distributed data sources, yet its application to large-scale speech language models (SpeechLLMs) remains unexplored. This paper presents the first systematic study of federated training for SpeechLLM-based end-to-end ASR systems. We design a communication-efficient federated optimization strategy tailored to the unique challenges of SpeechLLM architectures, addressing high-dimensional parameter spaces, gradient communication overhead, and computational constraints in distributed settings. Through extensive empirical evaluation on monolingual ASR tasks in English and Italian, we demonstrate the effectiveness and stability of our federated approach compared to centralized training baselines across diverse acoustic conditions and speaking styles. Additionally, we conduct a comprehensive ablation study analyzing the impact of different speech encoder architectures on monolingual English ASR performance within the federated framework, providing insights into optimal model configurations for decentralized training. Our results achieve competitive word error rates while reducing communication costs, establishing practical foundations for federated SpeechLLM deployment in real-world multilingual scenarios.

AI.tldr: First systematic study applying federated learning to SpeechLLM-based end-to-end ASR, proposing a communication-efficient optimization strategy that achieves competitive word error rates while reducing communication costs across English and Italian monolingual tasks.
AI.motivation: Federated learning for ASR preserves privacy across distributed data, but its application to large-scale speech language models (SpeechLLMs) remains unexplored due to challenges like high-dimensional parameter spaces, gradient communication overhead, and computational constraints.
AI.method: The authors design a communication-efficient federated optimization strategy specifically for SpeechLLM architectures, and validate it through empirical evaluation on monolingual English and Italian ASR tasks, plus an ablation study on speech encoder architectures.
AI.result: The federated approach achieves competitive word error rates (WER) compared to centralized training baselines, across diverse acoustic conditions and speaking styles, while reducing communication costs. The ablation study provides insights into optimal encoder configurations for decentralized training.
AI.conclusion: Federated SpeechLLM training is both effective and stable, establishing practical foundations for real-world multilingual deployment of privacy-preserving SpeechLLM-based ASR systems.

title: Does Runtime Topology Context Improve LLM-Generated Kubernetes Security Patches?
comment: Accepted at the Workshop on the Use of Large Language Models for Cybersecurity (LLMSec), co-located with ESORICS 2026
summary: Kubernetes is central to the cloud-native ecosystem, orchestrating containerised workloads. Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) can automate cluster security remediation, generating configuration patches from Kubernetes Security Posture Management (KSPM) findings without human authoring. Such systems, however, prompt the model with each finding in isolation from the live service call graph, assuming general hardening knowledge suffices. This assumption breaks down whenever a patch must preserve a runtime service dependency invisible to the model: an otherwise compliant fix then carries a destructive functional blast radius, crashing downstream callers or silently severing call edges across the cluster. Whether live cluster context improves patch correctness has not been measured under controlled conditions across multiple dependency classes. We introduce KuTIE (Kubernetes Topology Intelligence Engine), which builds a live cluster context from Istio call edges, Trivy KSPM findings, and the service-account bindings a workload reads, and conditions LLM patch generation on it. It is evaluated on VulnCare, a purpose-built 36-deployment, four-namespace healthcare cluster with 31 injectable findings across seven dependency classes, each labelled by topology dependence against cluster ground truth. Across 248 trials, topology context raises topology-dependent patch correctness from 11.1% to 78.0% ($Δ= 0.669$), a gap that holds for every model and for six of seven classes, from credential and network-policy ($Δ= 0.95$) to role-based access control ($Δ= 0.31$); a topology-independent control exhibits no such effect ($Δ= 0.0$), isolating the result from generic prompt enrichment. Supplying the live service-call graph and the service-account bindings it exposes thus improves remediation of topology-dependent findings well beyond scanner-only context.

AI.tldr: KuTIE leverages live cluster topology (Istio call edges, KSPM findings, service-account bindings) to condition LLM-based Kubernetes security patch generation, boosting topology-dependent fix correctness from 11.1% to 78.0% across 248 trials on a custom 36-deployment healthcare cluster.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based KSPM remediation systems process each security finding in isolation, lacking visibility into runtime service dependencies. This causes otherwise compliant patches to break downstream callers or sever call edges, producing a destructive functional blast radius. No prior work has measured whether live cluster context improves patch correctness under controlled conditions across multiple dependency classes.
AI.method: KuTIE constructs live cluster context from Istio service-call edges, Trivy KSPM findings, and workload service-account bindings, then conditions LLM patch generation on this topology. Evaluation uses VulnCare, a purpose-built 36-deployment, four-namespace healthcare cluster with 31 injectable findings spanning seven dependency classes, each labeled for topology dependence against cluster ground truth. 248 trials were run across multiple models.
AI.result: Topology context raised topology-dependent patch correctness from 11.1% to 78.0% (Δ = 0.669), with the effect holding across all models and six of seven dependency classes. Gains ranged from Δ = 0.95 for credential and network-policy classes to Δ = 0.31 for RBAC. A topology-independent control showed no effect (Δ = 0.0), confirming the result is not due to generic prompt enrichment.
AI.conclusion: Supplying the live service-call graph and exposed service-account bindings significantly improves LLM-based remediation of topology-dependent Kubernetes security findings, well beyond scanner-only context. The effect is robust across models and dependency classes.

title: Bridging Compute- and Data-Optimal Pretraining
summary: Classical compute-optimal scaling laws assume an unbounded supply of fresh pretraining data, yet pretraining is increasingly entering a regime in which compute grows faster than the availability of high-quality data. We propose Compute-Data (CD) scaling laws, a unified framework that bridges compute-optimal scaling, where data scales freely with compute, and data-optimal scaling, where the corpus is fixed while compute can grow without bound. CD scaling extends classical scaling laws by introducing a token-effectiveness function, $η$, which quantifies the value of a derived token-produced, for example, through multi-epoch repetition or paraphrasing-relative to a fresh token, ranging from a perfect substitute to having no value. We fit $η$ for two data-expansion strategies, multi-epoch repetition and paraphrasing, across model sizes from 14M to 600M parameters using the Dolma-3 corpus. We find that token effectiveness is far from constant: it depends jointly on model size, the tokens-per-parameter ratio, and the amount of derived data, and it saturates as the corpus is expanded. The functional form of $η$ implies diminishing returns when substituting compute for data as either model size or data availability increases. It also partitions training into three operational regimes---compute-bound, data-bound, and model-bound---and shows that classical compute-optimal allocation is suboptimal across most practically relevant settings.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Compute-Data (CD) scaling laws, which unify compute-optimal and data-optimal scaling by modeling token effectiveness (η) for derived data (e.g., repeated or paraphrased tokens). It shows that classical compute-optimal scaling is suboptimal in most practical settings.
AI.motivation: Classical scaling laws assume unlimited fresh data, but in practice, compute growth is outpacing the availability of high-quality pretraining data. There is a need for scaling laws that account for limited data regimes where strategies like multi-epoch repetition and paraphrasing are used.
AI.method: Introduces a token-effectiveness function η that quantifies the value of derived tokens relative to fresh tokens (from perfect substitute to zero value). Fits η empirically for multi-epoch repetition and paraphrasing across model sizes (14M–600M parameters) using the Dolma-3 corpus. Derives CD scaling laws that partition training into three regimes: compute-bound, data-bound, and model-bound.
AI.result: Token effectiveness η is not constant — it depends jointly on model size, tokens-per-parameter ratio, and amount of derived data, and saturates as the corpus is expanded. The functional form exhibits diminishing returns when substituting compute for data. Classical compute-optimal allocation is shown to be suboptimal across most practically relevant settings.
AI.conclusion: CD scaling laws provide a more realistic framework for allocating compute when data is limited. The three-regime partition offers practical guidance: practitioners should identify whether they are compute-bound, data-bound, or model-bound to optimally allocate resources.

title: Two Views, One Voice: Evidence-Grounded Conversational Music Recommendation
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. 4th-place solution (team swyoo) in the Blind-B industry track of the ACM RecSys Challenge 2026
summary: Traditional conversational recommenders entangle retrieval and response generation within a single text interface, so exact entity cues fade as the dialogue's intent evolves, which compromises explanation credibility. We address this within the ACM RecSys Challenge 2026, which mandates both top-20 ranking and evidence-grounded response generation. This paper presents the third-place solution by team "swyoo" for the Blind-B industry track. We decouple retrieval and response into separate pipelines connected strictly via ranked tracks and metadata. Retrieval combines a hybrid lexical-dense pool for exact matching with a task-adapted pool driven by fine-tuned Qwen 8B adapters. Candidates are calibrated via LightGBM, then routed to an evidence-grounded propose-assign-select (PAS) framework to structure responses. This system also ranked second on the explanation-quality leaderboard in the final blind evaluation. Our findings demonstrate that: (i) isolating retrieval and response preserves both catalog cues and fluid intent; (ii) structuring generation via explicit evidence assignment is key to this near-best-in-class explanation reliability.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a third-place solution for the ACM RecSys Challenge 2026 Blind-B track, which decouples retrieval and response generation to improve explanation credibility in conversational recommenders. The system combines hybrid retrieval, LightGBM calibration, and a propose-assign-select (PAS) framework for evidence-grounded responses, achieving second place on explanation quality.
AI.motivation: Traditional conversational recommenders entangle retrieval and response generation in a single interface, causing exact entity cues to fade as dialogue intent evolves, which undermines explanation credibility. The RecSys Challenge 2026 mandates both top-20 ranking and evidence-grounded response generation, motivating a decoupled architecture.
AI.method: The system decouples retrieval and response into separate pipelines connected via ranked tracks and metadata. Retrieval uses a hybrid lexical-dense pool for exact matching plus a task-adapted pool with fine-tuned Qwen 8B adapters. Candidates are calibrated via LightGBM and then routed to an evidence-grounded propose-assign-select (PAS) framework for structured response generation.
AI.result: The system achieved third place overall in the Blind-B industry track and ranked second on the explanation-quality leaderboard in the final blind evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Two key findings: (i) isolating retrieval and response preserves both catalog cues and fluid conversational intent; (ii) structuring generation via explicit evidence assignment (PAS) is critical for achieving near-best-in-class explanation reliability.

title: AdaKP: Online Adaptive Knowledge-Point Selection for Reasoning-Oriented Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is a powerful paradigm for eliciting reasoning in large language models, yet it suffers from severe reward sparsity on competition-level mathematics. A common remedy injects atomic knowledge points (KPs) - short natural-language hints distilled from gold solutions - into the prompt. Existing methods, however, either fix this selection once offline or merely scale the monolithic quantity of injected text, leaving untouched the most informative axis of choice: which subset of atomic KPs to inject, and when. We introduce AdaKP, an online selector that re-chooses each problem's KP subset over the course of RL training. At its core is an entropy proxy that scores a KP by the reduction in next-token entropy it induces - a single inexpensive forward pass, with a provable bound on its truncation bias - in place of expensive rollout-based estimation. Three lightweight mechanisms make this signal usable online: a momentum smoother that absorbs per-step noise, a retirement-and-revival manager that prunes weak KPs while preserving exploration, and an adaptive scheduler that front-loads re-evaluations into early training. AdaKP further contributes a pre-flight validation gate that certifies the proxy against a leave-one-out ground truth before any expensive run is launched, turning method-level risk into a falsifiable check. Realized as a fully additive fork of a standard DAPO+GRPO trainer with no optimizer changes, AdaKP improves over a strong static-selection baseline on all eight competition-mathematics benchmarks at negligible added cost, positioning online, validated KP-subset selection as a practical and as-yet under-explored axis for reasoning-oriented reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: AdaKP is an online knowledge-point selector for RL-based mathematical reasoning in LLMs that dynamically chooses which atomic hints to inject during training, using an entropy-based proxy instead of expensive rollouts, with mechanisms for smoothing, pruning, and adaptive scheduling.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards on competition-level math suffers from severe reward sparsity. Existing methods inject atomic knowledge points (KPs) as hints but fix the selection offline or merely scale quantity — missing the critical axis of *which* KPs and *when* to inject them during training.
AI.method: AdaKP uses an entropy proxy that scores KPs by measuring next-token entropy reduction via a single forward pass (with provable truncation bias bounds), avoiding costly rollout-based estimation. Three mechanisms make this practical online: (1) a momentum smoother for per-step noise, (2) a retirement-and-revival manager that prunes weak KPs while preserving exploration, and (3) an adaptive scheduler that concentrates re-evaluations early in training. A pre-flight validation gate certifies the proxy against leave-one-out ground truth before expensive runs.
AI.result: AdaKP, implemented as a fully additive fork of DAPO+GRPO with no optimizer changes, outperforms strong static-selection baselines across all eight competition-mathematics benchmarks at negligible added computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Online, validated KP-subset selection is a practical and under-explored axis for improving reasoning-oriented RL, and AdaKP demonstrates that lightweight entropy-based proxy signals can effectively guide dynamic hint injection without expensive rollouts.

title: WorkSurface-Bench: Benchmarking Enterprise Agents on Multi-Surface Knowledge Routing
summary: Enterprise agents often need to integrate heterogeneous knowledge sources: documents for narrative facts, tables for computation, and dependency graphs for file relationships. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate retrieval or tool use without distinguishing whether an agent first selects the appropriate knowledge sources. We introduce WorkSurface-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating this capability as surface routing. It contains 1,151 atomic tasks derived from persona-scoped Workspace-Bench-Lite workspaces, spanning document, table, graph, and cross-surface questions. Its reference answers are auditable: table answers are reproduced through executed DuckDB queries, document answers are grounded in verified text spans, and graph answers are traced to source dependency annotations. We evaluate four model backbones across six controlled agent settings, yielding 27,624 protocol-error-free trajectories. Under gold-constrained tool access, agents achieve 98.7-99.8 Route F1, while Answer remains only 56.1-75.3 percent, showing that correct surface selection is necessary but insufficient for task completion. Matched interventions further show that surface hints improve Answer for three of four models, whereas removing irrelevant tools primarily improves routing and efficiency. In an independent three-annotator audit, all 200 sampled tasks pass all six quality criteria by majority vote, with 192 receiving unanimous judgments on every criterion. We release the dataset, construction pipeline, scoring code, and agent harness at https://github.com/haolpku/WorkSurface-Bench.

AI.tldr: WorkSurface-Bench is a benchmark of 1,151 tasks for evaluating how agents route questions to the correct knowledge surface (document, table, graph, or cross-surface) before attempting to answer. It shows that near-perfect surface routing (>98% F1) still yields only 56-75% answer accuracy, demonstrating that correct surface selection is necessary but insufficient.
AI.motivation: Enterprise agents must integrate heterogeneous knowledge sources—documents, tables, and dependency graphs—but existing benchmarks conflate retrieval/tool-use quality with the prior decision of which knowledge surface to query. There is no benchmark that isolates and evaluates surface routing as a distinct capability.
AI.method: The authors constructed WorkSurface-Bench with 1,151 atomic tasks from persona-scoped workspaces. Tasks span document, table, graph, and cross-surface questions. Reference answers are auditable: table answers via executed DuckDB queries, document answers via verified text spans, and graph answers via source dependency annotations. Four model backbones were evaluated across six controlled agent settings (gold-constrained tool access, surface hints, irrelevant tool removal), yielding 27,624 protocol-error-free trajectories. An independent three-annotator audit assessed 200 sampled tasks on six quality criteria.
AI.result: Under gold-constrained tool access, agents achieved 98.7–99.8 Route F1, but Answer accuracy remained only 56.1–75.3%. Surface hints improved Answer for three of four models, while removing irrelevant tools primarily improved routing and efficiency. In the audit, all 200 sampled tasks passed all six quality criteria by majority vote; 192 received unanimous judgments on every criterion.
AI.conclusion: Surface routing is a distinct and measurable capability that is necessary but insufficient for task completion. WorkSurface-Bench provides a rigorous, auditable framework for evaluating this capability, and the authors release the full dataset, pipeline, scoring code, and agent harness to facilitate further research.

title: ScoreShield: Differentially Private Release of Similarity Scores
summary: A growing number of applications, such as biometrics and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), rely on cosine similarity scores computed between vector embeddings of text, images, or audio. These systems return similarity scores through their APIs for ranking and verification. However, such releases can leak information about individual records and enable membership inference attacks. While differential privacy (DP) provides a principled metric for quantifying attack risks, naïve application of DP mechanisms---such as adding i.i.d. Gaussian noise to vector entries---leads to excessive distortion (i.e., low utility) at a given privacy constraint that scales poorly with the number of released scores. We propose \textsc{ScoreShield}, a perturb-then-project mechanism that adds Gaussian noise calibrated to global sensitivity of the chosen score release regime and then projects the result onto the feasibility set of valid cosine objects. \textsc{ScoreShield} satisfies $(\varepsilon,δ)$-DP for releasing similarity score vectors and Gram matrices. We provide utility guarantees for the exact Frobenius metric projection used in the risk analysis, and prove convergence to feasibility for the practical averaged alternating-projection solver used for large-scale Gram releases. For full pairwise cosine Gram release under record-level replacement adjacency, the exact-projection bound improves the $n$-dependence of squared Frobenius risk from $Θ(n^3)$ for the naïve Gaussian baseline to $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ for fixed privacy parameters, with sharper local bounds at low-rank Grams. We evaluate the mechanism across RAG, face recognition, semantic retrieval, image similarity, and recommender-system tasks.

AI.tldr: ScoreShield introduces a perturb-then-project mechanism for differentially private release of cosine similarity scores and Gram matrices. By adding Gaussian noise calibrated to global sensitivity and projecting onto the feasibility set of valid cosine objects, it significantly improves utility over naïve i.i.d. Gaussian perturbation, reducing squared Frobenius risk dependence from Θ(n³) to O(n²) for full pairwise Gram release.
AI.motivation: Many applications (biometrics, RAG, retrieval systems) expose cosine similarity scores via APIs, creating vulnerability to membership inference attacks. While DP offers principled protection, the naïve approach of adding i.i.d. Gaussian noise to vector entries causes excessive distortion that scales poorly with the number of released scores, motivating a more structure-aware mechanism.
AI.method: ScoreShield uses a perturb-then-project framework: (1) add Gaussian noise calibrated to the global sensitivity of the chosen score release regime (similarity vectors or Gram matrices), then (2) project the noisy result onto the feasibility set of valid cosine objects via Frobenius metric projection. For large-scale Gram releases, an averaged alternating-projection solver is used with proven convergence to feasibility. Privacy guarantees satisfy (ε,δ)-DP under record-level replacement adjacency.
AI.result: The exact-projection bound improves squared Frobenius risk dependence on n from Θ(n³) (naïve Gaussian) to O(n²) for fixed privacy parameters, with sharper local bounds at low-rank Grams. Empirical evaluation across RAG, face recognition, semantic retrieval, image similarity, and recommender-system tasks demonstrates practical utility gains.
AI.conclusion: ScoreShield demonstrates that enforcing geometric consistency (projecting onto the feasible cosine similarity manifold) after perturbation substantially reduces distortion compared to unstructured noise addition, enabling practical DP-protected cosine similarity release at scale.

title: Explanation-Bound Tool Execution for AI Agents: Server-Verified Action Claims Without Trusting Model Rationales
summary: Tool-using agents expose structured calls but commonly attach free-form rationales. Such rationales are neither authorization nor reliable introspection. We present Explanation-Bound Tool Execution (EBTE), a claim-carrying mediation layer that converts decision-relevant rationale content into typed action claims and checks them against server-held intent, policy, payload, tool, risk, provenance, and freshness facts. EBTE cannot widen baseline authority: conflicts deny, incomplete or uncertain claims review, and only matching claims remain eligible for governed execution. We formalize this composition under explicit mediation and trusted-fact assumptions and implement a versioned reference profile with minimized audit packets. Across 136 authored conformance scenarios, the full profile matches all specified dispositions, admits none of 96 designated hard contradictions, and passes 232 metamorphic checks; these results validate the included profile rather than population performance. A draft-only reference integration forwards none of 48 authored hard cases under EBTE while preserving all 16 soft-review and 4 aligned draft paths. In a frozen 2026-07-12 exploratory 224-attempt hosted-model record, the historical generation/runner agreement counts are 71/96, 66/96, and 19/32; a separately labeled zero-call post-hoc revalidation of the preserved minimized claims under the current pipeline yields 70/96, 65/96, and 17/32. In an AgentDojo-derived semantic check, existing high-risk controls already make all 12 attack proposals non-allow; EBTE additionally resolves them as deny. These results support the feasibility and diagnostic value of server-checked action claims, not rationale faithfulness, human-review benefit, representative attack resistance, or production safety.

AI.tldr: EBTE introduces a mediation layer that converts free-form agent rationales into typed, verifiable action claims, then checks them against server-held facts (intent, policy, risk, etc.). Conflicting claims are denied; only matching claims execute. The paper formalizes this composition, implements a reference profile, and validates it across conformance scenarios, hard-contradiction tests, and metamorphic checks, demonstrating feasibility of server-checked action claims.
AI.motivation: Tool-using AI agents typically emit structured function calls alongside unstructured rationales. These rationales are neither authoritative for authorization nor reliable for introspection—they can be inconsistent, deceptive, or misaligned with actual actions. The motivation is to bridge this gap by making rationale content verifiable and actionable through a typed claim mechanism, enabling the server (tool provider) to mediate execution based on trustworthy checks rather than trusting agent self-reporting.
AI.method: EBTE operates as a claim-carrying mediation layer. The agent attaches typed action claims (covering intent, policy, payload, tool, risk, provenance, and freshness) to its tool calls. The server checks these claims against its own held facts. The composition is formalized under explicit mediation and trusted-fact assumptions. Three outcomes are possible: (1) conflicts result in denial, (2) incomplete/uncertain claims trigger review, and (3) matched claims proceed to governed execution. EBTE cannot expand baseline authority beyond what the server already permits. A versioned reference profile with minimized audit packets is implemented. Evaluation uses 136 authored conformance scenarios, 96 hard contradictions, 232 metamorphic checks, plus AgentDojo-derived semantic attacks and a frozen 2026-07-12 exploratory hosted-model record.
AI.result: The full reference profile matches all specified dispositions across 136 conformance scenarios, admits none of 96 hard contradictions, and passes 232 metamorphic checks. A draft-only integration forwards none of 48 hard cases but preserves all 16 soft-review and 4 aligned paths. In the 224-attempt hosted-model record, historical agreement counts are 71/96, 66/96, and 19/32; post-hoc revalidation yields 70/96, 65/96, and 17/32. In the AgentDojo semantic check, existing high-risk controls already block all 12 attacks; EBTE additionally resolves them as deny. The authors emphasize these results validate the included profile, not population performance, rationale faithfulness, human-review benefit, representative attack resistance, or production safety.
AI.conclusion: EBTE demonstrates the feasibility and diagnostic value of server-checked action claims as a mediation mechanism between agent rationales and tool execution. The work does not claim to improve rationale faithfulness, provide human-review benefits, resist representative attacks, or achieve production safety. Instead, it establishes that typed, fact-checked claims can reliably govern tool execution within explicit mediation boundaries, offering a structured alternative to trusting unstructured agent rationales.

title: HeAD-CP: Heterophily-Aware Diffused Conformal Prediction Sets for Graph Neural Networks
summary: Conformal prediction (CP) provides distribution-free uncertainty quantification, and its extension to graphs is an active research direction. Diffused Adaptive Prediction Sets (DAPS) is a widely used graph-aware diffusion baseline, propagating Adaptive Prediction Sets (APS) non-conformity scores along edges with a uniform coefficient $λ$. We identify a fundamental shortcoming of this design: the uniform low-pass diffusion presupposes graph homophily and proves detrimental on heterophilic graphs, enlarging the mean prediction-set size by up to 10.6% relative to plain APS. To mitigate this, we propose HeAD-CP, a family of node-wise diffusion variants whose coefficients are determined by a label-free local-homophily estimate derived from the GNN softmax. Three variants, namely signed-$γ$, edge-compatibility, and a DAPS-baseline-with-correction, are most effective at extreme heterophily, intermediate heterophily, and moderate-to-high homophily, respectively, and all preserve the marginal coverage guarantee. On ten benchmarks, the HeAD-CP family stays at or below plain APS on every dataset, while DAPS exceeds APS on six. The post-hoc oracle over the family improves over DAPS on 8/10 datasets at $p<0.01$ (paired Wilcoxon), with the largest gains on heterophilic graphs (10.3% on Texas); on the two homophilic datasets where DAPS still wins (CiteSeer, PubMed), it retains a marginal advantage of at most 0.002, statistically insignificant on CiteSeer ($p=0.23$). Designing a calibrated label-free selector that approaches this oracle is the main outstanding empirical question.

AI.tldr: HeAD-CP improves conformal prediction on graphs by replacing DAPS's uniform diffusion coefficient with node-wise, homophily-aware variants, preventing prediction-set inflation on heterophilic graphs while preserving coverage guarantees.
AI.motivation: DAPS applies uniform low-pass diffusion to propagate APS non-conformity scores, which implicitly assumes graph homophily. On heterophilic graphs, this assumption fails catastrophically, inflating mean prediction-set size by up to 10.6% relative to plain APS. A graph-aware CP method that adapts to both homophilic and heterophilic regimes is needed.
AI.method: HeAD-CP introduces three node-wise diffusion coefficient variants based on a label-free local-homophily estimate from GNN softmax outputs: (1) signed-γ for extreme heterophily, (2) edge-compatibility for intermediate heterophily, and (3) a DAPS-baseline-with-correction for moderate-to-high homophily. All variants preserve the marginal coverage guarantee. A post-hoc oracle selector over the family is also evaluated.
AI.result: The HeAD-CP family matches or beats plain APS on all 10 benchmarks, while DAPS exceeds APS on 6. The oracle improves over DAPS on 8/10 datasets at p<0.01 (paired Wilcoxon), with largest gains on heterophilic graphs (10.3% on Texas). On CiteSeer and PubMed, DAPS's advantage is ≤0.002 and statistically insignificant (p=0.23 on CiteSeer).
AI.conclusion: Homophily-aware, node-wise diffusion coefficients are critical for effective graph conformal prediction across the homophily spectrum. The remaining challenge is designing a calibrated label-free selector to approximate the oracle performance in practice.

title: SearchArt: Training Long-Horizon Search Agent with Scalable Synthetic and Verified Task
summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled search agents to autonomously tackle complex tasks across extended search and reasoning horizons. However, training effective search agents remains challenging due to the lack of scalable and long-horizon tasks, and the difficulty of evaluating and correcting intermediate reasoning and tool-use behaviors. We introduce SearchArt, a scalable framework for training long-horizon search agents through verification-driven task synthesis and a multi-stage post-training pipeline. SearchArt constructs large-scale datasets for complex search-, research- and user-oriented tasks by synthesizing diverse information-seeking QA pairs and corresponding search trajectories from web documents and automatically generated evidence graphs. To ensure the reliability of the synthesized data, we design a verification pipeline that jointly evaluates QA consistency, trajectory quality, and the relevance of retrieved evidence. The verified trajectories are subsequently used in a multi-stage training process comprising supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning-based policy optimization. Search agents trained with SearchArt exhibit adaptive search planning, iterative evidence aggregation, and complex reasoning over extended interaction horizons. Experimental results demonstrate that, with only (Qwen3.5-) 27B parameters, SearchArt scores 74.39 on BrowseComp-ZH, 70.06 on BrowseComp, and 52.55 on Deepresearch-bench, matching or surpassing frontier closed-source agents on both deepsearch and deepresearch benchmarks.

AI.tldr: SearchArt is a scalable framework that trains long-horizon search agents by synthesizing complex QA pairs and search trajectories from web documents, verified through a multi-stage pipeline, then fine-tuned with supervised and reinforcement learning. A 27B model trained with SearchArt matches or surpasses frontier closed-source agents on deepsearch and deepresearch benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Training effective search agents is difficult due to (1) the scarcity of scalable, long-horizon tasks and (2) the challenge of evaluating and correcting intermediate reasoning and tool-use behaviors during training.
AI.method: SearchArt consists of two core components: (1) a verification-driven task synthesis pipeline that constructs large-scale datasets by synthesizing diverse information-seeking QA pairs and search trajectories from web documents, using automatically generated evidence graphs and a verification module that jointly evaluates QA consistency, trajectory quality, and evidence relevance; (2) a multi-stage post-training pipeline combining supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning-based policy optimization on the verified trajectories.
AI.result: A SearchArt-trained agent based on Qwen3.5-27B achieves 74.39 on BrowseComp-ZH, 70.06 on BrowseComp, and 52.55 on Deepresearch-bench, matching or surpassing frontier closed-source agents on both deepsearch and deepresearch benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: SearchArt demonstrates that verification-driven synthesis of long-horizon search tasks, combined with multi-stage post-training, enables relatively small open models to rival much larger proprietary systems on complex search and research benchmarks.

title: MusiChat: Vibe Composing for Music Creation
summary: Recent advances in AI music generation have enabled users to create complete musical pieces from natural-language prompts. However, most existing systems follow a prompt-and-regenerate paradigm, making iterative refinement difficult because users must repeatedly recreate compositions instead of directly evolving existing musical ideas. We present MusiChat, a conversational vibe composing system that enables collaborative human-AI music creation through natural-language interaction and iterative refinement. At the core of MusiChat is a hierarchical controllable music generation framework that separates lyric-aligned musical structure generation from expressive surface realization, allowing flexible stylistic transformations and structure-preserving edits. The system integrates a large language model with a hybrid symbolic music engine through a memory-augmented architecture that maintains the active composition state and user history across interactions. A hybrid intent-routing mechanism further enables efficient interpretation of both precise musical edits and open-ended creative requests. Rather than regenerating compositions from scratch, MusiChat incrementally transforms an evolving musical artifact while preserving relevant musical structure and user intent. We evaluate MusiChat through objective analysis and human studies, achieving 95.31% and 100% accuracy for single- and multi-turn interactions, respectively, and obtaining like-to-dislike ratios of 2:1 for melody naturalness and 3:1 for musical quality. Our results demonstrate that MusiChat supports coherent multi-turn music authoring and interactive human-AI co-creation through a conversational interface.

AI.tldr: MusiChat is a conversational AI music co-creation system that enables iterative, multi-turn refinement of musical compositions through natural language, using a hierarchical generation framework that separates structure from surface realization, achieving high interaction accuracy and favorable human ratings.
AI.motivation: Existing AI music generation systems rely on a prompt-and-regenerate paradigm, forcing users to recreate entire compositions rather than incrementally refine existing musical ideas. This limits iterative, collaborative creativity.
AI.method: A hierarchical controllable music generation framework decouples lyric-aligned musical structure generation from expressive surface realization. The system integrates a large language model with a hybrid symbolic music engine via a memory-augmented architecture that tracks composition state and interaction history. A hybrid intent-routing mechanism interprets both precise edits and open-ended creative requests, enabling incremental transformation rather than full regeneration.
AI.result: MusiChat achieved 95.31% accuracy for single-turn interactions and 100% accuracy for multi-turn interactions. Human evaluations yielded like-to-dislike ratios of 2:1 for melody naturalness and 3:1 for overall musical quality.
AI.conclusion: MusiChat demonstrates that conversational interfaces with iterative, structure-preserving refinement can support coherent multi-turn music authoring and effective human-AI co-creation.

title: Evaluation of Adversarial Robustness in Arabic Language Models
summary: The emergence of the recent outstanding capabilities of Arabic Language Models has opened doors for exposing their vulnerabilities. One of the major security risks associated with such Natural Language Processing models is adversarial attacks. These attacks can deceive the model into the wrong prediction, raising critical model security and safety concerns. This study aims to assess the robustness of five state-of-the-art Arabic Language Models under a distinct set of Arabic adversarial attacks applied at various levels of granularity and using different example generation strategies. We also explore a defense technique based on adversarial training to enhance model robustness. The results show that insertion of diacritics can reduce the accuracy of some models by 92% while maintaining a low perturbation distance. For word-level attacks, manipulating Arabic conjunctions preserves high semantic similarity scores, low perturbation distance, and leads to an accuracy degradation of up to 58%. For sentence-level attacks, paraphrasing proves its effectiveness by an average reduction of 76% in the victim models' performance. While adversarial training improves overall resilience, with MARBERT being the most robust and AraBERT showing the greatest relative gains, challenges persist, particularly against character-level noise. These findings highlight both the potential and limitations of current defense strategies in morphologically rich languages like Arabic.

AI.tldr: Assesses robustness of five Arabic language models against adversarial attacks at character, word, and sentence levels; finds diacritic insertion reduces accuracy by up to 92%, while adversarial training offers partial but incomplete defense.
AI.motivation: Arabic language models have shown remarkable capabilities, yet their vulnerability to adversarial attacks remains underexplored. Given the morphological richness of Arabic, there is a pressing need to systematically evaluate model robustness across different attack granularities and to test whether adversarial training can mitigate these vulnerabilities.
AI.method: Five state-of-the-art Arabic LMs (including MARBERT and AraBERT) are evaluated under adversarial attacks at three levels: character-level (diacritic insertion), word-level (manipulation of Arabic conjunctions), and sentence-level (paraphrasing). Attack generation strategies vary. Adversarial training is explored as a defense technique, and metrics include accuracy degradation, perturbation distance, and semantic similarity.
AI.result: Diacritic insertion achieves up to 92% accuracy reduction with minimal perturbation distance. Word-level conjunction manipulation yields up to 58% degradation with high semantic similarity. Sentence-level paraphrasing causes an average 76% performance drop. MARBERT proves most robust overall; AraBERT shows the greatest relative improvement under adversarial training, yet character-level noise remains a persistent challenge.
AI.conclusion: Adversarial training improves resilience but does not fully resolve vulnerabilities, especially character-level attacks. The findings underscore both the promise and limitations of current defenses in morphologically rich languages, highlighting the need for more robust strategies tailored to Arabic.

title: When Does Deep Representation Learning Help Single-Cell Clustering? A Sensitivity-Aware Diagnostic Benchmark for Biomedical AI Pipelines
summary: Single-cell ribonucleic acid sequencing (scRNA-seq) is a foundational technology for precision-medicine workflows that contribute to United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 3 on Good Health and Well-being, and unsupervised clustering is the analytical step that turns raw expression matrices into interpretable cell populations. Practitioners therefore face a recurring engineering decision: is an additional deep representation stage worth its compute and tuning cost, or do classical principal component analysis (PCA) pipelines already suffice? We address this question with a diagnostic benchmark of nine clustering pipelines on ten real datasets (90-5,685 cells, 19,046-41,480 genes, 4-11 cell types), augmented by a partial scVI V2 specialized comparison on seven datasets. The protocol integrates Optuna hyperparameter search, repeated-run robustness, Friedman/Wilcoxon-Holm/TOST testing, and Sobol total-order sensitivity analysis. The contrastive autoencoder achieved the highest mean Adjusted Rand Index (0.7872), but Holm-corrected tests did not establish dominance over the strongest baselines. Per-dataset analysis reveals three reproducible regimes: probabilistic variational autoencoder (VAE) variants help on the smallest datasets, deep autoencoders win on mid-scale data with multi-batch or many-type structure, and classical PCA pipelines remain competitive when linear projection already captures the dominant variation. Sobol indices identify learning rate ($S_T=0.70$) and latent dimensionality ($S_T=0.56$) as the dominant variance contributors, indicating where limited tuning budgets should be allocated. The contribution is therefore a dataset-aware and compute-conscious decision framework for biomedical AI pipelines supporting sustainable healthcare analytics, rather than a universal superiority claim.

AI.tldr: A benchmark of nine scRNA-seq clustering pipelines (deep vs. classical PCA) across ten datasets reveals no universal winner; contrastive autoencoders achieve the highest mean ARI (0.7872) but lack statistical dominance. Three data-dependent regimes emerge: VAE variants for small datasets, deep autoencoders for mid-scale multi-batch data, and PCA pipelines where linear projection suffices. Learning rate and latent dimensionality dominate sensitivity indices, guiding hyperparameter budget allocation.
AI.motivation: Practitioners face a recurring engineering decision in scRNA-seq workflows: whether the added computational cost and tuning effort of deep representation learning methods justifies their use over classical PCA-based clustering pipelines. The paper addresses this question to support precision medicine and sustainable healthcare analytics (aligned with UN SDG 3).
AI.method: A diagnostic benchmark evaluating nine clustering pipelines on ten real scRNA-seq datasets (90–5,685 cells; 19,046–41,480 genes; 4–11 cell types), supplemented by a scVI V2 comparison on seven datasets. The protocol integrates Optuna hyperparameter search, repeated-run robustness assessment, Friedman and Wilcoxon-Holm statistical testing, TOST equivalence testing, and Sobol total-order sensitivity analysis to identify dominant hyperparameters.
AI.result: The contrastive autoencoder achieved the highest mean Adjusted Rand Index (0.7872), but Holm-corrected tests did not establish significant dominance over strongest baselines. Three reproducible regimes were identified: (1) probabilistic VAE variants benefit small datasets; (2) deep autoencoders excel on mid-scale data with multi-batch or many-type structure; (3) classical PCA pipelines remain competitive when linear projection captures dominant variation. Sobol indices identified learning rate (S_T=0.70) and latent dimensionality (S_T=0.56) as dominant variance contributors.
AI.conclusion: There is no universal superiority among clustering pipelines. Instead, a dataset-aware, compute-conscious decision framework is needed. The contribution provides practical guidance for selecting scRNA-seq clustering methods in biomedical AI pipelines, recommending allocation of limited tuning budgets to learning rate and latent dimensionality.

title: HVM-GraphRAG: Holistic-View Multimodal Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Complex Document
summary: Question answering (QA) over complex documents requires models to retrieve and integrate evidence distributed across distant document regions and modalities. Multimodal GraphRAG provides a promising direction by organizing document evidence with graph structures. However, existing methods often suffer from unreliable cross-modal evidence indexing and expensive graph traversal. To address these issues, we propose HVM-GraphRAG, a holistic-view multimodal GraphRAG framework on complex document. HVM-GraphRAG uses a holistic view to guide graph construction, thereby reducing noisy and conflicting graph updates and building reliable indices between concept-level graph nodes and supporting multimodal chunks. During retrieval, HVM-GraphRAG searches over a compact concept-level graph and directly accesses supporting evidence through the constructed index, avoiding costly traversal over dense entity-level graphs. After obtaining the retrieved evidence, HVM-GraphRAG further reorganizes chunks into modality-specific groups, enabling the answering model to better integrate heterogeneous evidence. Experiments on three datasets show that HVM-GraphRAG achieves the best answer performance in most evaluated settings while substantially improving online retrieval efficiency over representative graph-based baselines.

AI.tldr: HVM-GraphRAG proposes a holistic-view multimodal GraphRAG framework for QA over complex documents, using concept-level graph indexing with direct evidence access to replace costly entity-level graph traversal, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy and improved retrieval efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal GraphRAG methods suffer from two key problems: (1) unreliable cross-modal evidence indexing due to noisy and conflicting graph updates, and (2) expensive graph traversal over dense entity-level graphs during retrieval. These limitations hinder both retrieval quality and efficiency for QA over complex documents.
AI.method: HVM-GraphRAG introduces three main components: (1) a holistic view to guide graph construction, reducing noise and conflicts while building reliable indices between concept-level nodes and supporting multimodal chunks; (2) retrieval over a compact concept-level graph with direct evidence access via the pre-built index, avoiding costly entity-level traversal; and (3) post-retrieval reorganization of chunks into modality-specific groups to help the answering model better integrate heterogeneous evidence.
AI.result: Experiments on three datasets demonstrate that HVM-GraphRAG achieves the best answer performance in most evaluated settings while substantially improving online retrieval efficiency over representative graph-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: HVM-GraphRAG effectively addresses the reliability and efficiency limitations of existing multimodal GraphRAG methods through holistic-view-guided graph construction and compact concept-level retrieval, offering a more practical solution for complex document QA.

title: Understanding Semantic IDs: From Item Representation to Item Selection in Generative Recommendation
summary: Semantic IDs (SIDs) are now a central component of generative recommendation. Current SID-based systems assign three roles to the same token sequence. Shared prefixes are intended to organize related items, the complete SID identifies an individual item, and each generated token narrows the items that can still be returned. We systematically investigate SIDs from item encoding and SID construction to autoregressive generation and final recommendation. We examine how SID construction changes item representations and how those changes affect generation. Across three Amazon domains and eight SID constructions, SID neighborhoods recover only 32.2% of the encoder's ten nearest neighbors on average. Alternative item descriptions still retrieve the corresponding item first in 99.57% of controlled cases, yet change 38.4% of exact SIDs. These results show that SIDs retain broad organization but lose much of the encoder's fine local structure, while their exact tokens are not determined by item meaning alone. This loss becomes consequential during generation. After the final semantic token, TIGER retains only 29.9% of held-out targets that were plausible recommendations before SID filtering. Motivated by these findings, we propose Item-Supported Decoding (ISD), a lightweight inference-time method that allows a user-specific item ranking to support corresponding SID prefixes before beam search discards them. The same ranking then orders the generated items. ISD requires no additional parameters or retraining of the SID constructor or decoder. We empirically show that ISD improves NDCG@10 over the corresponding SID backbone in every evaluated setting, with relative gains of up to 31.2%. Our results show that SIDs provide useful coarse item organization, but their fine boundaries should not alone determine which items remain available during generation.

AI.tldr: Semantic IDs (SIDs) in generative recommendation sacrifice fine-grained item similarity and allow SID tokens to vary independently of item meaning, hurting generation quality. The authors propose Item-Supported Decoding (ISD), a lightweight inference-time fix that uses item rankings to guide SID generation and re-rank outputs, yielding up to 31.2% relative NDCG@10 gains without retraining.
AI.motivation: Current SID-based generative recommendation systems conflate three roles in a single token sequence: organizing items hierarchically, uniquely identifying items, and constraining the candidate set during autoregressive decoding. The authors hypothesize that this conflation leads to a loss of the encoder's fine-grained local structure and that SID tokens are not fully determined by item semantics, which in turn harms recommendation performance during generation.
AI.method: The paper systematically analyzes SIDs across three stages: (1) item encoding and SID construction, measuring how well SID neighborhoods recover encoder neighborhoods across eight SID methods on three Amazon domains; (2) controlled item description experiments to test whether SID tokens are determined by item meaning; (3) generation analysis measuring how many plausible recommendations survive after SID filtering. Based on these findings, the authors propose Item-Supported Decoding (ISD), which at inference time uses a user-specific item ranking to support SID prefixes that would otherwise be pruned by beam search, then re-ranks generated items using the same ranking. ISD requires no additional parameters or retraining.
AI.result: SID neighborhoods recover only 32.2% of the encoder's 10 nearest neighbors on average across three Amazon domains and eight SID constructions. Alternative item descriptions retrieve the correct item first in 99.57% of controlled cases but change 38.4% of exact SIDs. After the final semantic token, TIGER retains only 29.9% of held-out targets that were plausible before SID filtering. ISD improves NDCG@10 over the SID backbone in every evaluated setting, with relative gains up to 31.2%.
AI.conclusion: SIDs provide useful coarse item organization but their fine boundaries should not alone determine which items remain available during generation. ISD offers a simple, retraining-free solution that preserves SIDs' organizational benefits while mitigating their local structural limitations, improving recommendation performance across all tested settings.

title: AngelSpec: Towards Real-World High Performance Inference with Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference without changing the target distribution, but no single drafting structure performs best across real-world workloads. Autoregressive multi-token prediction (MTP) is a lightweight, stable proposal mechanism, whereas block-parallel diffusion amortizes drafting latency over much longer candidate sequences; the better choice depends strongly on the output distribution. We present AngelSpec, a unified training framework for MTP and block-parallel speculative decoding that addresses this heterogeneity at three levels. At the training level, rather than fitting one universal drafter to a uniform data mixture, we co-specialize structure and data: the MTP drafter is trained on diverse conversational data for high-entropy open-ended chat, and the block-diffusion drafter on code and mathematics data for longer predictable continuations. At the architecture level, we propose DFly, a block-diffusion framework combining a hybrid target-conditioning backbone with a predecessor-conditioned autoregressive head, improving target-feature utilization and intra-block dependency modeling while keeping generation parallel. At the inference level, both acceptance length and verification cost vary with domain, request, online load, and hardware, so DFly treats verification as a shared batch-level resource: it reallocates compute toward high-confidence prefixes across requests and combines expected utility with a profiled cost model to adapt verification depth online. Across the Hy3 series, DFly raises the average accepted length on Hy3-A21B by roughly 30% and attains the highest average throughput at every tested concurrency from 4 to 64, a 1.98-2.40x speedup over autoregressive decoding and 10.5-11.8% higher throughput than DFlash. We release AngelSpec to support training and extending these methods.

AI.tldr: AngelSpec is a unified training framework that co-specializes autoregressive multi-token prediction (MTP) and block-parallel diffusion drafters for speculative decoding. It introduces DFly, a hybrid block-diffusion architecture, and online adaptive verification. Across the Hy3 model series, DFly achieves 1.98–2.40× speedup over autoregressive decoding and 10.5–11.8% higher throughput than DFlash.
AI.motivation: No single drafting structure performs optimally across diverse real-world LLM workloads. MTP excels in high-entropy, open-ended chat, while block-parallel diffusion suits longer, predictable continuations like code and math. The choice depends on the output distribution, creating a need for a unified framework that adapts drafting strategy to data domain and inference conditions.
AI.method: AngelSpec operates at three levels: (1) Training — co-specializes MTP on conversational data and block-diffusion on code/math data rather than fitting a universal drafter. (2) Architecture — DFly, a block-diffusion framework with a hybrid target-conditioning backbone and a predecessor-conditioned autoregressive head, improving target-feature utilization and intra-block dependency modeling. (3) Inference — treats verification as a shared batch-level resource, reallocating compute toward high-confidence prefixes and using expected utility with a profiled cost model to adapt verification depth online.
AI.result: On the Hy3 series, DFly raises average accepted length on Hy3-A21B by ~30% and achieves the highest average throughput at every tested concurrency (4–64). It delivers a 1.98–2.40× speedup over autoregressive decoding and 10.5–11.8% higher throughput than DFlash.
AI.conclusion: Co-specializing drafter architectures to data domains and adaptively managing verification as a shared resource yields robust, workload-aware speculative decoding. AngelSpec provides a unified training and inference framework that significantly outperforms both autoregressive baselines and prior speculative decoding methods.

title: ContractHIL-HLS: Contract-Aligned Multi-Agent Workflow with Hardware-in-the-Loop Feedback for HLS Design
summary: This paper presents ContractHIL-HLS, a contract-aligned multi-agent workflow for practical high-level synthesis (HLS) engineering. The workflow makes three contributions. First, it introduces a structured contract as the semantic-alignment and task-execution artifact that translates natural language requirements into explicit interfaces, constraints, validation checks, and rollback rules. Second, it incorporates hardware information into the feedback loop by feeding HLS, Vivado, PYNQ runtime, power, and failure evidence back into generation, thereby extending LLM-assisted HLS from kernel code toward system- and board-level closure. Third, it decomposes agents by semantic lowering and execution tasks rather than by conversational roles: a Contract Agent lowers natural language into the contract, an HTML Agent renders the contract as persistent structured HTML, and a Hardware-in-the-Loop Agent implements and revises the design with measured evidence. We evaluate ContractHIL-HLS in two parts. On 94 locally executable HLS-Eval tasks, the structured contract provides the largest small design gain, improving the estimated single-sample testbench pass rate from 64.0% to 70.2%; the full flow reaches 70.4% pass@1 and 76.6% pass@5. Because HLS-Eval does not exercise board-level design, we also validate ContractHIL-HLS on a board tested ML-KEM/ML-DSA post-quantum cryptography (PQC) secure-message accelerator, where the retained dual-bitstream organization reduces six-message average text runtime from 207.3 ms to 52.4 ms with positive routed WNS on both images while preserving decrypted-message verification. We open-source our work at BJUT-CS316-LAB/ContractHIL-HLS (https://github.com/BJUT-CS316-LAB/ContractHIL-HLS).

AI.tldr: ContractHIL-HLS introduces a contract-aligned multi-agent workflow for HLS engineering that translates natural language requirements into structured contracts, incorporates hardware feedback loops, and decomposes agents by task semantics. On HLS-Eval, it improves pass@1 from 64.0% to 70.4%; on a PQC accelerator, it reduces runtime from 207.3ms to 52.4ms.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-assisted HLS approaches lack structured semantic alignment between natural language requirements and hardware implementation, fail to incorporate board-level hardware feedback (synthesis, power, runtime evidence), and rely on conversational agent roles rather than task-oriented decomposition. This limits practical closure from kernel code to system/board-level designs.
AI.method: Three contributions: (1) a structured contract serving as a semantic-alignment artifact that captures interfaces, constraints, validation checks, and rollback rules; (2) hardware-in-the-loop feedback integrating HLS tool, Vivado, PYNQ runtime, power, and failure evidence into the generation loop; (3) task-based agent decomposition: a Contract Agent (NL→contract), an HTML Agent (contract→persistent structured HTML), and a Hardware-in-the-Loop Agent (implementation + revision with measured evidence). Evaluation spans 94 HLS-Eval tasks plus a board-tested ML-KEM/ML-DSA PQC secure-message accelerator.
AI.result: On 94 HLS-Eval tasks, the structured contract alone boosts estimated single-sample testbench pass rate from 64.0% to 70.2%; the full flow achieves 70.4% pass@1 and 76.6% pass@5. On the PQC board-tested accelerator, the retained dual-bitstream organization cuts six-message average text runtime from 207.3ms to 52.4ms with positive routed WNS on both images, while preserving decrypted-message verification.
AI.conclusion: A contract-aligned, task-decomposed multi-agent architecture with hardware-in-the-loop feedback significantly improves practical HLS outcomes, spanning both benchmark-level pass rates and board-level system performance. The structured contract emerges as the single most impactful component for small designs, and the full flow demonstrates scalable closure to real hardware.

title: A Machine-Learning-Based Gas Lift Optimization Workflow for Unconventional Fields
summary: In this paper, we present an automated data-driven workflow using Machine Learning (ML) for gas lift optimization in unconventional fields. This workflow integrates a ML model that accurately forecasts the Gas Lift Performance Curve, and a Bayesian Optimization Framework to solve for the optimal gas injection rates under the constraints of facility capacity. The ML model leverages the historical production time series data without requiring downhole gauges or multi-rate well tests. We piloted this workflow on 30 wells across 5 well pads in Bakken and obtained >5% production uplift on average. With the success of the pilot, we have now fully-deployed this workflow in Bakken across 200+ gas lift and plunger-assisted gas lift (PAGL) wells. Moreover, the ML-based gas lift optimization workflow presented in this paper is an effective and economic solution for other assets where downhole data or multi-rate testing are not available/feasible due to cost or facility constraints.

AI.tldr: An ML-driven workflow combining gas lift performance curve prediction with Bayesian optimization achieves 5%+ production uplift, validated on 30 wells and deployed across 200+ wells in the Bakken.
AI.motivation: Traditional gas lift optimization requires expensive downhole gauges or multi-rate well tests, which are often infeasible in unconventional fields due to cost and facility constraints. A data-driven alternative is needed.
AI.method: The workflow integrates two components: (1) an ML model trained on historical production time series data to forecast the Gas Lift Performance Curve without requiring downhole data, and (2) a Bayesian Optimization Framework that solves for optimal gas injection rates subject to facility capacity constraints.
AI.result: A pilot on 30 wells across 5 well pads in the Bakken yielded >5% average production uplift. The workflow has subsequently been fully deployed across 200+ gas lift and plunger-assisted gas lift (PAGL) wells.
AI.conclusion: The ML-based gas lift optimization workflow is an effective, economical solution applicable to assets where downhole data or multi-rate testing are unavailable or cost-prohibitive.

title: AMRD: Adaptive Multi-Teacher Relational Distillation for Lightweight Speech Emotion Recognition
summary: On-device speech emotion recognition (SER) is critical for real-time applications, yet large self-supervised models that excel at SER are too costly for edge devices. Multi-teacher knowledge distillation can compress them into a lightweight student, but two challenges remain: teacher reliability varies across batches, and logit-level distillation ignores inter-sample relational structure. We propose Adaptive Multi-teacher Relational Distillation (AMRD) to address both. A one-class SVM on each teacher's logit similarity matrix assigns per-batch weights favoring more coherent teachers. A relational distillation loss aligns teacher and student similarity matrices, capturing structure that logit matching misses. On IEMOCAP and CREMA-D datasets across four student architectures, AMRD outperforms single-teacher distillation baselines in most settings, and ablations confirm both components yield complementary gains.

AI.tldr: AMRD proposes adaptive multi-teacher relational knowledge distillation for on-device SER, using per-batch teacher weighting via one-class SVM and relational distillation to capture inter-sample structure, outperforming single-teacher baselines on IEMOCAP and CREMA-D.
AI.motivation: Large self-supervised SER models are prohibitively expensive for edge devices, and existing multi-teacher knowledge distillation suffers from (1) unreliable teachers whose quality varies across batches, and (2) logit-level distillation that fails to capture inter-sample relational structure.
AI.method: AMRD combines two components: (1) a one-class SVM applied to each teacher's logit similarity matrix to assign per-batch weights favoring more coherent teachers, and (2) a relational distillation loss that aligns teacher and student similarity matrices to capture inter-sample structure missed by standard logit matching.
