AI.result: AMRD outperforms single-teacher distillation baselines across four student architectures on both IEMOCAP and CREMA-D datasets in most settings; ablation studies confirm both the adaptive teacher weighting and relational distillation components provide complementary performance gains.
AI.conclusion: AMRD effectively compresses large SER models for on-device deployment by adaptively weighting teachers per batch and incorporating relational structure, offering a practical solution for real-time edge SER applications.

title: KuaiLive-M3: A Multi-Modal, Multi-Domain, and Multi-Feedback Dataset for Live Streaming Recommendation
summary: Existing public live streaming datasets suffer from three major limitations: they provide limited access to temporally evolving multimodal live content, overlook users' cross-domain interactions between short videos and live streams, and contain only implicit behavioral signals without explicit feedback that captures users' perceived content quality and satisfaction. These limitations prevent existing benchmarks from faithfully reflecting real-world live streaming scenarios and hinder comprehensive research on live streaming recommendation. To address these limitations, we introduce KuaiLive-M3, a multi-modal, multi-domain, and multi-feedback dataset for live streaming recommendation, collected from Kuaishou, a leading live streaming and short video platform in China. KuaiLive-M3 covers 21,938 users and contains 35 million live streaming interactions and 111 million short video interactions, with fine-grained timestamps and diverse user behaviors. It further provides approximately 88 million timestamped segment-level multi-modal embeddings that capture the temporal evolution of live streaming content, as well as 25,403 questionnaire-based feedback records that bridge implicit user behaviors and explicit user preferences. Based on these unique signals, we establish benchmarks for cross-domain recommendation, live stream highlight prediction, and questionnaire-enhanced recommendation. Extensive experiments with representative baselines demonstrate that KuaiLive-M3 provides a challenging and realistic benchmark for future live streaming recommendation research. The results further highlight the importance of modeling temporally evolving content, transferring user preferences across domains, and bridging the gap between implicit behaviors and explicit user feedback. The dataset and benchmark code are publicly available at https://imgkkk574.github.io/KuaiLive-M3/.

AI.tldr: KuaiLive-M3 is a large-scale, multi-modal, multi-domain, multi-feedback dataset for live streaming recommendation, addressing gaps in temporal content modeling, cross-domain interactions, and explicit user feedback. It includes 35M live streaming and 111M short video interactions from 21,938 users, plus segment-level embeddings and questionnaire data, with established benchmarks showing the importance of these unique signals.
AI.motivation: Existing live streaming datasets suffer from three key limitations: (1) limited access to temporally evolving multimodal content, (2) neglect of cross-domain interactions between short videos and live streams, and (3) reliance on implicit behavioral signals without explicit user feedback on content quality and satisfaction. These gaps prevent realistic benchmarking and hinder live streaming recommendation research.
AI.method: The authors construct KuaiLive-M3, a dataset collected from Kuaishou, containing: (1) 35M live streaming and 111M short video interactions with fine-grained timestamps from 21,938 users; (2) ~88M timestamped segment-level multi-modal embeddings capturing temporal content evolution; and (3) 25,403 questionnaire-based explicit feedback records bridging implicit and explicit preferences. They establish three benchmarks: cross-domain recommendation, live stream highlight prediction, and questionnaire-enhanced recommendation, evaluating representative baselines on each.
AI.result: Extensive experiments with representative baselines demonstrate that KuaiLive-M3 presents a challenging and realistic benchmark. Results highlight the critical importance of (1) modeling temporally evolving live streaming content, (2) transferring user preferences across short video and live streaming domains, and (3) bridging the gap between implicit behavioral signals and explicit user feedback for improved recommendation performance.
AI.conclusion: KuaiLive-M3 fills a critical gap in live streaming recommendation research by providing multi-modal, multi-domain, and multi-feedback signals lacking in prior datasets. The benchmarks and experimental findings underscore the value of temporal content modeling, cross-domain preference transfer, and explicit feedback integration, offering a foundation for future research in realistic live streaming recommendation scenarios.

title: Localized Anomaly Detection via Differentiable D-vine Copulas
comment: Workshop paper accepted for presentation at the CAESAR workshop within ECML-PKDD (September 2026, Naples)
summary: Vine copulas provide a flexible framework for modeling complex multivariate distributions through a hierarchical decomposition into bivariate pair-copulas. Fitting a D-vine requires selecting a copula family and parameter configuration for each pair-copula from a set of candidates encoding different dependence patterns. As the number of variables and candidate families increases, the number of possible configurations grows combinatorially. Existing fitting procedures address this challenge through sequential greedy decisions, committing to a single locally optimal family at each step and potentially discarding configurations that would yield a better global fit. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel estimation framework that combines gradient-based maximum likelihood estimation, enabled by our fully differentiable implementation, with a beam-search strategy that maintains multiple competing D-vine configurations throughout the fitting process. This allows a broader exploration of the configuration space while remaining computationally tractable. Building on the fitted D-vine, we introduce a localized anomaly detection framework that exploits the hierarchical decomposition to produce both global anomaly scores and edge-level explanations. Statistical guarantees are provided through Mondrian conformal prediction, while the pair-copula structure enables the localization of anomalies to specific variable relationships. We evaluate the proposed framework on both benchmark and real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness for interpretable anomaly detection with uncertainty quantification.

AI.tldr: A new D-vine copula fitting method uses gradient-based maximum likelihood with beam search to explore multiple configurations globally, avoiding greedy local decisions. The fitted model enables localized anomaly detection with edge-level explanations and Mondrian conformal prediction for uncertainty quantification.
AI.motivation: Existing D-vine fitting procedures rely on sequential greedy decisions that commit to a single locally optimal copula family at each step, potentially discarding configurations that would yield a better global fit. As variables and candidate families increase, exhaustive search becomes combinatorially intractable.
AI.method: The authors propose a fully differentiable D-vine implementation that enables gradient-based maximum likelihood estimation, combined with a beam-search strategy that maintains multiple competing D-vine configurations throughout fitting. For anomaly detection, they exploit the hierarchical pair-copula decomposition to produce global anomaly scores and edge-level explanations, with statistical guarantees via Mondrian conformal prediction.
AI.result: The framework is evaluated on both benchmark and real-world datasets, demonstrating effectiveness for interpretable anomaly detection with uncertainty quantification.
AI.conclusion: The beam-search approach with differentiable estimation overcomes the limitations of greedy sequential fitting in D-vine copulas, and the resulting model provides a principled, interpretable anomaly detection framework with formal statistical guarantees.

title: Shieldstral
summary: We introduce Shieldstral, a 3B-parameter policy-adaptive multimodal safety classifier that matches or outperforms models nearly 7$\times$ its size on text safety benchmarks and sets a new state of the art on multimodal safety classification. Shieldstral formulates content moderation as a binary question-answering task. This simple formulation unifies diverse moderation tasks into a single yes/no problem, enabling heterogeneous safety datasets with divergent taxonomies to be consolidated under one training framework. We present the data construction recipe, covering curation and generation of approximately 54.1M samples and a fine-grained evaluation set to evaluate policy adaptability. Together, these enable a small adaptive model to match or outperform much larger models.

AI.tldr: Shieldstral is a 3B-parameter multimodal safety classifier that uses a binary question-answering formulation to unify diverse content moderation tasks, achieving state-of-the-art performance while matching models 7× its size.
AI.motivation: Current safety classification models are either large and computationally expensive or lack multimodal capabilities and policy adaptability. There is a need for a compact, efficient model that can unify heterogeneous safety datasets with divergent taxonomies under a single training framework while remaining adaptable to different content policies.
AI.method: Shieldstral formulates content moderation as a binary question-answering task (yes/no), which unifies diverse moderation tasks into one framework. The authors construct a large training dataset of approximately 54.1M samples through curation and generation, along with a fine-grained evaluation set for assessing policy adaptability. The model is a 3B-parameter policy-adaptive multimodal classifier.
AI.result: Shieldstral matches or outperforms models nearly 7× its size on text safety benchmarks and sets a new state of the art on multimodal safety classification.
AI.conclusion: A simple binary QA formulation combined with careful data construction at scale enables a small (3B) adaptive model to achieve competitive or superior safety classification performance compared to much larger models, demonstrating that scale is not the sole determinant of effectiveness in content moderation.

title: The Disruptive Impact of Large Language Models on Capture the Flag Competitions and the Path Toward Fair Play
summary: Capture the Flag (CTF) competitions are among cybersecurity's most effective training grounds, developing practical skill across cryptography, web exploitation, and binary exploitation. Large language models (LLMs) can now solve a growing share of challenges with minimal human input, raising urgent questions about fairness, the validity of rankings, and whether participation still delivers the learning that justifies the effort. This paper reports a mixed-methods study of LLM impact on modern CTFs, combining a synthesis of published benchmarks, including a recent government evaluation, case studies of live competition across three challenge categories, structured observation of the public channels where the community debates AI use, and semi-structured interviews with experienced players and organisers. We map the current human-machine capability boundary by category, showing that easy and intermediate challenges in cryptography, web, and binary exploitation are now reliably automated while narrower sub-categories continue to resist. We find that community disagreement about whether AI should be permitted is downstream of an undeclared prior question: what a competition is for. Against this backdrop we contribute a four-component safeguard framework, combining tiered competition divisions, LLM-resistant challenge design, telemetry used investigatively, and a draft community code of conduct, together with a decision tool that ties the combination of safeguards to a competition's declared purpose. The argument reaches beyond CTFs to any setting in cybersecurity where a demonstrated result is taken as evidence of an underlying ability.

AI.tldr: LLMs now reliably solve easy and intermediate CTF challenges across cryptography, web, and binary exploitation, raising questions of fairness and learning value. The paper maps the human-machine capability boundary by category, identifies an undeclared conflict about CTF purpose as the root of AI-use disagreements, and proposes a four-component safeguard framework with a decision tool aligning protections to a competition's stated purpose.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly capable of solving CTF challenges autonomously, threatening the fairness of rankings and undermining CTFs' core function as practical cybersecurity training grounds. The community lacks both a clear map of which challenge categories resist automation and a structured approach to deciding whether and how to permit AI use.
AI.method: Mixed-methods design combining: (1) synthesis of published LLM-on-CTF benchmarks including a government evaluation; (2) case studies of live competition performance across three categories (cryptography, web exploitation, binary exploitation); (3) structured observation of public community channels debating AI use; and (4) semi-structured interviews with experienced players and organisers.
AI.result: Easy/intermediate challenges in all three studied categories are now reliably automatable; narrower sub-categories still resist. Community disagreement about AI permissibility stems from an unstated divergence on what CTFs are fundamentally for — a prior question left undeclared. The paper contributes a four-component safeguard framework (tiered divisions, LLM-resistant challenge design, investigatory telemetry, community code of conduct) and a decision tool linking safeguard choices to a competition's declared purpose.
AI.conclusion: The core issue is not whether AI should be allowed in CTFs but that the community has not first agreed on the purpose of the competitions themselves. The safeguard framework and decision tool provide a principled way to align AI policy with purpose, and the argument generalises to any cybersecurity context where a demonstrated result is taken as evidence of underlying competence.

title: Breaking the Periodicity Assumption: Robust Tensorial Multi-View Clustering via Graph-Spectral Low-Rank Learning
summary: Tensorial multi-view clustering (TMC) has achieved strong performance due to its ability to capture high-order correlations across multiple views. Most existing t-SVD-based TMC frameworks apply the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) along the sample mode to impose frequency-domain low-rank constraints. However, we reveal that this widely adopted design critically relies on an implicit ``periodicity assumption'' induced by the sample arrangement. When samples are ordered by class, neighboring indices tend to be semantically similar, creating artificial local continuity along the sample mode and a favorable spectral structure for FFT-based low-rank regularization. Once this ordering is removed by random permutation, existing t-SVD-based TMC methods suffer severe performance degradation. This strong sensitivity to class ordering conflicts with the permutation-invariant nature of clustering and indicates that part of the reported performance may be attributed to a privileged sample arrangement rather than genuine high-order structure modeling. In this paper, we systematically investigate this phenomenon and its underlying algebraic and spectral mechanisms. To address this fundamental flaw, we further propose a graph-spectral low-rank tensor learning framework based on the Graph Fourier Transform (GFT), which replaces the fixed Fourier basis along the sample mode with a data-driven graph spectral basis, thereby capturing the intrinsic manifold structure without relying on a particular sample ordering. Moreover, we develop an anchor-based variant to address large-scale datasets efficiently. Extensive experiments on various benchmarks validate our findings and demonstrate the competitive or superior performance of the proposed methods compared with state-of-the-art TMC approaches.

AI.tldr: Existing t-SVD-based multi-view clustering methods rely on FFT along the sample mode, which implicitly assumes a favorable sample ordering (e.g., by class). Random permutation destroys performance, revealing that gains partly stem from privileged arrangement rather than genuine high-order modeling. The authors propose a Graph Fourier Transform (GFT)-based tensor learning framework that uses a data-driven graph spectral basis to capture intrinsic manifold structure without depending on sample ordering, plus an anchor-based variant for scalability.
AI.motivation: Expose a critical flaw in t-SVD-based tensorial multi-view clustering (TMC): FFT-based low-rank regularization along the sample mode relies on an implicit "periodicity assumption" tied to sample ordering by class. Random permutation severely degrades performance, contradicting the permutation-invariant nature of clustering and suggesting that reported gains are partly artifacts of privileged sample arrangement rather than genuine high-order structure modeling.
AI.method: Replace the fixed FFT basis along the sample mode with a Graph Fourier Transform (GFT) derived from a data-driven similarity graph. This yields a graph-spectral low-rank tensor learning framework that captures intrinsic manifold structure invariant to sample permutation. An anchor-based variant is also developed for efficient large-scale processing.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks validate the identified flaw in FFT-based TMC methods and demonstrate that the proposed GFT-based framework achieves competitive or superior performance compared to state-of-the-art TMC approaches.
AI.conclusion: The periodicity assumption in FFT-based TMC is a fundamental weakness. Graph-spectral low-rank tensor learning via GFT provides a principled, permutation-invariant solution that recovers genuine multi-view clustering performance and scales to large datasets with the anchor-based variant.

title: Tokens are All You Need: Dual-purpose Semantic IDs for Achieving LLM-Level I/O Efficiency in recommendation systems
summary: Large-scale recommendation systems face "Memory Wall" bottlenecks due to massive, dense embedding tables. While generative retrieval uses discrete tokens for IDs, high-dimensional context still relies on inefficient dense formats. Inspired by computer vision data compression, we propose Dual-purpose Semantic IDs to achieve LLM-level I/O efficiency. Our methodology uses hierarchical quantization to condense continuous embeddings into discrete Semantic IDs performing two concurrent roles: (1) Collaborative Identity: modeling user-item interactions via learnable embedding table; and (2) Content Reconstruction: using a lightweight Semantic Decoder for on-the-fly embedding approximation. This approach replaces massive vector storage with on-demand reconstruction, reducing system overhead and data footprints. We demonstrate the efficacy of our framework through offline evaluations and successful online deployment in production-scale ranking and retrieval systems at a major video sharing platform, showing that discrete tokens are indeed all you need for highly efficient, content-rich recommendation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Dual-purpose Semantic IDs — a hierarchical quantization framework that converts dense embeddings into discrete tokens serving dual roles (collaborative identity and content reconstruction). This replaces massive vector storage with on-demand decoding, achieving LLM-level I/O efficiency and demonstrating success in production-scale recommendation systems.
AI.motivation: Large-scale recommendation systems suffer from the "Memory Wall" bottleneck caused by massive, dense embedding tables. While generative retrieval has moved toward discrete token-based IDs, high-dimensional context representations still rely on inefficient dense formats, creating storage and I/O inefficiencies at scale.
AI.method: The authors propose Dual-purpose Semantic IDs using hierarchical quantization to condense continuous embeddings into discrete tokens. These Semantic IDs serve two concurrent roles: (1) Collaborative Identity — modeling user-item interactions through a learnable embedding table, and (2) Content Reconstruction — employing a lightweight Semantic Decoder for on-the-fly embedding approximation. The framework replaces persistent vector storage with on-demand reconstruction.
AI.result: The framework was validated through offline evaluations and successful online deployment in production-scale ranking and retrieval systems at a major video sharing platform, demonstrating significant reductions in system overhead and data footprint while maintaining recommendation quality.
AI.conclusion: Discrete tokens are sufficient for highly efficient, content-rich recommendation. The dual-purpose Semantic ID approach effectively overcomes the Memory Wall bottleneck, enabling LLM-level I/O efficiency in large-scale production recommendation systems.

title: AI's Capability in Assisting Scientific Research in Physics, Astrophysics, and Cosmology II: Project Planning and Proposal Evaluation
summary: We investigate how well large language models (LLMs) can assist scientific project planning and proposal evaluation. One-page project plans were independently generated for eight expert-conceived research projects in physics, astrophysics, and cosmology by human researchers and three contemporary LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek; mid-2025 models, used with their default tool access). The resulting 32 proposals were blindly evaluated by four human reviewers and two newer frontier LLMs (Claude Opus 4.8 and ChatGPT Pro 5.5) using a four-aspect evaluation rubric. Reviewers were also asked to identify whether each proposal was written by a human or an AI. Human reviewers rated human- and AI-written proposals similarly overall, whereas both AI reviewers scored AI-written proposals about one point higher (on a five-point scale) than human-written proposals. Human reviewers correctly identified human- and AI-written proposals 72% and 79% of the time, respectively, while both AI reviewers correctly classified all 32 proposals (100%). These results suggest that current LLMs can produce project plans comparable to human-written ones in the eyes of human reviewers, but that AI reviewers show a systematic preference for AI-generated proposals. Our results suggest caution when deploying LLMs widely in proposal preparation and evaluation.

AI.tldr: A study tested whether LLMs can generate scientific project proposals comparable to human-written ones. Human reviewers rated both similarly, but AI reviewers systematically favored AI-generated proposals (≈1 point higher on a 5-point scale) and correctly identified authorship 100% of the time, while humans achieved ~72–79% accuracy. The findings urge caution in deploying LLMs for proposal preparation and evaluation.
AI.motivation: To assess the capability of contemporary LLMs in assisting scientific project planning and proposal evaluation, and to determine whether AI and human reviewers exhibit biases when evaluating AI-generated versus human-written research proposals.
AI.method: Eight expert-conceived research projects in physics, astrophysics, and cosmology were used to generate one-page project plans independently by human researchers and three LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek; mid-2025 models with default tool access), yielding 32 proposals. These were blindly evaluated by four human reviewers and two frontier LLMs (Claude Opus 4.8, ChatGPT Pro 5.5) using a four-aspect rubric on a five-point scale. Reviewers also attempted to identify whether each proposal was human- or AI-written.
AI.result: Human reviewers rated human- and AI-written proposals similarly overall. AI reviewers scored AI-written proposals approximately one point higher on a five-point scale than human-written ones. Human reviewers correctly identified human-written proposals 72% of the time and AI-written ones 79% of the time; AI reviewers achieved 100% classification accuracy for all 32 proposals.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs can produce project plans comparable to human-written ones as judged by human reviewers, but AI reviewers exhibit a systematic preference for AI-generated content. Caution is warranted when deploying LLMs broadly in proposal preparation and evaluation contexts.

title: Bits and Memories: Measuring Verbatim Extraction Across LLM Quantization
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures. Code: https://github.com/AkshaySasi/bits-and-memories. Data and results: https://huggingface.co/datasets/AkshaySasi/bits-and-memories
summary: Language models are almost always quantized before they are deployed, and a growing line of work asks whether quantization also lowers their privacy risk. That work measures privacy almost entirely with membership inference. We think this is the wrong thing to measure for the risk that most people actually worry about, namely a model reproducing its training data word for word, and we measure that directly. Using the Pythia models and the public set of sequences each of them is known to have memorized, we track verbatim extraction across five precision levels, from full precision down to four bits, and across three model sizes, while measuring general capability (perplexity) at every point. We find two things. Quantization is a selective forgetter: verbatim memorization falls off faster than capability at every precision and every model size we tried, and this holds under two unrelated quantization algorithms and two evaluation corpora. But the selectivity is not enough to make quantization a privacy defense, which cuts against the optimistic reading of earlier membership-inference results. At the largest model we study, four-bit quantization still reproduces most of the memorized sequences while giving up only a few percent of capability, and the fraction of memorized data that survives quantization grows with model size. We conclude that compression should not be treated as a way to remove memorized training data, and that extraction, not membership inference, is the number practitioners should be watching. All code, sampled evaluation data, and per-configuration results are released.

AI.tldr: Quantization selectively reduces verbatim memorization faster than general capability, but not enough to serve as a privacy defense — larger models retain most memorized sequences even at 4-bit precision. The paper argues extraction, not membership inference, is the right metric for privacy risk.
AI.motivation: Prior work evaluates whether quantization reduces privacy risk using membership inference attacks, but the authors argue this misses the real concern: models reproducing training data verbatim. They aim to directly measure how quantization affects memorized sequence extraction across precision levels and model sizes.
AI.method: Using Pythia models (three sizes) and a public set of known memorized sequences, the authors track verbatim extraction across five precision levels (full precision down to 4-bit) under two unrelated quantization algorithms and two evaluation corpora, while measuring perplexity as a capability proxy at every point.
AI.result: Quantization acts as a "selective forgetter": verbatim memorization degrades faster than capability. However, at the largest model size, 4-bit quantization still reproduces most memorized sequences while losing only a small percentage of capability. The fraction of memorized data surviving quantization grows with model size.
AI.conclusion: Compression/quantization should not be treated as a way to remove memorized training data. Extraction, not membership inference, should be the primary metric practitioners monitor for privacy risk. All code, data, and results are released.

title: Zhinv: Real-time hub-height wind field reconstruction using only local sparse observations
summary: The high proportion of wind power connected to the grid places higher demands on fine-grained knowledge of regional wind fields. Since the wind information directly obtainable in actual operations is mostly sparse, discrete, and irregularly distributed local observations, it is difficult to directly meet the needs of tasks such as wind power regulation, wind resource assessment, and low-altitude environmental perception of continuous regional wind fields. Therefore, we propose Zhinv, an end-to-end reconstruction framework that directly weaves sparse and irregular observations into a fine-grid wind field at hub-height. Experiments in Northeast China, Europe, and Southeast Asia demonstrate that Zhinv can accurately, robustly, and efficiently reconstruct fine-grid wind fields from sparse observations, reducing the error by about 66% compared with Kriging. With local wind-power observations as input, Zhinv enables wind power centers to bypass NWP and complex assimilation processes, supporting direct and real-time wind resource assessment from locally available data.

AI.tldr: Zhinv is an end-to-end framework that reconstructs fine-grid hub-height wind fields directly from sparse, irregularly distributed local observations, achieving ~66% error reduction compared to Kriging and enabling real-time wind resource assessment without NWP.
AI.motivation: With high wind power penetration, fine-grained regional wind field knowledge is critical for regulation, resource assessment, and environmental perception. However, directly obtainable observations are sparse, discrete, and irregularly distributed, making continuous regional wind field reconstruction challenging.
AI.method: An end-to-end reconstruction framework called Zhinv that directly weaves sparse and irregular observations into a fine-grid wind field at hub-height, bypassing numerical weather prediction (NWP) and complex assimilation processes.
AI.result: Experiments across Northeast China, Europe, and Southeast Asia show Zhinv reconstructs fine-grid wind fields accurately, robustly, and efficiently, reducing error by approximately 66% compared to Kriging. It also supports direct real-time wind resource assessment from local wind-power observations.
AI.conclusion: Zhinv enables wind power centers to bypass traditional NWP and assimilation workflows, providing a direct, real-time, and accurate means of regional wind field reconstruction and resource assessment from locally available sparse observations.

title: Ranked by Position: Order Sensitivity as an Exploitable Attack Surface in LLM Listwise Recommenders
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 11 tables. Code and data available at https://github.com/geoz-lab/position_bias_attack
summary: Large language models (LLMs) used as listwise rerankers in recommendation systems suffer from position bias when serializing candidate sets into prompts. We show this order sensitivity creates an exploitable attack surface: an attacker can promote a label-0 target into the top-$k$ solely by reordering candidates, without changing item content, labels, or model parameters. We introduce $\mathrm{promo}@k$ to quantify this vulnerability, measuring the fraction of label-0 targets that can be elevated into top-$k$ rankings via permutation. Evaluating across three domains (MovieLens, Amazon Books, and Amazon Fashion), $\mathrm{promo}@5$ reaches up to 0.57 at an attack budget of $R$ = 50 orderings. Furthermore, ordinary permutation stability predicts vulnerability without running the attack. While a bidirectional T5 encoder scorer reduces exposure, permutation-consistency regularization and architectural invariance effectively mitigate it. Pointwise scoring avoids the bias issue but degrades ranking quality. These results demonstrate that input candidate order in listwise LLM reranking is a security-relevant attack vector. Code and data are available at https://github.com/geoz-lab/position_bias_attack.

AI.tldr: LLM listwise rerankers are vulnerable to order-based adversarial attacks where an attacker can elevate irrelevant items into top-k recommendations solely by permuting candidate order, without modifying content, labels, or model parameters.
AI.motivation: LLM-based listwise rerankers suffer from position bias when candidate sets are serialized into prompts. This paper investigates whether this order sensitivity constitutes an exploitable security vulnerability rather than merely a ranking quality degradation.
AI.method: The authors formalize the attack as maximizing a target item's rank via permutation of other candidates within a budget R of orderings. They introduce the promo@k metric to quantify vulnerability — the fraction of label-0 (irrelevant) targets promotable into top-k. Empirical evaluation spans MovieLens, Amazon Books, and Amazon Fashion datasets with multiple LLM rerankers. Defenses tested include bidirectional T5 encoder scoring, permutation-consistency regularization, architectural invariance, and pointwise scoring baselines.
AI.result: promo@5 reaches up to 0.57 at R=50 orderings, demonstrating substantial vulnerability. Ordinary permutation stability (rank variance under random orderings) strongly predicts attack vulnerability without executing the attack. A bidirectional T5 encoder reduces but does not eliminate exposure. Permutation-consistency regularization and architectural invariance effectively mitigate the attack. Pointwise scoring avoids position bias entirely but sacrifices ranking quality.
AI.conclusion: Input candidate order in listwise LLM reranking constitutes a security-relevant attack vector. The proposed promo@k metric and permutation stability proxy enable practical vulnerability assessment. Architectural and regularization-based defenses can mitigate the risk, though pointwise approaches trade ranking quality for immunity.

title: Evaluating Multi-Turn Multimodal Diagnostic Reasoning on Challenging Real-World Clinical Cases
summary: Clinical diagnostic evaluation should not only assess whether models can provide correct diagnoses, but also reflect the realities of clinical practice, including progressive disclosure of multimodal information, dynamic updating of diagnostic hypotheses, and continuous refinement of clinical reasoning. However, existing evaluations of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) typically rely on single-turn or isolated tasks, making it difficult to fully capture the complexity of real-world clinical diagnosis. To bridge this gap, we developed ClinMM-Bench, the largest multi-turn multimodal clinical diagnostic evaluation benchmark to date. ClinMM-Bench contains 1,089 challenging real-world clinical cases and 3,760 medical images across eight specialties. We systematically evaluated 15 representative MLLMs using a two-level evaluation framework that assessed both diagnostic accuracy and diagnostic reasoning quality. Results showed that proprietary models achieved the highest overall diagnostic accuracy, but the proportion of completely correct diagnoses remained limited across all models. In terms of diagnostic reasoning quality, current models can identify plausible diagnostic directions but still have considerable limitations in generating reliable diagnostic reasoning. Error analysis further identified five representative failure modes: information synthesis failure, knowledge mapping error, perception error, premature closure, and visual hallucination.

AI.tldr: ClinMM-Bench is a large-scale, multi-turn, multimodal benchmark for clinical diagnosis using 1,089 cases and 3,760 images across eight specialties. Evaluation of 15 MLLMs reveals that even top proprietary models struggle with fully correct diagnoses and exhibit five characteristic failure modes in diagnostic reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal LLM evaluations use single-turn or isolated tasks, failing to capture real-world clinical diagnosis which involves progressive information disclosure, dynamic hypothesis updating, and iterative reasoning refinement.
AI.method: The authors constructed ClinMM-Bench (1,089 cases, 3,760 images, 8 specialties) and evaluated 15 MLLMs using a two-level framework assessing diagnostic accuracy and diagnostic reasoning quality, followed by systematic error analysis to identify failure modes.
AI.result: Proprietary models led in overall diagnostic accuracy, but the proportion of completely correct diagnoses was low across all models. All models showed limitations in generating reliable diagnostic reasoning. Five failure modes were identified: information synthesis failure, knowledge mapping error, perception error, premature closure, and visual hallucination.
AI.conclusion: Current MLLMs are not yet reliable for real-world clinical diagnosis. The ClinMM-Bench benchmark provides a more ecologically valid evaluation framework, and the identified failure modes offer clear directions for future model improvement.

title: Anti-Backdoor Coreset Selection via Cumulative Entropy
summary: Recent training-time defenses against neural backdoors isolate a benign subset from poisoned training data, to learn a backdoor-free model from it. In this paper, we formulate this defense strategy as a coreset selection problem, giving rise to so-called "Anti-Backdoor Coreset Selection." Since poisonous samples have (a) lower prediction uncertainty and are (b) less frequent than benign samples, coreset selection naturally focuses more on samples associated with benign functionality than the backdoor functionality. We use the Cumulative Entropy as selection criterion to further facilitate this effect. The metric tracks the learning dynamics of training samples and allowing us to select benign samples with high informativeness for the coreset. Additionally, we unlearn the chosen samples in each epoch to facilitate the separability between benign and poisonous samples. Together, this yields an exceptionally effective training-time defense that constructs a benign coreset to train a backdoor-free model. Unlike prior defenses that compromise natural accuracy and fail against certain attacks, our method mitigates backdooring attacks consistently with a negligible impact on natural performance.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates training-time backdoor defense as a coreset selection problem, leveraging the observation that poisonous samples exhibit lower prediction uncertainty and lower frequency than benign samples. Using Cumulative Entropy as a selection criterion and per-epoch unlearning, the method constructs a benign coreset to train backdoor-free models with negligible natural accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Existing training-time defenses isolate benign subsets from poisoned data but lack a principled formulation. The authors aim to formalize this as a coreset selection problem, exploiting inherent differences between benign and poisonous samples — namely, poisonous samples' lower prediction uncertainty and lower relative frequency — to achieve more robust and consistent backdoor mitigation without sacrificing natural accuracy.
AI.method: The approach, called Anti-Backdoor Coreset Selection, uses Cumulative Entropy as the selection metric to track sample learning dynamics and identify high-informativeness benign samples. In each epoch, the method selects a coreset of benign samples for training and applies an unlearning step to the chosen samples, which enhances the separability between benign and poisonous data. This iterative process yields a progressively purer benign coreset for training a backdoor-free model.
AI.result: The method mitigates backdoor attacks consistently across diverse attack types, unlike prior defenses that fail against certain attacks. It achieves this with negligible impact on natural (clean) performance, avoiding the accuracy degradation common in existing defenses.
AI.conclusion: Framing training-time backdoor defense as coreset selection, guided by Cumulative Entropy and augmented with per-epoch unlearning, provides an exceptionally effective defense that consistently neutralizes backdoors while preserving natural model accuracy.

title: Psychological Influences of Conversational AI: Research and Design Directions for Reducing Harm and Promoting Well-Being
summary: As conversational AI systems become increasingly integrated into daily life, their potential effects on user well-being require ongoing attention. While consumer-facing generalist models can provide benefits, including improved access to information, learning, productivity, self-reflection, and companionship, they also introduce risks, such as emotional entanglement, unhealthy dependence, and the amplification of psychological vulnerabilities. Drawing on prior research and empirical observations of AI chatbot behavior, we propose a set of aspirational directions for guiding the behavior of general-purpose AI systems in ways that may reduce potential psychological harms and support user well-being. We acknowledge the difficulty of systematically assessing the long-term impacts of AI chatbot use and frame these directions as hypotheses for studying how AI behavior may influence users across general interactions, role-playing scenarios, and contexts that could be characterized as providing psychological support. While some proposed directions are supported by existing research and expert insights, others identify open questions and areas requiring deeper study. We hope that this formulation and these hypotheses encourage further discussion, empirical investigation, and exploration of interactive design approaches aimed at better accommodating users' psychological needs and promoting their well-being.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes aspirational behavioral guidelines for general-purpose conversational AI systems to mitigate psychological harms (e.g., emotional dependence, vulnerability amplification) while preserving benefits (e.g., companionship, learning), framing these as testable hypotheses for future empirical research on AI's long-term impact on user well-being.
AI.motivation: As conversational AI becomes ubiquitous in daily life, there is growing concern about psychological risks — emotional entanglement, unhealthy dependence, and exacerbation of vulnerabilities — that lack systematic study. The authors aim to catalyze proactive design and empirical investigation before harms become widespread.
AI.method: Drawing on prior research and empirical observations of AI chatbot behavior, the authors propose a set of aspirational behavioral directions for general-purpose AI systems. These directions are framed as falsifiable hypotheses regarding AI behavior across general interactions, role-playing, and psychological support contexts, intended to guide future empirical studies and interactive design exploration.
AI.result: The paper does not report empirical results; instead, it yields a structured framework of testable hypotheses about how AI behavior may influence user well-being. Some directions are grounded in existing evidence and expert insight, while others identify open research questions requiring deeper investigation.
AI.conclusion: The authors call for further discussion, empirical investigation, and iterative design approaches to better accommodate users' psychological needs. They emphasize that systematically assessing long-term impacts remains challenging but essential for responsible AI deployment.

title: Retraction-Free Optimization over the Stiefel Manifold for the LoRA Fine-Tuning
summary: Optimization over the Stiefel manifold plays a significant role in various machine learning tasks. Existing methods either use the retraction operators, requiring costly orthonormalization for large-scale matrices, or employ landing methods that rely on careful step size selection and penalty parameter tuning. To address these challenges, we propose a retraction-free and penalty parameter-free algorithm that directly lands on the manifold. By leveraging the strongly-convex-like property of the quadratic penalty function and the proximal smoothness of the Stiefel manifold, we establish global convergence guarantees with the best-known iteration complexities under both constant and diminishing step sizes. Then, we reformulate the low-rank adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning problem for large language models as a manifold optimization problem, introducing Manifold-LoRA for geometry-accelerated adaptation. This approach employs the proposed landing technique and a carefully designed step size strategy to accelerate the training process. Numerical experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficiency and strong downstream performance of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: A retraction-free, penalty-free algorithm for Stiefel manifold optimization with global convergence guarantees, applied to accelerate LoRA fine-tuning for large language models.
AI.motivation: Existing Stiefel manifold optimization methods either require costly retraction/orthonormalization or rely on sensitive penalty parameters and step size tuning. There is a need for a simpler, more robust algorithm that avoids these issues, especially for large-scale applications like LLM fine-tuning.
AI.method: The authors propose a landing algorithm that directly lands on the Stiefel manifold without retractions or penalty parameters. The method exploits the strongly-convex-like property of the quadratic penalty function and proximal smoothness of the Stiefel manifold to establish convergence. This algorithm is then integrated into a manifold optimization reformulation of LoRA fine-tuning (Manifold-LoRA) with a tailored step size strategy.
AI.result: Global convergence is established with the best-known iteration complexities under both constant and diminishing step sizes. Numerical experiments on benchmark datasets show that Manifold-LoRA achieves efficient training and strong downstream performance compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed retraction-free, penalty-free landing algorithm offers a simpler and theoretically grounded alternative for Stiefel manifold optimization, with practical advantages demonstrated through Manifold-LoRA for accelerating LLM fine-tuning.

title: Agent Retrieval Bench: Evaluating Repository Context Retrieval for Coding Agents
summary: Modern coding agents are usually evaluated by whether they eventually produce a correct patch, but patch generation depends on an earlier context-acquisition stage: finding the repository files needed for the task. We introduce Agent Retrieval Bench, a file-level benchmark for this upstream retrieval problem. Samples are built from real coding-workflow signals and evaluated against frozen base-commit repositories, with relevance defined by what an agent needs next rather than direct query-file semantic similarity. The benchmark covers four positive-retrieval tasks: code2test, comment2context, trace2code, and edit2ripple; a fifth subset evaluates selective retrieval using natural evidence-backed no-gold cases and counterfactual wrong-repository controls. Agent Retrieval Bench contains 427 samples across 25 repositories: 345 positive examples, 50 natural no-gold examples, and 32 counterfactual controls. The corpus includes 308 base-commit snapshots, 392,000 files, and 7.9 million chunks. We evaluate lexical retrieval, RepoMap, open-source embeddings, selective abstention, and logged agent context selection. No single retrieval family dominates: Qwen3-Embedding-4B has the best sample-weighted MRR on positive samples, Qwen3-Embedding-8B the best Recall@20, and RepoMap the best budgeted context yield at 8K tokens, with task-level winners differing substantially. Selective thresholds calibrated with counterfactual controls do not improve selective success on natural no-gold cases, revealing a calibration gap. Logged trajectories also miss every gold file on 27-35 percent of samples. A controlled seed-intervention pilot finds that retrieval-derived initial context yields higher file F1 with less post-seed exploration than random non-gold context, while oracle gold context shows substantial remaining headroom.

AI.tldr: Introduces Agent Retrieval Bench (ARB), a file-level benchmark evaluating how well coding agents retrieve relevant repository context before patch generation. Across 427 samples and 25 repositories, no single retrieval method dominates; selective retrieval thresholds show a calibration gap, and initial context quality significantly impacts downstream coding performance.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of coding agents focus on end-to-end patch correctness, ignoring the critical upstream retrieval stage where agents must identify relevant files from large repositories. Current retrieval benchmarks rely on semantic similarity between queries and files, which does not match what agents actually need next during real workflows. There is no standardized benchmark for this context-acquisition problem.
AI.method: ARB constructs samples from real coding-workflow signals (not synthetic queries) across four positive-retrieval tasks: code2test, comment2context, trace2code, and edit2ripple. It also includes natural no-gold examples and counterfactual wrong-repository controls for evaluating selective retrieval. Relevance is defined by what an agent needs next, not query-file similarity. Evaluation covers lexical retrieval (BM25), RepoMap, open-source embeddings (multiple Qwen3 variants), selective abstention strategies, and logged agent context selection. A seed-intervention pilot measures how retrieval-derived context affects downstream file F1.
AI.result: No single retriever dominates: Qwen3-Embedding-4B achieves best sample-weighted MRR, Qwen3-Embedding-8B best Recall@20, and RepoMap best budgeted context yield at 8K tokens. Task-level winners vary substantially. Selective thresholds calibrated on counterfactual controls fail to improve success on natural no-gold cases, revealing a calibration gap. Logged trajectories miss every gold file on 27-35% of samples. Retrieval-derived initial context yields higher file F1 with less post-seed exploration than random non-gold context; oracle gold context shows substantial remaining headroom.
AI.conclusion: Context retrieval is a distinct, measurable bottleneck in coding agent pipelines deserving independent evaluation. The calibration gap between controlled and natural no-gold cases suggests current selective retrieval methods are unreliable. Retrieval quality directly impacts downstream coding performance, and significant headroom remains between best retrievers and oracle performance, motivating further research in retrieval-augmented code generation.

title: CogEEGAgent: Toward Autonomous Cognitive EEG Analysis with Grounded Execution and Selection-Aware Verification
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures, and 16 tables. The supplementary material is included in the same PDF
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) analysis in cognitive studies requires specialized expertise and involves many defensible choices over contrasts, channels, time windows, and statistical tests. LLM agents can translate varied natural-language questions into analysis choices, offering a flexible interface for automation. Yet fluent reports alone cannot establish that an agent selected the requested analysis or evaluated a confirmatory claim independently of adaptive search. We present CogEEGAgent, a cognitive-EEG analysis agent grounded in MNE-Python. Its EEG-specific scientific harness separates semantic from scientific authority. The LLM interprets intent and proposes registered analyses, while deterministic components validate typed contracts, control confirmation access, and authorize evidence-bound release. On a prespecified routing benchmark, CogEEGAgent maps language to registered analyses more accurately than a matched deterministic router, while matched preflight makes both systems abstain whenever required. In an externally model-authored, outcome-blind campaign, the complete system releases supported analyses with participant-disjoint confirmation and blocks prespecified capability hazards and lifecycle-reuse requests. Policy stress testing shows that held-out confirmation curbs false positives from uncorrected adaptive search. Together, these studies establish bounded autonomy and an auditable automation framework for cognitive-EEG workflows. More broadly, they show how scientific agents can combine flexible language understanding with fail-closed control over inference and release.

AI.tldr: CogEEGAgent combines an LLM for natural-language understanding with deterministic scientific harnesses to automate cognitive EEG analysis while enforcing bounded autonomy — separating semantic interpretation from scientific authority, blocking unauthorized analyses, and curbing false positives from adaptive search.
AI.motivation: EEG analysis in cognitive studies requires specialized expertise and involves many defensible but arbitrary choices (contrasts, channels, time windows, statistical tests). While LLMs offer flexible natural-language interfaces for automating such workflows, fluent outputs alone cannot guarantee that the agent correctly selected the requested analysis or evaluated confirmatory claims without engaging in uncorrected adaptive search. There is a need for auditable automation that combines LLM flexibility with rigorous scientific control.
AI.method: The authors introduce CogEEGAgent, an agent grounded in MNE-Python with a scientific harness that separates semantic authority (LLM interpreting intent and proposing registered analyses) from scientific authority (deterministic components validating typed contracts, controlling confirmation access, and authorizing evidence-bound release). Evaluation proceeds through: (1) a prespecified routing benchmark comparing CogEEGAgent against a matched deterministic router; (2) an externally model-authored, outcome-blind campaign testing complete system behavior; and (3) policy stress testing with held-out confirmation to assess false-positive control under adaptive search.
AI.result: On the routing benchmark, CogEEGAgent maps natural language to registered analyses more accurately than a matched deterministic router, while matched preflight causes both systems to abstain when required. In the outcome-blind campaign, the system releases supported analyses with participant-disjoint confirmation and successfully blocks prespecified capability hazards and lifecycle-reuse requests. Policy stress testing demonstrates that held-out confirmation effectively curbs false positives that would otherwise arise from uncorrected adaptive search.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes bounded autonomy and an auditable automation framework for cognitive-EEG workflows. More broadly, it demonstrates how scientific agents can combine flexible language understanding with fail-closed control over inference and release, offering a principled blueprint for responsible LLM integration into scientific analysis pipelines.

title: Polistemics: Evaluating LLMs as Information Mediators in Politics & Elections
summary: As LLMs increasingly mediate the political information citizens rely on, there is still no standardized way to assess whether they do so responsibly. We introduce Polistemics, a theory-grounded benchmark for evaluating LLMs as mediators of political information in elections. Prior work has treated this task as reproduction rather than mediation, leaving its epistemic dimensions and interaction with imperfect information unaddressed. We ground the evaluation in Epistemic Modesty, a normative standard derived from citizens' epistemic agency, and test it across controlled settings that vary informational properties such as clarity, noise, and consistency. Applying the benchmark to three state-of-the-art LLMs on the 2025 German and Dutch elections, we find that high aggregate scores mask systematic failures. Models mediate reliably under clear evidence but break down under absent, vague, or contradictory information, while flattening the intensity of political language. These failures are likely driven by party priors, influenced by party labels and output language. Reliable mediation appears achievable, but no model delivers it consistently.

AI.tldr: Presents Polistemics, a benchmark evaluating LLMs as political information mediators during elections. Using Epistemic Modesty as a normative standard, the study tests three LLMs on 2025 German and Dutch elections and finds that high aggregate scores conceal systematic breakdowns under absent, vague, or contradictory information, with performance influenced by party priors and language.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly mediating political information that citizens rely on, yet no standardized method exists to evaluate whether they do so responsibly. Prior work frames this as a reproduction task, neglecting the epistemic dimensions of mediation and how models handle imperfect (noisy, vague, inconsistent) information.
AI.method: Introduces Polistemics, a theory-grounded benchmark rooted in Epistemic Modesty—a normative standard derived from citizens' epistemic agency. The benchmark tests LLM mediation across controlled settings varying informational properties (clarity, noise, consistency). Applied to three state-of-the-art LLMs on the 2025 German and Dutch elections.
AI.result: High aggregate scores mask systematic failures: models mediate reliably under clear evidence but fail under absent, vague, or contradictory information. Models also flatten the intensity of political language. Failures are driven by party priors, influenced by party labels and output language. No model achieves consistently reliable mediation.
AI.conclusion: Reliable political information mediation is theoretically achievable but not yet consistently delivered by current LLMs. The benchmark reveals that aggregate evaluation metrics are insufficient and that epistemic standards like Epistemic Modesty are necessary for responsible deployment in electoral contexts.

title: Guiding Posterior Exploration with Optimizer-Derived Geometry
comment: Accepted for presentation at the OPTIMAL Workshop at AISTATS 2026
summary: Sampling-based methods offer a principled approach to uncertainty quantification in Bayesian neural networks. Their practical use, however, is often challenged by the computational cost of exploring high-dimensional and multimodal posterior distributions. To overcome these difficulties, Bayesian Deep Ensembles, i.e., warmstarting the sampling from several optimized solutions, have proven to be an effective strategy. In this paper, we demonstrate that curvature estimates computed during the warmstart as a byproduct in adaptive optimizers such as AdamW can inform the sampling phase at negligible additional cost. Specifically, our proposed preconditioned sampling strategy based on optimizer-derived geometries can substantially reduce or even eliminate the need for a lengthy sampling burn-in phase and leads to greater numerical stability. This approach consistently maintains or improves predictive performance and uncertainty quantification without any additional computational costs. We confirm the consistency of our findings across various datasets and network architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a preconditioned sampling strategy for Bayesian Deep Ensembles that reuses curvature estimates from adaptive optimizers (e.g., AdamW) as a preconditioner during MCMC sampling, eliminating burn-in and improving numerical stability at no extra cost.
AI.motivation: Sampling-based uncertainty quantification in Bayesian neural networks is computationally expensive due to high-dimensional, multimodal posteriors. While Bayesian Deep Ensembles (warm-starting MCMC from multiple optimized solutions) help, the burn-in phase remains costly. The authors aim to leverage optimizer-derived curvature information — already computed during warmstart — to accelerate the sampling phase.
AI.method: The authors propose using curvature estimates (e.g., the preconditioner from AdamW's second-moment estimates) computed as a byproduct during the warmstart optimization phase to precondition the subsequent MCMC sampling. This preconditioned sampling strategy employs the adaptive optimizer's geometry to inform the proposal distribution in the sampling phase, reducing or eliminating burn-in and enhancing numerical stability, all without additional computational overhead.
AI.result: The proposed strategy consistently maintains or improves predictive performance and uncertainty quantification across various datasets and network architectures. It substantially reduces or eliminates the burn-in phase and yields greater numerical stability, all at negligible additional cost.
AI.conclusion: Optimizer-derived geometries from the warmstart phase can effectively inform sampling in Bayesian Deep Ensembles, eliminating the burn-in phase and improving stability without extra computation. The findings are consistent across diverse datasets and architectures, making this a practical, cost-free enhancement to existing Bayesian deep learning pipelines.

title: Grounded in Consensus, In Step With Emerging Science: A Consensus-Anchored Multi-Corpus Clinical Chatbot for Long COVID
summary: Long COVID (LC) poses a challenge for clinical decision support because relevant evidence is distributed across sources with different update cycles, evidentiary roles, and levels of clinical maturity. We present a clinician-facing chatbot that organizes four sources within a retrieval-augmented workflow: expert-curated consensus guidance, current PubMed literature, registered interventional trials, and evidence from living systematic reviews. Consensus guidance is always included to frame responses, while the remaining sources are retrieved in parallel when selected by the user. In an exploratory automated evaluation on 50 clinician-facing questions, our chatbot showed comparable mean ratings to OpenEvidence, with numerically higher scores and lower score variability in an LLM-judged comparison.

AI.tldr: A clinician-facing chatbot for Long COVID uses a retrieval-augmented workflow that integrates four sources — expert consensus guidance, PubMed literature, interventional trials, and living systematic reviews — with consensus guidance always framing responses. In automated evaluation on 50 questions, it performed comparably to OpenEvidence, with numerically higher and less variable LLM-judged scores.
AI.motivation: Long COVID clinical decision support is challenging because relevant evidence is fragmented across sources with heterogeneous update cycles, evidentiary roles, and clinical maturity levels. No single source provides timely, comprehensive guidance, necessitating a system that can orchestrate multiple evidence streams.
AI.method: The authors built a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) chatbot that always retrieves expert-curated consensus guidance to frame responses, while optionally retrieving PubMed articles, registered interventional trials, and living systematic review evidence in parallel based on user selection. An exploratory automated evaluation used 50 clinician-facing questions, comparing the chatbot against OpenEvidence via LLM-as-judge scoring.
AI.result: The chatbot achieved mean ratings comparable to OpenEvidence, with numerically higher scores and lower score variability in the LLM-judged comparison.
AI.conclusion: A multi-source RAG architecture that anchors responses in expert consensus while supplementing with parallel retrieval from complementary evidence sources is a viable approach for Long COVID clinical decision support, showing competitive performance against existing tools like OpenEvidence.

title: Detecting Knowledge Inconsistencies Across Text, Tables, and Knowledge Graphs
summary: Wikipedia and Wikidata are widely used for information access, LLM pre-training, and retrieval-augmented generation. Their knowledge is deeply connected but scattered across text, tables, and knowledge graphs. This raises a practical question: when these modalities disagree, how can we detect and explain the conflict? We study this problem as \emph{modality-level inconsistency detection}. We first introduce a taxonomy of cross-modal knowledge inconsistencies, covering information granularity differences, direct conflicts, temporal changes, and KG incompleteness. We then present \textsc{Kontrast}, an automatic framework that uses Text-to-SPARQL and LLM reasoning to compare table-based answers with KG evidence and categorize the resulting inconsistencies. Experiments on various Table-QA datasets show that cross-modal inconsistencies are common and informative. They reveal not only true knowledge conflicts, but also missing KG structure and temporal mismatches while being limited by Text-to-SPARQL errors and noise. Our analysis shows that text, tables, and KGs can complement and correct one another through systematic comparison. \textsc{Kontrast} provides a practical tool for large-scale knowledge auditing and establishes a benchmark for future work on cross-modal knowledge consistency. Code and data are available at https://github.com/ECLADATTA/KONTRAST.

AI.tldr: Kontrast is an automatic framework that detects and categorizes cross-modal knowledge inconsistencies between Wikipedia text/tables and Wikidata KGs using Text-to-SPARQL and LLM reasoning, revealing that such discrepancies are common and can be used for knowledge auditing.
AI.motivation: Wikipedia and Wikidata knowledge is deeply connected but scattered across text, tables, and knowledge graphs, with no systematic way to detect and explain conflicts when these modalities disagree.
AI.method: The authors introduce a taxonomy of cross-modal knowledge inconsistencies (granularity differences, direct conflicts, temporal changes, KG incompleteness) and build Kontrast, which uses Text-to-SPARQL conversion and LLM reasoning to compare table-based QA answers against KG evidence, then categorizes detected inconsistencies.
AI.result: Experiments on Table-QA datasets show cross-modal inconsistencies are common and informative, revealing true knowledge conflicts, missing KG structure, and temporal mismatches, though limited by Text-to-SPARQL errors and noise.
AI.conclusion: Text, tables, and KGs can complement and correct one another through systematic comparison. Kontrast serves as a practical tool for large-scale knowledge auditing and a benchmark for future cross-modal consistency research.

title: Beyond Epistemia: Epistemic Schizologia and Large Language Models as Techno-Semiotic Machines
summary: Quattrociocchi and colleagues warn that the fluent outputs of large language models may allow linguistic plausibility to substitute for epistemic evaluation, producing the condition they call *Epistemia*: the experience of possessing knowledge without undertaking the practices through which judgment would ordinarily be warranted. This article accepts that diagnosis but challenges its explanatory framework, which compares an embodied, socially situated human knower with an isolated generative model thereby locating epistemic legitimacy in capacities internal to autonomous agents. Drawing on Carlo Sini's philosophy of practices, writing, signs, and technics, we propose instead to understand a large language model (LLM) as a *techno-semiotic machine* that automates a phase of written semiosis by producing plausible linguistic configurations from the sedimented archive of human writing. From this perspective, *Epistemia* is one consequence of a broader phenomenon that we call *epistemic schizologia*: the socio-technical cleavage between signs as linguistically accomplished expressions and signs as moments within socially embedded circuits of interpretation, evidence, criticism, verification, and responsibility. This cleavage is reinforced by *eikotic closure*, through which a plausible continuation is presented with the finality of an epistemic result, and by algorithmic authority and epistemic self-misrecognition. The relevant unit is therefore not the model alone but the complete practice in which generated inscriptions are prompted, interpreted, verified, contested, used, and made consequential. This reframing preserves the distinction between linguistic production and responsible understanding while grounding a design programme centred on inspectable genealogy, contestability, distributed responsibility, epistemic agency, and the evaluation of hybrid human--AIpractices.

AI.tldr: This paper critiques Quattrociocchi et al.'s concept of *Epistemia* (mistaking linguistic plausibility for knowledge) for its individualistic framework. Drawing on Carlo Sini's philosophy, it reframes LLMs as "techno-semiotic machines" and introduces *epistemic schizologia*—the socio-technical cleavage between linguistically accomplished signs and signs embedded in socially accountable interpretive practices—along with *eikotic closure*, advocating a design programme centered on inspectability, contestability, and distributed epistemic agency.
AI.motivation: The authors accept Quattrociocchi et al.'s diagnosis that LLMs foster *Epistemia* but find its explanatory framework inadequate because it locates epistemic legitimacy in the internal capacities of autonomous agents, comparing an embodied human knower against an isolated model. This misses the socio-technical and semiotic dimensions of knowledge production, prompting a search for a more robust philosophical grounding.
AI.method: The paper deploys philosophical analysis grounded in Carlo Sini's philosophy of practices, writing, signs, and technics. It reconceptualizes the LLM as a *techno-semiotic machine* that automates a phase of written semiosis. It then introduces two novel concepts—*epistemic schizologia* and *eikotic closure*—to redescribe the problem at the level of complete socio-technical practices (prompting, interpreting, verifying, contesting, using) rather than at the level of individual agent-model dyads.
AI.result: The reframing yields: (1) a diagnosis of *epistemic schizologia* as the cleavage between signs as plausible linguistic completions and signs as moments within socially embedded circuits of evidence, criticism, and responsibility; (2) identification of *eikotic closure* (plausible continuation mistaken for epistemic finality), algorithmic authority, and epistemic self-misrecognition as reinforcing mechanisms; and (3) a design programme organized around inspectable genealogy, contestability, distributed responsibility, epistemic agency, and evaluation of hybrid human-AI practices.
AI.conclusion: The relevant unit of analysis is not the LLM alone but the complete practice in which generated inscriptions are made consequential. This preserves the distinction between linguistic production and responsible understanding while grounding actionable design principles for hybrid epistemic systems.

title: Explainable AI for Chronic Kidney Disease Prediction Using Simulated Federated Learning
summary: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD), characterized by the gradual loss of kidney function, remains a significant public health challenge. Early detection is crucial for preventing severe complications and enhancing patient outcomes. In this study, Federated Learning (FL) with a VotingClassifier was used to predict CKD using a clinical dataset, where Random Forest, AdaBoost, and XGBoost were utilized to compare and identify the best-fitting model for the global server. Additionally, GridSearchCV was applied to optimize the models' performance on the client's side. To enhance model transparency and trustworthiness, explainable AI (XAI) techniques were incorporated to interpret the prediction mechanisms. The global model's average accuracy was 99%, highlighting the potential of interpretable FL models in supporting early CKD diagnosis and advancing data-driven healthcare solutions.

AI.tldr: A federated learning system using a VotingClassifier (Random Forest, AdaBoost, XGBoost) with GridSearchCV optimization and XAI interpretation achieves 99% accuracy for early CKD prediction.
AI.motivation: CKD poses a major public health burden, and early detection is critical for preventing severe complications and improving patient outcomes. Privacy-preserving, interpretable machine learning models are needed for clinical adoption.
AI.method: Federated Learning with a VotingClassifier ensemble (Random Forest, AdaBoost, XGBoost) trained on a clinical CKD dataset. GridSearchCV is applied client-side for hyperparameter tuning. Explainable AI (XAI) techniques are used to interpret model predictions and enhance transparency.
AI.result: The global model achieved an average accuracy of 99%, demonstrating strong predictive performance for CKD detection.
AI.conclusion: Interpretable FL models hold significant promise for supporting early CKD diagnosis and advancing privacy-preserving, data-driven healthcare solutions.

title: Similar Models Learn Differently: Final-Window Pretraining Shapes Post-Training Beyond SFT
summary: Developers judge a model checkpoint by how it behaves. After supervised fine-tuning (SFT), two checkpoints that perform about the same across relevant benchmarks are treated as interchangeable, equally ready for the next alignment stage, typically preference optimization. We ask whether this judgment misses a pretraining imprint: a difference that no post-SFT benchmark reveals, yet that decides how each checkpoint responds to further training. To find out, we run a controlled experiment on the final window of pretraining, the last data trained on before instruction tuning. Six branches fork from one partially pretrained checkpoint and differ only in this window: 500 million tokens, 0.1% to 1% of the tokens that precede it. Each branch trains its window on a single data source: generic web text, filtered web text, normative discourse, safety text, mathematical text, or synthetic educational text. SFT and post-training are then identical. After SFT the branches behave near-identically, within about one point on instruction following, refusal, and capability, yet the same post-training carries them to very different endpoints, under both a direct preference optimization update and a reinforcement learning update with a verifiable reward. We measure this deviation through refusal of harmful requests: when post-training begins the safety text branch refuses no more than the web text branch, yet by the end it has lost far less of its refusal. The other four branches gain little or no protection, so the effect is selective to what the window contained. The protection requires the safety text to arrive last rather than earlier in pretraining, and it reproduces on a second model family. What a model is pretrained on last shapes how it reacts to alignment. Therefore, a checkpoint should not be evaluated by its post-SFT behavior alone, and what it was trained on last should be reported with it.

AI.tldr: Checkpoints that appear identical after SFT can harbor a "pretraining imprint" from the final pretraining window — specifically, the last data seen before instruction tuning. When the last window contains safety text, the model retains refusal behavior after alignment far better than when it contains web text, even though post-SFT benchmarks show no difference. This effect is selective to content type, sensitive to recency, and reproducible across model families.
AI.motivation: Standard practice evaluates checkpoints post-SFT using benchmarks; checkpoints with similar scores are considered interchangeable for downstream alignment (e.g., preference optimization). The authors hypothesize this misses a critical latent factor: the final pretraining data window leaves an imprint that is invisible after SFT but dictates how the model responds to subsequent alignment training.
AI.method: A controlled experiment: one partially pretrained checkpoint is forked into six branches, each trained on a final 500M-token window (0.1%–1% of prior tokens) from a distinct source — generic web text, filtered web text, normative discourse, safety text, mathematical text, or synthetic educational text. All branches then undergo identical SFT and post-training (DPO and RL with a verifiable reward). Outcomes are measured via harmful-request refusal rates and other behavioral metrics.
AI.result: After SFT, all branches perform within ~1 point on instruction-following, refusal, and capability benchmarks. After identical post-training, the safety-text branch retains significantly more refusal of harmful requests than the web-text branch, while the other four branches show little to no protection. The effect requires safety text to appear last (not earlier) and replicates on a second model family.
AI.conclusion: A checkpoint cannot be adequately assessed by post-SFT behavior alone; the final pretraining data composition decisively shapes alignment outcomes. Authors recommend that the last-trained-on data be reported alongside any model checkpoint release.

title: Instruction-Tuned Models Locally Reuse Human Syntax More Than Humans Do
summary: Syntactic convergence (the tendency of speakers to adapt in language towards the grammatical profiles of their interlocutors) is a well-documented feature of human dialogue widely considered to operate below conscious awareness. Whether large language models exhibit analogous syntactic convergence toward human users relative to human baselines and across a broad range of syntactic constructions remains an open question. Using substitution-paradigm data in which model generations replace one speaker's turns in pre-existing human dialogues, this study measures turn-adjacent reuse of context-free grammar (CFG) rules across sixteen open-weight Llama and Gemma models (1B-70B, pretrained and instruction-tuned) at 1,901 matched positions per model. Every model showed greater CFG-rule overlap with the preceding human turn than with a sampled unrelated human prime, and in every model this actual-versus-random difference was larger for lower-frequency rules. Each instruction-tuned model also showed greater natural-output overlap with the actual prime than the human response it replaced, and all eight matched architecture pairs exhibited greater actual-prime overlap after instruction tuning. However, relative to pretrained variants, instruction-tuned outputs overlapped more with unrelated primes, showed a smaller actual-versus-random increment, and had lower conditional rule-reuse odds once target rule-set size was held constant. In exploratory analyses, each model exhibited greater mean lexical and semantic similarity to the preceding turn than the matched human responses did. Instruction-tuned models additionally produced responses with greater mean semantic similarity than their pretrained counterparts in all eight architecture pairs, whereas the lexical similarity results were more heterogeneous.

AI.tldr: This study investigates whether large language models exhibit syntactic convergence—the tendency to reuse grammatical structures from a preceding human turn—finding that all 16 tested Llama and Gemma models (1B–70B) show significant CFG-rule overlap with the actual prime compared to random baselines, with stronger effects for low-frequency rules. Instruction tuning increases overall syntactic overlap but also raises baseline similarity to unrelated primes, reducing the actual-versus-random increment and lowering conditional rule-reuse odds when controlling for rule-set size.
