AI.motivation: Syntactic convergence is a well-established, largely unconscious phenomenon in human dialogue, yet whether LLMs exhibit analogous behavior across diverse syntactic constructions relative to human baselines remains unexplored. The study addresses this gap by systematically measuring whether open-weight models adapt their grammatical output to match preceding human interlocutors.
AI.method: The authors employ a substitution-paradigm design: model generations replace one speaker's turns in pre-existing human dialogues, matched at 1,901 positions per model across 16 open-weight Llama and Gemma models. Syntactic convergence is operationalized as turn-adjacent reuse of context-free grammar (CFG) rules, comparing overlap with the actual preceding human turn versus a sampled unrelated human prime. Analyses also examine lexical and semantic similarity, with comparisons between pretrained and instruction-tuned variants across matched architecture pairs.
AI.result: Every model showed greater CFG-rule overlap with the actual human prime than random baselines, with larger actual-versus-random differences for lower-frequency rules. Instruction-tuned models exhibited greater natural-output overlap with the actual prime than the human response they replaced. All eight matched architecture pairs showed greater actual-prime overlap after instruction tuning. However, instruction-tuned outputs also overlapped more with unrelated primes, showed smaller actual-versus-random increments, and had lower conditional rule-reuse odds once target rule-set size was controlled. Lexically and semantically, all models showed greater similarity to the preceding turn than matched human responses; instruction-tuned models also produced greater semantic similarity than pretrained counterparts across all pairs, with more heterogeneous lexical similarity results.
AI.conclusion: LLMs reliably exhibit syntactic convergence toward human interlocutors, particularly for low-frequency constructions, but instruction tuning produces a complex pattern: while it increases raw syntactic overlap, it also elevates baseline similarity to any prime, reducing the selectivity of convergence. This suggests instruction tuning may promote more generic syntactic accommodation rather than enhancing context-specific adaptation.

title: Toward Standardized Cross-Vendor Agent Tool Trust Management in Autonomous Networks
summary: Autonomous Network Levels 4-5 require AI agents to invoke tools across vendor boundaries without human oversight, yet existing management standards lack a standardized mechanism for cross-vendor trust visibility. When a tool from Vendor B is compromised, agents from Vendor A continue invoking it -- unaware of the trust degradation -- causing cascading service impact. We present AgentToolMO, a proposed 3GPP NRM information model for agent tool trust management. The model comprises: a formally defined trust state machine with provable graduated enforcement, damped cascade propagation with bounded convergence, cross-vendor trust notifications via existing Management Services (MnS) interfaces, and retroactive impact assessment through NRM dependency graph traversal. Simulation-based evaluation across multi-vendor topologies shows that standardized cross-vendor notifications reduce blast radius from hours-scale undetected propagation to near-real-time containment bounded by MnS notification delivery, with cascade convergence guaranteed in bounded iterations and sub-linear notification scaling across vendor domains. The framework operates within existing 3GPP management infrastructure, leverages existing protocols, and provides a standardization pathway for trustworthy multi-vendor autonomous network management.

AI.tldr: Proposes AgentToolMO, a 3GPP NRM information model for managing trust of AI agent-invoked tools in multi-vendor autonomous networks. Uses a trust state machine with damped cascade propagation and cross-vendor notifications via existing MnS interfaces to achieve near-real-time containment of compromised tools, with provable convergence guarantees.
AI.motivation: Autonomous Networks at Levels 4-5 require AI agents to invoke tools across vendor boundaries without human oversight. Existing management standards lack a standardized mechanism for cross-vendor trust visibility, creating a critical vulnerability: when a tool from one vendor is compromised, agents from other vendors continue invoking it unaware, causing cascading service impact.
AI.method: The paper introduces AgentToolMO, a 3GPP NRM (Network Resource Model) information model with four core components: (1) a formally defined trust state machine with provable graduated enforcement, (2) damped cascade propagation with bounded convergence, (3) cross-vendor trust notifications via existing Management Services (MnS) interfaces, and (4) retroactive impact assessment using NRM dependency graph traversal. Evaluation is simulation-based across multi-vendor topologies.
AI.result: Standardized cross-vendor notifications reduce blast radius from hours-scale undetected propagation to near-real-time containment bounded by MnS notification delivery latency. Cascade convergence is guaranteed in bounded iterations, and notification scaling across vendor domains is sub-linear.
AI.conclusion: The AgentToolMO framework operates within existing 3GPP management infrastructure, leverages existing protocols, and provides a viable standardization pathway for trustworthy multi-vendor autonomous network management.

title: Raven: High-Recall Sequence Modeling with Sparse Memory Routing
summary: Long-context recall in linear-time sequence models highlights a tradeoff in how they write to memory. State-based linear models, such as state-space models (SSMs) and linear Transformers, write densely, updating the entire state for each newly arrived token, which leads to interference and makes specific past tokens hard to recover. Sliding-window attention (SWA) exhibits the opposite behavior: it writes sparsely by storing explicit token representations, but only within a fixed window, so recall drops once the relevant token is evicted. Interpolating between these models, we introduce Raven, a linear-time sequence model that maintains a fixed set of memory slots and, at each step, decays and updates only a selected subset via learned, input-dependent routing. This lets Raven mitigate SWA's position-based overwriting and hard eviction while reducing interference from dense state updates in SSMs, thereby preserving long-range content much more effectively. Across recall-intensive benchmarks, Raven is competitive with or outperforms prior linear-time baselines, achieving strong long-context recall where both SWA and SSMs sharply degrade. It remains effective when extrapolating to context lengths as large as 16x its training length, with similar gains in hybrid architectures.

AI.tldr: Raven is a linear-time sequence model that uses a fixed set of memory slots with learned, input-dependent sparse routing — updating only a subset of slots per token — to combine the strengths of dense state updates (SSMs) and sparse token storage (sliding-window attention) while mitigating their respective weaknesses in long-context recall.
AI.motivation: Linear-time sequence models face a fundamental tradeoff in memory writing: dense state updates (as in SSMs and linear Transformers) cause interference that obscures past tokens, while sparse sliding-window attention evicts tokens entirely outside the window, causing recall to fail at long range. The authors aim to unify these paradigms into a single model that avoids both failure modes.
AI.method: Raven maintains a fixed-size set of memory slots. At each time step, it uses learned, input-dependent routing to decay and update only a selected subset of slots, rather than all slots (dense) or only the newest token's position (SWA). This sparse, content-aware write strategy reduces interference and prevents hard eviction based purely on recency.
AI.result: On recall-intensive benchmarks, Raven matches or surpasses prior linear-time baselines. It maintains strong long-context recall where both SWA and SSMs degrade sharply, and extrapolates effectively to context lengths up to 16× training length, with similar benefits observed in hybrid architectures.
AI.conclusion: Sparse, input-dependent memory routing offers a principled middle ground between dense state updates and position-based windowing, yielding a linear-time model that preserves long-range recall significantly better than either extreme, even under substantial length extrapolation.

title: On the Convergent Validity of Offline Evaluation Designs for Recommender Systems
comment: 9 pages, Accepted at ACM RecSys 2026 Main Track
summary: Offline evaluation on historical interaction logs is the most common evaluation methodology for recommender systems. However, such evaluations depend on sparse, incomplete, or biased data, which raises concerns about whether commonly used evaluation setups reliably reflect true user preferences. In this work, we study how offline evaluation design choices affect the validity of recommender system comparisons. We evaluate a set of recommendation models across several evaluation setups that vary key factors such as data filtering thresholds and candidate set construction. To assess the validity of these configurations, we measure the correlation between model rankings obtained from conventional train-test splits on sparse interaction data and rankings from evaluations based on dense ground-truth user feedback. We use this agreement as an indication of their validity with respect to true user preferences. Our results show that the validity of sparse evaluation depends on the dataset and the specific dense evaluation targets, and that there is no uniformly best offline evaluation design.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether standard offline recommender system evaluations—based on sparse interaction logs—reliably reflect true user preferences. By comparing model rankings from sparse train-test splits against those from dense ground-truth feedback, the authors find that no single evaluation setup is universally valid; results depend on the dataset and the dense evaluation target used.
AI.motivation: Offline evaluation of recommender systems typically relies on historical interaction logs that are sparse, incomplete, or biased. There is growing concern that conventional evaluation setups may not faithfully represent true user preferences, yet the field lacks a systematic understanding of how specific design choices (e.g., data filtering thresholds, candidate set construction) impact evaluation validity.
AI.method: The authors evaluate multiple recommendation models across various offline evaluation setups, systematically varying data filtering thresholds and candidate set construction strategies. They measure the correlation (agreement) between model rankings derived from conventional train-test splits on sparse data and rankings from evaluations using dense ground-truth user feedback. This agreement serves as a proxy for validity with respect to true user preferences.
AI.result: The validity of sparse offline evaluation is dataset-dependent and varies with the specific dense evaluation target. No single offline evaluation design emerges as uniformly optimal across all conditions.
AI.conclusion: There is no universally best offline evaluation setup for recommender systems. Researchers and practitioners should be cautious when interpreting results from any single evaluation configuration and should consider multiple setups tailored to the specific dataset and evaluation goals.

title: Addressable Recall Compaction for Long Context-Window Control in AI Agents
summary: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate reasoning traces, actions, and tool observations that can eventually exceed a model's fixed context window. Existing compaction methods address this limitation by discarding, summarizing, or retrieving earlier information, but they may remove task-critical details or fail to recover them reliably. We propose ARC (Addressable Recall Compaction), a context-management framework that separates archival storage from active-context presentation. ARC stores tool observations in an append-only, ID-addressable log and replaces older observations with compact citations when compaction is required. The agent can subsequently use these identifiers to request stored content without re-executing the corresponding tools or depending solely on similarity-based retrieval. We evaluate ARC using Qwen3-8B with a 16k context window and Qwen3-32B with a 32k context window. On the Needle-in-a-Haystack evaluation, ARC achieves an average exact-answer accuracy of 99.40%, compared with 88.12% for the best-performing baseline in our evaluation. ARC also reduces estimated serving time and HBM traffic under our hardware-cost model. On the LongBench-v2 Hard subset, ARC obtains an average accuracy of 29.97%, compared with 28.25% for the best-performing baseline. These results indicate that explicit, address-based recall can improve information retention and serving efficiency relative to the evaluated context-management baselines under the tested settings.

AI.tldr: ARC is a context-management framework that stores tool observations in an ID-addressable log and uses compact citations to replace older observations when the context window fills up, enabling explicit, address-based recall of archived content without re-executing tools or relying solely on similarity retrieval.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate extensive reasoning traces, actions, and tool observations that exceed fixed context windows. Existing compaction methods (discarding, summarizing, retrieval) risk dropping task-critical details or cannot reliably recover them. There is a need for a framework that preserves the ability to precisely recall any past observation without tool re-execution.
AI.method: ARC separates archival storage from active-context presentation using an append-only, ID-addressable log. Tool observations are stored upon generation and, when compaction is triggered, older observations in the active context are replaced with compact citations (containing IDs). The agent can later use these IDs to explicitly request the full stored content, bypassing imprecise similarity-based retrieval and avoiding tool re-execution.
AI.result: On Needle-in-a-Haystack, ARC (with Qwen3-8B/16k and Qwen3-32B/32k) achieves 99.40% average exact-answer accuracy vs. 88.12% for the best baseline. On LongBench-v2 Hard, ARC achieves 29.97% vs. 28.25% for the best baseline. ARC also demonstrates reduced estimated serving time and HBM traffic under a hardware-cost model.
AI.conclusion: Explicit, address-based recall via ARC improves information retention and serving efficiency over standard compaction baselines, offering a more reliable mechanism for long-horizon LLM agents to access past observations without losing task-critical details.

title: UniMem: Complementary Episodic-to-Parametric Memory for Boundary-Agnostic Task Streams
summary: Memory is essential for LLM agents to accumulate task experience and reuse task-specific execution strategies. However, real-world deployment over boundary-agnostic and evolving task streams exposes a fundamental stability-plasticity dilemma. External retrieval-based memory can rapidly absorb new evidence, but it often fails to internalize recurring execution patterns and incurs inference-time retrieval overhead. Parametric memory enables stable and efficient execution once learned, but typically relies on explicit task boundaries and fixed parameter budgets. Inspired by the human brain, which balances plasticity and stability through complementary episodic storage and gradual consolidation, we propose UniMem, a self-routing framework for autonomous memory management. UniMem uses learnable routing tokens as memory controllers, enabling adaptive coordination between complementary memory pathways: novel or sparse tasks are retained in an episodic buffer for retrieval-augmented execution, while recurring and reliable patterns are consolidated into expandable parametric memory. By decoupling task identification from task execution with routing tokens and parametric memory blocks, UniMem expands memory on demand without task labels during deployment or uncontrolled parameter growth. Experiments on long-horizon streaming task sequences show that UniMem consistently outperforms baselines while maintaining execution fidelity, achieving an average gain of 4.0 EM points across three backbone models.

AI.tldr: UniMem is a self-routing framework that resolves the stability-plasticity dilemma in LLM agents by adaptively coordinating episodic retrieval (for novel/sparse tasks) with expandable parametric memory (for recurring patterns), using learnable routing tokens as memory controllers.
AI.motivation: LLM agents deployed on boundary-agnostic, evolving task streams face a stability-plasticity dilemma: retrieval-based memory absorbs new evidence but incurs overhead and fails to internalize patterns; parametric memory is stable and efficient but requires explicit task boundaries and fixed parameter budgets. No existing approach balances both demands effectively.
AI.method: UniMem introduces learnable routing tokens that act as memory controllers, enabling adaptive coordination between two complementary memory pathways. Novel or sparse tasks are stored in an episodic buffer for retrieval-augmented execution. Recurring, reliable patterns are consolidated into expandable parametric memory blocks. Crucially, UniMem decouples task identification from task execution, allowing on-demand memory expansion without requiring task labels during deployment or uncontrolled parameter growth.
AI.result: On long-horizon streaming task sequences, UniMem consistently outperforms baselines while maintaining execution fidelity, achieving an average gain of 4.0 exact match (EM) points across three different backbone models.
AI.conclusion: UniMem effectively mirrors the human brain's complementary episodic storage and gradual consolidation, providing a practical solution for autonomous memory management in continually deployed LLM agents without relying on explicit task boundaries.

title: Rethinking Likelihood distributions: Student's t Likelihood Boosts Bayesian Neural Network Performance
summary: In Bayesian neural networks (BNNs), variational inference is a widely adopted framework for modeling uncertainty in a distributional way, with the evidence lower bound (ELBO) serving as the standard objective function. Several distributions contribute to the ELBO loss, such as the prior, approximated posterior, and likelihood distribution. Typically, these distributions are all approximated by a Gaussian distribution, since it is easy to compute, allows for reparameterized gradients, and provides a closed-form loss for training. However, several works have highlighted that this assumption may not generally hold, posing the risk of model misspecification. Alternative distributions have been proposed for the prior specifically, while the effect of distribution choice on the likelihood distribution remains unexplored. In this work, our aim is to close this gap by investigating whether alternative assumptions for the likelihood distribution can outperform the commonly used Gaussian. We compare several likelihood distribution assumptions, such as skewed or heavy-tailed, across regression tasks on both artificial and real-world datasets using standard multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). Our findings demonstrate that Student's t yields better predictive performance than a Gaussian likelihood distribution, independent of the data distribution and MLP architecture (depth and width). In some cases, Student's t can also lead to shorter training times, while still being easy to implement.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether alternative likelihood distributions in Bayesian neural networks can outperform the standard Gaussian assumption. Across regression tasks with both artificial and real-world datasets, the authors find that Student's t distribution consistently yields better predictive performance than Gaussian, regardless of data distribution or network architecture, and can sometimes reduce training time.
AI.motivation: Variational inference in BNNs typically assumes Gaussian distributions for the prior, approximate posterior, and likelihood. While prior misspecification has been studied, the effect of likelihood distribution choice remains unexplored — the authors aim to close this gap by systematically evaluating alternative likelihood assumptions.
AI.method: The authors compare multiple likelihood distribution assumptions (e.g., skewed, heavy-tailed) against the standard Gaussian likelihood in BNNs using MLPs. Evaluation is conducted on regression tasks spanning both artificial and real-world datasets, across varying network depths and widths.
AI.result: Student's t likelihood consistently outperforms Gaussian likelihood in predictive performance, independent of the underlying data distribution and MLP architecture. In some cases, it also leads to shorter training times while remaining straightforward to implement.
AI.conclusion: The Gaussian assumption for the likelihood distribution in BNNs may be suboptimal. Adopting a Student's t likelihood is a simple, effective alternative that improves predictive performance across diverse regression settings without added implementation complexity.

title: Memory Layer: Train the In-Model Cache for Recommendation Models
summary: Early ranking stages in recommendation systems precompute item embeddings and cache them in-model for scoring within strict latency constraints. Because this cache exists only at serving time, outside the training loop, training and serving use different item representations, a structural discrepancy that limits quality and adds operational fragility. We show that co-designing the training and serving paths removes this representation discrepancy at its source. We introduce the memory layer, an in-model key-value embedding cache co-trained with the model: the item tower writes embeddings during training and the model reads them at serving, one source of truth for item representations by construction. Always-on embeddings cover items not yet cached, so every item receives a prediction, and the design consolidates three separate trainer-to-predictor update paths into a single self-contained pipeline. Deployed in production on Instagram Reels, the memory layer raises prediction coverage from 96% to 100%, improves embedding freshness from $O(5\text{ min})$ to $O(20\text{ s})$, and narrows the training-serving Normalized Entropy (NE) gap by up to 86%, yielding over $2\times$ recall for the freshest content and a 5-6% cold start engagement lift. Because embeddings are produced during training, the system needs no separate bulk-evaluation or publish-time recomputation, cutting training-and-publish computational cost by 30% at neutral serving computational cost.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a "memory layer" — an in-model key-value embedding cache co-trained with the recommendation model — that eliminates the training-serving representation discrepancy in early-stage ranking systems. Deployed on Instagram Reels, it achieves 100% prediction coverage, significantly fresher embeddings (O(20s) vs O(5min)), up to 86% reduction in the training-serving NE gap, and 5–6% cold-start engagement lift, while reducing training-and-publish computational cost by 30%.
AI.motivation: In production recommendation systems, early ranking stages precompute item embeddings and cache them for low-latency scoring. This cache exists only at serving time, outside the training loop, creating a structural discrepancy between training and serving item representations. This discrepancy degrades model quality, introduces operational fragility, and requires multiple separate update paths (bulk evaluation, publish-time recomputation) that add complexity and computational cost.
AI.method: The authors introduce a "memory layer" — an in-model key-value embedding cache that is co-trained with the recommendation model. During training, the item tower writes embeddings into this cache; at serving time, the model reads from the same cache, ensuring a single source of truth for item representations. An "always-on" embedding mechanism covers items not yet cached, guaranteeing 100% prediction coverage. This design consolidates three previously separate trainer-to-predictor update paths into one self-contained pipeline.
AI.result: Deployed on Instagram Reels, the memory layer raises prediction coverage from 96% to 100%, improves embedding freshness from O(5 min) to O(20 s), and narrows the training-serving Normalized Entropy (NE) gap by up to 86%. It yields over 2× recall for the freshest content and a 5–6% cold-start engagement lift. The system eliminates separate bulk-evaluation and publish-time recomputation, cutting training-and-publish computational cost by 30% while maintaining neutral serving computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Co-designing training and serving paths via an in-model memory layer removes the root cause of training-serving representation discrepancy in recommendation systems. The approach simplifies operational pipelines, improves model quality (especially for fresh/cold-start content), and reduces infrastructure cost, demonstrating a practical and impactful design pattern for large-scale production recommenders.

title: How Often Should a Recommender Call an LLM? Value-Weighted Routing, Monitoring, and Seasonal Robustness
summary: Routing decisions between a cheap heuristic and an expensive large language model (LLM) are typically framed as a difficulty problem: send the hard cases to the expensive path. We argue this framing is incomplete because difficulty and business value are distinct axes - a difficult cheap item and a difficult costly item do not have the same cost of error. We present Value Router, a fully synthetic simulation of a retail merchandising pipeline that routes items using only estimated difficulty and estimated value, never ground truth. The study has three stages. First, a value-weighted threshold router is compared with a difficulty-only and a random baseline on a synthetic catalog with an inverse correlation between category volume and value. Value-weighting matches the difficulty-only baseline's recall of true high-value items (60%) while achieving substantially higher precision (98.3% vs. 94.3%). Second, a decision logger and monitor expose a failure mode hidden by aggregate metrics showing that the aggregate result is driven almost entirely by between-category differences rather than per-item discrimination. Third, a simulated Black Friday demand surge (2.5 volume with a shift toward higher-value categories) compares a static router, a seasonally tuned router, and two slow-path budget policies. All results are from a controlled synthetic simulation with experimenter-defined ground truth and illustrate design principles for cost-aware routing systems rather than validated real-world claims.

AI.tldr: Value Router argues that LLM routing should consider both difficulty and business value, not difficulty alone. Using a synthetic retail simulation, the authors show value-weighted routing achieves comparable recall but higher precision than difficulty-only baselines, expose a hidden failure mode in aggregate metrics, and demonstrate seasonal adaptability during a simulated Black Friday surge.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM routing systems treat routing as purely a difficulty estimation problem — send hard cases to the expensive model. The authors argue this framing is incomplete because difficulty and business value are independent axes: misclassifying a high-value item carries a different cost than misclassifying a low-value item. A routing system should account for the asymmetric cost of errors based on item value, yet ground-truth value labels are unavailable in practice.
AI.method: The authors construct Value Router, a fully synthetic retail merchandising pipeline where items are routed between a cheap heuristic and an expensive LLM using only estimated difficulty and estimated value (never ground truth). The study proceeds in three stages: (1) comparing a value-weighted threshold router against difficulty-only and random baselines on a synthetic catalog with inverse correlation between category volume and value; (2) deploying a decision logger and monitor to expose failure modes hidden by aggregate metrics, revealing that aggregate performance is driven by between-category differences rather than per-item discrimination; (3) simulating a Black Friday demand surge (2.5× volume, shift toward higher-value categories) to compare a static router, a seasonally tuned router, and two slow-path budget policies.
AI.result: The value-weighted router matches the difficulty-only baseline's recall of true high-value items (60%) while achieving substantially higher precision (98.3% vs. 94.3%). The decision logger reveals that aggregate results are driven almost entirely by between-category differences, masking poor per-item discrimination. In the Black Friday simulation, seasonal tuning and budget policies demonstrate trade-offs under shifting demand patterns. All results derive from controlled synthetic simulation with experimenter-defined ground truth.
AI.conclusion: Routing systems for LLM pipelines should incorporate estimated business value alongside estimated difficulty, as value-weighted routing can improve precision without sacrificing recall on high-value items. The authors caution that aggregate metrics can conceal important failure modes (category-level effects dominating item-level decisions) and recommend decision logging and monitoring for production systems. The work illustrates design principles rather than making validated real-world claims.

title: Pass the Baton: Trajectory-Relayed On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) grounds token-level supervision in the student's own trajectory, yet suffers from prefix failure: once the student commits to a wrong reasoning direction, all subsequent generation builds on this deviation, producing misdirected continuations that elicit unreliable supervision and waste compute. We identify a teacher-student continuation asymmetry on failed prefixes, where the teacher tends to redirect while the student continues along the original direction, and convert it into a label-free handoff trigger in Relay On-Policy Distillation (Relay-OPD). During training, Relay-OPD constructs relay trajectories by letting the teacher briefly take over at detected trigger points to produce a teacher leg, after which the student resumes and is optimized on the resulting trajectory. A limited relay budget concentrates intervention on critical early positions while limiting departure from the student policy. With a Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 teacher and Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B-Non-Thinking students on eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, Relay-OPD achieves the best or second-best results on every benchmark, outperforming standard OPD by +5.73% and the strongest baseline FastOPD by +1.49% on average for 1.7B, with consistent gains at 0.6B. Training trajectory length is reduced by over 50%.

AI.tldr: Relay-OPD introduces a mechanism where the teacher model briefly takes over when the student begins to fail during training, creating "relay trajectories" that correct course early. This label-free handoff approach outperforms standard on-policy distillation and prior baselines while cutting training trajectory length by over half.
AI.motivation: Standard on-policy distillation (OPD) suffers from prefix failure: once the student generates a wrong token, all subsequent tokens build on this error, yielding unreliable teacher supervision and wasted computation. The key insight is a teacher-student continuation asymmetry — on failed prefixes, the teacher tends to redirect while the student persists in the wrong direction.
AI.method: Relay-OPD detects trigger points where teacher-student continuation diverges (label-free handoff). At these points, the teacher briefly takes over to produce a "teacher leg," after which the student resumes generation. The resulting relay trajectory — mixing student and teacher segments — serves as the optimization target. A limited relay budget ensures interventions concentrate on critical early positions without straying too far from the student's own policy.
AI.result: Using a Qwen3-4B-Instruct teacher with 0.6B/1.7B students across 8 math reasoning benchmarks, Relay-OPD achieves best or second-best on every benchmark. For the 1.7B student, it outperforms standard OPD by +5.73% and the strongest baseline FastOPD by +1.49% on average, with consistent gains at 0.6B. Training trajectory length is reduced by over 50%.
AI.conclusion: Relay-OPD effectively addresses prefix failure in on-policy distillation through strategic, budget-constrained teacher intervention, yielding substantial accuracy gains and significant training efficiency improvements.

title: Learned, Relied Upon, or Necessary? Separating Checkpoint Dependence from Task-Level Value in Sheaf GNNs
summary: Learned restriction maps in sheaf graph neural networks are often treated as proof that the model has discovered useful edge geometry. That conclusion does not follow from parameter movement or from a post-hoc ablation: both can show how one checkpoint is organized while leaving open whether learned transport still helps after the rest of the model adapts. We separate these claims with two estimands. Checkpoint reliance intervenes on the maps of a fixed predictor; protocol-relative replacement retrains matched families that remove map capacity, edge variation, or persistent edge assignment. A task-null theorem shows why the claims can diverge: labels identify only the transported classifier directions, leaving $d^2-d$ invisible degrees of freedom in every full $d\times d$ map. An exact frame model then gives the boundary at which reliance becomes unreplaced task value. Label-only training realizes the predicted separation, while audits of public NSD, DNSD, and Directed Sheaf Neural Network (DSNN) implementations recover both replaceable and unreplaced transport regimes on real graphs. All five DNSD benchmarks exhibit fixed-checkpoint reliance. After retraining, assignment-breaking or shared-map controls recover Full performance on four; Roman-Empire retains a $.0675$ advantage over continually resampled assignment and a $.0391$ advantage over a parameter-matched shared map across ten official splits. Thus, a learned map can govern a fitted computation without constituting indispensable edge geometry. Claims of learned transport should pair checkpoint interventions with matched retraining.

AI.tldr: Learned restriction maps in sheaf graph neural networks may appear to encode meaningful edge geometry, but this paper shows that apparent reliance on learned maps at a fixed checkpoint often disappears after retraining with matched controls, revealing that label-only training leaves most map degrees of freedom invisible. The authors provide theoretical and empirical evidence that claims of learned transport require both checkpoint interventions and protocol-relative retraining.
AI.motivation: Prior work treats learned restriction maps in sheaf GNNs as evidence of useful edge geometry, but this conclusion conflates two distinct claims: (1) checkpoint reliance (a fixed predictor depends on the maps) and (2) protocol-relative replacement value (whether learned maps remain beneficial after retraining). The paper aims to rigorously separate these and expose when and why they diverge.
AI.method: The authors introduce two estimands: checkpoint reliance (intervening on maps of a fixed, trained predictor) and protocol-relative replacement (retraining matched families of models with map capacity removed, edge variation ablated, or persistent assignment broken). A task-null theorem proves that label supervision identifies only $d$ transported classifier directions, leaving $d^2-d$ degrees of freedom invisible. An exact frame model analytically derives the boundary where reliance becomes unreplaced task value. Empirical audits cover public NSD, DNSD, and DSNN implementations across five benchmarks with ten official splits.
AI.result: All five DNSD benchmarks show fixed-checkpoint reliance. However, after matched retraining, assignment-breaking or shared-map controls recover full performance on four benchmarks. Roman-Empire retains only a 0.0675 advantage over continually resampled assignment and a 0.0391 advantage over a parameter-matched shared map, indicating that learned maps do not constitute indispensable edge geometry in most cases.
AI.conclusion: A learned restriction map can govern a fitted computation without being indispensable edge geometry. Claims of learned transport should always be validated by pairing checkpoint interventions with matched retraining under protocol-relative replacement to distinguish transient parameter organization from genuine representational value.

title: HiEviDR-Bench: A Benchmark for Hierarchical Evidence Aggregation in Deep Research
comment: Code and data are available at https://ai9stars.github.io/HiEviDR-Bench.github.io
summary: Deep research requires models to retrieve, connect, and synthesize evidence from large-scale heterogeneous sources to answer complex queries and produce analytical reports. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate final outcomes, such as answer correctness, report quality, or citation alignment, while providing limited visibility into whether evidence is correctly selected, linked, and aggregated into supported claims and conclusions. To address this gap, we introduce HiEviDR-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating Hierarchical Evidence Aggregation in Deep Research. HiEviDR-Bench covers open-domain and academic-domain settings under both text-only and multimodal conditions, and represents each instance with an explicit evidence graph that captures evidence selection, cross-source linking, and aggregation from evidence to intermediate claims and final conclusions. Based on this formulation, we develop a traceability-oriented evaluation framework with five dimensions: report quality, evidence traceability, citation accuracy, claim verification, and answer correctness, together with a progressive gating mechanism for fine-grained error localization. HiEviDR-Bench contains 2,000 human-validated questions with evidence graphs across multiple difficulty levels. Experiments on 16 representative multimodal large language models show that, although many systems achieve strong report quality, their performance drops markedly on citation accuracy, claim construction, and answer correctness. Further analysis shows that the main bottlenecks lie in evidence identification and intermediate claim construction, revealing that strong surface-level report quality does not necessarily imply grounded multi-stage reasoning on our benchmark.

AI.tldr: HiEviDR-Bench is a benchmark for evaluating hierarchical evidence aggregation in deep research. It uses explicit evidence graphs to trace evidence selection, cross-source linking, and aggregation into claims and conclusions. Experiments on 16 multimodal LLMs reveal that strong report quality often masks poor citation accuracy, claim construction, and evidence grounding.
AI.motivation: Existing deep research benchmarks evaluate only final outputs (answer correctness, report quality, citation alignment) without revealing whether models correctly select, link, and aggregate evidence into supported claims. There is a need for fine-grained, traceability-oriented evaluation.
AI.method: The authors construct HiEviDR-Bench with 2,000 human-validated questions across open-domain and academic-domain settings (text-only and multimodal). Each instance includes an explicit evidence graph capturing evidence selection, cross-source linking, and aggregation from evidence to intermediate claims and final conclusions. Evaluation uses five dimensions (report quality, evidence traceability, citation accuracy, claim verification, answer correctness) with a progressive gating mechanism for error localization.
AI.result: Across 16 multimodal LLMs, systems achieve strong report quality but underperform on citation accuracy, claim construction, and answer correctness. Bottlenecks lie in evidence identification and intermediate claim construction, showing that surface-level report quality does not guarantee grounded multi-stage reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Strong surface-level report generation does not imply faithful, grounded evidence aggregation. HiEviDR-Bench exposes critical weaknesses in evidence identification and claim construction, providing a traceability-focused framework to guide improvements in deep research systems.

title: Towards an Agent Operating System - Lessons from Classical and Cloud OS
summary: Every major wave of platform software follows the same arc: an initial period of experimentation with competing frameworks and ad-hoc implementations, followed by the articulation of a small set of stable abstractions with well-defined semantics, and finally consolidation around those abstractions into a platform that applications can portably target. POSIX did this for classical operating systems; Kubernetes did it for the cloud. Agentic AI systems - autonomous, LLM-driven agents that plan, use tools, maintain memory, and collaborate - are currently in the experimentation phase of the third such wave. dozens of frameworks and protocols have emerged, but no community consensus exists on what the core abstractions are or what guarantees they carry. Without that consensus, agentic applications cannot be written portably, platforms cannot compose reliably, and the field cannot advance beyond prototype deployments. We argue that the path forward is to follow the prior-wave methodology: derive new agentic abstractions by extending classical OS and cloud OS primitives to stochastic, natural-language-mediated execution, specify their semantics precisely, and consolidate around them - just as POSIX and Kubernetes consolidated their respective waves.

AI.tldr: Agentic AI systems lack standardized abstractions. This paper argues for deriving core primitives by extending classical OS and cloud OS concepts to stochastic, LLM-driven execution, then consolidating around them—mirroring the POSIX and Kubernetes consolidation patterns.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI is in an experimentation phase with dozens of competing frameworks and no consensus on core abstractions or their semantics. Without stable, portable abstractions, agentic applications cannot be written portably, platforms cannot compose reliably, and the field cannot advance beyond prototypes—echoing the pre-POSIX and pre-Kubernetes eras.
AI.method: The authors propose applying the historical methodology from prior platform waves (POSIX for classical OS, Kubernetes for cloud): extend established OS and cloud OS primitives to accommodate stochastic, natural-language-mediated execution; precisely specify their semantics; and drive community consolidation around those abstractions to form a stable agentic platform.
AI.result: The paper is a position/vision paper and does not present empirical results. It offers a conceptual framework and call to action rather than experimental findings.
AI.conclusion: The agentic AI field must deliberately consolidate around a small set of well-specified abstractions—derived from classical and cloud OS primitives—to enable portable applications, reliable composition, and progression beyond prototype deployments, just as POSIX and Kubernetes enabled their respective ecosystems to mature.

title: Multi-Objective Structured Pruning of LLMs for Latency and Model Size Optimization
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved widespread adoption because of their strong reasoning and query-response capabilities. However, deploying them in embedded and edge computing environments remains challenging because of strict latency, memory, and energy constraints. Their large parameter counts and computational demands hinder efficient execution on resource-constrained platforms. Although model pruning has emerged as a viable solution for reducing scale while preserving performance, jointly optimizing layers, attention heads, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) dimensions remains highly complex. Exhaustively exploring this combined design space is computationally expensive and often leads to local optima or unstable configurations. To address these limitations, we propose a hardware-aware, multi-objective structured pruning framework. The proposed two-stage method explicitly targets latency and model size for efficient deployment on edge devices. In the coarse-grained stage, multi-objective depth pruning removes entire attention and MLP blocks to reduce computational load and memory usage. In the subsequent fine-grained stage, Parallel Bayesian Optimization (PBO) searches for the optimal layer-wise pruning ratios for pruning under latency constraints, while importance-based strategies rank the specific components to be pruned within each layer's allocated budget. Experimental results show that our approach reduces model complexity with minimal impact on commonsense reasoning tasks and zero-shot performance. Our method achieves a favorable trade-off among accuracy, latency, and model size, making it suitable for edge deployment. Across multiple LLMs at 37.5% and 50% pruning ratios, the proposed approach achieves better performance on commonsense reasoning tasks than existing methods while significantly reducing inference cost.

AI.tldr: A two-stage hardware-aware structured pruning framework for LLMs that combines coarse-grained depth pruning with fine-grained Parallel Bayesian Optimization to optimize latency and model size under edge deployment constraints.
AI.motivation: Deploying LLMs on edge/embedded devices is hindered by latency, memory, and energy constraints. Existing pruning methods struggle with the combinatorial complexity of jointly optimizing layers, attention heads, and MLP dimensions, often leading to local optima or unstable configurations.
AI.method: A two-stage structured pruning framework: (1) Coarse-grained multi-objective depth pruning that removes entire attention/MLP blocks to reduce computation and memory; (2) Fine-grained Parallel Bayesian Optimization (PBO) that searches for optimal layer-wise pruning ratios under latency constraints, combined with importance-based ranking to select specific components within each layer's budget.
AI.result: At 37.5% and 50% pruning ratios across multiple LLMs, the method outperforms existing approaches on commonsense reasoning tasks while significantly reducing inference cost, achieving favorable accuracy-latency-model size trade-offs with minimal impact on zero-shot performance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hardware-aware, multi-objective structured pruning framework effectively enables LLM deployment on edge devices by jointly optimizing depth and width dimensions, achieving superior performance compared to existing methods under strict resource constraints.

title: TWICE: Two-Clock, Two-Window Learning for Long-Horizon Conversion Prediction in Online Advertising
summary:
Long-horizon conversion prediction under delayed feedback creates a two-clock, two-window learning problem in online advertising. A short base observation window releases recent clicks on the click clock before their outcomes mature, whereas conversions continue to arrive on the conversion clock throughout a longer target conversion window. The click clock provides timely but partially observed status supervision. The conversion clock reveals long-tail delays, but the delay composition within an arrival-time slice is weighted by historical click cohorts with different traffic volumes and target-window conversion rates.
  We present TWICE, a framework that factorizes long-horizon post-click conversion rate (CVR) into a target-window conversion probability and a grouped elapsed-delay cumulative distribution function (CDF). The two clocks provide complementary supervision. Click-clock records train the target-window CVR head through a current-status likelihood over the base observation window. Newly arrived conversions train the delay model on the conversion clock. To account for the cohort mixture, TWICE uses fixed click-time predicted CVR (pCVR) mass as cohort exposure in an arrival-conditioned likelihood. This accounts for differences in cohort traffic and conversion propensity. The resulting aggregate records are self-contained. A single learned CDF produces monotone predictions for all requested horizons up to the target conversion window. Serving requires neither historical lookup nor convolution. Experiments on a public benchmark and an industrial advertising dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of TWICE. In an online A/B test in Kwai's advertising system, TWICE increased expected revenue, revenue, and conversions by 2.486%, 1.858%, and 2.061%, respectively. It was subsequently deployed to full traffic.

AI.tldr: TWICE factorizes long-horizon CVR prediction into a target-window conversion probability and a grouped elapsed-delay CDF, using dual-clock supervision (click clock and conversion clock) to handle delayed feedback. It achieves monotone multi-horizon predictions without historical lookup, delivering significant revenue and conversion gains in production.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon conversion prediction in online advertising suffers from a two-clock, two-window problem: the click clock provides timely but partial labels within a short base window, while the conversion clock reveals full outcomes with long-tail delays. Existing methods struggle because delay composition within arrival-time slices is confounded by historical click cohorts with heterogeneous traffic volumes and conversion rates. A method is needed that leverages both sources of supervision without requiring expensive convolution or historical lookups at serving time.
AI.method: TWICE factorizes post-click CVR into (1) a target-window conversion probability and (2) a grouped elapsed-delay cumulative distribution function (CDF). The click clock trains the CVR head via a current-status likelihood over the base observation window. The conversion clock trains the delay model using newly arrived conversions. To address cohort mixture, TWICE weights each conversion by its fixed click-time predicted CVR (pCVR) mass as cohort exposure in an arrival-conditioned likelihood, accounting for differences in cohort traffic and conversion propensity. A single learned CDF produces monotone multi-horizon predictions up to the target window, requiring no historical lookup or convolution at serving.
AI.result: On a public benchmark and an industrial advertising dataset, TWICE demonstrated strong predictive performance. In an online A/B test within Kwai's advertising system, TWICE improved expected revenue by 2.486%, actual revenue by 1.858%, and conversions by 2.061%. The method was subsequently deployed to full traffic.
AI.conclusion: TWICE effectively addresses the delayed feedback problem in long-horizon conversion prediction by factorizing CVR and leveraging dual-clock supervision with cohort-aware likelihood. It is computationally efficient at serving time and delivers substantial business metrics improvements in a real-world, large-scale advertising system.

title: Bekko Embedding: Parameter-Efficient Multilingual Retrieval with Ultra-Compact Encoders
comment: 45 pages, 9 figures. Model weights and training data: https://huggingface.co/hotchpotch
summary: How small can a competitive multilingual retrieval model be? We present Bekko Embedding: its smallest model, bekko-embedding-v1-a8m, has just under 8M Active Parameters (AP) -- the non-embedding parameters that dominate inference compute -- yet on official MMTEB Multilingual v2 Retrieval (nDCG@10) it scores 56.2, above the multilingual-e5 family and BGE-M3 (40x the AP) in our comparison. The higher-quality bekko-embedding-v1-a25m (just under 25M AP) reaches 57.5, on par with gte-multilingual-base, and Multilingual NanoBEIR (14 languages) confirms the trend. Both models handle inputs of up to 8192 tokens, and on long-input retrieval (NanoLongEmbed) a25m is the strongest dense model in our comparison. The recipe is deliberately simple. We prune the 22-layer multilingual encoder mmBERT-small to 4 / 13 layers and train the pruned models in two stages -- large-scale contrastive learning on about 1.1 billion multilingual pairs from our public corpus, followed by hard-negative fine-tuning with 8192-token long-document negatives -- with a masked contrastive loss whose direction depends on pair type, plus the Matryoshka objective. No teacher distillation is used, and all training completes on a single GPU in about 3 days for a8m. Small AP pays off directly in speed: among the compared models measured under identical conditions, a8m is the fastest on both CPU and GPU -- 1.6x multilingual-e5-small on x86 CPU -- and the fastest on a Raspberry Pi 5. The 384-dimensional output (truncatable to 256/128/64) keeps similarity search and indexing cheap, and row-wise int8 quantization of the vocabulary embedding shrinks the a8m ONNX / OpenVINO build to 124 MiB, which runs in the browser via Transformers.js. To support reproducible research, we release the model weights, the complete stage-1 corpus, and the independently mined stage-2 hard negatives.

AI.tldr: Bekko Embedding introduces ultra-compact multilingual retrieval models (8M and 25M active parameters) that achieve competitive performance through aggressive pruning of mmBERT-small and a simple two-stage contrastive training recipe, all on a single GPU in ~3 days.
AI.motivation: To explore how small a competitive multilingual retrieval model can be while maintaining strong retrieval performance, addressing the trade-off between model size, inference speed, and retrieval quality.
AI.method: The authors prune the 22-layer multilingual encoder mmBERT-small to 4 layers (a8m) or 13 layers (a25m), then train in two stages: (1) large-scale contrastive learning on ~1.1B multilingual pairs, (2) hard-negative fine-tuning with 8192-token long-document negatives. Training uses a masked contrastive loss with pair-type-dependent direction and a Matryoshka objective. No teacher distillation is employed. Post-training, int8 quantization of vocabulary embeddings and ONNX/OpenVINO builds enable browser deployment.
AI.result: bekko-embedding-v1-a8m (8M AP) achieves 56.2 nDCG@10 on MMTEB Multilingual v2 Retrieval, surpassing multilingual-e5 family and BGE-M3 (40× more AP). a25m (25M AP) reaches 57.5, on par with gte-multilingual-base. On Multilingual NanoBEIR (14 languages), the trend holds. a25m is the strongest dense model on NanoLongEmbed. a8m is the fastest model on CPU/GPU and Raspberry Pi 5 (1.6× faster than multilingual-e5-small on x86). The 384-dim output with Matryoshka truncation and 124 MiB quantized build enables efficient browser inference.
AI.conclusion: Aggressive pruning combined with a simple, distillation-free two-stage contrastive training recipe yields highly competitive multilingual retrieval models with dramatically fewer parameters, enabling fast, low-cost deployment across diverse hardware including CPUs, edge devices, and browsers.

title: SPARC Segmentation to Prediction via Affine Regression and Counterfactuals
summary: Transaction propensity prediction in B2B e commerce presents unique challenges distinct from B2C contexts, primarily due to the heterogeneous procurement behaviors of organizational entities, which violate SMOTE's implicit assumption of within class feature homogeneity. Specifically, B2B buyers exhibit multi modal procurement cycles that render linear interpolation between minority class samples structurally invalid, producing synthetic data that does not represent real purchasing behavior. This paper introduces a production deployed propensity modeling framework designed to address these complexities through two primary contributions. First, we replace conventional SMOTE based augmentation with a synthetic data generation approach leveraging Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE). This method produces minority class samples with superior distributional fidelity compared to SMOTE, as validated through quantitative proximity analysis and UMAP cluster visualization. Second, we adapt the PyPARC piecewise affine classification framework to generate calibrated propensity probabilities, facilitating the interpretable segmentation of customers into actionable risk tiers. Evaluated on two years of longitudinal data from a large scale B2B e commerce platform with a 1 to 9 class imbalance ratio, the proposed architecture achieves 93.1% precision at a decision threshold of 0.8, a 9.2 percentage point improvement over SMOTE based baselines at the same threshold (83.9%), and a 26.1 point improvement over SMOTE at threshold 0.7 (66.04%), demonstrating consistent superiority across operating points. These results demonstrate the framework's efficacy in enabling high precision marketing campaigns with significant improvements in customer activation and return on investment.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a B2B transaction propensity prediction framework that replaces SMOTE with DiCE-based counterfactual data augmentation and uses PyPARC for calibrated probability estimation, achieving 93.1% precision (a 9.2pp improvement over SMOTE baselines) on a real-world platform with 1:9 class imbalance.
AI.motivation: B2B e-commerce transaction propensity prediction is fundamentally different from B2C due to heterogeneous, multi-modal organizational procurement behaviors. SMOTE's core assumption of within-class feature homogeneity fails because linear interpolation between minority class samples produces structurally invalid synthetic data that misrepresents genuine purchasing patterns. A production-ready solution is needed that respects the distributional complexity of B2B buyer behavior.
AI.method: Two main contributions: (1) Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE) replaces SMOTE for minority class oversampling, generating synthetic samples with superior distributional fidelity validated via proximity analysis and UMAP visualization. (2) The PyPARC piecewise affine classification framework is adapted to output calibrated propensity probabilities, enabling interpretable customer segmentation into actionable risk tiers. The system is evaluated on two years of longitudinal B2B platform data with a 1:9 class imbalance ratio.
AI.result: At a decision threshold of 0.8, the proposed method achieves 93.1% precision, outperforming SMOTE-based baselines at the same threshold (83.9%) by 9.2 percentage points. At threshold 0.7, the improvement is 26.1 points over SMOTE (66.04%). The framework demonstrates consistent superiority across operating points, enabling high-precision marketing campaigns with improved customer activation and ROI.
AI.conclusion: The DiCE + PyPARC framework effectively addresses B2B transaction propensity prediction by generating distributionally faithful synthetic minority samples and producing well-calibrated propensity scores. The substantial and consistent precision gains over SMOTE across multiple decision thresholds validate the approach for production deployment in large-scale B2B e-commerce settings, directly translating to improved marketing efficiency and return on investment.

title: VaLiDRec: Variable-Length LLM-Aligned Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation
summary: Generative recommendation commonly represents items using fixed-length semantic identifiers (SIDs) constructed through clustering and quantization. However, these artificial codes may overcompress item semantics, remain misaligned with pretrained LLM vocabularies, and require costly autoregressive decoding. In light of this, we propose VaLiDRec, a generative recommendation framework based on variable-length, LLM-aligned semantic identifiers. VaLiDRec constructs SIDs directly from informative native LLM vocabulary tokens via token importance estimation, semantic-quality-aware pruning, and collision-aware refinement, allowing identifier lengths to adapt to item semantic complexity. To model user preferences, VaLiDRec incorporates graph-aware soft prompts and reformulates recommendation as token-set prediction with token-level item scoring, eliminating autoregressive SID generation and beam search. Experiments on four real-world datasets show that VaLiDRec consistently outperforms strong sequential and generative recommendation baselines across all evaluation metrics. It further achieves superior zero-shot item cold-start performance and 87.49$\times$ faster inference than LC-Rec. These results demonstrate that LLM-native variable-length semantic identifiers provide a more expressive and efficient paradigm for generative recommendation.

AI.tldr: VaLiDRec proposes variable-length, LLM-native semantic identifiers for generative recommendation, replacing fixed-length artificial codes. It constructs identifiers from LLM vocabulary tokens via importance estimation, quality pruning, and collision refinement, then reformulates recommendation as token-set prediction — achieving superior performance and 87× faster inference than autoregressive baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing generative recommendation methods use fixed-length semantic identifiers (SIDs) from clustering/quantization, which suffer from three key limitations: (1) overcompression of item semantics into rigid-length codes, (2) misalignment with pretrained LLM vocabularies, and (3) costly autoregressive decoding with beam search. The authors aim to overcome these issues with more expressive, efficient identifiers that naturally integrate with LLMs.
AI.method: VaLiDRec has two main components: (1) **Variable-length SID construction**: Starting from an item's textual description, token-level importance is estimated (e.g., via attention or gradient-based methods). A semantic-quality-aware pruning step removes low-importance tokens, and collision-aware refinement ensures identifier uniqueness across items — yielding SIDs whose length adapts to item semantic complexity. (2) **Recommendation as token-set prediction**: User preferences are modeled using graph-aware soft prompts. Instead of autoregressively generating SIDs token-by-token, the model scores all candidate items by computing token-level match scores between user representations and each item's SID token set, enabling parallelized, beam-search-free inference.
AI.result: Experiments on four real-world datasets show VaLiDRec consistently outperforms both sequential and generative recommendation baselines across all metrics. It achieves superior zero-shot item cold-start performance and demonstrates 87.49× faster inference compared to LC-Rec (an autoregressive generative baseline).
AI.conclusion: LLM-native variable-length semantic identifiers offer a more expressive and efficient paradigm for generative recommendation. By aligning identifiers with LLM vocabularies and reformulating recommendation as token-set prediction rather than autoregressive generation, VaLiDRec achieves both state-of-the-art accuracy and dramatic inference speedups, while naturally handling items of varying semantic complexity.

title: Matryoshka Agent: Unfolding Sub-Agents for Long-Horizon Machine Learning Engineering
summary: Machine learning engineering (MLE) tasks require long-horizon decision making over iterative solution debugging and refinement, under expensive and feedback-driven environment interactions. Developing and training a monolithic agent for such tasks is fundamentally challenging, as it must simultaneously manage extremely long and noisy contexts, explore vast solution spaces, and remain effective under limited model capacity and computational budgets. To address these challenges, we propose Matryoshka Agent, a unified hierarchical agent framework for complex long-horizon tasks. Matryoshka Agent decomposes agentic problem solving into a coordinated hierarchy of decision making and execution: a high-level Orchestrator maintains compact, long-horizon exploration states and issues strategic instructions, while lower-level Sub-Agents execute concrete solution attempts through direct environment interaction, mediated by standardized Tool interface. This design decouples strategic exploration from costly execution, substantially reducing the burden of long-context reasoning and enabling efficient iterative refinement. We further develop an efficient training paradigm for Matryoshka Agent. Experimental results on a broad range of MLE tasks with diverse model types and scales demonstrate that Matryoshka Agent is an effective and scalable paradigm for long-horizon MLE tasks and complex agentic problem solving. Notably, Matryoshka Agent enables Qwen3-4B-Instruct to reach Orchestrator performance comparable to o4-mini. Applying Matryoshka Agent to Qwen3-30B-Coder results in at most 36.7% relative performance gain.

AI.tldr: Matryoshka Agent is a hierarchical agent framework that decomposes long-horizon machine learning engineering tasks into a high-level Orchestrator for strategic planning and low-level Sub-Agents for direct environment execution, decoupling exploration from costly interaction to improve efficiency and scalability.
AI.motivation: Monolithic agents struggle with long-horizon MLE tasks due to the need to simultaneously handle extremely long and noisy contexts, explore vast solution spaces, and operate under limited model capacity and compute budgets. A decompositional approach is needed to reduce the burden of long-context reasoning and enable efficient iterative refinement.
AI.method: Matryoshka Agent introduces a two-level hierarchy: a high-level Orchestrator maintains compact exploration states and issues strategic instructions, while lower-level Sub-Agents execute solution attempts via direct environment interaction through standardized Tool interfaces. An efficient training paradigm is also developed for the framework.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse MLE tasks, model types, and scales show Matryoshka Agent is effective and scalable. Qwen3-4B-Instruct with the framework achieves Orchestrator performance comparable to o4-mini. Applied to Qwen3-30B-Coder, it yields up to a 36.7% relative performance gain.
AI.conclusion: Matryoshka Agent is an effective, scalable paradigm for long-horizon MLE and complex agentic problem solving, demonstrating that hierarchical decomposition significantly improves performance across model scales.

title: PIcsC: Partitioning-Induced Covariate Shift Correction
summary: Covariate shift across training-data partitions biases model selection and parameter estimation in cross-validation, lifelong learning, and federated learning. We propose \textit{Partition-Induced Covariate-shift Correction} (\texttt{PIcsC}), a Fisher information-based regularization framework that mitigates distribution mismatch between data partitions and a reference distribution. \texttt{PIcsC} approximates partition divergence using the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) and incorporates the resulting statistic as a regularizer during optimization. The same formulation applies to both centrally partitioned datasets (batches or cross-validation folds) and inherently distributed data (federated clients or decentralized nodes), requiring only partition-local gradient statistics rather than raw data. We further introduce a conditional adaptation mechanism that combines FIM shift with KL divergence to detect significant distribution shifts and activates regularization only when necessary. Experiments on more than 40 datasets demonstrate consistent improvements under both natural and synthetic covariate shift. On fragmented batch and fold settings, \texttt{PIcsC} reduces fragmentation-induced performance degradation by more than 20\% and 25\%, respectively. On seven federated learning benchmarks, it consistently outperforms FedAvg, FedProx, and SCAFFOLD by 3 -5 percentage points without requiring client-specific personalization. These results demonstrate that Fisher information provides an effective and unified mechanism for mitigating partition-induced covariate shift across both centralized and distributed learning.

AI.tldr: PIcsC is a Fisher information-based regularization framework that corrects partition-induced covariate shift across cross-validation, lifelong learning, and federated learning, achieving consistent performance gains on 40+ datasets without requiring raw data sharing.
AI.motivation: Covariate shift across training-data partitions (e.g., batches, folds, federated clients) biases model selection and parameter estimation. Existing methods often require raw data sharing, client-specific personalization, or fail to unify centralized and distributed settings under a single correction framework.
AI.method: PIcsC uses the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) to approximate divergence between data partitions and a reference distribution, incorporating this statistic as a regularizer during optimization. It requires only partition-local gradient statistics, not raw data. A conditional adaptation mechanism combining FIM shift with KL divergence detects significant distribution shifts and activates regularization selectively.
AI.result: On fragmented batch and fold settings, PIcsC reduces fragmentation-induced performance degradation by over 20% and 25%, respectively. Across seven federated learning benchmarks, it outperforms FedAvg, FedProx, and SCAFFOLD by 3–5 percentage points without client-specific personalization. Consistent improvements are observed on 40+ datasets under natural and synthetic covariate shift.
AI.conclusion: Fisher information provides an effective, unified mechanism for mitigating partition-induced covariate shift across both centralized and distributed learning paradigms, enabling robust model selection and training without compromising data locality.

title: TopoGR: Revealing and Preserving Latent Structure of Semantic ID in Generative Recommendation
summary: Semantic ID-based generative recommendation tokenizes each item into a sequence of discrete semantic IDs and predicts the next item by generating semantic IDs. However, existing methods typically regard SIDs as independent discrete symbols, while often overlooking the topology of the learned semantic ID space. We identify a structural mismatch between tokenization and generation: the tokenizer learns a structured code space with semantic neighborhood relations, whereas the generator consumes semantic ID tokens as independent categorical symbols. Consequently, item relatedness is reduced to exact semantic ID overlap, making it difficult to identify semantically similar items whose semantic IDs do not overlap. To address this issue, we propose TopoGR, a topology-preserving generative recommendation framework based on Bit-decomposable Semantic ID(Binary SID). Each Binary SID is learned in a bit-decomposable form and can be deterministically converted to a standard integer SID, while exposing an explicit Hamming geometry. TopoGR exploits this topology at three stages: binary SID features preserve Hamming proximity at the input layer; Hamming soft targets inject topology-aware supervision; and Hamming-consistent reranking aligns candidate items with the predicted binary prototype during inference. We further verify that the Hamming topology can capture item relatedness beyond exact SID matching. Experiments on four benchmark datasets show that TopoGR consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines in recommendation performance.

AI.tldr: Existing semantic ID-based generative recommendation methods treat SIDs as independent symbols, ignoring the topological structure of the semantic ID space. This paper proposes TopoGR, which uses Bit-decomposable Semantic IDs with explicit Hamming geometry to preserve this topology across input encoding, training supervision, and inference reranking, achieving consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.motivation: Current generative recommendation systems suffer from a structural mismatch: the semantic ID tokenizer learns a structured code space with neighborhood relations, but the generator treats SID tokens as independent categorical symbols. This makes it difficult to recognize semantically similar items whose SIDs do not exactly overlap, reducing recommendation quality.
AI.method: The authors propose TopoGR, which learns Binary SIDs in a bit-decomposable form that can be converted to standard integer SIDs while exposing Hamming geometry. TopoGR leverages this topology through three mechanisms: (1) binary SID features that preserve Hamming proximity at the input layer, (2) Hamming soft targets for topology-aware supervision, and (3) Hamming-consistent reranking during inference to align candidates with the predicted binary prototype.
AI.result: Experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that TopoGR consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines in recommendation performance. The Hamming topology is also verified to capture item relatedness beyond exact SID matching.
AI.conclusion: Preserving the topological structure of the semantic ID space is crucial for generative recommendation. By exploiting Hamming geometry through Binary SIDs, TopoGR effectively bridges the gap between tokenization and generation, enabling the model to recognize semantic similarity beyond exact ID overlap.

title: Towards Robust Reinforcement Learning for Small-Scale Language Model Agents
comment: Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics (SMC), Bellevue, WA, USA
summary: The alignment of Small Language Models (SLMs) in the 70--500M parameter range using reinforcement learning is often considered unstable, though the underlying failure mechanisms have not been systematically investigated. In the State-of-the-Art (SOTA) research, fifteen (model, corpus) configurations were trained using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). The experiments included Pythia-70M, 160M, 410M and SmolLM2-135M, 360M on the TinyStories, CNN/DailyMail, and Wikitext-103 corpora. Three reproducible failure modes were identified in small-scale language models: silent LoRA parameter freezing in standard PEFT/TRL pipelines, numerical overflow in importance ratios when using bfloat16, and catastrophic policy collapse due to reward-model error. These issues were addressed using a merge-and-reinitialize adapter technique, float32 precision during PPO updates, and a three-layer safety mechanism comprising reward whitening, importance-ratio guarding, and weight rollback. In this paper, a capacity-headroom hypothesis is proposed, which states that PPO performance at the SLM scale depends on both a fluent supervised model ($\text{PPL}<20$) and a discriminative reward signal, rather than on the number of model parameters. The proposed system converged stably in all experiments and improved preference win rate over the SFT baseline in configurations with a fluent prior and an informative reward signal. Furthermore, it outperformed instruction-tuned baselines while requiring significantly less training data. All checkpoints, preference datasets, and training scripts are publicly released$^§$.

AI.tldr: Investigates failure modes of PPO-based RL alignment for SLMs (70–500M params), identifies three reproducible issues (LoRA freezing, bfloat16 overflow, reward-model collapse), proposes fixes, and introduces a capacity-headroom hypothesis stating PPO success depends on fluent prior and discriminative reward rather than model size.
AI.motivation: RL-based alignment of Small Language Models (70–500M parameters) is often considered unstable, yet the underlying failure mechanisms have not been systematically studied. The authors aim to identify, reproduce, and resolve these failure modes to enable reliable PPO training at the SLM scale.
AI.method: Fifteen (model, corpus) configurations were trained using PPO with Pythia (70M, 160M, 410M) and SmolLM2 (135M, 360M) on TinyStories, CNN/DailyMail, and Wikitext-103. Three fixes were applied: (1) merge-and-reinitialize adapter technique for silent LoRA freezing, (2) float32 precision during PPO updates to prevent bfloat16 numerical overflow in importance ratios, and (3) a three-layer safety mechanism (reward whitening, importance-ratio guarding, weight rollback) to prevent catastrophic policy collapse from reward-model error.
AI.result: The proposed system converged stably across all experiments. Improved preference win rate over the SFT baseline was achieved in configurations with a fluent prior (PPL < 20) and an informative reward signal. The system outperformed instruction-tuned baselines while using significantly less training data.
AI.conclusion: The capacity-headroom hypothesis posits that PPO performance at the SLM scale depends on a fluent supervised model (PPL < 20) and a discriminative reward signal, not parameter count. With the proposed stabilization techniques, reliable RL alignment of SLMs is feasible. All artifacts are publicly released.

title: Structure-aware Relative Policy Optimization for Ranking
summary: Ranking is a fundamental component of modern information access systems. Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a flexible framework for directly optimizing coarse-grained feedback and system-level objectives defined over the complete ranking list. However, existing RL-based ranking methods typically treat each sampled permutation as an atomic output and evaluate it primarily through a scalar reward, overlooking the structural relationships among different ranking lists. Consequently, permutations with similar rewards but substantially different permutation patterns may receive comparable optimization signals, potentially leading to inaccurate credit assignment and overly aggressive policy updates. To address this limitation, we propose SRPO, a \textbf{S}tructure-aware \textbf{R}elative \textbf{P}olicy \textbf{O}ptimization framework for listwise ranking. SRPO measures the discrepancy between sampled permutations using a top-weighted Kendall-tau distance and normalizes their pairwise reward differences by the corresponding distances. It quantifies the reward improvement per unit of ranking change, thereby emphasizing efficient local refinements, particularly those involving top-ranked positions. Experimental results across two ranking scenarios demonstrate that explicitly modeling permutation-level differences improves the effectiveness and stability of listwise ranking, with particularly favorable performance in limited-feedback and complex list-level optimization settings.

AI.tldr: SRPO introduces a structure-aware relative policy optimization framework for listwise ranking that normalizes pairwise reward differences by top-weighted Kendall-tau distance, improving credit assignment and optimization stability in RL-based ranking.
AI.motivation: Existing RL-based ranking methods treat each sampled permutation atomically and evaluate via scalar reward, ignoring structural relationships between ranking lists. This leads to similar optimization signals for permutations with comparable rewards but different patterns, causing inaccurate credit assignment and overly aggressive policy updates.
