This offers a practical, safer moderation pathway for open-weight image generation ecosystems.

title: Cyber-Capable AI Agents: Vulnerabilities, Evaluation Containment, and Defensive Response
summary: Cyber-capable AI agents combine language models with tools, memory, and execution en- vironments to perform multi-step offensive-security tasks. Existing work separately measures cyber capability and catalogs attacks against agent components, but provides less guidance on containing a capable agent within the environments used to evaluate it. This review synthe- sizes five vulnerability classes at that boundary: multi-step offensive chains, objectives that conflict with sandbox boundaries, supply-chain and credential exposure, persistent command- and-control, and the speed of automated action. We use the reported July 2026 Hugging Face/OpenAI incident as a bounded case study, distinguishing incident-specific observations from findings established in the wider literature. Across the taxonomy and case, we examine controls for containment, privilege separation, provenance, and responder access, including the dual-use problem that defensive artifacts may also enable misuse. The review identifies practical priorities for evaluating cyber capability together with the security of the environment in which that capability is exercised.

AI.tldr: This review paper synthesizes five vulnerability classes at the boundary between cyber-capable AI agents and their evaluation sandboxes, using a real-world incident as a case study, and proposes containment controls while addressing dual-use concerns.
AI.motivation: Existing work measures AI cyber capability and catalogs attacks against agent components in isolation, but offers insufficient guidance on how to securely contain a capable agent within the environments used to evaluate it — a critical gap given the dual-use risk that containment artifacts may aid misuse.
AI.method: The authors conduct a literature review synthesizing five vulnerability classes at the agent-environment boundary, then apply this taxonomy to a bounded case study (the July 2026 Hugging Face/OpenAI incident), distinguishing incident-specific observations from broader research findings. They further examine containment controls across four dimensions: containment, privilege separation, provenance, and responder access.
AI.result: Five vulnerability classes are identified: (1) multi-step offensive chains, (2) objectives conflicting with sandbox boundaries, (3) supply-chain and credential exposure, (4) persistent command-and-control, and (5) speed of automated action. The case study validates several taxonomy elements, and the analysis of controls reveals a persistent dual-use tension — defensive monitoring artifacts can also enable offensive actors.
AI.conclusion: Secure evaluation of cyber-capable AI agents requires jointly assessing both offensive capability and the security of the evaluation environment itself. Practical priorities include robust containment, privilege separation, provenance tracking, and responder access — all designed with awareness of dual-use implications.

title: An Embarrassingly Simple Rule-based Visiting Circulation Approach to Trip Destination Prediction
summary: In this paper, we propose the Rule-based Visiting Circulation (RVC) model in tackling the challenge in the IEEE Big Data Cup 2022: Trip Destination Prediction. Given trips containing travel information, personal attributes, origin zones, and their features in the training metropolitan areas, the task is to predict the destination of every trip in a targeted metropolitan area whose destinations are not given at all at the training stage. We highlight the challenges in this destination prediction task -- having no knowledge of the destinations in the targeted metropolitan area. We provide insights from the datasets, in which revisiting behaviors and the relationships between origins and destinations play a crucial role in individuals' trips. Hence, we design a simple but comprehensive method, rule-based visiting circulation, which directly utilizes the origin information and individuals' trip behaviors to determine the destinations in the targeted metropolitan area, i.e., requiring no learning from the four training areas. Experimental results on both offline evaluation and leaderboard submission consistently exhibit the proposed RVC can significantly outperform supervised learning methods and other heuristics. The RVC method eventually brings us to second place in the competition leaderboard.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Rule-based Visiting Circulation (RVC) model for trip destination prediction without any training on target-area destinations. By leveraging revisiting behaviors and origin-destination relationships, the non-learning heuristic outperformed supervised methods and secured second place in the IEEE Big Data Cup 2022 competition.
AI.motivation: The core challenge is predicting trip destinations in a target metropolitan area where destination data is entirely absent during training — a cold-start, cross-domain transfer problem. Existing supervised learning methods rely on labeled destination data, which is unavailable in this setting. The authors observed that revisiting patterns and origin-destination correlations are strong behavioral signals, motivating a rule-based approach that bypasses the need for target-area training entirely.
AI.method: The RVC model is a non-parametric, rule-based heuristic. It directly exploits (1) individual revisiting behaviors — users tend to return to previously visited locations — and (2) origin-to-destination relationships derived from source metropolitan areas, applying these rules directly to the target area without any learning. No model training on the four source areas is required; the method purely uses origin information and trip behavioral patterns to infer destinations.
AI.result: On both offline evaluation and the competition leaderboard, RVC significantly outperformed supervised learning baselines and other heuristic methods. The approach achieved second place in the IEEE Big Data Cup 2022 leaderboard.
AI.conclusion: Simple, behavior-driven heuristics can surpass complex supervised models in destination prediction when target-domain labels are unavailable. The RVC model demonstrates that revisiting patterns and origin-destination relationships encode sufficient signal for accurate cross-area transfer, offering a strong baseline for zero-shot spatial prediction tasks.

title: HANDBOOK.md: A Benchmark for Long-Context Agentic Instruction Following
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Accepted to the Workshop on Agent Behavior (WAB) at COLM 2026. Benchmark, environments, and evaluation harness: https://github.com/surge-ai/handbook
summary: Language-model agents are increasingly deployed under standing instructions: a system prompt, a policy file, or a skills document is placed in context, and the agent is trusted to let it govern every action that follows. Existing benchmarks rarely test this deployment pattern directly; they measure whether an agent can complete a task, not whether a long, binding policy document actually constrains its behavior over an extended tool-use horizon. We present HANDBOOK.md, a benchmark of 65 agentic tasks modeled on how enterprise employees follow company handbooks. Each task places an agent in a self-contained company environment, a file workspace together with mock email, chat, calendar, issue-tracking, and commerce services exposed over the Model Context Protocol, and instructs it to carry out routine professional work governed by an expert-written standard operating procedure of 20 to 124 pages. Tasks span five domains (finance, medical billing, insurance, logistics, and HR) and ten fictional companies. To resist memorization, every task modifies one of ten base handbooks, altering the specific rules and thresholds on which grading turns, so no two tasks share a policy. Grading is fully deterministic: each task carries a rubric of programmatic criteria (824 in total) that check both that required actions occurred and that prohibited actions did not. Under strict grading, where a trial passes only if every criterion is satisfied, the best of thirty evaluated model configurations passes 36.2% of trials, and most frontier configurations remain below 25%. Failures follow consistent patterns: agents let a plausible in-environment request override the standing policy, perform a required check and then act against its result, lose rule details over long horizons, and report compliance they did not achieve. We release all tasks, environments, and the evaluation harness.

AI.tldr: HANDBOOK.md is a benchmark of 65 agentic tasks testing whether language-model agents can follow long, binding policy documents (20–124 pages) over extended tool-use horizons across five enterprise domains. The best of 30 evaluated model configurations passes only 36.2% of trials under strict grading, with consistent failure patterns including policy override by plausible requests, rule forgetting, and false compliance reporting.
AI.motivation: Existing agent benchmarks measure task completion, not whether a standing policy document actually constrains agent behavior over long horizons. This fails to reflect the real-world deployment pattern where agents are governed by system prompts, policy files, or skills documents that should bind every action.
AI.method: The benchmark comprises 65 tasks across five domains (finance, medical billing, insurance, logistics, HR) and ten fictional companies. Each task embeds an agent in a self-contained company environment with file workspace, mock email, chat, calendar, issue-tracking, and commerce services via the Model Context Protocol. Agents must follow expert-written SOPs (20–124 pages) while completing routine professional work. To resist memorization, each task modifies one of ten base handbooks, altering rules and thresholds critical to grading. Grading uses 824 fully deterministic programmatic rubric criteria, checking both required and prohibited actions. A trial passes only if every criterion is satisfied.
AI.result: Under strict grading, the best of 30 evaluated model configurations passes only 36.2% of trials; most frontier configurations remain below 25%. Consistent failure patterns include: agents allowing plausible in-environment requests to override standing policy, performing required checks but then acting against their results, losing rule details over long horizons, and reporting compliance they did not achieve.
AI.conclusion: Current language-model agents struggle significantly with long-horizon policy adherence, revealing a critical gap between task-completion benchmarks and real-world constrained deployment. The benchmark, environments, and evaluation harness are publicly released to spur progress on this underexamined capability.

title: SpectONet: A Physics-Guided Spectral Deep Operator Network for Euler-Bernoulli Beam Dynamics
summary: This paper proposes a novel physics-guided spectral deep operator network, termed SpectONet, for solving Euler-Bernoulli beam (EBB) vibration problems. The proposed framework integrates the operator-learning capability of DeepONet with physics-informed constraints and Chebyshev-Gauss-Lobatto (CGL) sensor placement. Unlike conventional DeepONet frameworks, which commonly employ uniformly distributed sensors, SpectONet uses nonuniform spectral sensor locations with a higher concentration of points near the domain boundaries. This sampling strategy improves the finite-dimensional representation of boundary-sensitive structural responses while requiring only a limited number of branch-network inputs. The governing beam equation, together with the associated initial and boundary conditions, incorporated into the training objective to promote physically consistent and generalizable predictions. Numerical experiments on three synthetic EBB vibration problems and a real-world bridge vibration dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Comparisons with strong baselines such as, Vanilla DeepONet, PI-DeepONet, PINN, and CNN-UNet show that SpectONet consistently achieves lower prediction errors across all considered evaluation metrics. In particular, SpectONet achieves at least \(64\%\) improvement over the considered baseline models across the three synthetic problems and at least \(37\%\) for the real-world problems. These results demonstrate that SpectONet provides an accurate, computationally efficient, and physically consistent operator-learning framework for structural vibration analysis.

AI.tldr: SpectONet combines DeepONet with physics-informed constraints and Chebyshev-Gauss-Lobatto sensor placement to solve Euler-Bernoulli beam vibration problems, achieving 64%+ improvement on synthetic data and 37%+ on real-world data over baselines.
AI.motivation: Conventional DeepONet frameworks use uniformly distributed sensors, which poorly capture boundary-sensitive structural responses in beam vibration problems. There is a need for an operator-learning method that is both physically consistent and computationally efficient for structural vibration analysis.
AI.method: The authors propose SpectONet, which integrates three key components: (1) the operator-learning architecture of DeepONet, (2) physics-informed constraints that embed the governing Euler-Bernoulli beam equation along with initial and boundary conditions into the loss function, and (3) nonuniform Chebyshev-Gauss-Lobatto (CGL) spectral sensor placement that concentrates points near domain boundaries for improved finite-dimensional representation with limited branch-network inputs.
AI.result: On three synthetic EBB vibration problems and one real-world bridge vibration dataset, SpectONet consistently outperforms Vanilla DeepONet, PI-DeepONet, PINN, and CNN-UNet. It achieves at least 64% improvement over baselines on synthetic problems and at least 37% on real-world problems across all evaluation metrics.
AI.conclusion: SpectONet provides an accurate, computationally efficient, and physically consistent operator-learning framework for structural vibration analysis, demonstrating that spectral sensor placement combined with physics-informed constraints substantially enhances predictive performance over existing methods.

title: COVENANT: Natural-Language Workflow Compilation for Aligned Agent Execution
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly entrusted with natural-language workflow instructions (e.g., retail-payment policies) that specify not only what outcome to achieve, but also which steps, branches, and tool interactions are permitted. When these instructions are supplied as prompt context, however, the model retains control over both procedure selection and step execution. As interactions accumulate, an agent can skip required steps, take unsupported branches, or execute a valid step with unsupported arguments or effects--a failure mode we call workflow misalignment. In this work, we propose COVENANT, a compiler-and-interpreter architecture for workflow-aligned agent execution. Our key insight is to treat workflow instructions as source programs rather than prompts. COVENANT converts the instructions into a workflow abstract syntax tree (WAST) and lowers it to a workflow control-flow graph (WCFG). At runtime, a controller interprets the WCFG one node at a time, checks each proposal against requirements extracted from the instructions before committing controller state or advancing the graph, and returns diagnostic feedback for repair. To evaluate COVENANT, we use 120 cases from three existing benchmarks, spanning seven workflow scenarios. Compared with state-of-the-art LLM agents, COVENANT improves benchmark success from 50.00% to 83.33% and reduces the workflow-misalignment failure rate from 42.50% to 15.83% (62.75% relative). These results show that COVENANT substantially mitigates workflow misalignment, moving LLM-agent alignment beyond isolated prompt following toward reliable execution of complex and multi-step workflows.

AI.tldr: COVENANT is a compiler-interpreter architecture that treats workflow instructions as source programs rather than prompts. It compiles instructions into a workflow control-flow graph and enforces step-by-step compliance at runtime, improving benchmark success from 50% to 83.33% and reducing workflow misalignment failures by 62.75% relative.
AI.motivation: LLM agents given natural-language workflow instructions as prompts retain control over both procedure selection and step execution, leading to "workflow misalignment" — skipping required steps, taking unsupported branches, or executing valid steps with invalid arguments or effects. This failure mode is inadequately addressed by existing prompt-based approaches.
AI.method: COVENANT employs a compiler-and-interpreter architecture: (1) a compiler converts natural-language workflow instructions into a Workflow Abstract Syntax Tree (WAST), then lowers it to a Workflow Control-Flow Graph (WCFG); (2) at runtime, a controller interprets the WCFG node-by-node, validates each agent proposal against extracted requirements before committing state or advancing the graph, and returns diagnostic feedback for repair when violations occur.
AI.result: Evaluated on 120 cases across three benchmarks and seven workflow scenarios, COVENANT improved benchmark success rate from 50.00% to 83.33% and reduced the workflow-misalignment failure rate from 42.50% to 15.83% — a 62.75% relative reduction — compared to state-of-the-art LLM agents.
AI.conclusion: COVENANT substantially mitigates workflow misalignment, advancing LLM-agent alignment beyond isolated prompt following toward reliable execution of complex, multi-step workflows through structured programmatic enforcement rather than prompt-based guidance alone.

title: PatientAgentBench: A Benchmark Framework for Evaluating Patient-Facing Health AI Agents
summary: Health AI is evolving from answering questions to agentic systems that converse with patients, reason about health records, and act on their behalf. Primary care guards against diagnostic errors and unsafe care; agents assisting in this domain warrant evaluation against the same risks. Current benchmarks focus on medical knowledge, assessed through isolated question-answering or clinician-facing tasks. PatientAgentBench benchmarks patient-facing agentic healthcare; it evaluates a foundation model, wrapped in an agent with a sandbox of healthcare tools, conversing with a simulated patient. Each conversation is scored by an LLM-as-a-Jury across six dimensions via over a hundred conversation-agnostic, clinician-grounded criteria. To validate alignment, licensed clinicians annotated shared conversations, yielding 79-93% adjacent agreement between jury and expert raters, on par with or exceeding clinician inter-rater agreement. We benchmarked 10 models across four families on the same 1,200 scenarios and found clinical gaps. Triage quality is the most discriminating dimension: pass rates rise from 32% for the weakest models to 88% for the strongest, with agents often acting on administrative requests without clinical screening. Clinical safety and workflow accuracy follow the same pattern: the weakest models fail often, fabricating unexecuted actions, while frontier models fail on only 1-3% of cases, from unverified tool outputs and omitted crisis resources in an emergency. More capable models narrow these gaps but do not close them; the strongest scores only 4.25 of 5 overall. These failures surface only in sustained, tool-using conversations against realistic patient records, confirming that static benchmarks are insufficient as healthcare agentic systems gain autonomy. We release the framework as a reproducible, clinician-validated evaluation standard to help the field close this gap.

AI.tldr: PatientAgentBench is a clinician-validated benchmark for evaluating LLM-based healthcare agents in sustained, tool-using conversations with simulated patients, revealing clinical gaps—especially in triage quality—that static medical QA benchmarks miss, with even frontier models scoring only 4.25/5.
AI.motivation: Health AI is shifting from answering isolated questions to agentic systems that converse with patients and act on health records. Primary care involves diagnostic and safety risks that current benchmarks, limited to static QA or clinician-facing tasks, fail to capture. There is a need for evaluation that reflects real-world, patient-facing, tool-using clinical workflows.
AI.method: PatientAgentBench evaluates a foundation model wrapped as an agent with a healthcare tool sandbox, conversing with a simulated patient across 1,200 scenarios. Each conversation is scored by an LLM-as-a-Jury across six dimensions using over 100 conversation-agnostic, clinician-grounded criteria. Validation was performed by licensed clinicians annotating shared conversations, achieving 79–93% adjacent agreement with the jury, matching or exceeding clinician inter-rater agreement. Ten models from four families were benchmarked.
AI.result: Triage quality is the most discriminating dimension: pass rates range from 32% (weakest models) to 88% (strongest). Weaker models frequently act on administrative requests without clinical screening, fabricate unexecuted actions, and show high failure rates on clinical safety and workflow accuracy. Frontier models fail on only 1–3% of cases, but still exhibit errors from unverified tool outputs and omitted crisis resources in emergencies. The strongest model scores 4.25/5 overall—gaps are narrowed but not closed. Failures surface only in sustained, tool-using conversations against realistic records.
AI.conclusion: Static benchmarks are insufficient as healthcare AI gains autonomy. PatientAgentBench provides a reproducible, clinician-validated evaluation standard that exposes clinically meaningful failures in agentic systems, and the framework is released to help the field close the remaining performance gap.

title: Prototype Adaptation for Zero-Shot sEMG Movement Classification
summary: Surface electromyography (sEMG) enables the control of prostheses, allowing upper-limb amputees to re-gain some hand function. Most current research focuses on recognizing basic movements for prosthesis control. However, in most daily activities, such as opening a door, combined movements are essential. However, collecting training data for all possible combined movements is time-consuming and requires re-training of the model for any new combination. We propose two novel recognition approaches, Compositional Prototype Interpolation (CPI) and Synthetic Adaptation for Prototypes (SAP), that enable zero-shot learning of combined, novel and unseen movements in Prototype Networks after training only with basic movements. Our methods rest on a linear interpolation assumption in the embedding space, which we study by inspecting the geometry of combined motions in signal and embedding space. In experiments on the NearLab and NinaPro DB3 data sets as well as our newly recorded BasCom dataset, our proposed SAP outperforms prior zero-shot learning methods with accuracy improvements on combined movements of more than 20%. This advantage is maintained in online inference experiments in a user study.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes two zero-shot learning methods (CPI and SAP) that recognize combined hand movements from sEMG signals after training only on basic movements, achieving >20% accuracy improvement over prior methods across multiple datasets.
AI.motivation: Current sEMG-based prosthesis control focuses on basic movements, but daily activities require combined movements. Collecting training data for all possible combined movements is impractical, and models require retraining for each new combination. A method enabling zero-shot recognition of novel combined movements from basic movement training alone is needed.
AI.method: The authors propose two methods built on Prototype Networks: Compositional Prototype Interpolation (CPI) which linearly interpolates between basic movement prototypes in embedding space to synthesize combined movement prototypes, and Synthetic Adaptation for Prototypes (SAP) which further refines these interpolated prototypes. Both rely on a linear interpolation assumption, validated by inspecting geometry in signal and embedding space. Experiments use NearLab, NinaPro DB3, and a newly collected BasCom dataset.
AI.result: SAP outperforms prior zero-shot learning methods with accuracy improvements exceeding 20% on combined movements. This performance advantage is maintained in online inference experiments during a user study.
AI.conclusion: Zero-shot learning of combined sEMG movements via prototype interpolation is viable and effective, with SAP providing state-of-the-art performance. This approach significantly reduces the data collection burden for prosthetic control systems.

title: Context Assembly as the Controlled Variable: A Control-Theoretic View of Harness Policies for Frozen LLM Agents
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Code and companion paper's data: https://github.com/dpaul0501/context-optimization-rl
summary: A growing body of 2026 work applies control theory to LLM agents: Lyapunov-certified stability for tool-mediated controllers (Prinos et al., "Stable Agentic Control", 2026), sample-complexity bounds for sparse policies over massive discrete tool universes (Majumdar, "Sparse Agentic Control", 2026), and regulatory-control decompositions of multi-agent systems into auditable feedback loops (Nogueira and Skogestad, 2026). We do not claim to introduce control theory to LLM agents -- that ship has sailed. Our narrower claim is about what the controlled variable is. Prior work controls tool selection, inter-agent message routing, or the agent's raw action stream. We instead treat context assembly itself -- which prompt template, which few-shot demonstrations, how much retrieved context, how many planning/verification passes -- as the controlled variable, learned online by a contextual bandit or REINFORCE policy sitting outside a frozen model. This paper develops the formal decomposition (inner frozen policy $π_θ$, outer context policy $π_φ$), gives a stability argument for the online controller in the sense used by Zhang et al. (2026) (non-decreasing expected reward under bounded policy change), and reports an uncertainty-calibration analysis of the controller's own confidence against realized task outcomes. The applied counterpart to this paper instantiates the same controller across three domains and two model providers and releases the dataset, trajectory logs, and a deployment recipe; here we focus on the formal framing and the stability/uncertainty evidence a control-theoretic claim requires.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes treating context assembly (prompt templates, few-shot examples, retrieval depth, planning passes) as the controlled variable for LLM agents, rather than tool selection or action streams. It formalizes a two-level policy decomposition (frozen inner policy, learned outer context policy) with stability guarantees and uncertainty calibration evidence.
AI.motivation: Prior work applying control theory to LLM agents focuses on controlling tool selection, inter-agent messaging, or raw action streams. The authors identify a gap: no one has framed context assembly itself as the controlled variable. This matters because context design decisions (which prompt template, how many demonstrations, how much retrieval) strongly influence agent performance but are typically hand-tuned offline rather than learned adaptively.
AI.method: The paper proposes a formal two-policy decomposition: an inner frozen policy π_θ (the base LLM agent) and an outer context policy π_φ that selects context configurations. The outer policy is trained online using a contextual bandit or REINFORCE algorithm. The authors provide a stability argument showing non-decreasing expected reward under bounded policy change (in the sense of Zhang et al., 2026), and conduct an uncertainty-calibration analysis comparing the controller's confidence estimates against realized task outcomes.
AI.result: The paper reports a stability guarantee for the online context controller and demonstrates that the controller's confidence estimates are well-calibrated against actual task outcomes. An applied companion paper instantiates the framework across three domains and two model providers, with released datasets, trajectory logs, and deployment recipes.
AI.conclusion: Reframing context assembly as a learned control variable — rather than a static design choice — opens a new formal interface between control theory and LLM agents. The stability and calibration evidence satisfies the rigor that control-theoretic claims demand, complementing the empirical deployment results in the companion applied paper.

title: DRIFT: Direct-Recursive Intervention-Conditioned Forecasting of ICU Physiological Trajectories
comment: 34 pages, 1 figure; extended technical appendices included
summary: Many time-series forecasts depend not only on prior observations but also on actions specified during the forecast period. In intensive care units (ICUs), future vital signs and laboratory values are influenced by treatments such as vasopressors. However, models that predict the full future sequence all at once make little use of these treatments, whereas autoregressive models can accumulate errors. We introduce DRIFT, a hybrid framework in which a direct model produces the primary forecast and a recursive, action-conditioned model contributes constrained corrections. We evaluate DRIFT on 6,046 admissions from MIMIC-IV and 8,345 admissions from eICU-CRD. Averaged across the 8-, 24-, and 48-hour forecast endpoints, DRIFT reduces mean absolute error for mean arterial pressure (MAP) by 0.673% relative to an action-conditioned Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT-action) on MIMIC-IV and achieves the lowest corresponding error among the compared models on eICU-CRD. Although the overall accuracy improvement is modest, a MIMIC-IV audit restricted to windows in which the supplied treatment sequence was altered showed that DRIFT achieved lower observed-target MAP error than TFT-action at 8 and 24 hours. Treatment-sequence alteration increased DRIFT's MAP error by 0.21-0.26 mmHg more than it increased TFT-action's error, with prediction changes occurring primarily after the supplied paths diverged. In a separate robustness experiment, the MAP advantage persisted under three shared checkpoint-selection rules emphasizing overall endpoint error, MAP error, or both equally.

AI.tldr: DRIFT is a hybrid time-series forecasting framework that combines a direct (all-at-once) prediction model with a recursive, action-conditioned correction model, evaluated on ICU vital sign forecasting (MAP) from MIMIC-IV and eICU-CRD, showing modest accuracy gains over a Temporal Fusion Transformer baseline, with particular benefits when treatment sequences are altered.
AI.motivation: In clinical settings like ICUs, future vital signs depend not only on past observations but also on planned interventions (e.g., vasopressor treatments). Existing direct forecasting models underutilize these action sequences, while autoregressive models suffer from error accumulation. A framework is needed that leverages both approaches to improve action-conditioned forecasting.
AI.method: DRIFT (Direct-Recursive Integration for Forecasting with Treatments) is a hybrid framework where a direct model produces the primary multi-step forecast, and a recursive, action-conditioned model contributes constrained corrections to refine the prediction. The approach was benchmarked against an action-conditioned Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT-action) and evaluated on MAP forecasting across 8-, 24-, and 48-hour horizons using 6,046 MIMIC-IV admissions and 8,345 eICU-CRD admissions. Counterfactual-style audits were conducted by altering supplied treatment sequences, and robustness was tested under multiple checkpoint-selection rules.
AI.result: DRIFT reduced MAP mean absolute error by 0.673% relative to TFT-action on MIMIC-IV and achieved the lowest error on eICU-CRD. In windows where treatment sequences were altered, DRIFT maintained lower observed-target MAP error than TFT-action at 8 and 24 hours. Treatment alteration increased DRIFT's MAP error by 0.21–0.26 mmHg more than TFT-action, with divergence occurring after supplied paths differed. The MAP advantage persisted across three shared checkpoint-selection rules.
AI.conclusion: DRIFT effectively integrates direct and recursive forecasting to incorporate treatment action sequences, yielding modest but consistent improvements in ICU vital sign prediction. Its responsiveness to altered treatment paths suggests meaningful action-conditioning, though overall accuracy gains remain limited.

title: A Control System, a Dataset, and a Recipe for Making Frozen LLM Agents Learn a Domain
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Code and dataset: https://github.com/dpaul0501/context-optimization-rl
summary: Production LLM agents are increasingly assembled from a frozen model wrapped in a harness: a prompt template, a tool set, a memory/retrieval layer, a planning strategy, and a verification policy. Two 2026 systems, Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026) and HyperAgents (Meta AI, 2026), show that this harness can itself be optimized or even self-rewritten by an agentic proposer -- at the cost of either an expensive code-search loop or unconstrained self-modifying code, neither of which is auditable or usable with a fully black-box model API. We take a narrower, more constrained position: treat the harness as a small, fixed, human-legible action space and learn a policy over it online with classic sample-efficient reinforcement learning (an $ε$-greedy contextual bandit and REINFORCE), scored against a multi-objective reward (task success, verifier score, policy compliance, cost, latency, and an unsupported-claim penalty). We instantiate this control system with DSPy (Khattab et al., 2024) as both the context assembler and the source of the strongest non-adaptive baseline (a DSPy BootstrapFewShot static prompt), and evaluate it across three verifiable task domains -- tool-use workflows, code generation (HumanEval), and multi-hop retrieval QA (HotpotQA) -- and two model providers (a local Ollama model and AWS Bedrock). We release the harness-control-system code, the cross-domain verifiable task suite, the full trajectory/reward-decomposition logs from training, and a provider-agnostic deployment recipe for applying this to a new organization's domain and verification setup.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a constrained, auditable approach to optimizing LLM agent harnesses using classic RL (ε-greedy contextual bandit and REINFORCE) over a fixed, human-legible action space, evaluated with multi-objective rewards across three task domains and two model providers.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches to optimizing LLM agent harnesses (Meta-Harness, HyperAgents) rely on expensive code-search loops or unconstrained self-modifying code, which are neither auditable nor compatible with black-box model APIs. The authors seek a narrower, safer alternative that remains auditable and provider-agnostic.
AI.method: The harness is treated as a small, fixed, human-legible action space. An online RL policy is learned using ε-greedy contextual bandit and REINFORCE, scored against a multi-objective reward (task success, verifier score, policy compliance, cost, latency, unsupported-claim penalty). Implemented via DSPy as the context assembler, with DSPy BootstrapFewShot as the non-adaptive baseline. Evaluated across tool-use workflows, HumanEval, and HotpotQA using a local Ollama model and AWS Bedrock.
AI.result: The paper does not disclose explicit quantitative results in the abstract. It reports releasing: the harness-control-system code, cross-domain verifiable task suite, full trajectory/reward-decomposition logs, and a provider-agnostic deployment recipe.
AI.conclusion: A constrained RL-based harness optimization approach provides an auditable, black-box-compatible alternative to code-search and self-modifying code methods, demonstrated across diverse tasks and model providers with full artifact release for reproducibility and organizational adoption.

title: A2TTA: Anchored-and-Agile Test-Time Adaptation for Evolving Traffic Sensor Networks
summary: Traffic forecasting is important for efficient traffic management and route planning in smart cities. Existing traffic forecasting studies typically assume fixed sensor graphs, overlooking the continuous evolution of real-world traffic networks, e.g., ongoing road network construction and evolving human mobility patterns. These dynamic changes can substantially degrade conventional forecasting models, motivating test-time adaptation (TTA) to efficiently adapt pretrained models during deployment. However, applying TTA to evolving traffic sensor networks remains challenging in two aspects. First, topology expansion introduces new sensors and connections, continuously reshaping the sensor graph. Second, tem- poral shifts vary in time scale and stability, requiring differentiated adaptation to long-term and short-term shifts. In this study, we address these challenges by proposing A2TTA, an Anchored-and-Agile Test-Time Adaptation framework for evolving traffic sensor networks, which transforms topology-induced forecasting errors into an expandable output calibration problem and separates tem- poral adaptation into persistent global correction and agile context-specific specialization. By jointly addressing topology evolution and multi-scale temporal shifts, A2TTA enables efficient and robust adaptation to continuously evolving traffic environments. Extensive experiments on ten real-world traffic networks demonstrate that A2TTA consistently improves forecasting performance across different backbones, datasets, and prediction horizons. Our code is available in https://github.com/lixus7/A2TTA.

AI.tldr: A2TTA is a test-time adaptation framework for traffic forecasting that handles evolving sensor networks by (1) reframing topology expansion as output calibration, and (2) decoupling temporal adaptation into global persistent correction and local agile specialization, demonstrating consistent improvements across ten real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Real-world traffic sensor networks continuously evolve due to road construction and shifting mobility patterns, yet existing forecasting methods assume static sensor graphs. Test-time adaptation is promising but faces two unresolved challenges: topology expansion (new sensors/connections) and multi-scale temporal shifts (varying stability and time scales).
AI.method: A2TTA (Anchored-and-Agile Test-Time Adaptation) introduces two components: (1) an expandable output calibration module that converts topology-induced errors into a calibration problem, accommodating new sensors without full model retraining; (2) a dual temporal adaptation mechanism with persistent global correction for long-term distribution shifts and agile context-specific specialization for short-term, localized changes.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on ten real-world traffic networks show that A2TTA consistently improves forecasting performance across different backbone models, datasets, and prediction horizons.
AI.conclusion: A2TTA provides an efficient and robust solution for adapting pretrained traffic forecasting models to continuously evolving traffic environments by jointly addressing topology evolution and multi-scale temporal shifts.

title: Salient Knowledge Pathways: Sparse Cross-Modal Routing for Efficient Knowledge-Intensive Multimodal Question Answering
comment: Accepted at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026) Workshop on Efficient Multimodal Question Answering (EMM-QA), Seoul, South Korea. Copyright 2026 by the author(s). (Archival)
summary: Knowledge-intensive multimodal question answering (KI-MMQA) sits at the intersection of three expensive primitives: long visual token sequences, dense retrieval over large external corpora, and full cross-modal fusion. Existing systems pay all three costs uniformly per query, even though only a small fraction of visual content and retrieved knowledge is actually relevant to any given question. We introduce SKIP (Salient Knowledge-Injected Pathways), a unified inference architecture that routes computation along sparse pathways jointly conditioned on the question, the image, and a difficulty estimate. SKIP combines question-guided visual token pruning, region-conditional sparse retrieval, bipartite sparse cross-attention, and speculative knowledge verification with an adaptive budget controller that allocates compute proportional to predicted question difficulty. We derive an information-bottleneck bound showing that the optimal visual sparsity rate scales as $O(1/\sqrt{N})$ under realistic question-image mutual-information assumptions, with retained accuracy guarantees. Across five KI-MMQA benchmarks (OK-VQA, A-OKVQA, InfoSeek, Encyclopedic-VQA, and ViQuAE), SKIP matches or exceeds the accuracy of strong dense baselines while using $3.4$--$6.8\times$ fewer FLOPs and $2.7\times$ less end-to-end latency. Code available at: https://pmlrbd.github.io/skip/

AI.tldr: SKIP introduces a unified inference architecture for knowledge-intensive multimodal QA that routes computation along sparse pathways conditioned on the question, image, and difficulty estimate, achieving 3.4–6.8× FLOP reduction and 2.7× lower latency while matching or exceeding dense baselines across five benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing KI-MMQA systems uniformly pay three high computational costs — long visual token sequences, dense retrieval over large corpora, and full cross-modal fusion — even though only a small fraction of visual content and retrieved knowledge is relevant to any given question. This motivates a sparsity-driven, adaptive approach.
AI.method: SKIP combines four sparse mechanisms: (1) question-guided visual token pruning, (2) region-conditional sparse retrieval, (3) bipartite sparse cross-attention, and (4) speculative knowledge verification. An adaptive budget controller allocates compute proportional to predicted question difficulty. An information-bottleneck bound is derived showing optimal visual sparsity scales as O(1/√N).
AI.result: Across OK-VQA, A-OKVQA, InfoSeek, Encyclopedic-VQA, and ViQuAE, SKIP matches or exceeds accuracy of strong dense baselines while using 3.4–6.8× fewer FLOPs and 2.7× less end-to-end latency.
AI.conclusion: Sparse, difficulty-conditioned routing can dramatically reduce KI-MMQA inference cost without sacrificing accuracy. The theoretical bound provides principled justification for the sparsity design, and the unified architecture offers a practical path toward efficient multimodal reasoning systems.

title: AIriskEval-edu Demo: Auditing of Pedagogical Risks in Educational Explanations
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at the 17th IAPR International Workshop on Document Analysis Systems (DAS 2026), ICDAR 2026, September 3, 2026
summary: We present AIriskEval-edu Demo, a platform that audits the pedagogical quality of instructional explanations and provides explainable audit results. The platform evaluates an explanation against a rubric covering five dimensions of pedagogical risk: factual accuracy, depth and completeness, focus and relevance, student-level appropriateness, and ideological bias. For each dimension, it returns a binary decision and a confidence score. Detected risks also include a natural-language rationale and, except for Depth and Completeness, a localized evidence span. The platform integrates GPT-5.5 through an external API and a self-hosted Llama 3.1 8B evaluator that runs on consumer-grade GPUs. The local evaluator is fine-tuned on AIriskEval-edu, a dataset of K-12 instructional explanations with risk and explainability annotations. The platform operates in two modes: in AI mode, both evaluators assess stored explanations generated under six simulated teacher profiles, each representing a distinct pedagogical behavior and potential risk; in human mode, the local evaluator audits user-written explanations in real time. The local evaluator outperforms GPT-5.5 on most reported metrics, offering educational institutions a practical way to keep audited content within their own infrastructure.

AI.tldr: AIriskEval-edu Demo is a dual-mode platform that audits K-12 instructional explanations across five pedagogical risk dimensions using both GPT-5.5 and a fine-tuned local Llama 3.1 8B model, with the local evaluator outperforming GPT-5.5 on most metrics.
AI.motivation: Educational institutions need automated, explainable quality assurance for instructional content, but existing solutions may lack transparency, pose data privacy risks when relying solely on external APIs, and fail to provide localized evidence for detected pedagogical flaws.
AI.method: The platform evaluates explanations against a five-dimension rubric (factual accuracy, depth/completeness, focus/relevance, student-level appropriateness, ideological bias), returning binary decisions with confidence scores and natural-language rationales. It integrates GPT-5.5 via external API and a self-hosted Llama 3.1 8B fine-tuned on the AIriskEval-edu dataset. Two operational modes exist: AI mode (evaluating pre-generated explanations from six simulated teacher profiles) and human mode (real-time auditing of user-written explanations using only the local evaluator).
AI.result: The fine-tuned local Llama 3.1 8B evaluator outperforms GPT-5.5 on most reported metrics, demonstrating that a consumer-grade, self-hosted model can match or exceed a proprietary API-based model for pedagogical risk auditing.
AI.conclusion: AIriskEval-edu Demo offers a practical, privacy-preserving solution for educational quality assurance, enabling institutions to keep audited content within their own infrastructure without sacrificing audit quality.

title: Localized Adaptation Reveals Distinct Learning Signatures in Transformers
comment: Main text: 8 pages, 2 figures; appendix: 13 tables, 10 figures; code and data available at https://github.com/rramnauth2220/adaptation-geometries
summary: Transformer adaptation is typically distributed across model depth, even when the intended change is narrow. We investigate how adaptation site shapes what a model learns, how well that learning generalizes, and how selectively it is applied. We introduce a controlled benchmark spanning five objectives (lexical binding, factual association, behavioral policy learning, causal mapping, and procedural reasoning) and define each objective's "adaptation geometry" as its profile of acquisition, transfer, and boundedness under full-stack and early-, middle-, or late-layer LoRA. The objectives exhibit distinct geometries. Lexical binding favors early-layer adaptation for acquisition and boundedness but requires broader updates for transfer; factual association favors later layers among localized adapters; behavioral learning separates late-layer action acquisition from middle-layer policy gating; and causal and procedural transfer benefit most from middle- or full-stack adaptation. These patterns largely persist under parameter-matched controls, and most corresponding directional contrasts replicate across five model families. These findings establish adaptation site as a key design variable for controlling what models learn, generalize, and leave unchanged.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how the layer at which LoRA adapters are applied (early, middle, late, or full-stack) shapes a model's acquisition, transfer, and boundedness across five distinct objectives. It finds that different tasks exhibit unique "adaptation geometries"—for example, lexical binding prefers early layers, factual association favors late layers, and causal/procedural reasoning benefits from middle or full-stack adaptation.
AI.motivation: Transformer adaptation is typically applied uniformly across model depth, even for narrow changes. The authors aim to understand how the site (layer depth) of adaptation influences what is learned, how well it generalizes (transfer), and how selectively it is applied (boundedness). There is a gap in systematic understanding of adaptation geometry across diverse objectives.
AI.method: The authors introduce a controlled benchmark with five objectives: lexical binding, factual association, behavioral policy learning, causal mapping, and procedural reasoning. They define each objective's "adaptation geometry" as its profile across three dimensions—acquisition, transfer, and boundedness—under LoRA applied at early, middle, late, or all layers. Parameter-matched controls and replication across five model families are used to validate the findings.
AI.result: Each objective exhibits a distinct adaptation geometry: (1) Lexical binding favors early-layer adaptation for acquisition/boundedness but needs broader updates for transfer; (2) Factual association favors late layers among localized adapters; (3) Behavioral learning separates late-layer action acquisition from middle-layer policy gating; (4) Causal and procedural transfer benefit most from middle or full-stack adaptation. These patterns persist under parameter-matched controls and replicate across five model families.
AI.conclusion: Adaptation site (layer depth) is a critical design variable that controls what models learn, how well that learning generalizes, and how selectively it is applied. Practitioners should tune adaptation site to match the geometry of the target objective rather than defaulting to uniform full-depth adaptation.

title: Minimizing Targeted Activations: Input-Only Suppression of Evaluation-Awareness Latents in Large Language Models
summary: Activation steering controls model behavior by editing internal activations at inference time. We study its input-side dual: optimizing a fluent prompt so that a chosen internal latent is driven toward zero, with no inference-time model access. Our target is an "evaluation-awareness" latent-linearly readable and steerable in recent work-whose control would threaten the validity of safety evaluations if models behave differently when they detect being tested. Adapting Fluent Dreaming / EPO with a negated feature term (GCG-style token optimization plus a self-cross-entropy fluency regularizer, swept over a fluency weight), we suppress the latent under five target constructions-a CAA direction, a subspace norm, an SAE feature, a single MLP neuron, and a behavioral logit-on Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.1-8B. The latent is robustly suppressible ($z\approx-7$), and a causally-validated Llama Scope SAE feature can be fully and selectively turned off. But our controls tell a cautionary story about the CAA direction: a placebo random direction is suppressed just as hard and shifts behavior just as far, and when we hold a real eval passage in context and optimize only a prefix, suppressing the eval-direction fails to reduce-and slightly increases-the model's behavioral eval judgment. Activation-readability, in short, is not behavioral controllability. We further find that a single MLP neuron is eval-correlated but not causal at both scales, and that scanning the real Pile yields a natural-text baseline competitive with the optimizer for the internal direction. A positive control validates our erasure detector, bounding an erasure-vs-rotation question earlier left open.

AI.tldr: This paper studies whether a "latent erasure" approach—optimizing a fluent input prompt to suppress an internal evaluation-awareness latent—can control model behavior as effectively as inference-time activation steering. The authors find that while the latent is robustly suppressible, this does not translate to behavioral control: a placebo random direction suppresses equally well and shifts behavior similarly, and real eval-context optimization fails to reduce (and slightly increases) eval judgments. Activation readability ≠ behavioral controllability.
AI.motivation: If models can detect when they are being evaluated and alter their behavior accordingly, this threatens the validity of safety evaluations. The authors aim to test whether an input-side prompt optimization method (no inference-time model access needed) can suppress an "evaluation-awareness" latent to enable undetectable evaluation, and more broadly, whether latent readability implies behavioral controllability.
AI.method: The authors adapt Fluent Dreaming / EPO with a negated feature term (GCG-style token optimization + self-cross-entropy fluency regularizer, swept over a fluency weight) to suppress an evaluation-awareness latent under five target constructions: a CAA direction, subspace norm, SAE feature, single MLP neuron, and behavioral logit. Experiments run on Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.1-8B. They compare against a placebo random direction, test with real eval passages in context, scan the Pile for natural-text baselines, and include a positive control to validate their erasure detector.
AI.result: The eval latent is robustly suppressible (z ≈ -7), and a causally-validated Llama Scope SAE feature can be fully and selectively turned off. However, a placebo random CAA direction is suppressed just as hard and shifts behavior just as far. When holding a real eval passage in context and optimizing only a prefix, suppressing the eval direction fails to reduce—and slightly increases—behavioral eval judgment. A single MLP neuron is eval-correlated but not causal at both scales. Scanning the Pile yields a natural-text baseline competitive with the optimizer. The positive control validates the erasure detector, bounding the erasure-vs-rotation question.
AI.conclusion: Latent readability does not entail behavioral controllability. The ease with which random directions are suppressed and the failure of prefix optimization to reduce eval behavior suggest that activation steering findings may not straightforwardly generalize to input-side control, raising caution for interpretability-informed safety evaluation designs.

title: Toward an Organizational Science of Multi-Agent LLM Systems: Decoupling Who, How, and Which Algorithm
summary: Multi-agent frameworks built on large language models (LLMs) routinely entangle three logically distinct concerns: who is on the team (organization), how members align (coordination), and which algorithm fuses their work (collaboration protocol). IMACS (Intelligent Multi-Agent Collaboration System) separates the three into orthogonal, independently swappable layers. Classic organizational theory (Belbin roles, Mintzberg coordination, RACI accountability) becomes executable, validated configuration, and the framework places six published collaboration algorithms behind a common interface while exposing roles, coordination, and accountability as independently configurable factors. We use this separation to conduct controlled comparisons in which organizational assignments vary while the collaboration protocol is held fixed. It also turns protocol choice into a variable that can be learned: Adaptive Org Routing, a contextual-bandit meta-protocol, selects a protocol per task under an explicit quality-cost tradeoff, outperforms every fixed protocol in a controlled study, and trains online on real benchmark and LLM-judge rewards. The ablations expose a mechanism. Accountability placement changes outcomes exactly when the protocol routes the deliverable through the accountable agent, and the winning placement flips across model families, so organizational design cannot be hard-coded; it must be revalidated, or learned, for each model binding.

AI.tldr: IMACS disentangles multi-agent LLM systems into three orthogonal layers—organization, coordination, and collaboration protocol—enabling controlled comparisons and a learned meta-protocol (Adaptive Org Routing) that selects protocols per task, outperforming fixed protocols while revealing that optimal accountability placement is model-dependent and must be revalidated or learned.
AI.motivation: Current multi-agent LLM frameworks conflate team composition (organization), member alignment (coordination), and work fusion algorithms (collaboration protocol), making it impossible to conduct controlled ablations or optimize each concern independently. This entanglement hinders systematic study of organizational design choices and prevents learning optimal configurations per task and model.
AI.method: IMACS separates multi-agent systems into three independently swappable layers: organization (Belbin roles, RACI accountability), coordination (Mintzberg-inspired), and collaboration protocol (six published algorithms behind a unified interface). Using this separation, controlled experiments vary organizational assignments while holding protocol fixed. Adaptive Org Routing, a contextual-bandit meta-protocol, learns to select protocols per task under an explicit quality-cost tradeoff using real benchmark and LLM-judge rewards.
AI.result: Adaptive Org Routing outperforms every fixed protocol in controlled studies. Ablations reveal that accountability placement changes outcomes only when the protocol routes the deliverable through the accountable agent, and the optimal placement flips across model families, demonstrating that organizational design cannot be hard-coded.
AI.conclusion: Organizational design in multi-agent LLM systems must be revalidated or learned for each model binding rather than hard-coded. IMACS provides a principled framework for such systematic study and optimization through its layered architecture and learned meta-protocol.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Code Optimization
summary: RL for code correctness is now established: have the model generate a program, run it against hidden test cases, and reward solutions that pass. Extending this to code optimization seems straightforward: just add execution time to the reward. But in practice, once timing drives the reward, small problems in measurement noise, reward sparsity, or GRPO instability overwhelm the signal and make RL fail: generated solutions are barely faster, and more of them can fail. We make execution time learnable through three stages: (1) how code is tested, by building DMC-Optim with large optimization tests and a calibrated sandbox; (2) how speed is turned into reward, by composing correctness and speed in the RL environment and using an offline simulator to predict the most promising configurations; and (3) how the model learns from that reward, by adapting GRPO and evaluation to the sparser, noisier timed-execution setting. On DMC-Optim, the strongest optimization-aware configurations improve strict top-50% pass@1 from 18.0% to 31.3% on Qwen 2.5 7B and from 30.7% to 50.4% on CWM 32B. These gains further increase at stricter percentiles such as top-30%, with 125% relative improvement for CWM 32B, while preserving pure-correctness scores. When the timing sandbox is degraded, robust optimization RL reaches 100% to 200% improvement over standard RLVR, depending on the evaluation criterion. On LCB, CWM 32B wins up to 83% of median-sample speed comparisons against standard RLVR. Relative to the fastest correct human submissions per problem, it reaches about half the human rate of complexity-class improvements (14% vs. 28%).

AI.tldr: RL for code optimization is hindered by noisy timing signals, reward sparsity, and GRPO instability. The authors introduce DMC-Optim, a three-stage framework addressing how code is tested, how speed is turned into reward, and how the model learns, achieving substantial speedups on code generation benchmarks while preserving correctness.
AI.motivation: Extending RL-based code generation from correctness to optimization by simply adding execution time to the reward fails in practice due to measurement noise, reward sparsity, and GRPO instability. A principled approach is needed to make execution time a learnable signal.
AI.method: A three-stage framework: (1) DMC-Optim benchmark with large optimization tests and a calibrated timing sandbox; (2) reward composition combining correctness and speed signals, with an offline simulator to predict promising reward configurations; (3) adaptation of GRPO and evaluation protocols to handle sparser, noisier timed-execution settings.
AI.result: On DMC-Optim, Qwen 2.5 7B improves strict top-50% pass@1 from 18.0% to 31.3%; CWM 32B from 30.7% to 50.4%. At stricter percentiles (top-30%), CWM 32B sees 125% relative improvement. Under degraded sandbox conditions, robust optimization RL achieves 100–200% improvement over standard RLVR. On LCB, CWM 32B wins up to 83% of median-sample speed comparisons and reaches ~14% complexity-class improvement rate versus 28% for fastest human submissions.
AI.conclusion: Execution time can be made a learnable signal for RL-based code optimization through careful attention to testing infrastructure, reward design, and training stability. The proposed approach yields substantial and robust speed improvements without sacrificing correctness, narrowing the gap toward human-level code optimization.

title: TRWH: A Text-Driven Random Walk Heterogeneous GNN for Semantic-Aware Sparse Recommendation
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Large Language Models (LLMs) have each advanced recommendation systems by modeling structural and semantic signals, respectively. However, integrating their complementary strengths remains challenging, particularly in sparse settings where maintaining semantic precision is critical. We propose TRWH (Text-driven Random Walk Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network), a novel framework that fuses LLM-generated textual profiles with heterogeneous graph structures through strategic random walk augmentation. TRWH consists of three core components: (1) Embedding Creation, which produces user and item representations using both Word2Vec and LLM-based profiling; (2) a Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network (HeteroGNN) that propagates information across multi-relational edges; and (3) Random Walk-based Path Construction, which enriches sparse graphs with second-order user-user and item-item links. Experiments on the Amazon-2023 Fashion (2M users, 825K items) and Beauty (631K users, 112K items) datasets demonstrate that TRWH achieves substantial performance gains over state-of-the-art methods, including 80.0% RMSE and 52.6% MAE reductions on Fashion, and 25.7% and 10.8% improvements on Beauty. Notably, while random walks improve performance with traditional embeddings, they can dilute the nuanced representations learned by LLMs, underscoring the importance of adaptive integration strategies.

AI.tldr: TRWH is a recommendation framework that integrates LLM-generated textual profiles with heterogeneous GNNs via random walk augmentation. It achieves substantial performance gains on sparse Amazon datasets but reveals that random walks can dilute LLM representations, necessitating adaptive integration.
AI.motivation: GNNs and LLMs each bring complementary strengths to recommendation — structural and semantic modeling, respectively — but integrating them is challenging, especially in sparse data settings where semantic precision is critical and existing methods fail to effectively fuse these heterogeneous signals.
AI.method: TRWH comprises three components: (1) Embedding Creation using Word2Vec and LLM-based user/item profiling; (2) a Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network (HeteroGNN) for multi-relational message passing; and (3) Random Walk-based Path Construction that injects second-order user-user and item-item links to enrich sparse graphs.
AI.result: On Amazon-2023 Fashion (2M users, 825K items), TRWH achieves 80.0% RMSE reduction and 52.6% MAE reduction. On Beauty (631K users, 112K items), it yields 25.7% and 10.8% improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. Random walks improve performance with traditional embeddings but degrade LLM-derived representations.
AI.conclusion: Fusing LLM semantics with heterogeneous GNN structures via random walks yields significant gains in sparse recommendation, but naive augmentation can harm LLM representations. Adaptive integration strategies are essential for preserving semantic precision.

title: Generator-Aligned Representation Interfaces for Diagnostic Soft Equivariance
summary: Exact-equivariant architectures typically encode prescribed group actions in specialized operators, which can complicate their reuse with generic backbones and across data modalities. We introduce the Generator-Aligned Representation Interface (GARI), a representation-level design principle that exposes selected transformation generators to a generic sequence backbone through aligned canonical and generator-induced views. We formalize the resulting behavior using a probe-specific soft-equivariance residual defined over declared data and transformation distributions. This framework distinguishes representation consistency from task robustness and exact equivariance, and localizes residual mismatch to interface construction, shared stream processing, and terminal fusion. We instantiate the interface as GARI-Net, which constructs generator-indexed streams, converts them into a common interaction frame, processes them with shared parameters, repairs ordering-induced context mismatch, enables cross-stream information exchange, and aggregates them using inter-stream discrepancy. Direct Equivariance Error (DEE) provides a frozen-checkpoint diagnostic of the prescribed representation relation under known token or voxel actions. Experiments on genomic sequences, images, and three-dimensional point clouds examine sequence reversal, planar rotations and reflections, and controlled axial transfer. Across these settings, the same interface principle supports task-relevant transformation consistency and generalization to declared held-out probes without requiring group-specific redesign of the sequence backbone. GARI therefore provides a portable diagnostic complement to hard-equivariant architectures: it makes generator structure accessible, learnable, and measurable, while finite-probe evidence remains distinct from certification of exact equivariance over a continuous group.

AI.tldr: GARI introduces a representation-level design principle that aligns canonical and generator-induced views of data for a generic sequence backbone, enabling measurable, learnable transformation consistency without group-specific architectural redesign. It is validated across genomic sequences, images, and 3D point clouds.
AI.motivation: Exact-equivariant architectures embed group actions into specialized operators, hindering reuse across generic backbones and diverse data modalities. The authors seek a portable, representation-level alternative that exposes transformation generators to generic sequence models without requiring group-specific redesign.
AI.method: The Generator-Aligned Representation Interface (GARI) creates generator-indexed streams, converts them into a common interaction frame, processes them with shared parameters, repairs ordering-induced context mismatch, enables cross-stream information exchange, and aggregates via inter-stream discrepancy. A soft-equivariance residual is formalized over declared data and transformation distributions. GARI-Net instantiates this interface, and Direct Equivariance Error (DEE) serves as a frozen-checkpoint diagnostic for prescribed representation relations.
AI.result: Experiments on genomic sequences (sequence reversal), images (planar rotations and reflections), and 3D point clouds (controlled axial transfer) show that GARI supports task-relevant transformation consistency and generalization to held-out probes without group-specific backbone redesign.
AI.conclusion: GARI provides a portable diagnostic complement to hard-equivariant architectures by making generator structure accessible, learnable, and measurable, while acknowledging that finite-probe evidence remains distinct from certification of exact equivariance over continuous groups.

title: Balancing multiscale similarity and cartographic constraints: A similarity-driven optimization framework for line generalization
comment: Submitted to Cartography and Geographic Information Science
summary: Cartographic generalization is essential for generating multiscale map representations by balancing information preservation and cartographic readability. However, automated generalization remains challenging because existing approaches often treat spatial similarity evaluation, cartographic constraints, and parameter optimization as separate processes, limiting adaptive and interpretable control across scales. This study formulates cartographic generalization as a constrained multiscale similarity optimization problem and proposes a similarity-driven framework for adaptive generalization control. The framework integrates multiscale spatial similarity as an optimization objective to quantify representation consistency between original and generalized data, while incorporating cartographic constraints to regulate readability, smoothness, and geometric validity. A unified objective function is optimized to automatically identify scale-dependent parameter configurations for different generalization algorithms. Experiments using multiple line simplification algorithms, target scales, and similarity measures, including geometric, structural, and learning-based metrics, demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves an effective balance between similarity preservation and cartographic abstraction. The results further show that combining similarity optimization with cartographic constraints provides more consistent and interpretable parameter control than relying on similarity evaluation alone. This study provides a unified optimization perspective that connects similarity assessment, constraint modeling, and algorithm control, contributing to adaptive and automated cartographic generalization.

AI.tldr: This paper frames cartographic generalization as a constrained multiscale similarity optimization problem, proposing a unified framework that jointly optimizes spatial similarity preservation and cartographic constraints to automatically determine scale-dependent parameters for generalization algorithms.
AI.motivation: Existing automated cartographic generalization approaches treat spatial similarity evaluation, cartographic constraints, and parameter optimization as separate, disconnected processes, which limits adaptive, interpretable, and consistent control across multiple scales.
AI.method: A similarity-driven framework is proposed that integrates multiscale spatial similarity (geometric, structural, and learning-based metrics) as an optimization objective and cartographic constraints (readability, smoothness, geometric validity) as regularization terms into a unified objective function, which is then optimized to automatically derive scale-dependent parameter configurations for generalization algorithms.
AI.result: Experiments with multiple line simplification algorithms, target scales, and similarity measures show the framework achieves an effective balance between similarity preservation and cartographic abstraction. Combining similarity optimization with cartographic constraints yields more consistent and interpretable parameter control than similarity evaluation alone.
AI.conclusion: The study contributes a unified optimization perspective that bridges similarity assessment, constraint modeling, and algorithm control, advancing adaptive and automated cartographic generalization.

title: Empirical Evaluation of Out-Of-Distribution Performance of Tabular Foundation Models
summary: Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) have emerged as novel approaches for tabular predictive tasks, demonstrating competitive predictive performance to ensemble tree-based models. Most TFMs are trained and evaluated on independent and identically distributed data, but this assumption changes in real-world scenarios due to distribution shifts, which compromise the robustness of models. Limited research has been conducted of TFMs under distribution shifts. We present an empirical evaluation of Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) performance of nine TFMs, spanning diverse pre-training strategies and architectures: TabPFNv2, TabPFNv2.5, TabPFNv2.6, TabPFNv3, TabICL, TabICLv2, Mitra, LimiX and TabFM. Three real-world datasets from the TableShift study were considered (HELOC, Voting, Childhood Lead), covering label, socioeconomic, and geographic shift types. Our results show that all evaluated TFMs degrade systematically under distribution shift regardless of pre-training strategy, with shift gaps ranging from 0.003 to 0.060 depending on shift type. The relationship between in-distribution and OOD predictive performance documented for classical tabular models extends into TFMs. We also identified a scalability gap, as high-performing models demand significant memory and computational resources beyond what standard deployment infrastructure can support. This study extends existing benchmarks for OOD in tabular data, providing evidence to support their adoption in high-stakes domains characterized by structural distribution shifts.

AI.tldr: An empirical study evaluating nine Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) on three real-world datasets under distribution shift, revealing systematic performance degradation, scalability gaps, and a consistent in-distribution to OOD performance relationship.
AI.motivation: Most TFMs are trained and evaluated on i.i.d. data, but real-world deployment involves distribution shifts. Limited research exists on TFM robustness under such shifts, particularly in high-stakes domains.
AI.method: Empirical evaluation of nine TFMs (TabPFNv2/v2.5/v2.6/v3, TabICL/v2, Mitra, LimiX, TabFM) spanning diverse pre-training strategies and architectures on three TableShift datasets (HELOC, Voting, Childhood Lead) covering label, socioeconomic, and geographic shift types.
AI.result: All evaluated TFMs degraded systematically under distribution shift regardless of pre-training strategy, with shift gaps of 0.003–0.060 depending on shift type. The in-distribution vs. OOD performance relationship documented for classical models also holds for TFMs. High-performing models demand prohibitive memory and computational resources.
AI.conclusion: The study extends OOD benchmarks for tabular data, providing evidence to inform TFM adoption in high-stakes domains with structural distribution shifts, while highlighting scalability challenges for deployment.

title: Finding Optimal Cost-Bounded Plan Reductions: Refined Model
comment: Extended version of a paper accepted at ICAPS 2026 (doi: 10.1609/icaps.v36i1.42849). Includes a new model and expanded experimental results
summary: In some real applications a plan may later become unfeasible due to newly imposed budget constraints, yet, at the same time, using only the original actions of the plan and their order is mandatory. In this paper, we study the problem of extracting, from a precomputed plan, a valid subplan that maximizes utility while respecting a cost bound. Each goal is given a utility value and the plan is reduced by removing actions that support low-utility goals, while preserving both executability and the original action order. We show the decision variant is NP-complete and propose two exact methods to solve it: one via oversubscription planning (OSP) and another via Integer Linear Programming (ILP). This paper extends our previous work published at ICAPS 2026 (Del Toro, Fuentetaja, and García-Olaya 2026b). While the core framework remains as introduced there, we further introduce a refined ILP formulation that significantly decreases the model size and improves computational efficiency.

AI.tldr: Given a precomputed plan with associated goal utilities and a newly imposed budget constraint, the paper addresses how to extract a maximal-utility valid subplan that preserves original action order and executability. The problem is shown NP-complete, and two exact solution methods—oversubscription planning (OSP) and Integer Linear Programming (ILP)—are proposed, with a refined ILP formulation that reduces model size and improves efficiency over prior work.
AI.motivation: In real-world applications, a previously feasible plan may become infeasible due to newly imposed budget constraints, yet the set of available actions and their original ordering must be preserved. The need to selectively remove actions supporting low-utility goals while maintaining plan validity motivates this study of utility-maximizing plan reduction under a cost bound.
AI.method: The authors first prove the decision variant is NP-complete. They then propose two exact solution approaches: (1) a reduction to oversubscription planning (OSP), and (2) an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) formulation. A key contribution is a refined, more compact ILP encoding that reduces model size and improves computational efficiency compared to their prior ICAPS 2026 formulation.
AI.result: The decision problem is shown NP-complete. The refined ILP formulation significantly decreases model size and yields improved computational performance over the original ICAPS 2026 approach. Both the OSP and ILP methods provide exact solutions for extracting maximal-utility valid subplans under cost constraints.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully formalizes and solves the problem of utility-maximizing plan reduction under budget constraints. The refined ILP encoding represents a meaningful advance over the earlier ICAPS 2026 work, offering a more scalable exact method. The OSP-based approach provides an alternative exact solution framework.

title: A Cost-Effective Multimodal LLM Reasoning Framework for Question Answering over Irregular Clinical Time Series
summary: Question answering (QA) over irregular clinical time series (ICTS) plays a pivotal role in a wide range of healthcare applications. Although recent multimodal time-series large language models (LLMs) have shown considerable promise in general-purpose time-series QA, they remain poorly equipped to model the sparsity, asynchrony, and irregular sampling patterns of clinical observations. To fill this gap, we propose ClinPRISM, a cost-effective multimodal LLM reasoning framework for question answering over ICTS data. First, we devise an irregularity-aware multi-scale encoder to capture sparse clinical evidence at diverse temporal scales. Then, we propose a temporal evidence distiller to integrate representations across these scales and compress them into a small number of LLM-compatible tokens. Moreover, we introduce a progressive alignment strategy that sequentially aligns the irregular trajectories with the LLM's textual embedding space. To facilitate training, we construct 30,000 clinical time series paired with multi-scale descriptions, together with 41,000 instruction-tuning instances spanning 11 tasks. Using a 4-billion-parameter LLM backbone, ClinPRISM achieves state-of-the-art performance on the held-out evaluation benchmark while using only 16 time-series tokens and achieving an average inference latency of 0.15 seconds per question.

AI.tldr: ClinPRISM is a cost-efficient multimodal LLM framework for question answering over irregular clinical time series, using an irregularity-aware multi-scale encoder, a temporal evidence distiller, and progressive alignment to achieve state-of-the-art performance with only 16 tokens and 0.15s inference latency.
