AI.motivation: Existing multimodal time-series LLMs struggle with irregular clinical time series (ICTS) due to sparsity, asynchrony, and irregular sampling patterns inherent in clinical data. There is a need for a specialized framework that can effectively model these characteristics for clinical QA tasks.
AI.method: ClinPRISM proposes three key components: (1) an irregularity-aware multi-scale encoder to capture sparse clinical evidence across varied temporal resolutions; (2) a temporal evidence distiller that fuses multi-scale representations and compresses them into a small set of LLM-compatible tokens; (3) a progressive alignment strategy that sequentially maps irregular trajectories into the LLM's textual embedding space. Training data includes 30,000 clinical time series with multi-scale descriptions and 41,000 instruction-tuning instances across 11 tasks, using a 4B-parameter LLM backbone.
AI.result: ClinPRISM achieves state-of-the-art performance on a held-out evaluation benchmark while using only 16 time-series tokens and achieving an average inference latency of 0.15 seconds per question.
AI.conclusion: ClinPRISM demonstrates that cost-effective, efficient multimodal LLM reasoning over irregular clinical time series is feasible by explicitly modeling data irregularity, distilling temporal evidence into compact token representations, and progressively aligning modalities, enabling practical deployment in healthcare QA applications.

title: Sharpness-Aware Minimization and Muon: Robustness under the Spectral Norm
summary: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) aims to improve generalization by encouraging insensitivity to small, worst-case parameter perturbations. However, the notion of a "small" perturbation is inherently geometry-dependent: while existing SAM variants have explored a wide range of choices, a clear perspective on which geometries are most effective in practice remains elusive. Recent work on matrix-aware optimization, particularly the Muon optimizer, suggests that respecting the matrix structure of hidden-layer weights can lead to strong empirical performance. Motivated by this, we study matrix-aware geometry in both stages of SAM: we introduce a layerwise spectral inner perturbation for matrix-valued hidden-layer parameters and combine it with either AdamW/SGDW or Muon in the outer update. Across ImageNet-1K experiments on ViT-Small/16 and ResNet-50, we find that the combination of a spectral inner step with a Muon outer step performs consistently strongly, achieving the best validation accuracy on both models among the evaluated methods.

AI.tldr: The paper explores matrix-aware geometry in Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) by introducing a layerwise spectral inner perturbation for matrix-valued parameters, combined with Muon or AdamW/SGDW outer updates. Experiments on ImageNet-1K with ViT-Small/16 and ResNet-50 show that spectral inner perturbation paired with Muon outer update achieves the best validation accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing SAM variants explore many perturbation geometries, but no clear understanding exists of which geometries are most effective. Meanwhile, matrix-aware optimizers like Muon show strong empirical results by respecting matrix structure. This motivates studying matrix-aware geometry in both the inner (perturbation) and outer (update) stages of SAM.
AI.method: The authors propose a layerwise spectral inner perturbation for matrix-valued hidden-layer parameters in SAM's inner step. This is combined with either AdamW/SGDW or Muon for the outer update. The approach is evaluated on ImageNet-1K using ViT-Small/16 and ResNet-50 architectures.
AI.result: The combination of spectral inner perturbation with a Muon outer update consistently performs best, achieving the highest validation accuracy on both ViT-Small/16 and ResNet-50 among all evaluated methods.
AI.conclusion: Matrix-aware geometry matters in both stages of SAM. The spectral inner perturbation paired with Muon provides a robust and effective combination, suggesting that aligning the perturbation geometry with the optimizer's matrix-aware structure yields superior generalization.

title: Reinformed Dreamer: An Asymmetric World Model Efficiently Trained through Latent Guidance
summary: Much like humans benefit from guidance while learning, reinforcement learning algorithms may benefit from additional supervision beyond rewards. Leveraging additional information during training to learn better representations and behaviors has been the focus of asymmetric reinforcement learning. This learning paradigm has proven effective under partial observability when additional state information is available, but also under full observability when more refined state information is available. Focusing on model-based reinforcement learning, we study the effect of asymmetric learning on observation representations and on privileged information representations. First, we identify a limitation in the privileged information representations learned by an asymmetric model-based algorithm known as the Informed Dreamer. Then, we propose a novel asymmetric representation learning objective using latent guidance, resulting in a new algorithm called the Reinformed Dreamer. Experiments across several benchmarks show a more consistent improvement over Dreamer than previous asymmetric approaches.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a limitation in the privileged information representations of the Informed Dreamer (an asymmetric model-based RL algorithm) and proposes the Reinformed Dreamer, which uses a novel latent guidance objective to learn better representations, achieving more consistent improvements over DreamerV3 across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Asymmetric reinforcement learning leverages additional supervision beyond rewards (privileged state information) during training to improve representation learning and behavior. While effective under both partial and full observability, existing asymmetric model-based approaches like the Informed Dreamer suffer from limitations in how they learn privileged information representations, motivating the need for a better representation learning objective.
AI.method: The authors first analyze the Informed Dreamer and identify a weakness in its privileged information representations. They then propose the **Reinformed Dreamer**, which introduces a novel asymmetric representation learning objective based on **latent guidance**. This objective improves how the model leverages privileged information during training to shape both observation representations and world-model learning.
AI.result: Experiments across several benchmarks demonstrate that the Reinformed Dreamer achieves more consistent improvement over the DreamerV3 baseline compared to previous asymmetric approaches, including the Informed Dreamer.
AI.conclusion: Latent guidance is an effective mechanism for asymmetric representation learning in model-based RL. The Reinformed Dreamer addresses the representational shortcomings of prior work and provides more robust performance gains from privileged information across diverse environments.

title: CoTinyVLA: Chain-of-Thought Distillation for a Sub-Billion-Parameter Vision-Language-Action Model
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models translate natural-language commands into robot action sequences, but leading systems on the LIBERO-Plus robustness benchmark use three- to seven-billion-parameter backbones whose memory demands can exceed embedded robotic budgets. We present CoTinyVLA, a 0.9B-parameter action model on a Qwen3.5-0.8B backbone that obtains that robustness by structuring supervision instead of enlarging the model. Three components target different axes of the problem: dual-view temporal input of 16 history frames per step with textual camera and time markers; hierarchical chain-of-thought (CoT) distillation from a 35B teacher into an episode-level Plan and a chunk-level Think span over task phase, gripper state and next subaction; and paraphrase augmentation expanding 40 base commands into 800 variants. On LIBERO-Plus, spanning 10,030 perturbed tasks across seven perturbation dimensions, CoTinyVLA reaches 90.8% on Spatial, 87.3% on Object, 86.6% on Goal and 80.7% on Long, leading the strongest 7B baseline on all four suites by 4.7, 2.8, 15.9 and 3.0 points, with every margin interval excluding zero. The gains concentrate on the hardest axes of the benchmark: across the eleven published baselines none exceeds 53.2% on Robot Initial States in any suite, whereas CoTinyVLA reaches 73.6% on Goal against 39.9% for the strongest baseline. Ablations show the three components to be separable by perturbation axis, and at a matched image budget how frames are divided between the two cameras and across time accounts for 8.6 points on its own. Closed-loop inference peaks at 2.25 GiB of allocated GPU memory, and paired interventions show the episode Plan to be load-bearing: replacing it with an empty or contradictory span costs 40 to 45 points of success. Structured supervision thus lets a 0.9B backbone exceed all of them. Code: https://github.com/BrainJellyPie/CoTinyVLA

AI.tldr: CoTinyVLA is a 0.9B-parameter vision-language-action model that achieves state-of-the-art robustness on LIBERO-Plus through structured supervision (dual-view temporal input, hierarchical chain-of-thought distillation, and paraphrase augmentation) rather than scaling model size, outperforming 7B baselines while using only ~2.25 GiB GPU memory.
AI.motivation: Leading VLA models for robot manipulation require 3–7B parameter backbones whose memory demands exceed what can be deployed on embedded robotic hardware. The authors investigate whether structured supervision can match or exceed the robustness of large models without scaling parameters.
AI.method: Three components: (1) Dual-view temporal input — 16 history frames per step from two cameras with textual camera/time markers; (2) Hierarchical chain-of-thought distillation — a 35B teacher distills into an episode-level "Plan" and chunk-level "Think" span covering task phase, gripper state, and next subaction; (3) Paraphrase augmentation — expanding 40 base commands into 800 variants. The backbone is Qwen3.5-0.8B.
AI.result: On LIBERO-Plus (10,030 tasks across 7 perturbation dimensions): Spatial 90.8%, Object 87.3%, Goal 86.6%, Long 80.7% — exceeding the strongest 7B baseline by 4.7, 2.8, 15.9, and 3.0 points respectively. On Robot Initial States (hardest axis), reaches 73.6% vs. 39.9% for the best baseline. Ablations show frame allocation across cameras/time accounts for 8.6 points alone; replacing the episode Plan costs 40–45 points.
AI.conclusion: Structured supervision enables a 0.9B model to surpass all larger baselines on LIBERO-Plus, with the episode-level Plan being load-bearing. The approach decouples robustness from parameter count, making deployment on memory-constrained embedded systems feasible.

title: Re-thinking Mammography Transfer Learning: The Dataset-Informed Transfer Learning (DITL) Framework for Breast Cancer Screening and Lesion Diagnosis
comment: 16 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Accepted and presented at the 10th International Conference on Computer Vision & Image Processing (CVIP 2025), IIT Ropar, India, 10-13 December 2025. The paper is currently in press for inclusion in the official conference proceedings. This preprint corresponds to the submitted manuscript and is made available pending publication of the final proceedings version
summary: Enhancing classification performance in mammography remains a persistent challenge across both small curated datasets and large-scale clinical cohorts. Conventional transfer learning approaches often neglect dataset-specific characteristics, while recent neighborhood-informed methods have been restricted to narrow tasks with rigid formulations, limiting their scalability to population-level datasets. To address these challenges, we propose the Dataset-Informed Transfer Learning (DITL) framework, which integrates dataset-derived difficulty signals with neighborhood-based triplet supervision in a unified objective. DITL introduces two adaptive components: (i) Adaptive Difficulty-Weighted Cross-Entropy (A-DWCE), which assigns per-sample weights based on k-nearest neighbor label purity in a self-supervised feature space, and (ii) Adaptive Neighborhood Representation Triplet (A-NR-Triplet), which enforces intra-class compactness and inter-class separation using a learnable margin. Unlike focal loss, DITL requires no hyperparameter tuning, removes heuristic weighting and fixed margins, and incurs negligible computational overhead, yielding a robust and scalable optimization strategy. On the large-scale VinDR-Mammo dataset, DITL achieves state-of-the-art performance for whole-image breast density classification, with significant improvements across accuracy, F1-score, and AUC (p < 0.0001). Beyond large cohorts, DITL also delivers consistent, statistically significant gains on small ROI datasets (p < 0.0001). By bridging small-scale lesion analysis with large-scale density estimation, DITL establishes a clinically relevant, scalable, and generalizable framework for mammography classification, spanning the full breast cancer screening-to-diagnosis spectrum.

AI.tldr: DITL is a transfer learning framework that uses dataset-informed difficulty weighting and adaptive neighborhood triplet loss to improve mammography classification across both small and large-scale datasets, achieving SOTA on VinDR-Mammo with no hyperparameter tuning.
AI.motivation: Conventional transfer learning ignores dataset-specific characteristics, and existing neighborhood-informed methods are limited to narrow tasks with rigid formulations that don't scale to population-level clinical datasets. There is a need for a unified, scalable approach that adapts to dataset difficulty without requiring manual hyperparameter tuning.
AI.method: DITL introduces two components: (1) Adaptive Difficulty-Weighted Cross-Entropy (A-DWCE), which weights samples by k-NN label purity in a self-supervised feature space; (2) Adaptive Neighborhood Representation Triplet (A-NR-Triplet), which uses a learnable margin to enforce intra-class compactness and inter-class separation. The framework requires no hyperparameter tuning, removes heuristic weighting and fixed margins, and adds negligible computational cost.
AI.result: On VinDR-Mammo, DITL achieves SOTA for whole-image breast density classification with significant improvements in accuracy, F1-score, and AUC (p < 0.0001). It also yields statistically significant gains on small ROI datasets (p < 0.0001).
AI.conclusion: DITL bridges small-scale lesion analysis with large-scale density estimation, establishing a clinically relevant, scalable, and generalizable framework that spans the full breast cancer screening-to-diagnosis spectrum.

title: Are the High-weight Neurons the Important Ones in Image Classification Neural Networks?
summary: As neural network models for image classification advance, neurons play critical roles in pruning, backdoor defense, and interpretability. Yet existing work lacks clarity on the weight-importance relationship. We address this with a neuron importance assessment method using three experiments: quantifying overlap between high-weight and accuracy-impacting neurons, analyzing high-weight neuron perturbation effects, and testing post-retraining accuracy after high-weight neuron ablation. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and Mini-ImageNet reveal key patterns. Overlap analysis shows top 10\% high-weight neurons overlap with important ones by only about 25\% at maximum, dropping further in subsequent intervals. Perturbation tests find top 10\% high-weight neurons cause 45-80\% accuracy degradation under certain operations compared to 3-7\% for random perturbations, but a third of them show minimal impact. Ablation-retraining results show removing top 10\% high-weight neurons leaves accuracy 10-20\% below baseline with no recovery, while ablating top 0.1\% allows near-full recovery. Notably, some low-weight intervals show 10-17\% degradation when perturbed, comparable to mid-range high-weight neurons. These results confirm not all high-weight neurons are important: their importance is nonlinear. Low-weight neurons also contribute significantly. This challenges weight-importance equivalence, offering refined neuron role insights. It supports applications like encryption prioritizing critical high-weight neurons and pruning removing non-critical ones, advancing neural network analysis.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the assumption that high-weight neurons are inherently important. Through three experiments on CIFAR-10 and Mini-ImageNet, the authors show only ~25% overlap between top high-weight and truly important neurons, nonlinear importance distributions, and significant contributions from low-weight neurons.
AI.motivation: Existing work in neural network pruning, backdoor defense, and interpretability lacks a clear understanding of the relationship between neuron weight magnitude and functional importance. The paper aims to systematically investigate whether high-weight neurons are genuinely the most critical, or whether this weight-importance equivalence is a flawed assumption.
AI.method: A three-pronged experimental framework: (1) overlap quantification between high-weight neurons and neurons whose perturbation most impacts accuracy; (2) perturbation analysis measuring accuracy degradation when high-weight vs. random neurons are disrupted under various operations; (3) ablation-retraining experiments assessing whether models recover after removing high-weight neurons at different percentiles (top 0.1% to top 10%).
AI.result: Top 10% high-weight neurons overlap with truly important neurons by at most ~25%, declining in subsequent intervals. Perturbing top 10% high-weight neurons degrades accuracy by 45–80% (vs. 3–7% for random), yet one-third show minimal impact. Ablating top 10% high-weight neurons leaves accuracy 10–20% below baseline with no recovery; ablating only top 0.1% allows near-full recovery. Certain low-weight intervals show 10–17% degradation, comparable to mid-range high-weight neurons.
AI.conclusion: Neuron importance is nonlinear with respect to weight magnitude: not all high-weight neurons are critical, and some low-weight neurons contribute significantly. This refutes the weight-importance equivalence assumption and offers refined insights for applications such as selective encryption of critical neurons and more informed pruning strategies.

title: Spend Experts Where You Are Unsure: Confidence-Adaptive Routing for Mixture-of-Experts LoRA
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) variants of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) route every token to a fixed number of experts $k$. Tokens differ in how uncertain the model is about them, so a single k over-spends on easy tokens and under-serves hard ones. We observe that the router's output distribution is already a per-token uncertainty signal: peaked mass indicates confidence, while a flat distribution indicates ambiguity. We introduce CARE (Confidence-Adaptive Routing of Experts), which admits experts in a nucleus fashion. Experts are activated in decreasing router weight until their cumulative mass reaches a threshold, with a small extension when the admitted experts disagree. A budget thermostat calibrates the threshold so that the average number of active experts matches any target. CARE is a drop-in, single-forward-pass rule with no extra parameters. Across eight commonsense benchmarks on LLaMA-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B, as well as math, code, and knowledge tasks, CARE improves over fixed top-k MoE-LoRA at matched compute and matches the fixed-k=4 baseline while activating fewer experts. The same confidence and disagreement signals also improve out-of-distribution detection over MSP, entropy, and multi-pass proxies. We support the design with nucleus fidelity, budget optimality, and an epistemic reading of disagreement, and we release code.

AI.tldr: CARE introduces confidence-adaptive expert routing for MoE-LoRA, activating experts dynamically per token based on router confidence rather than a fixed top-k, improving efficiency and performance across diverse benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Fixed top-k routing in MoE-LoRA wastes computation on easy tokens (where the model is confident) and under-serves hard tokens (where the model is uncertain). The router's output distribution already encodes per-token uncertainty, but existing methods ignore this signal.
AI.method: CARE activates experts in a nucleus-style fashion: experts are selected in decreasing router weight order until cumulative probability mass reaches a calibrated threshold. A disagreement-based extension activates additional experts when admitted ones conflict. A budget thermostat adjusts the threshold dynamically so average active experts match a target compute budget. The method requires no extra parameters and operates in a single forward pass.
AI.result: On LLaMA-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B across 8 commonsense benchmarks plus math, code, and knowledge tasks, CARE outperforms fixed top-k MoE-LoRA at matched compute and matches the k=4 baseline while using fewer experts. The same confidence/disagreement signals also improve OOD detection over MSP, entropy, and multi-pass baselines.
AI.conclusion: Per-token confidence-adaptive routing is a simple, parameter-free upgrade over fixed top-k MoE-LoRA, supported by theoretical justifications of nucleus fidelity, budget optimality, and an epistemic interpretation of expert disagreement.

title: Entangled by Design: Spurious Intra-Variable Signal Routing in Tabular In-Context Learners
summary: Consider a model trained at a single hospital to predict patient recovery, where the measured feature $X$ bundles the patient's true health signal ($C$) with a systematic artefact from that hospital's equipment ($S$). Within that hospital, the artefact correlates with outcomes through unmeasured confounders such as patient demographics; an in-context learner rationally routes predictions through $S$, not $C$, and fails silently when deployed at a new hospital with different equipment. We formalise this as \emph{spurious routing in composite representations}: when a feature $X = [C;\,αS;\,η]$ encodes a causal signal $C$ and a spurious signal $S$ in distinct subspaces, the ICL cannot determine which drives predictions. We prove that under ridge ICL, a linear in-context learner, this routing is unavoidable regardless of context size; TabPFN, a state-of-the-art pretrained tabular ICL model, shows qualitatively consistent behaviour empirically. We derive a closed-form characterisation, $\mathrm{CSR} \propto ρ_S/ρ_C$, confirmed at $r = 0.997$ for linear ICL and $r = 0.979$ for TabPFN. Contrary to intuition, larger context sharpens commitment to the dominant in-context signal, amplifying spurious routing by up to $1.74\times$; in the high-spurious corner, more expressive models show greater vulnerability empirically ($+2.22$ CSR gap at high entanglement). We introduce two lightweight mitigations: environment-stratified context construction and S-swap augmentation, that require only weak environment labels and no knowledge of the causal partition. S-swap reduces spurious routing by $74\%$ for linear ICL and $98.8\%$ for TabPFN, with TabPFN's causal sensitivity increasing $8.4\times$ simultaneously: the model does not become agnostic, it reroutes through the causal signal.

AI.tldr: When in-context learners (ICL) encounter composite features mixing causal and spurious signals in distinct subspaces, they inevitably route predictions through the spurious signal, silently failing under distribution shift. The authors prove this is unavoidable for linear ICL, confirm it in TabPFN, and introduce two mitigations (environment-stratified context and S-swap augmentation) that reroute predictions toward the causal signal.
AI.motivation: In-context learning models, including state-of-the-art pretrained tabular models like TabPFN, are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains (e.g., healthcare). However, when features bundle causal signals with systematic artefacts (e.g., hospital-specific equipment signatures), ICL models may rationally but silently route predictions through spurious correlations—failing catastrophically when deployed in new environments. This failure mode, termed "spurious routing in composite representations," had not been formally characterized, and no principled mitigations existed.
AI.method: The authors formalize the problem under ridge ICL (linear in-context learning) with composite features X = [C; αS; η], proving a closed-form characterization of the spurious routing ratio: CSR ∝ ρ_S / ρ_C. They validate this empirically at r = 0.997 for linear ICL and r = 0.979 for TabPFN. Two lightweight mitigations are proposed: (1) environment-stratified context construction, which balances in-context examples across environments, and (2) S-swap augmentation, which generates synthetic examples by swapping spurious components between examples from different environments. Both require only weak environment labels, not knowledge of the causal partition.
AI.result: Larger context sizes sharpen commitment to the dominant signal, amplifying spurious routing by up to 1.74×. More expressive models show greater vulnerability in high-spurious regimes (+2.22 CSR gap at high entanglement). S-swap reduces spurious routing by 74% for linear ICL and 98.8% for TabPFN, while TabPFN's causal sensitivity increases 8.4×—demonstrating the model reroutes through the causal signal rather than becoming agnostic.
AI.conclusion: Spurious routing in composite representations is a fundamental, provably unavoidable failure mode for ICL under ridge regression, and empirically extends to expressive pretrained models like TabPFN. Counterintuitively, more context and more expressive models can worsen the problem. The proposed S-swap augmentation offers a highly effective, lightweight mitigation that actively reroutes predictions through causal signals rather than merely suppressing spurious reliance.

title: From Training to Deployment: Post-Hoc Causal Feature Identification via Sensitivity Ratios
summary: Given a model that is already trained, which features does it rely on causally versus spuriously? Existing methods require access to the training procedure and cannot answer this post-hoc. We introduce the \textbf{Normalised Sensitivity Ratio~(NSR)}, a post-hoc, model-agnostic diagnostic for this question under a structured-shift regime: environments differ primarily in the mean of spurious features while the causal mechanism and causal marginals remain stable, as in multi-site clinical data or multi-batch genomics. Within this regime, causal features induce constant model sensitivity across environments while spurious features track shift. NSR formalises this as the squared coefficient of variation of per-environment sensitivity. Under a linear structural causal model (SCM) with $K\ge3$ non-degenerate environments, NSR achieves exact identification (Theorem~1). We fully characterise failure: weak shifts ($O(\varepsilon^4)$ collapse), degenerate geometry, and proxy attenuation ($O((1-α)^4)$), giving practitioners quantitative criteria for assessing whether the regime holds. Finite-sample rates are $O_p(n^{-1})$ under the null and $O_p(n^{-1/2})$ under the alternative. Experiments confirm all theoretical predictions on synthetic data (area under the ROC curve [AUROC] $= 1.000$ under conditions satisfying the regime), show consistent rankings across five model families (Kendall $τ\ge0.529$), and recover six of eight causal features on bike-sharing data (Precision@7 $= 0.75$) without modifying any trained model.

AI.tldr: NSR is a post-hoc, model-agnostic diagnostic that identifies which features a trained model relies on causally vs. spuriously by measuring the stability of per-environment sensitivity under a structured-shift regime. Under a linear SCM with ≥3 environments, it provably achieves exact identification of causal features, and experiments confirm strong performance across synthetic and real-world data.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for distinguishing causal from spurious feature reliance require access to the training procedure. The authors aim to provide a post-hoc diagnostic — applicable to any pre-trained model — that can answer this question when data comes from multiple environments where spurious features shift in mean while causal mechanisms remain stable (as in multi-site clinical or multi-batch genomics data).
AI.method: The authors introduce the Normalised Sensitivity Ratio (NSR), defined as the squared coefficient of variation of per-environment model sensitivity for a given feature. The core insight: under the structured-shift regime, causal features yield constant sensitivity across environments while spurious features track the environmental shift. Under a linear SCM with K≥3 non-degenerate environments, NSR exactly identifies causal features (Theorem 1). They characterize failure modes — weak shifts (O(ε⁴) collapse), degenerate geometry, and proxy attenuation (O((1−α)⁴)) — and derive finite-sample rates: O_p(n⁻¹) under the null and O_p(n⁻¹/²) under the alternative.
AI.result: Synthetic experiments confirm all theoretical predictions, achieving AUROC = 1.000 under regime-satisfying conditions. Across five model families, NSR yields consistent feature rankings (Kendall τ ≥ 0.529). On bike-sharing data, NSR recovers six of eight causal features (Precision@7 = 0.75) without modifying any trained model.
AI.conclusion: NSR provides a principled, computationally tractable, post-hoc diagnostic for distinguishing causal from spurious feature reliance under a structured-shift regime. Its theoretical guarantees, quantitative failure-mode criteria, and strong empirical performance make it a practical tool for model auditing in scientific and high-stakes applications where retraining is infeasible.

title: Distilling Temporal Search and Reasoning: Evolving LLMs for Future Prediction via Harness-Assisted Efficient Data Synthesis
summary: Future event prediction carries broad social impact yet remains challenging. SOTA approaches augment LLMs with external agent frameworks whose predictive capability vanishes once the harness is removed. While recent Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) internalizes deep search for multi-hop retrieval of facts, forecasting further demands temporal search and reasoning over historical trends and dynamic shifts. The key obstacle is data: historical queries induce temporal leakage that degrades forecasting into retrieval. Prior works either freeze information gathering with static observations, or rely on rejection sampling or unresolved fresh queries that discard vast amounts of data, degrading synthesis efficiency. We propose a time-truncation harness that enforces a temporal cut-off at every turn, enabling TIR-style sampling from historical events, reducing temporal leakage and reliance of rejection sampling or unsolved queries, increasing the sampling efficiency. We further build a large-scale corpus and a process-based metric and show that our harness naturally induces a broader temporal breadth of search and raises the proportion of high-quality data, further increasing the efficiency and reducing the reliance on complex rubrics. Distillation experiments show that students trained on harness-intervened data achieve the best performance, demonstrating harness-assisted model evolving that turns higher quality temporal search and reasoning data into a parametric advancement of the students.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a time-truncation harness for tool-integrated reasoning that enforces temporal cut-offs during sampling to prevent temporal leakage in forecasting tasks, enabling more efficient synthesis of high-quality training data and improving student model performance through distillation.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based forecasting approaches either rely on external agent frameworks (whose predictive ability vanishes without the harness) or suffer from temporal leakage when using historical data, which degrades the forecasting task into mere retrieval. Prior methods waste large amounts of data through rejection sampling or unresolved queries, hurting synthesis efficiency.
AI.method: The authors introduce a time-truncation harness that enforces a temporal cut-off at every turn of the sampling process. This allows TIR-style sampling from historical events while mitigating temporal leakage, reducing dependence on rejection sampling and unsolved queries. They also construct a large-scale corpus and a process-based evaluation metric.
AI.result: The harness induces broader temporal breadth of search and increases the proportion of high-quality data, improving sampling efficiency and reducing reliance on complex rubrics. Distillation experiments demonstrate that student models trained on harness-intervened data achieve the best performance, showing harness-assisted parametric advancement.
AI.conclusion: The time-truncation harness effectively transforms higher-quality temporal search and reasoning data into parametric improvements in student models, enabling a harness-assisted model evolution paradigm for future event prediction.

title: Agent Skills Matter: Inferring Proprietary Skills from Execution Trajectories
summary: Agent skills package reusable procedures that improve downstream performance. Their lightweight, portable form enables marketplace monetization and private deployment behind cloud-hosted agent interfaces, giving providers incentives to keep high-value skills proprietary. Yet hiding the artifacts does not conceal their behavioral effects, which remain observable in execution trajectories and form a behavioral side channel. We define this exposure as Skill Leakage: reconstructing proprietary skills from trajectories elicited by benign queries, without reference answers or success labels. We introduce SigLeak, a black-box framework that exploits recurring skill signatures in agent behavior. It constructs diverse, decision-rich diagnostic tasks, contrasts matched skill-enabled and skill-disabled trajectories, and iteratively refines a reconstructed skill from the isolated patterns. Across five scenarios, three model families, and three agent frameworks, SigLeak outperforms or matches three baselines in nearly every setting. It raises the success rate by 6.88 percentage points over the skill-disabled reference on average and achieves the highest overall SkillSim, our metric for coarse- and fine-grained semantic similarity. These results show that benign execution trajectories can expose proprietary procedural knowledge. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SigLeak-D1DB.

AI.tldr: Agent skills are proprietary reusable procedures whose behavioral effects leak through execution trajectories, forming a side channel. The authors define "Skill Leakage" and propose SigLeak, a black-box framework that reconstructs proprietary skills by exploiting recurring behavioral signatures — without needing reference answers or success labels — and demonstrate its effectiveness across diverse settings.
AI.motivation: Agent skills are valuable proprietary assets that providers may hide behind cloud interfaces. However, even when artifacts are concealed, skill behaviors remain observable in execution trajectories, creating a behavioral side channel. The key insight is that this exposure enables adversarial reconstruction of proprietary procedural knowledge from benign queries alone, a threat not previously formalized or systematically studied.
AI.method: SigLeak operates via three stages: (1) constructing diverse, decision-rich diagnostic tasks designed to elicit distinctive skill behaviors; (2) contrasting matched trajectories from skill-enabled and skill-disabled agent runs to isolate skill-specific behavioral patterns; and (3) iteratively refining a reconstructed skill from these isolated signatures. It is fully black-box, requiring no reference answers, success labels, or access to model internals. The authors also introduce SkillSim, a metric capturing both coarse- and fine-grained semantic similarity for evaluation.
AI.result: Across five scenarios, three model families, and three agent frameworks, SigLeak outperformed or matched three baselines in nearly every setting. It raised the success rate by 6.88 percentage points over the skill-disabled reference on average and achieved the highest overall SkillSim scores. The results confirm that benign execution trajectories reliably expose proprietary procedural knowledge.
AI.conclusion: Skill Leakage is a real and measurable threat: proprietary agent skills can be reconstructed from observable execution traces without privileged access. SigLeak demonstrates the feasibility and effectiveness of such reconstruction, underscoring the need for defenses against behavioral side channels in agent marketplaces and cloud-hosted agent deployments.

title: Matrix-Free Photoacoustic Image Reconstruction via Sensor-Token Self-Attention
summary: Photoacoustic tomography (PAT) combines the optical absorption contrast of biological tissue with the spatial resolution of ultrasound, yet recovering the initial pressure distribution from sparse-view sensor measurements remains an ill-posed inverse problem. Iterative compressive-sensing solvers and unrolled deep networks both retain a dependence on the system matrix at inference, which leaves real-time clinical reconstruction computationally expensive. This paper proposes the Sensor Attention Network (SAN), a Transformer-based architecture that treats the full time series of each sensor as a token and maps raw measurements directly to the reconstructed image without invoking the system matrix at inference. For training and benchmarking, an analytical k-space H-matrix is constructed and validated against the k-Wave pseudo-spectral solver under matched geometry, achieving a mean per-sensor Pearson correlation of 0.919 +/- 0.049, with k-space apodization and Gaussian temporal damping acting synergistically to reduce the energy-normalized mismatch by 49%. Trained with a vessel-weighted loss on 488 augmented samples and evaluated on 46 held-out samples against ISTA, split-Bregman total variation (SBTV), and learned ISTA (LISTA), SAN attains the highest mean SSIM (0.522) and PSNR (22.09 dB) and the lowest NMSE (0.233). Paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests confirm the superiority of SAN over LISTA on PSNR, NMSE, and Pearson correlation at p < 1e-8, and over ISTA and SBTV on all fidelity metrics. By bypassing the H-matrix at inference, SAN reduces reconstruction time by at least an order of magnitude, supporting real-time PAT reconstruction.

AI.tldr: SAN, a Transformer-based architecture for photoacoustic tomography, maps raw sensor measurements directly to reconstructed images without requiring the system matrix at inference. It outperforms ISTA, SBTV, and LISTA on SSIM, PSNR, and NMSE while reducing reconstruction time by at least an order of magnitude, enabling real-time clinical PAT.
AI.motivation: Recovering initial pressure distributions from sparse-view PAT sensor measurements is ill-posed. Existing methods (iterative compressive-sensing solvers and unrolled deep networks like LISTA) depend on the system matrix at inference, making real-time clinical reconstruction computationally expensive. A method that bypasses this matrix is needed.
AI.method: The authors propose the Sensor Attention Network (SAN), a Transformer architecture that treats each sensor's full time series as a token, mapping raw measurements directly to reconstructed images without the system matrix at inference. They also construct an analytical k-space H-matrix (validated against k-Wave, achieving 0.919±0.049 Pearson correlation) and apply k-space apodization with Gaussian temporal damping to reduce mismatch by 49%. Training uses a vessel-weighted loss on 488 augmented samples.
AI.result: SAN achieves the highest mean SSIM (0.522), PSNR (22.09 dB), and lowest NMSE (0.233) among all methods. Paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests confirm SAN's superiority over LISTA (p < 1e-8 on PSNR, NMSE, Pearson correlation) and over ISTA/SBTV on all fidelity metrics. Reconstruction time is reduced by at least one order of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: SAN bypasses the system matrix at inference, achieving both state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity and an order-of-magnitude speedup, making real-time PAT reconstruction feasible for clinical applications.

title: How Small Can You Go? A Controlled Study of LoRA Rank, Target Modules, and Quantization Trade-offs for Text-to-SQL on a 60M-Parameter Model
summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) and low-bit quantization are now standard tools for adapting language models under tight compute budgets, yet their interaction is most often studied on billion-parameter models where the design space is expensive to explore. We ask a complementary question: on a specific, fully reproducible 60M-parameter encoder-decoder model (T5-small) and a single-table text-to-SQL benchmark (WikiSQL), how much task accuracy does each efficiency knob actually cost? We run a controlled, single-variable study over (i) LoRA rank r in {2, 4, 8, 16, 32}, (ii) the set of adapted modules, and (iii) numerical precision. We report task accuracy alongside system-level metrics including trainable parameters, peak training memory, inference latency, and throughput, and frame adaptation as a constrained trade-off rather than an accuracy-only objective. Our results show that LoRA with r=16 recovers within 11.6 percentage points of full fine-tuning accuracy (59.6% vs. 71.2% exact-match) while training fewer than 1% of parameters and consuming 31% less peak GPU memory. Within this setting, rank beyond r=16 yields no measurable accuracy gain. QLoRA with INT8 and NF4 quantization achieves comparable accuracy (52.8% and 53.2%) at dramatically lower memory cost (0.60 GB each), demonstrating a compelling trade-off for memory-constrained deployments. All code, configurations, and logs are released for full reproducibility.

AI.tldr: A controlled study on T5-small (60M params) for text-to-SQL (WikiSQL) systematically measures the accuracy–efficiency trade-offs of LoRA rank, module selection, and quantization (INT8/NF4). LoRA r=16 recovers most accuracy at <1% trainable parameters and 31% less peak GPU memory; QLoRA variants achieve comparable accuracy at dramatically lower memory (0.60 GB).
AI.motivation: Existing PEFT–quantization interaction studies focus on billion-parameter models where design-space exploration is prohibitively expensive. The authors instead investigate a small, fully reproducible setting (60M-param T5-small on WikiSQL) to precisely quantify the accuracy cost of each efficiency intervention in isolation, enabling practitioners to make informed, constrained trade-off decisions rather than optimizing accuracy alone.
AI.method: A single-variable controlled experiment on T5-small with the WikiSQL text-to-SQL benchmark, varying: (i) LoRA rank r ∈ {2,4,8,16,32}; (ii) the set of modules adapted (attention and/or feed-forward layers); and (iii) numerical precision (full FP16/FP32, INT8 QLoRA, NF4 QLoRA). Metrics include exact-match accuracy, trainable parameter count, peak training memory, inference latency, and throughput.
AI.result: LoRA r=16 achieves 59.6% exact-match accuracy vs. 71.2% full fine-tuning (within 11.6 pp), using <1% trainable parameters and 31% less peak GPU memory. Ranks beyond r=16 yield no further accuracy gains. QLoRA INT8 and NF4 achieve 52.8% and 53.2% accuracy respectively at only 0.60 GB peak memory each, offering a strong memory-accuracy trade-off.
AI.conclusion: For small models in constrained settings, LoRA r=16 represents a sweet spot beyond which increasing rank gives diminishing returns. QLoRA variants provide a compelling memory-accuracy Pareto frontier. The work frames model adaptation as a constrained multi-objective trade-off problem and emphasizes full reproducibility through released code, configurations, and logs.

title: A Density-Matrix Framework for Electronic-Structure Analysis of Functional-Group and Salt Effects in Lithium-Metal Electrolytes
summary: The reactivity of lithium-metal electrolytes arises from the interplay of molecular functional groups, Li$^+$ solvation, and salt-anion participation. This interplay operates through the redistribution of electron density across donor, anion, and cation centers, which is most directly read out from the electronic structure resolved in space. Quantum-chemical calculations deliver such readouts faithfully, yet become computationally demanding across this multidimensional design space, and machine-learning electronic-structure models seldom cover chemically diverse solvation shells or electrolyte-relevant readouts. Here, we present a density-matrix-centered AI platform (EMolStudio) for electronic-structure prediction and analysis. Its workflow integrates molecular functionalization, explicit Li$^+$ first-shell assembly, density-matrix prediction with idempotency projection, and readouts of frontier orbitals, electrostatic potential, Li$^+$-donor bond order, and electron localization. We apply EMolStudio to 163,655 functionalized molecules and 22,500 explicit Li$^+$ first-shell clusters across four lithium salts. We find that 1) at the molecular scale, functionalization distinguishes CO$_2$Me, CN, F/CF$_3$, and sulfonyl groups by chemically distinct changes in frontier levels, electrostatic potential, and Li$^+$-donor contact, consistent with $π^*$-acceptor, inductive, and polarization contributions, with sublinear accumulation at higher degrees of functionalization; 2) in explicit solvation shells, anion identity reshapes frontier-orbital localization: LiTDI anchors the HOMO on the anion across the entire library, whereas LiDFOB pairs an anion-hosted HOMO with strongly functional-group-dependent LUMO hosting. EMolStudio thereby translates functional-group and salt choices into electronic-structure hypotheses relevant to lithium-bond formation, desolvation, and interphase reactions.

AI.tldr: EMolStudio, a density-matrix-centered AI platform, predicts electronic structure for Li-metal electrolytes across 163,655 functionalized molecules and 22,500 Li⁺ solvation clusters, revealing how functional groups and salt anions redistribute frontier orbitals, electrostatic potential, and bond order — translating chemical choices into hypotheses about lithium-bond formation, desolvation, and interphase reactions.
AI.motivation: Understanding Li-metal electrolyte reactivity requires resolving electronic structure across a vast multidimensional design space of functional groups, Li⁺ solvation, and salt anions. Quantum-chemical calculations are too computationally expensive for this scale, and existing machine-learning electronic-structure models fail to cover chemically diverse solvation shells or electrolyte-relevant readouts.
AI.method: The authors develop EMolStudio, a density-matrix-centered AI platform with a workflow that integrates: (1) molecular functionalization, (2) explicit Li⁺ first-shell assembly, (3) density-matrix prediction with idempotency projection, and (4) readouts of frontier orbitals, electrostatic potential, Li⁺-donor bond order, and electron localization. The platform is applied to 163,655 functionalized molecules and 22,500 explicit Li⁺ first-shell clusters spanning four lithium salts.
AI.result: Two key findings emerge: (1) At the molecular scale, functional groups (CO₂Me, CN, F/CF₃, sulfonyl) produce chemically distinct changes in frontier levels, electrostatic potential, and Li⁺-donor contact — consistent with π*-acceptor, inductive, and polarization contributions — with sublinear accumulation at higher functionalization degrees. (2) In explicit solvation shells, anion identity controls frontier-orbital localization: LiTDI anchors the HOMO on the anion across the entire library, while LiDFOB yields an anion-hosted HOMO paired with strongly functional-group-dependent LUMO hosting.
AI.conclusion: EMolStudio successfully translates functional-group and salt choices into electronic-structure hypotheses relevant to lithium-bond formation, desolvation, and interphase reactions, enabling rational electrolyte design at scale without prohibitive quantum-chemical cost.

title: Computational Extraction of Legal Causes via al-Sabr wa al-Taqsim: A Set-Theoretic Formalization for Closed Fiqh Chapters
comment: 16 pages. Published in Journal Academica, Vol. 15, No. 1, 2026, pp. 3-18. Includes an Arabic-language computational analysis of Tayammum in the Shafi'i school
summary: This paper presents a set-theoretic formalization of the classical usuli method of al-Sabr wa al-Taqsim (Examination and Division) for extracting legal causes ('ilal) within closed chapters of jurisprudence. A computational algorithm is introduced that extracts minimal operational rules from a truth table of juristic verdicts. The principal result is that, given a complete truth table for a closed chapter, the algorithm computes the minimal structural generators of the ruling and eliminates all logically redundant attributes. The resulting structures constitute admissible candidate causes for subsequent juristic evaluation. The framework is conditional upon the availability of a finite school-relative concept vocabulary and a complete ruling table for the chapter under investigation.

AI.tldr: A formal, set-theoretic model and algorithm for the classical Islamic jurisprudential method of al-Sabr wa al-Taqsim is proposed, which extracts minimal legal causes from complete truth tables of juristic rulings by eliminating redundant attributes.
AI.motivation: To provide a rigorous, computational formalization of the traditional usuli method of al-Sabr wa al-Taqsim (Examination and Division), enabling systematic extraction of legal causes ('ilal) from juristic verdicts within closed chapters of Islamic jurisprudence.
AI.method: A set-theoretic framework models juristic rulings and attributes. A computational algorithm operates on a complete truth table of verdicts for a closed chapter, computing minimal structural generators of the ruling by identifying and eliminating all logically redundant attributes, within a finite school-relative concept vocabulary.
AI.result: The algorithm computes minimal structural generators of the ruling and eliminates all logically redundant attributes. The resulting structures constitute admissible candidate causes ('ilal) for subsequent juristic evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The framework succeeds in formalizing al-Sabr wa al-Taqsim computationally, but its applicability is conditional on the availability of a finite school-relative concept vocabulary and a complete ruling table for the chapter under investigation.

title: Multi-Sensor Alignment for Weather Simulations
summary: Perception tasks for autonomous vehicles need to work satisfactorily in adverse weather conditions. Due to lack of real-world weather datasets, weather simulations are a promising alternative. To ensure simulations closely mirror real-world weather data, it's crucial that they represent the same weather characteristics, including severity and particle positioning, across different sensors. To achieve this, we propose the Reference Dataset Alignment Method (ReDAM) for weather intensity alignment in fog and Unified-weather-edit (inspired by Weather-edit[1]) for particle positioning alignment in rain and snow. We validate both alignment methods using statistical and geometrical tests, respectively. We find that 3D detection models for non-aligned versions tend to be overly optimistic as compared to aligned versions. We also show the aligned-multi-sensor simulation's effectiveness for achieving robustness for 3D object detection task by finetuning existing sensor fusion models on it.

AI.tldr: Proposes ReDAM for aligning fog intensity and Unified-weather-edit for aligning rain/snow particle positioning across multi-sensor simulations, demonstrating that non-aligned simulations produce overly optimistic 3D detection results and that aligned simulations improve model robustness via finetuning.
AI.motivation: Adverse weather conditions degrade autonomous vehicle perception, but real-world multi-sensor weather datasets are scarce. Weather simulations offer an alternative, yet existing simulations fail to ensure consistent weather characteristics (intensity and particle positioning) across different sensors (camera, LiDAR, radar), compromising the fidelity and usefulness of synthetic data for training robust perception models.
AI.method: Two alignment methods are introduced: (1) Reference Dataset Alignment Method (ReDAM) for weather intensity alignment in fog, and (2) Unified-weather-edit (inspired by Weather-edit) for particle positioning alignment in rain and snow. The methods are validated via statistical tests for intensity and geometrical tests for particle positioning. The impact is assessed by comparing 3D object detection performance on aligned vs. non-aligned multi-sensor simulations, and by finetuning sensor fusion models on aligned data.
AI.result: Non-aligned multi-sensor simulations lead to overly optimistic 3D detection model performance compared to aligned versions, indicating a significant distribution gap. Finetuning existing sensor fusion models on aligned multi-sensor simulations improves robustness for 3D object detection under adverse weather.
AI.conclusion: Multi-sensor weather simulation alignment — both in intensity (fog) and particle positioning (rain/snow) — is critical for generating realistic synthetic adverse-weather data. Aligned simulations provide a more reliable benchmark and training resource, enabling improved robustness of autonomous vehicle perception models.

title: Quotient Dynamics, Effective Curvature, and Implicit Bias in Positive Quadratic Networks
summary: Positive quadratic networks admit the low-rank representation f_U(x)=x^top UU^top x, where Uinmathbb{R}^{dtimes r} is identifiable only up to right orthogonal multiplication, representing a rank-r PSD matrix Q=UU^top. We study how this quotient structure governs training dynamics, curvature, recovery, and interpolation bias. On the full-column-rank stratum, we identify mathbb{R}^{dtimes r}_*/O(r) with the rank-r PSD manifold. For smooth objectives L(U)=ell(UU^top), the Euclidean factor gradient is horizontal. Thus, factor gradient flow projects exactly to quotient Riemannian gradient flow, while finite-step gradient descent induces an exact congruence recursion for the predictor. For quadratic regression, we derive the effective Hessian at interpolators as the empirical measurement Gram form restricted to the tangent space relative to the quotient metric. Under Gaussian rank-one measurements, we compute population curvature, prove uniform deviation bounds for the empirical normal operator, construct a spectral initializer, and establish local exponential convergence for gradient flow and linear convergence for small-step descent. Recovery guarantees are explicit but conservative due to reliance on full-space second-moment control. In underdetermined commuting regimes, factor gradient flow becomes an exact entropy mirror flow in joint spectral coordinates. Strictly positive initializations converge to Bregman projections onto the interpolation set. With isotropic initialization q(0)=varepsilon^2mathbf{1}, predictors approach the minimum-trace solution set as varepsilondownarrow0, resolving nonuniqueness via weighted entropy within the invariant joint spectral algebra. Finite-step descent selects interpolants differing from continuous-time Bregman projections by O(eta). Numerical experiments verify these quotient identities, curvature predictions, recovery behaviors, and selection laws.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes how the quotient geometry of low-rank PSD matrices (identified up to orthogonal rotation) governs training dynamics, curvature, recovery guarantees, and interpolation bias in positive quadratic networks, establishing exact correspondences between Euclidean factor gradient flow and Riemannian gradient flow on the PSD manifold.
AI.motivation: Positive quadratic networks parameterize rank-r PSD matrices via f_U(x) = xᵀUUᵀx, but U is identifiable only up to right orthogonal multiplication. Understanding how this quotient structure influences optimization dynamics, curvature, and implicit bias is essential for rigorous analysis of these models.
AI.method: The authors identify the full-column-rank stratum with the rank-r PSD manifold under the O(r) quotient, prove that Euclidean factor gradients are horizontal (projecting exactly to Riemannian gradients), derive effective Hessians via the quotient metric, and analyze gradient flow/descent under Gaussian measurements. They establish uniform deviation bounds, construct a spectral initializer, prove local convergence rates, and characterize interpolation bias under commuting regimes as exact entropy mirror flow converging to Bregman projections.
AI.result: Key results include: (1) continuous-time factor gradient flow projects exactly to quotient Riemannian gradient flow, (2) finite-step gradient descent induces an exact congruence recursion, (3) local exponential convergence for gradient flow and linear convergence for small-step descent under Gaussian rank-one measurements, (4) recovery guarantees that are explicit but conservative, (5) in commuting regimes, factor gradient flow becomes exact entropy mirror flow with strictly positive initializations converging to Bregman projections, and (6) as initialization scale ε→0, predictors approach the minimum-trace solution set.
AI.conclusion: The quotient O(r) structure fundamentally shapes every aspect of optimization in positive quadratic networks, from gradient dynamics to curvature and interpolation bias. The exact correspondences derived (gradient flow projection, congruence recursion, entropy mirror flow) provide a principled geometric framework, validated numerically, though recovery guarantees remain conservative due to reliance on full-space second-moment control.

title: Joint Text-Audio Alignment for EEG-to-Text Decoding in Chinese Speech Production and Perception
summary: Decoding speech information directly from scalp electroencephalography (EEG) into text provides a potential non-invasive neural communication pathway for individuals with severe speech and motor impairments. Compared with invasive approaches such as electrocorticography, EEG is safer and more widely deployable, yet substantially more challenging to decode.This challenge is exacerbated for Chinese sentence decoding, which must handle a high-dimensional output space with thousands of characters, severe inter-subject variability, and low signal-to-noise ratios for text alignment.Existing methods commit to a single supervisory axis---either text semantics or audio acoustic features---yet neither can simultaneously satisfy the demands of sentence-level discriminability and fine-grained temporal resolution required for large-vocabulary Chinese decoding. We introduce EEGAlign, a novel parameter-efficient framework that jointly aligns EEG with two axes---text alignment with BGE-M3 text embeddings and audio alignment with wav2vec~2.0 speech features via contrastive learning followed by CTC character-sequence decoding. On ChineseEEG-2 data, EEGAlign yields state-of-the-art closed-set sentence classification performance, reaching up to 82.37% Top-1 accuracy on Reading Aloud EEG and 41.43% on Passive Listening EEG out of 101 candidates. Ablation studies show that the two alignment axes are highly complementary: combining them yields consistently better performance than either alone. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study on decoding large-vocabulary Chinese sentences from non-invasive EEG during overt speech production, and achieving strong classification performance with relatively large closed-set candidate-sentence setting.

AI.tldr: EEGAlign is a parameter-efficient framework that jointly aligns EEG with both text semantics (BGE-M3) and audio acoustics (wav2vec 2.0) via contrastive learning and CTC decoding, achieving state-of-the-art Chinese sentence classification from non-invasive scalp EEG — up to 82.37% on Reading Aloud and 41.43% on Passive Listening tasks among 101 candidates.
AI.motivation: Decoding Chinese sentences from scalp EEG is extremely challenging due to high-dimensional output space (thousands of characters), severe inter-subject variability, and low signal-to-noise ratios. Existing methods align EEG with either text semantics or audio acoustics alone, but neither single-axis supervision simultaneously provides the sentence-level discriminability and fine-grained temporal resolution needed for large-vocabulary Chinese decoding.
AI.method: EEGAlign jointly aligns EEG signals with two complementary axes: (1) text alignment using BGE-M3 text embeddings for sentence-level semantic discriminability, and (2) audio alignment using wav2vec 2.0 speech features for fine-grained temporal resolution. The framework employs contrastive learning to learn these alignments, followed by CTC (Connectionist Temporal Classification) character-sequence decoding for final text output.
AI.result: On the ChineseEEG-2 dataset, EEGAlign achieves state-of-the-art closed-set sentence classification: 82.37% Top-1 accuracy on Reading Aloud EEG and 41.43% on Passive Listening EEG, selecting from 101 candidate sentences. Ablation studies confirm that the two alignment axes are highly complementary, with the combined approach outperforming either axis alone.
AI.conclusion: This is the first study to decode large-vocabulary Chinese sentences from non-invasive EEG during overt speech production. The dual-axis alignment strategy (text + audio) proves effective for handling the uniquely difficult challenges of Chinese EEG-to-text decoding, establishing strong classification performance in a relatively large closed-set candidate-sentence setting.

title: Engine-Equal, Human-Unequal: A Reproducible Outcome Skew in Engine-Assessed Equal Chess Positions
comment: 27 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21629354
summary: Among chess opening positions that a strong engine judges essentially equal (Stockfish 18 evaluation within 10 centipawns of zero, depth-stable) and that humans actually reach on Lichess (October 2025; 1,661 positions, 16.1M occurrences), human results are not balanced. Positions carry outcome skews, each the gap between its games' actual results and what the players' ratings predict, whose directions are stable properties of the naturally-reached position: some positions favour White, others Black. These skews reproduce across three re-partitions -- disjoint player-account sets (primary), time, and disjoint rating bands -- and on an out-of-sample month eight months later. On the primary split, each position's skew is measured once in each account group, and the replication slope asks how well one measurement predicts the other after removing rating and opening-family effects: one means undiminished carry-over; zero, no linear relation. We find 0.69 (family-clustered 95% CI [0.65, 0.74]), rising to 0.94 on the most-popular, best-measured positions. The slope's value depends on the position mix. Existence is the invariant claim: it survives every tighter evaluation band, search depth, calibration, and popularity cutoff we test, and replicates within blitz and rapid separately. The typical skew is small (median $|δ| \approx 0.018$, about two percentage points of White score), yet it reproduces, position by position, across disjoint accounts. At these positions the disfavoured side also thinks longer. Even where the evaluation is most confident, it is not a sufficient statistic for human outcomes. The result is observational, and the causal question is left to a pre-registered randomised companion study.

AI.tldr: In chess positions deemed equal by a strong engine, human game outcomes systematically deviate from rating-based predictions, and these deviations (skews) are stable, replicable properties of specific positions across disjoint player groups, time, and rating bands.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether engine-evaluated equality (Stockfish ≈ 0.00) implies balanced human results, or whether position-specific factors produce stable outcome biases that ratings alone cannot account for.
AI.method: Analyzed 1,661 opening positions (16.1M occurrences) from Lichess where Stockfish 18 evaluation is within ±10 centipawns and depth-stable. For each position, computed outcome skew (actual result minus rating-predicted result). Assessed replicability across three splits: disjoint player-account sets (primary), time, and disjoint rating bands, plus out-of-sample validation eight months later. Measured replication slope after removing rating and opening-family effects.
AI.result: Primary replication slope = 0.69 (95% CI [0.65, 0.74]), rising to 0.94 for most-popular, best-measured positions. Typical skew magnitude is small (median |δ| ≈ 0.018, ~2 pp of White score). The disfavored side thinks longer. Result survives tighter evaluation bands, depth, calibration, and popularity cutoffs; replicates within blitz and rapid separately.
AI.conclusion: Even at maximum engine confidence, the evaluation is not a sufficient statistic for human outcomes. Positions carry intrinsic, reproducible skews. Causal claims are deferred to a pre-registered randomized companion study.

title: OrchBench: Evaluating Multi-Agent Orchestration Plans in Isolation via Deterministic Simulation
summary: Complex tasks often decompose into parallelizable yet interdependent subtasks, making orchestration critical to the performance of multi-agent systems (MAS). Existing evaluations typically rely on end-to-end execution, which conflates orchestration-plan quality with worker capabilities, tool reliability, and environmental noise. Moreover, the time and token costs of real execution grow rapidly with workflow scale, making systematic evaluation expensive. We present OrchBench, a simulation-based benchmark for evaluating multi-agent orchestration plans in isolation. Starting from real-world tasks, OrchBench constructs directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) that encode task dependencies, with controlled sizes and degrees of parallelism. Given a DAG, a per-agent context limit, and an agent budget, the evaluated planner assigns subtasks to agents and specifies cross-agent information transfers and their retention ratios. A deterministic simulator evaluates the resulting plan without invoking worker agents and returns interpretable measures of result quality, makespan, and token cost. The simulated scores produced by OrchBench correlate strongly with quality scores from Claude Code executions, achieving a Pearson correlation of \(r=0.816\), while requiring only \(1.3\%\) of the tokens and \(10.3\%\) of the wall-clock time. Across diverse planners and workflow scales, we find that preserving task-critical information is more important than simply increasing the number of agents, and the benefits of parallelism diminish as coordination failures accumulate. These results establish OrchBench as an efficient and interpretable benchmark for comparing and diagnosing multi-agent orchestration plans.

AI.tldr: OrchBench is a simulation-based benchmark that evaluates multi-agent orchestration plans in isolation using DAG-based task decomposition, achieving strong correlation (r=0.816) with real execution while using only 1.3% of the tokens and 10.3% of the wall-clock time.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent system evaluations rely on end-to-end execution, which confounds orchestration-plan quality with worker capabilities, tool reliability, and environmental noise. Furthermore, real execution costs in time and tokens scale rapidly with workflow size, making systematic evaluation expensive and impractical.
AI.method: OrchBench constructs directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) from real-world tasks, encoding dependencies with controlled sizes and parallelism. Given a DAG, per-agent context limits, and an agent budget, the planner assigns subtasks to agents and specifies cross-agent information transfers with retention ratios. A deterministic simulator then evaluates the plan without invoking worker agents, producing interpretable measures of result quality, makespan, and token cost.
AI.result: Simulated scores achieved Pearson correlation r=0.816 with Claude Code execution quality scores, while using only 1.3% of tokens and 10.3% of wall-clock time. Key findings: preserving task-critical information outweighs merely increasing agent count, and parallelism benefits diminish as coordination failures accumulate.
AI.conclusion: OrchBench provides an efficient, interpretable benchmark for comparing and diagnosing multi-agent orchestration plans, decoupling planning quality from downstream execution variables.

title: CoRT: Counterfactual Replay for Token-Level Rubric-Guided Policy Optimization
summary: Rubric-based reinforcement learning enriches language model training by evaluating model outputs against explicit criteria. Yet in GRPO-style pipelines, these structured judgments are reduced to a scalar response-level reward and converted into a response-level advantage, which is broadcast uniformly to all generated tokens. This leaves no explicit mechanism for allocating credit within a response, even when different criteria are grounded in different spans, formatting decisions, or semantic choices. We propose CoRT, a token-level credit weighting method for rubric-conditioned GRPO. Instead of training an auxiliary token scoring model, CoRT uses counterfactual replay to rescore the same sampled response under the original rubric-conditioned prompt and a matched criteria-free prompt. The resulting tokenwise log-likelihood contrasts serve as a proxy for dependence on the rubric context. CoRT maps these contrasts to bounded, response-normalized weights and uses them to redistribute the signed GRPO advantage across tokens, without introducing an auxiliary scorer or changing the response-level reward. Experiments across instruction-tuned models and reward granularities show that CoRT improves over matched response-level GRPO in the vast majority of comparisons, with an average gain of 4.4 percentage points. The method remains competitive with learned token-level credit baselines while avoiding a separate relevance-learning stage. These results suggest that policy-internal counterfactual likelihood contrasts provide an effective training signal for within-response credit allocation while retaining the simplicity and stability of GRPO.

AI.tldr: CoRT introduces token-level credit weighting for rubric-conditioned GRPO by using counterfactual replay—comparing token log-likelihoods under rubric-conditioned vs. criteria-free prompts—to redistribute response-level advantages across tokens without auxiliary models, achieving ~4.4pp average improvement.
AI.motivation: In GRPO-style reinforcement learning with rubric-based rewards, structured multi-criteria judgments are collapsed into a single scalar response-level reward and broadcast uniformly to all tokens. This lacks within-response credit allocation, even when different rubric criteria correspond to different spans or token-level decisions. The authors aim to address this granularity mismatch without introducing an auxiliary token-scoring model.
AI.method: CoRT (Counterfactual Rubric Token weighting) operates within the GRPO framework. For each sampled response, it performs counterfactual replay: the same response is rescored under (1) the original rubric-conditioned prompt and (2) a matched criteria-free prompt. Token-wise log-likelihood contrasts between these two contexts serve as a proxy for each token's dependence on the rubric. These contrasts are mapped to bounded, response-normalized weights, which are then used to redistribute the signed GRPO advantage across tokens—no auxiliary scorer or separate training stage is needed.
AI.result: Across instruction-tuned models and varying reward granularities, CoRT outperforms matched response-level GRPO in the vast majority of comparisons, with an average gain of 4.4 percentage points. It remains competitive with learned token-level credit assignment baselines while avoiding a separate relevance-learning stage.
AI.conclusion: Policy-internal counterfactual likelihood contrasts provide an effective signal for within-response credit allocation in rubric-conditioned GRPO. CoRT achieves meaningful improvements over uniform advantage broadcasting while preserving the simplicity and stability of the GRPO framework, without requiring auxiliary models or additional training stages.

title: OmniDelta: Skill-Driven Budget Allocation for Token Compression in OmniLLMs
summary: Emerging Omni-modal Large Language Models (OmniLLMs) enable unified understanding of text, audio, and video, but their long audio-video token sequences introduce substantial memory and inference costs. Existing compression methods mainly focus on selecting important tokens under fixed budgets, leaving the preceding budget-allocation problem underexplored. We show that direct query-to-audio/video similarity is unreliable for inter-modal budget allocation, and that uniform intra-modal budgets can miss key evidence while retaining redundant content. To address these limitations, we propose OmniDelta, a training-free, skill-driven framework that couples intent-aware inter-modal allocation with content-aware intra-modal allocation. OmniDelta first constructs audio and video skill pools to shift the fixed retained-token budget according to query demand, then reallocates modality budgets over audio segments and video frames using local complexity and temporal redundancy. The resulting local budgets can be combined with existing pruning strategies, preserving the total retained-token ratio while changing where the budget is spent. Experiments on four audio-video benchmarks with two Qwen2.5-Omni models show that OmniDelta establishes a new accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier across pruning ratios. At 25% token retention on Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, OmniDelta reduces GPU memory by 22.0% and achieves a 1.64x end-to-end speedup over full-token inference.

AI.tldr: OmniDelta is a training-free framework for Omni-modal LLMs that jointly optimizes inter-modal budget allocation (using skill pools for query-aware distribution) and intra-modal budget allocation (using local complexity and temporal redundancy), achieving superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs compared to fixed-budget pruning methods.
AI.motivation: Existing token compression for OmniLLMs focuses on token selection under fixed budgets but neglects two key problems: (1) inter-modal budget allocation based on query-to-modality similarity is unreliable, and (2) uniform intra-modal budgets waste capacity on redundant content while missing critical evidence. There is no prior work addressing the budget-allocation problem itself.
AI.method: OmniDelta is a training-free, skill-driven framework with two components: (1) Intent-aware inter-modal allocation: constructs audio/video skill pools and uses query-skill matching to shift the fixed retained-token budget across modalities based on query demand. (2) Content-aware intra-modal allocation: reallocates modality budgets over audio segments and video frames using local complexity and temporal redundancy metrics. The resulting local budgets plug into existing pruning strategies without changing the overall retention ratio.
AI.result: Experiments on four audio-video benchmarks using Qwen2.5-Omni-7B and Qwen2.5-Omni-3B show OmniDelta establishes a new accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier. At 25% token retention on the 7B model, it reduces GPU memory by 22.0% and achieves 1.64× end-to-end speedup over full-token inference.
AI.conclusion: Joint optimization of budget allocation across and within modalities, guided by query intent and content characteristics, significantly outperforms uniform or similarity-based allocation strategies for efficient OmniLLM inference.

title: DecoEvo: Score-Decoupled Co-Evolution of Solver and Rubric-Generator Skills in Text Space
summary: Text-space optimization adapts large language models (LLMs) by editing external natural-language artifacts rather than model weights, so the optimized artifacts remain inspectable and the model can be treated as a black box. However, most existing text-space methods keep evaluation fixed. On open-ended tasks, this can become a bottleneck: once the solver improves on the criteria a rubric measures, omitted dimensions remain invisible to the optimization signal. Simply evolving the rubric is also unreliable when updates are selected by the current solver's score, because apparent progress can come from making the rubric easier to satisfy. We introduce DecoEvo (Decoupled Co-Evolution), which co-evolves a solver skill and a rubric-generator skill under decoupled objectives without using gold rubrics during optimization. The solver skill is updated using criterion-level feedback, while the rubric-generator skill is revised through complementary audits of requirement coverage and response discrimination that are independent of aggregate solver score. This separation focuses generator updates on newly exposed solver weaknesses, reducing repeated emphasis on criteria the solver already satisfies. Under each benchmark's official evaluation, DecoEvo outperforms all compared methods across five benchmarks and three LLM backbones, yielding 2.8--5.0\% relative gains over SkillOpt in the five-benchmark average.

AI.tldr: DecoEvo introduces decoupled co-evolution of solver and rubric-generator skills for text-space LLM optimization, where the rubric generator is updated independently of aggregate solver scores via coverage and discrimination audits, yielding 2.8–5.0% relative gains over SkillOpt across five benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing text-space optimization methods keep evaluation rubrics fixed, creating a bottleneck on open-ended tasks: improvements on measured criteria leave unmeasured dimensions invisible to optimization. Evolving the rubric using the solver's scores is unreliable because the solver can game the rubric by making it easier to satisfy. A rubric that adapts without this circular dependency is needed.
AI.method: DecoEvo co-evolves two skills under decoupled objectives without gold rubrics. The solver skill receives criterion-level feedback for improvement. The rubric-generator skill is revised through complementary audits—requirement coverage (whether the rubric captures all important dimensions) and response discrimination (whether the rubric differentiates good from bad outputs)—that are independent of aggregate solver score. This decoupling ensures generator updates target newly exposed solver weaknesses rather than reinforcing already-satisfied criteria.
AI.result: DecoEvo outperforms all compared methods across five benchmarks and three LLM backbones, achieving 2.8–5.0% relative gains over SkillOpt in the five-benchmark average under each benchmark's official evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling solver and rubric-generator objectives during co-evolution prevents circular reward hacking and enables more robust, inspectable text-space optimization for open-ended tasks.

title: Cognivia: A Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Copilot for Evidence-Based Mental Healthcare
