summary: Cognitive distortion amplifies negative emotions and contributes to mental health disorders. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is an effective way to address cognitive distortions, but its large-scale application is limited by the shortage of professional therapists. Although large language models (LLMs) have recently been explored for mental health applications, existing methods still suffer from limited domain specificity, overly flattering responses, and the absence of well-defined annotations for cognitive distortions. This paper proposes Cognivia, an evidence-based artificial intelligence therapist that integrates automatic cognitive distortion identification and rational response generation. Our framework is built on authoritative CBT texts widely regarded as core paradigms and standard references. It is further augmented with mental health question-answer (Q and A) data, and employs multi-stage prompting and structured generation strategies under the supervision of behavioral science experts. Then we fine-tune a lightweight LLM on this augmented CBT dataset to obtain Cognivia. In addition, we propose the first hierarchical quality evaluation framework for assessing LLM-generated rational responses, developed through collaboration between AI researchers and behavioral science experts. Cognivia is evaluated using lexical metrics, LLM-based Judges with two complementary criteria, and human evaluation by 10 behavioral science experts. It consistently outperforms the baseline methods in cognitive distortion recognition and rational response generation, demonstrating its effectiveness. Our code is available at https://github.com/SNOWTEAM2023/Cognivia.

AI.tldr: Cognivia is an AI therapist that integrates automatic cognitive distortion identification with rational response generation, built by fine-tuning a lightweight LLM on CBT-augmented data. It introduces the first hierarchical quality evaluation framework for LLM-generated rational responses and consistently outperforms baselines across lexical metrics, LLM-based judges, and human expert evaluation.
AI.motivation: Cognitive distortion amplifies negative emotions and contributes to mental health disorders. While CBT is effective, its scalability is limited by therapist shortages. Existing LLM-based mental health solutions suffer from limited domain specificity, overly flattering responses, and lack of well-defined cognitive distortion annotations.
AI.method: The framework builds on authoritative CBT texts augmented with mental health Q&A data. It employs multi-stage prompting and structured generation strategies supervised by behavioral science experts. A lightweight LLM is fine-tuned on this augmented CBT dataset. Additionally, a novel hierarchical quality evaluation framework is proposed, co-developed with behavioral science experts, assessing responses via lexical metrics, LLM-based judges with two complementary criteria, and evaluation by 10 behavioral science experts.
AI.result: Cognivia consistently outperforms baseline methods in both cognitive distortion recognition and rational response generation across all evaluation dimensions: lexical metrics, LLM-based judges, and human evaluation by 10 behavioral science experts.
AI.conclusion: Cognivia demonstrates that evidence-based, expert-supervised fine-tuning of lightweight LLMs on authoritative CBT resources can produce an effective AI therapist capable of both identifying cognitive distortions and generating high-quality rational responses, validated through a rigorous multi-tier evaluation framework.

title: Nudging Sustainable Choices through LLM-Generated Recommendation Explanations
summary: Recommender systems mediate everyday consumption, offering a promising channel for encouraging sustainable choices. Prior research shows that explanations influence users' perceptions of recommendations and can support more informed decisions. We argue that explanations can also serve as behavioral nudges by foregrounding sustainability information at the moment of choice. This study investigates how different behavioral framings of sustainability information in recommendation explanations affect user choices and perceptions. Using generative AI, we generate sustainability-aware explanations by drawing on nudge theory and validate them through human evaluation and LLM-as-a-judge audits. Building on this foundation, we conduct two randomized studies ($N = 529$) in a low involvement domain (instant coffee) and a high involvement domain (hotel bookings), in which participants choose among preference matched recommendations accompanied by these explanations. Our results show that, across both domains, merely disclosing sustainability information in explanations does not change choices, whereas framing that information or invoking a descriptive social norm significantly increases sustainable selections and eases decision-making. Notably, perception and behavior diverge, as plain disclosure improves explanation evaluations without translating into more sustainable selection behavior. Our work demonstrates how LLMs can generate theory-grounded explanations at scale, pointing toward practical explanation-based interventions for social good. We conclude by discussing implications for adaptive explanation design with generative AI.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how framing sustainability information in recommendation explanations (using generative AI and nudge theory) influences user choices. Two randomized studies show that plain disclosure of sustainability data doesn't change behavior, but behavioral framing and social norm framing significantly increase sustainable selections.
AI.motivation: Recommender systems mediate consumption at scale, yet sustainability information is rarely leveraged at the point of choice. While explanations improve user perceptions, their potential as behavioral nudges to promote sustainable consumption remains underexplored.
AI.method: The authors use generative AI to produce sustainability-aware explanations grounded in nudge theory (plain disclosure, behavioral framing, descriptive social norm framing). Explanations are validated via human evaluation and LLM-as-a-judge audits. Two randomized between-subjects studies (N=529) are conducted across a low-involvement domain (instant coffee) and a high-involvement domain (hotel bookings), where participants select among preference-matched recommendations with different explanation types.
AI.result: Plain sustainability disclosure in explanations does not change choice behavior in either domain. Behavioral framing and descriptive social norm framing significantly increase sustainable selections and ease decision-making. Perception and behavior diverge: plain disclosure improves explanation evaluations but fails to translate into more sustainable choices.
AI.conclusion: LLMs enable scalable generation of theory-grounded, sustainability-aware explanations. Effective behavioral nudges require framing beyond mere disclosure. The findings support adaptive explanation design with generative AI for social good, highlighting a perception-behavior gap in sustainability interventions.

title: Loss Invariance Determines What Concept Layers Encode: Volume Grounding in Echocardiography
summary:
Objective: Concept bottleneck models route prediction through interpretable intermediate variables, and their validity is normally judged by how accurately those variables are predicted. We ask whether that judgement is sufficient, using left ventricular volumes as the concepts underlying ejection fraction estimation from echocardiographic video.
  Methods: A video transformer encoder was trained on a publicly available echocardiography dataset. End-systolic and end-diastolic volumes formed a concept layer from which ejection fraction was computed analytically, with no residual path to the output. We compared training under an ejection fraction objective alone against training with additional supervision of the volumes in millilitres, and evaluated both on 1276 held-out studies.
  Results: The concept bottleneck did not increase ejection fraction error relative to direct regression, at 6.89 against 7.13 mean absolute error. Without volume supervision, however, the spread of predicted volumes collapsed to 0.1 millilitres against reference spreads of 35.7 and 45.7 millilitres, while correlation was partly preserved. We show that this follows from an invariance property of the objective: ejection fraction is a ratio and is unchanged when both volumes are rescaled, so the loss determines the concept layer only up to scale. Supervision in absolute units reduced volume error from 89.8 to 25.8 millilitres at a cost of 0.4 in ejection fraction error.
  Conclusion: Concept accuracy alone can conceal a concept layer that carries no physical scale.
  Significance: Interpretable intermediate variables in clinical models should be validated against the invariance structure of the training objective, not only against prediction accuracy.

AI.tldr: Concept bottleneck models can produce accurate predictions with intermediate variables that are physically meaningless due to objective invariance. The authors demonstrate that predicting ejection fraction from left ventricular volumes without volume supervision leads to correct EF but collapsed, unscaled volume estimates, because EF is a ratio invariant to rescaling.
AI.motivation: Concept bottleneck models are typically validated solely by how accurately their intermediate concepts are predicted. The authors challenge this sufficiency by investigating whether a concept layer can appear accurate while being physically meaningless, using the clinical task of ejection fraction estimation from echocardiographic video where EF is a ratio of end-systolic and end-diastolic volumes.
AI.method: A video transformer encoder was trained on a public echocardiography dataset. End-systolic and end-diastolic volumes formed a concept bottleneck layer from which ejection fraction was computed analytically (no residual connection bypassing the concepts). Two training regimes were compared: (1) EF objective only, and (2) EF with additional supervision on volumes in millilitres. Evaluation was performed on 1,276 held-out studies.
AI.result: The concept bottleneck achieved MAE of 6.89 vs. 7.13 for direct regression (no degradation). However, without volume supervision, predicted volume spread collapsed to 0.1 mL (vs. reference spreads of 35.7 and 45.7 mL) while EF correlation was partly preserved. Adding volume supervision reduced volume error from 89.8 to 25.8 mL at a cost of only 0.4 EF MAE. This follows analytically: EF = (EDV - ESV)/EDV is invariant to joint rescaling of both volumes.
AI.conclusion: Concept prediction accuracy alone is insufficient for validating concept bottleneck models; the concept layer may carry no physical scale while still producing correct downstream predictions. Clinically deployed interpretable models must be validated against the invariance structure of the training objective.

title: Speculate While You Reason: Teaching Agents to Predict Their Next Tool Call via Joint Agent-Speculator RL
summary: Large language model agents often spend substantial wall-clock time waiting for tool call results. Tool-call speculation can hide this latency by predicting and pre-executing an agent's next tool call if the prediction matches the agent's eventual tool call, but existing speculators are typically separate draft models or cached traces that are poorly aligned with the deployed agent's own behavior. We identify this speculator-agent gap and show that the target agent itself is a strong next-call speculator. This points to a simpler design: unifying the agent and speculator within the same model. In this paper, we introduce the self-speculating agent, a single model that both solves tasks in agent mode and predicts its next tool call from partial trajectories in speculator mode, fully reusing prefix KV cache. To enable this dual-mode agent without degrading performance, we propose a joint agent-speculator reinforcement learning method, which derives speculation targets from the agent's own rollouts and alternates agent and speculator updates. Across agentic search QA and conversational tool-use agentic tasks, our method improves average next tool-call Hit@1 from 44.1 to 61.2 for Qwen3-4B and from 48.9 to 66.3 for Qwen3.5-4B, while preserving agent task success.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the self-speculating agent: a unified model that acts as both the task-solving agent and its own tool-call speculator, eliminating the speculator-agent gap. A joint RL method alternates agent and speculator updates, improving next-tool-call prediction (Hit@1) by ~17 points on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3.5-4B while preserving task success.
AI.motivation: LLM agents waste wall-clock time waiting for tool call results. Existing speculation methods use separate draft models or cached traces that are poorly aligned with the deployed agent's behavior — the "speculator-agent gap." The authors observe that the target agent itself is a strong next-call speculator, motivating a unified design.
AI.method: The self-speculating agent operates in two modes: agent mode (solving tasks) and speculator mode (predicting next tool calls from partial trajectories), fully reusing prefix KV cache. A joint agent-speculator reinforcement learning method is proposed, which derives speculation targets from the agent's own rollouts and alternates between agent and speculator updates, avoiding performance degradation from the dual-mode setup.
AI.result: On agentic search QA and conversational tool-use tasks, the method improves average next tool-call Hit@1 from 44.1 to 61.2 for Qwen3-4B and from 48.9 to 66.3 for Qwen3.5-4B, while preserving agent task success rates.
AI.conclusion: Unifying agent and speculator in a single model with joint RL training effectively closes the speculator-agent gap, significantly boosting speculation accuracy without harming task performance.

title: Distributed Constraint Optimization via Online Learning and Iterative Pricing with Application to Large-Scale Satellite Scheduling
summary: Distributed constraint optimization problems (DCOPs) provide a popular framework for distributed decision making under limited communication, but many real-world instances are too large to solve monolithically. We address this challenge from two complementary directions. We revisit the connection between DCOPs and potential games, and adapt modern online learning algorithms for equilibrium finding to DCOPs. We show that these algorithms are competitive with representative incomplete DCOP algorithms. We then turn to decomposition frameworks for large-scale DCOPs, motivated by large-scale decentralized satellite scheduling. We propose a new framework that separates a DCOP into two interacting subproblems: a high-level meta-DCOP for task allocation, and independent local optimization problems for scheduling. To couple the two levels, we develop a novel iterative pricing method that updates the meta-level utilities using feedback from the local optimizers. Combining our online learning methods with our iterative pricing framework, we obtain near-optimal performance on real-world decentralized satellite scheduling problem instances, fulfilling over 99% of observation requests compared with 87% for state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses large-scale Distributed Constraint Optimization Problems (DCOPs) through two complementary approaches: (1) adapting online learning algorithms from potential game theory to DCOPs for competitive incomplete solving, and (2) proposing a novel decomposition framework with iterative pricing that separates DCOPs into a high-level task allocation meta-DCOP and local scheduling subproblems. The combined approach achieves over 99% fulfillment on real-world satellite scheduling, significantly outperforming the 87% baseline.
AI.motivation: Many real-world DCOP instances are too large to solve monolithically. The authors are motivated by large-scale decentralized satellite scheduling, where existing methods struggle to achieve high-quality solutions. There is an untapped connection between DCOPs and potential games that can be exploited, and a need for effective decomposition frameworks that preserve coordination while enabling scalability.
AI.method: The work proceeds in two complementary directions. First, the authors revisit the DCOP–potential game connection and adapt modern online learning algorithms (e.g., no-regret learning) for equilibrium finding to DCOP settings, demonstrating competitiveness with representative incomplete DCOP algorithms. Second, they propose a decomposition framework that splits a DCOP into: (a) a high-level meta-DCOP for task allocation, and (b) independent local optimization problems for scheduling. The two levels are coupled via a novel iterative pricing method, where meta-level utilities are updated using feedback from local optimizers. Finally, the online learning methods are combined with the iterative pricing framework.
AI.result: The combined approach achieves near-optimal performance on real-world decentralized satellite scheduling instances, fulfilling over 99% of observation requests compared to 87% for state-of-the-art baselines. The online learning algorithms alone are shown to be competitive with representative incomplete DCOP algorithms.
AI.conclusion: The DCOP–potential game connection enables effective application of online learning algorithms, and the proposed decomposition framework with iterative pricing successfully scales to large, real-world problems. The synergy of both contributions yields substantial performance gains over existing methods in decentralized satellite scheduling.

title: HiSkill: Empowering LLM Agents with Hierarchical Skill Graphs
summary: Skills have become an important abstraction for enabling large language model (LLM) agents to reuse past experience in long-horizon interactive tasks. However, existing trajectory-to-skill methods often produce flat collections of high-level textual skills that are stored and retrieved independently, leaving skill relations underutilized and maintaining a gap between high-level skills and executable actions. In this paper, we propose HiSkill, a hierarchical skill graph framework that organizes interaction trajectories into a directed graph with skill nodes, AtomicOp nodes, and typed edges. Specifically, the graph connects reusable high-level skills with executable action templates, while also capturing decomposition, temporal transition, compatibility, support, and recovery relations among them. At inference time, HiSkill retrieves a compact task-relevant subgraph and performs subgraph-guided task execution, where a symbolic task state, an active skill, and the retrieved subgraph guide the LLM agent to switch skills, select AtomicOps, and ground executable actions iteratively. Experiments on three interactive environments show that HiSkill outperforms state-of-the-art baselines while reducing inference token consumption, demonstrating the effectiveness of bridging high-level skills and executable action grounding through a hierarchical skill graph. Our data and code is available at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/HiSkill.

AI.tldr: HiSkill proposes a hierarchical skill graph framework that organizes LLM agent interaction trajectories into a directed graph with skills, AtomicOps, and typed edges. This bridges high-level textual skills with executable actions while capturing skill relations (decomposition, transitions, compatibility, support, recovery). At inference, a retrieved subgraph guides iterative task execution, outperforming baselines while reducing token consumption.
AI.motivation: Existing trajectory-to-skill methods produce flat collections of high-level textual skills stored independently, underutilizing skill relations and leaving a gap between abstract skills and concrete executable actions. This limits reuse and grounding in long-horizon interactive tasks.
AI.method: HiSkill constructs a hierarchical directed graph containing skill nodes, AtomicOp nodes (executable action templates), and typed edges encoding five relation types: decomposition, temporal transition, compatibility, support, and recovery. At inference, a compact task-relevant subgraph is retrieved. A symbolic task state, an active skill, and the subgraph jointly guide the LLM agent to switch skills, select AtomicOps, and ground actions iteratively.
AI.result: Experiments on three interactive environments demonstrate that HiSkill outperforms state-of-the-art baselines while reducing inference token consumption.
AI.conclusion: Bridging high-level skills and executable action grounding through a hierarchical skill graph is effective for improving LLM agent performance and efficiency in long-horizon interactive tasks.

title: Runtime Uncertainty Monitoring for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems Using Bayesian Networks
comment: This paper got accepted for Ninth International Workshop on Artificial Intelligence Safety Engineering (WAISE 2026): https://www.waise.org/
summary: This paper investigates how multi-agent systems (MAS)-based on large language models (LLMs) can support actuarial risk modelling, with a particular focus on uncertainty quantification. Actuarial workflows represent a high-stakes decision-support setting where unreliable outputs may lead to incorrect risk assessment, unfair pricing, and regulatory non-compliance. To address uncertainty introduced by the probabilistic nature of LLMs and dependencies between agents, a multi-agent framework is proposed in which specialised agents perform data preparation, modelling, review, and explanation tasks under a central hub. The main contribution is a novel approach to uncertainty propagation using token-level log-probabilities and a Bayesian Network. Importantly, log probabilities are not treated as direct probabilities of correctness or task success. Instead, length-normalised log-probability summaries are transformed into calibrated task-level confidence estimates before incorporation into the Bayesian Network. Results show that the framework reproduces baseline actuarial performance while providing additional insight into workflow stability and runtime uncertainty propagation.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent LLM framework for actuarial risk modelling that propagates uncertainty using token-level log-probabilities transformed into calibrated confidence estimates within a Bayesian Network, achieving baseline performance with added workflow stability insights.
AI.motivation: Actuarial workflows are high-stakes decision-support settings where unreliable LLM outputs can cause incorrect risk assessment, unfair pricing, and regulatory non-compliance. The probabilistic nature of LLMs and inter-agent dependencies introduce uncertainty that must be rigorously quantified.
AI.method: A multi-agent system with specialised agents (data preparation, modelling, review, explanation) coordinated by a central hub. Uncertainty propagation is handled via token-level log-probabilities that are length-normalised and calibrated into task-level confidence estimates, then fed into a Bayesian Network — crucially, log-probabilities are NOT treated as direct correctness probabilities.
AI.result: The framework reproduces baseline actuarial performance while providing additional insight into workflow stability and runtime uncertainty propagation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MAS framework successfully integrates LLMs into actuarial risk modelling with principled uncertainty quantification, maintaining performance parity with traditional baselines while enhancing transparency around model confidence and workflow reliability.

title: Distributing Security Controls Through Harness Engineering
summary: AI coding agents are being adopted at historic speed, yet security and risk concerns remain the primary barrier to scaling agentic AI across organizations. Existing security controls for coding agents are not systematically distributed to engineering teams, and vendor-native solutions introduce ecosystem dependencies that may not suit every deployment context. This paper investigates whether off-the-shelf security controls can be implemented on commercial AI coding agents and scaled to a distributed user base via a custom agent harness. A phased testing methodology was applied across four agent configurations --- two commercial agents with and without controls, a baseline harness, and a security-hardened harness --- using a 23-test suite derived from the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications. SHarD (Secure Harness Distribution), a distributable harness built on the Pi agent harness, demonstrated that three categories of security controls --- OS sandboxing, skill scanning, and tool restriction --- can be embedded and distributed via a single install command while retaining equivalent efficacy to direct installation on commercial agents. SHarD achieved an adjusted score of 100\%, matching the best securely configured commercial agent, with no regression across any test category. Notable observations include evidence that model non-determinism produces inconsistent security outcomes and that autonomous agent behavior can cross system boundaries in ways that OS sandboxing directly mitigates. Initial characteristics toward a control harness fitness framework are proposed, and a third research question is identified for future investigation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SHarD, a distributable security harness for AI coding agents that embeds OS sandboxing, skill scanning, and tool restriction controls into a single install command, achieving 100% adjusted security score — matching the best directly-configured commercial agent — without ecosystem lock-in.
AI.motivation: AI coding agents are being rapidly adopted, but security and risk concerns remain the primary barrier to scaling agentic AI. Existing security controls are not systematically distributed to engineering teams, and vendor-native solutions create ecosystem dependencies unsuitable for all deployment contexts.
AI.method: A phased testing methodology was applied across four agent configurations (two commercial agents with/without controls, a baseline harness, and a security-hardened harness) using a 23-test suite derived from the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications.
AI.result: SHarD achieved an adjusted score of 100%, matching the best securely configured commercial agent with no regression across any test category. Notable findings include model non-determinism producing inconsistent security outcomes, and autonomous agent behavior crossing system boundaries — which OS sandboxing directly mitigates.
AI.conclusion: Off-the-shelf security controls can be effectively embedded in a distributable harness and scaled across distributed user bases without sacrificing efficacy. Initial characteristics toward a control harness fitness framework are proposed, and a third research question is identified for future investigation.

title: Messier: A High-Resolution Corpus for Cross-Benchmark Agent Evaluation
summary: Evaluating AI agents in interactive environments is hindered by fragmented tasks, scaffolds, verifiers, and scoring rules. Existing efforts focus on narrow settings, remain limited in scale, or require costly reruns, leaving much of the empirical record incomparable. We introduce Messier, a unified corpus of 957,253 records that span 30 benchmarks, 714 agents, 11,891 tasks, and 74,205 verifiers. Messier consolidates public benchmark scores and supplements them with five-agent runs across six underrepresented professional and scientific domains, including a recent legal benchmark. Each record is standardized by model, scaffold, environment, task, verifier, and aggregation rule, with SOC/NAICS classifications for occupational and industry analysis. Using this corpus, we show frontier progress is uneven across benchmark types, with "function calling" saturated, "programming" improving the fastest, and "enterprise workflows" remaining the most challenging. Furthermore, counterfactual rescoring shows that strict all-pass aggregation in multi-verifier tasks can obscure progress and artificially alter agent rankings. From these standardized records, we derive capability scales that align with Epoch's Evaluation Capability Index rankings at Spearman \r{ho} = 0.81 and can be specialized by domain, occupation, action space, or verifier type. Messier provides a foundational, reusable infrastructure for agent capability scaling, benchmark auditing, and fine-grained analysis of evaluation failures.

AI.tldr: Messier is a unified corpus of ~1M standardized records spanning 30 benchmarks, 714 agents, and 11K+ tasks, enabling cross-benchmark analysis of AI agent capabilities. Key findings: frontier progress is uneven across benchmark types, strict all-pass aggregation obscures progress, and derived capability scales strongly correlate (ρ=0.81) with Epoch's Evaluation Capability Index.
AI.motivation: AI agent evaluation is fragmented across incompatible tasks, scaffolds, verifiers, and scoring rules. Existing efforts are narrow in scope, limited in scale, or require costly re-execution, rendering most empirical results incomparable. There is a need for a standardized, large-scale infrastructure to enable apples-to-apples comparison of agent capabilities across diverse benchmarks and domains.
AI.method: The authors construct Messier, a corpus of 957,253 standardized records by consolidating public benchmark scores and supplementing them with five-agent runs across six underrepresented professional/scientific domains (including a legal benchmark). Each record is normalized by model, scaffold, environment, task, verifier, and aggregation rule, with SOC/NAICS classifications for occupational and industry analysis. Counterfactual rescoring is used to assess the impact of different aggregation rules.
AI.result: (1) Frontier progress is uneven: "function calling" benchmarks are saturated, "programming" improves fastest, and "enterprise workflows" remain the hardest. (2) Strict all-pass aggregation in multi-verifier tasks artificially alters agent rankings and obscures meaningful progress. (3) Capability scales derived from the corpus align with Epoch's Evaluation Capability Index at Spearman ρ=0.81 and can be specialized by domain, occupation, action space, or verifier type.
AI.conclusion: Messier provides a foundational, reusable infrastructure for agent capability scaling, benchmark auditing, and fine-grained analysis of evaluation failures, enabling more principled and comparable assessment of AI agents.

title: Interactive Reward Agent: GUI Task Evaluation via Environment-State Verification
summary: Graphical user interface task evaluation aims to determine whether a GUI agent has successfully completed a user instruction. Automated GUI task evaluation has received increasing attention because the evaluation results can serve as reward signals for both test-time scaling and post-training. However, reliable GUI task evaluation remains challenging because the judgments often require access to environment states, such as system configurations, file data, and application settings, beyond the screenshots of execution trajectories. In this paper, we propose an interactive reward agent (IRA) based on a propose-then-verify framework to acquire and verify evidence from the post-execution environment. Given a task instruction and a GUI environment after the GUI agent execution, IRA first proposes the task completion conditions and then verifies them by invoking system tools, application tools, and GUI tools. This design combines evidence from both visible interfaces and the environment state in an interactive process. We further introduce GUI-RewardBench, a benchmark of 321 GUI task trajectories spanning 10 Ubuntu desktop application categories. Experiments show that IRA achieves 86.9% accuracy on GUI-RewardBench, outperforming existing evaluator baselines. We further apply IRA to reinforcement learning of GUI agents, achieving a 34.0% OSWorld success rate, which demonstrates that IRA can provide effective reward signals for training GUI agents.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces IRA (Interactive Reward Agent), a propose-then-verify framework for automated GUI task evaluation that accesses environment states beyond screenshots. IRA achieves 86.9% accuracy on the new GUI-RewardBench benchmark and, when used for RL training, yields a 34.0% OSWorld success rate.
AI.motivation: Automated GUI task evaluation is critical for providing reward signals in test-time scaling and post-training of GUI agents, but reliable evaluation is hard because it requires access to environment states (system configs, file data, app settings) beyond mere execution trajectory screenshots.
AI.method: IRA uses a propose-then-verify framework: given a task instruction and post-execution GUI environment, it proposes task completion conditions, then verifies them interactively by invoking system tools, application tools, and GUI tools, combining evidence from visible interfaces and environment state.
AI.result: IRA achieves 86.9% accuracy on GUI-RewardBench (a new benchmark of 321 GUI task trajectories across 10 Ubuntu desktop app categories), outperforming existing evaluator baselines. Applied to RL training of GUI agents, IRA helps achieve a 34.0% success rate on OSWorld.
AI.conclusion: IRA provides effective, reliable reward signals for GUI agent training by interactively verifying task completion through environment state access, validated by strong benchmark performance and downstream RL results.

title: Penelope: Localized Latent Recurrence for Efficient Structured Reasoning
summary: Complex structured reasoning tasks often require additional computation, yet current language models obtain it mainly by increasing parameter scale or by serializing intermediate steps as chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens. The former raises training and deployment costs, while the latter ties reasoning computation to autoregressive output length. We introduce Penelope, an efficient latent-reasoning framework for pretrained decoder-only Transformers that localizes recurrent computation to a selected decoder interval. The lower decoder prefix is evaluated once to construct a problem-conditioned boundary memory, which is then iteratively refined through time-modulated GRU dynamics and recurrent readout states before answer generation. A progressive CoT-to-latent curriculum transfers visible reasoning into this internal recurrent path, allowing additional computation to be allocated in latent space without repeatedly executing the complete decoder or generating a long intermediate trace. Experiments on open-source structured-reasoning benchmarks show that, at validation-selected latent budgets, Penelope attains competitive accuracy relative to established latent-reasoning models while reducing measured inference latency. These results show that latent refinement can be localized to a narrow decoder interval, reducing repeated full-decoder execution without generating a long visible reasoning trace and providing a practical accuracy-efficiency tradeoff for decoder-only Transformer models.

AI.tldr: Penelope introduces a latent-reasoning framework for decoder-only Transformers that localizes recurrent computation to a narrow decoder interval, using GRU-based iterative refinement of a boundary memory to achieve competitive accuracy with reduced inference latency compared to chain-of-thought approaches.
AI.motivation: Current LMs address complex reasoning by either scaling parameters (costly) or generating long chain-of-thought tokens (tying reasoning to autoregressive output length). Both approaches are inefficient. The authors seek a method that allocates additional computation in latent space without repeatedly executing the full decoder or producing long visible traces.
AI.method: Penelope selects a decoder interval where the lower prefix is evaluated once to build a problem-conditioned boundary memory. This memory is iteratively refined via time-modulated GRU dynamics and recurrent readout states. A progressive curriculum transfers CoT reasoning into the latent recurrent path. Only the interval undergoes recurrent refinement; the rest of the decoder is executed once.
AI.result: On open-source structured-reasoning benchmarks, Penelope achieves competitive accuracy relative to established latent-reasoning models at validation-selected latent budgets, while reducing measured inference latency.
AI.conclusion: Latent refinement can be effectively localized to a narrow decoder interval, avoiding repeated full-decoder execution and long visible reasoning traces. This provides a practical accuracy-efficiency tradeoff for decoder-only Transformer models.

title: dtControl2+$\varepsilon$: Trading Optimality for Explainability in MDPs via Decision Trees
comment: This paper is accepted at FMCAD26
summary: Over the past decade, decision trees have been used to represent controllers (a.k.a. policies) in an explainable way, with dtControl2 as a current state-of-the-art tool. However, for systems that are large or have many corner cases, even such representations tend to be too complex and not human-comprehensible. Unfortunately, reducing the size of the decision tree is not straightforward, as missing just a single crucial case might result in an incorrect controller. We tackle this issue in the setting of Markov decision processes, extending dtControl2 by "$\varepsilon$" functionality: Given an allowed imprecision $\varepsilon \geq 0$, we construct a smaller decision tree, distilling the essence of the controller, while still guaranteeing its $\varepsilon$-optimality. This enables us to provide tunably simpler explanations, omitting a controllable amount of detail. Our tool constructs decision trees that are orders of magnitude smaller than the state of the art.

AI.tldr: The paper extends dtControl2 for Markov decision processes by introducing an ε-approximation mechanism that produces significantly smaller decision trees while preserving ε-optimality, enabling tunably simpler and more comprehensible controller explanations.
AI.motivation: Decision-tree-based controller representations, while explainable, become too large and incomprehensible for complex systems with many corner cases. Naively reducing tree size risks omitting critical cases and producing incorrect controllers. The authors aim to enable principled simplification with formal guarantees.
AI.method: The authors extend the dtControl2 tool with an ε-functionality for Markov decision processes. Given an allowed imprecision ε ≥ 0, the method constructs a smaller decision tree that distills the controller's essence while provably guaranteeing ε-optimality — meaning the simplified controller's performance deviates from optimal by at most ε.
AI.result: The tool produces decision trees that are orders of magnitude smaller than the state of the art, offering tunable trade-offs between explanation simplicity and controller precision.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ε-approximation approach successfully addresses the interpretability–precision trade-off in controller representation, enabling human-comprehensible explanations without sacrificing formal correctness guarantees.

title: Large Language Model for Operations Research Formulation Selection in Multi-Warehouse Inventory Allocation
summary: Multi-warehouse inventory allocation is typically formulated as a mixed-integer programming (MIP) problem, yet no single formulation consistently matches heterogeneous instance-level regimes induced by demand concentration, inventory imbalance, replenishment scale, service constraints, and forecast volatility. We study this issue as instance-wise operations research (OR) formulation selection, where each allocation instance is assigned to a solver-executable formulation from a candidate OR expert library. We propose a solver-guided large language model (LLM) framework for OR formulation selection, in which each OR expert corresponds to a MIP formulation encoding a distinct allocation priority. To train the selector, the framework first constructs balanced expert-conditioned supervised fine-tuning (SFT) records for schema learning, and then uses MIP solver evaluation on historical instances to convert solver-evaluated allocation-quality gaps into margin-weighted identity preference optimization (IPO) preferences and per-instance expert-score metadata for reward lookup during group relative policy optimization (GRPO) to assign rewards to sampled responses. Experiments on multi-warehouse inventory allocation instances from JD$\mathord{.}$com, one of China's largest e-retailers, demonstrate that GRPO substantially improves expert-selection accuracy relative to the SFT+IPO selector and, more importantly, produces higher realized allocation quality than both the preference-trained selector and the best fixed formulation. With GRPO, Hit Ratio@1 and Hit Ratio@2 increase from 21.45% to 50.42% and from 70.47% to 82.31%. The resulting selector achieves an allocation accuracy gain of 12.57 percentage points over the incumbent baseline, outperforming both the SFT+IPO selector and the best fixed OR expert, and reduces the gap to the ex-post oracle to 4.85 percentage points.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses multi-warehouse inventory allocation by framing it as an instance-wise MIP formulation selection problem. The authors propose a solver-guided LLM framework that trains a selector to assign each allocation instance to the best-performing candidate formulation using a combination of SFT, IPO, and GRPO training stages, with rewards derived from actual MIP solver evaluations.
AI.motivation: No single MIP formulation for multi-warehouse inventory allocation performs consistently well across heterogeneous instance-level regimes (driven by demand concentration, inventory imbalance, replenishment scale, service constraints, and forecast volatility). There is a need for an adaptive, instance-wise formulation selection mechanism that can outperform any fixed formulation.
AI.method: The authors propose a solver-guided LLM framework with three training stages: (1) balanced expert-conditioned SFT for schema learning, (2) margin-weighted IPO using solver-evaluated allocation-quality gaps to train pairwise preferences, and (3) GRPO that leverages per-instance expert-score metadata for reward lookup, enabling the policy to assign rewards to sampled responses. The selector maps each instance to the best MIP formulation from a candidate OR expert library.
AI.result: On JD.com real-world data, GRPO lifts Hit Ratio@1 from 21.45% (SFT+IPO) to 50.42% and Hit Ratio@2 from 70.47% to 82.31%. The resulting selector achieves a 12.57 percentage point allocation accuracy gain over the incumbent baseline, outperforms both SFT+IPO and the best fixed formulation, and reduces the gap to the ex-post oracle to 4.85 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: GRPO substantially improves expert-selection accuracy over SFT+IPO and yields higher realized allocation quality than both preference-trained selectors and the best fixed formulation. The solver-guided LLM framework with GRPO is an effective approach for instance-wise MIP formulation selection in real-world inventory allocation.

title: CHARM: A Multimodal Graph Foundation Model with Hierarchical Context Modeling for Zero-Shot Transfer
summary: Graph foundation models (GFMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for transferring knowledge across graph domains and tasks. Real-world graphs associate nodes with text, images, and other modalities, making multimodal graphs essential for representing complex entities and relations. Moreover, collecting labels and adapting models for every new graph domain is costly and often infeasible, motivating zero-shot transfer. Unfortunately, zero-shot transfer on multimodal graphs remains underexplored. Existing GNN-based graph foundation models typically require downstream adaptation, whereas LLM-based graph methods mainly address unimodal graphs or tasks within a single domain. This setting presents two key challenges. First, models must generalize knowledge from individual modalities while capturing transferable cross-modal relations. Second, without target-domain fine-tuning, node representations remain entangled with domain-specific structures and modality-specific characteristics, obscuring shared concepts in unseen domains. To address these challenges, we propose CHARM, a multimodal graph foundation model with hierarchical context modeling for zero-shot transfer. CHARM replaces isolated raw nodes with hierarchical graph contexts that capture multimodal semantics and cross-modal relations. These contexts map domain-specific node patterns to shared high-level concepts, reducing reliance on target-domain supervision or adaptation. A modality-aware graph context encoder integrates multimodal information with graph structure and converts the resulting representations into graph tokens for a large language model . Experiments show consistent improvements on zero-shot multimodal graph tasks.

AI.tldr: CHARM is a multimodal graph foundation model that enables zero-shot transfer across graph domains by using hierarchical graph contexts and a modality-aware encoder to produce graph tokens for LLMs, outperforming existing methods on zero-shot multimodal graph tasks.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot transfer on multimodal graphs is underexplored. Existing GNN-based GFMs need downstream adaptation, while LLM-based methods focus on unimodal graphs or single-domain tasks. The core challenges are: (1) generalizing knowledge across modalities while capturing cross-modal relations, and (2) node representations entangled with domain-specific structures that obscure shared concepts in unseen domains.
AI.method: CHARM introduces hierarchical graph contexts to replace isolated raw nodes, capturing multimodal semantics and cross-modal relations. These contexts map domain-specific node patterns to shared high-level concepts, reducing reliance on target-domain supervision. A modality-aware graph context encoder integrates multimodal information with graph structure and converts representations into graph tokens for a large language model, enabling zero-shot transfer without target-domain fine-tuning.
AI.result: Experiments show consistent improvements on zero-shot multimodal graph tasks compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: CHARM effectively addresses the zero-shot multimodal graph transfer problem through hierarchical context modeling and modality-aware encoding, demonstrating that mapping domain-specific patterns to shared high-level concepts enables strong generalization without target-domain adaptation.

title: Falling Behind Drives Unsafe Development in an Idealised AI Race Experiment
summary: Technological races create tension between speed and safety: actors may gain by moving faster than competitors, even when risky development is harmful. This is prominent in debates about artificial intelligence (AI), where competitive pressure is often argued to incentivise riskier, less safety-conscious development. We study this using a framed behavioural experiment based on an idealised AI race, in which paired participants repeatedly chose between Safe and Unsafe development under an uncertain time horizon. Unsafe development gave faster progress and higher immediate payoffs but accumulated private risk up to a treatment-specific maximum of 10\%, 60\%, or 90\%; the race's competitive structure was held constant, and only this maximum risk varied. Neither the pre-registered comparison between risk levels nor the role of elicited risk preferences was supported by the data. Instead, exploratory analyses motivated by the task's repeated structure show that Unsafe behaviour is shaped less by risk preferences than by the evolving strategic state of the race: participants are more likely to choose Unsafe after their opponent does so, being ahead reduces Unsafe play while falling behind increases it, and first-round choices predict later behaviour. To interpret these effects we introduce a reduced evolutionary model with four strategies -- Always Safe, Always Unsafe, Conditionally Safe, and Conditionally Antisocial Safe -- which reproduces the treatment effect and shows how conditional Unsafe behaviour can be favoured by competitive race dynamics. Together, the experiment and model show that unsafe development can emerge from early behavioural momentum, opponent behaviour, and fear of falling behind, rather than from risk preferences alone, suggesting policy should focus on reducing competitive pressure and promoting cooperation in AI development rather than only individual risk.

AI.tldr: This paper uses a behavioral experiment framed as an idealized AI race to study how competitive pressure drives risky (Unsafe) development. Results show that Unsafe choices are driven more by strategic race dynamics — opponent behavior, being ahead/behind, and early momentum — than by individual risk preferences. An evolutionary model with four strategies reproduces these effects, suggesting policy should target competitive pressure and promote cooperation rather than focus solely on individual risk attitudes.
AI.motivation: Technological races, particularly in AI development, create a tension between speed and safety: competitive pressure may incentivize actors to cut corners on safety to gain an advantage. The authors aim to empirically test whether higher potential risks deter unsafe behavior and whether individual risk preferences predict such choices, or whether strategic race dynamics are the dominant driver.
AI.method: A framed behavioral experiment with paired participants repeatedly choosing between Safe and Unsafe development under an uncertain time horizon. Unsafe development offers faster progress and higher immediate payoffs but accumulates private risk up to a treatment-specific maximum (10%, 60%, or 90%). The competitive structure is held constant across treatments; only the maximum risk varies. Pre-registered hypotheses test risk-level effects and risk preferences. Exploratory analyses examine strategic state effects (opponent behavior, relative position, first-round choices). A reduced evolutionary model with four strategies (Always Safe, Always Unsafe, Conditionally Safe, Conditionally Antisocial Safe) is introduced to interpret the dynamics.
AI.result: Neither the pre-registered comparison between risk levels nor the role of elicited risk preferences was supported by the data. Instead, Unsafe behavior is shaped by strategic race dynamics: participants are more likely to choose Unsafe after their opponent does so; being ahead reduces Unsafe play while falling behind increases it; first-round choices predict later behavior. The evolutionary model reproduces the treatment effect and demonstrates how conditional Unsafe behavior is favored by competitive race dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Unsafe development in competitive AI races emerges from early behavioral momentum, opponent behavior, and fear of falling behind, rather than from risk preferences alone. Policy interventions should focus on reducing competitive pressure and promoting cooperation in AI development, rather than targeting only individual risk attitudes.

title: Desktop-Delta Bench: Do Computer-Use Models Understand Desktop GUI Transitions?
summary: Computer-use agents (CUAs) increasingly act through desktop GUIs to complete long-horizon tasks. Current benchmarks primarily measure end-task success or single-frame grounding. Neither isolates whether a model can reconstruct the causal, task-relevant transition produced by an action- crucial for rejecting stale observations, verifying progress, and recovering from failure. This is difficult because inference, remote input, app rendering, and screenshot capture are asynchronous: the next observation may be delayed, occluded, transient, or unrelated, then misread as progress and carried into subsequent planning. We introduce Desktop-Delta Bench (DDB), an offline step-level benchmark with 2,013 human-verified instances from novel, multi-app Linux trajectories across ~15 applications and 50 task domains. DDB trajectories targets 3 failure dimensions- state verification, source tracking, and context-aware control- through 2 complementary tasks: 463 3-frame temporal-ordering instances, including 105 with a cross-trajectory decoy, and 1,550 before-after pairs labeled from 5 actions + its payload. We evaluate 8 closed and open-source model families across 32 ordering and 16 single-action settings, observing consistent gaps. Ordering remains unsaturated: best non-decoy and decoy exact-match rates are 65.1% and 65.7%. Task context improves decoy identification by 6.9 percentage points but reduces non-decoy exact match by 2.2 points; error analysis reveals systematic copying of the presented A-B-C order. Single-action results show that inferring the action family is harder than locating it: click F1 is 0.96 vs, 0.76 for drag, while recognized drags are generally localized well. DDB, thus, complements end-to-end benchmarks by filling the missing diagnostic layer between GUI grounding and final task success, enabling targeted improvements to desktop CUA verification, reliability, and recovery.

AI.tldr: Desktop-Delta Bench (DDB) is a diagnostic benchmark with 2,013 human-verified instances that tests whether computer-use agents can reconstruct causal, task-relevant transitions from GUI screenshots, targeting three failure dimensions: state verification, source tracking, and context-aware control. Evaluations across 8 model families reveal unsaturated performance on temporal ordering and single-action inference, with systematic error patterns like copying presented order.
AI.motivation: Current CUA benchmarks only measure end-task success or single-frame grounding, failing to isolate whether models can reconstruct the causal transition produced by an action. This is critical for rejecting stale observations, verifying progress, and recovering from failure. The asynchronous nature of inference, remote input, app rendering, and screenshot capture makes this especially challenging, as delayed or transient observations can be misread as progress.
AI.method: The authors introduce DDB, an offline step-level benchmark with 2,013 human-verified instances from multi-app Linux trajectories across ~15 applications and 50 task domains. It targets 3 failure dimensions through 2 complementary tasks: (1) 463 3-frame temporal-ordering instances (including 105 with cross-trajectory decoys) and (2) 1,550 before-after pairs labeled with 5 actions plus payload. They evaluate 8 closed and open-source model families across 32 ordering and 16 single-action settings.
AI.result: Ordering performance is unsaturated: best non-decoy exact-match rate is 65.1% and decoy rate is 65.7%. Task context improves decoy identification by 6.9 percentage points but reduces non-decoy exact match by 2.2 points, with error analysis revealing systematic copying of the presented A-B-C order. For single-action inference, inferring the action family is harder than localizing it: click F1 is 0.96 vs. 0.76 for drag, though recognized drags are generally well-localized.
AI.conclusion: DDB complements end-to-end benchmarks by filling the missing diagnostic layer between GUI grounding and final task success, enabling targeted improvements to desktop CUA verification, reliability, and recovery.

title: Domain-Prior-Regularized Graph Modeling for Anomaly Detection in Cyber-Physical Systems
comment: 12 pages, ICML 2026 AI for Science Workshop
summary: Anomaly detection on multivariate sensor time series is critical for industrial monitoring of cyber-physical systems (CPS), where even subtle deviations from normal behavior can indicate process disruption. Recent graph-based approaches have made significant progress, but they often struggle in small-scale physical systems with scarce labeled anomalies and limited normal data. In such settings, graph-based models tend to capture spurious correlations and produce unstable sensor topologies. We propose DPR-GM (Domain-Prior-Regularized Graph Modeling), a forecasting-based framework that incorporates system design knowledge into graph construction. DPR-GM leverages a large language model (LLM) to extract directed physical couplings between sensor pairs from system documentation, which are encoded as a binary domain adjacency matrix serving as a structural gate over sensor relations. This gate is then modulated by Pearson correlations estimated from normal training data. The anomaly score is further weighted by sensor-level reliability derived from the coefficient of variation. All graph and weighting components are fixed prior to training and add no learnable parameters. On the SKAB benchmark, DPR-GM outperforms graph-based, statistical, and deep learning baselines across F1, AUROC, and AUPRC, showing that domain-structured graph priors are a practical alternative to fully learned topologies in data-scarce CPS.

AI.tldr: DPR-GM is a forecasting-based anomaly detection framework that uses LLM-extracted domain knowledge to regularize graph construction, outperforming baselines on the SKAB benchmark in data-scarce CPS settings.
AI.motivation: Graph-based anomaly detection methods for multivariate sensor time series often fail in small-scale cyber-physical systems where labeled anomalies are scarce and normal data is limited, because they learn spurious correlations and produce unstable sensor topologies.
AI.method: DPR-GM uses an LLM to extract directed physical couplings from system documentation, forming a binary domain adjacency matrix as a structural gate. This gate is modulated by Pearson correlations from normal training data. Anomaly scores are weighted by sensor-level reliability derived from the coefficient of variation. All graph and weighting components are fixed before training, adding no learnable parameters.
AI.result: On the SKAB benchmark, DPR-GM outperforms graph-based, statistical, and deep learning baselines across F1, AUROC, and AUPRC metrics.
AI.conclusion: Domain-structured graph priors offer a practical and effective alternative to fully learned topologies for anomaly detection in data-scarce cyber-physical systems.
